Before you accuse of this software as scam, let me tell you.
This app only do one thing. YES. ONE. THING.
It isolates your process into one core, and use another processes just for the game itself.
The final result depends on your hardware AND your game (very noticable for your hardware that can't meet the game requirements).
"Maximize your FPS" nametag is very suitable to this app, because this app try to "squeeze" your CPU so your CPU can focus on the game process than the system itself. It does not "increase" if your FPS is already at the maximum based on your hardware or your game is not "CPU-bound".
Have HyperThread? No problem. This app can disable it, unless you only have 2 cores, which is useless for games that need 4 threads.
I mainly use this app for games that always stutters, like GTA V, or another game that CPU-bound like Payday 2, because that's where the difference is very noticable.
If you test it to games that already have high stable FPS and you have beast PC (like CSGO), ofc it has a very little to none impact.
Really, anyone that says this app is "scam" never reads or do more research about the work of "CPU affinity" or having "FPS drops", like "hurrdurr csgo from 250 to 251, not noticeable, auto unrecommend".
This app do what it's advertised, and I love it.
Thank you, Tim, for your awesome software!

The best $10 I have ever spent.  Here's why:
Space adventures have always had a special place in my heart.  All the best ones let you explore the vast reaches of space, with all the dangers of rewards related to that.  FTL is able to deliver than in a compact, yet very satsifying way.  You spend the entire game moving from jump point to jump point, avoiding enemies, gathering resources, and meeting the intriguing residents of the galaxy.  Each event and instance in the game is scripted, giving choices on what to do on each area you meet.  You also have to contend with the many natural disasters found in the vast reaches of outer space, like a sun going nova.  Now take all the above features, and make every play session random, and you have a game for the adventurous.
Okay, so now you are probably thinking, "Now you've listed a bunch of features, but what exactly is this game about?"  Well, I'll tell you.  You play a lone starship captain in a middle of a war between the Federation and the Rebels (Wars meets Trek). If you weren't sure whose side you are on, you are with the Federation.  However, the Federation is losing the war and you contain a vital piece of information which can let your side win the conflict once and for all.  Your mission, travel to the other end of the galaxy, the Rebels hot on you tail, and deliver this vital information to the remaining Federation forces.
The Gameplay itself is simple.  You have a ship and a crew, and you move from jump point to jump point, facing a new event at each area.  Sometimes you are attacked by a hostile ship, sometimes you help a ship in distress. Other times, you run into some friendly wayfarers who will help you along your journey.  More often then not, you run into hostiles, and have to fight.  Combat is simple to understand, yet difficult to master.  Each ship is broken up into a collection of room. Most rooms have a system such as weapons, shields, oxygen, etc etc. When you attack a ship, you attack one of the sytems on the ship.  Obviously, disabling weapons keeps the enemy from firing back.  Of course, the ship will fire back at you, and one of your sytems will be disabled, so you'll need your crew to fix them.  On top of that, having a crew member operate a system makes it function better.  This turns into a game of "Where do I have my crew station and fix at this point."  One of the most important features is that you can run in the middle in battle if your engine is ready.  Oh and I should mention, it all happens in real time.  While you can pause the game, it makes combat frantic.  Did I say simp[le, well no it's not.  But it's all laid out, and the pause button makes it very easy to manage.
FTL has a lot to offer, and is a great stragey game which allows you to fully explore the dark reaches of space.  I loved it, and even with the repetitive content, the randomization makes it a gamble what you see.  If you've ever wanted to explore the depths of space, drop $10 and boot up Faster Than Light.

It's a nice classic TellTale game.
The game is 3 episodes so from the very start I have myself prepared for something VERY short.
Graphics wise it's the same thing we've seen with TellTales' TWD games (Telltale Tool graphics engine, same as The Wolf Among Us and others).
Voice acting is perfect, as to be expected from a TellTale game. Samira Wiley acting as Michonne and not Danai Gurira herself makes very little difference once you have gotten inside the game's character. However wether this game will deliver us a great and complete experience is yet to be seen.
So it is hard to say this is a review, this is how episodic games are, it's like reviewing a TV show, not knowing how the whole thing is going to be.
Episode 1:
We get to have a great entrance with some insight into Michonne's recent past in comparison to the time we see her for the first time in the TV show/comics (however this seems to what may be mainly based on the comics). There's great emphasis on her Mental state, her emotions and thoughts. The way the character is introduced is amazing.
However we don't get to see any key points about her past with the only exception of some dream or "hallucination" sequences if you like.
I really really REALLY hoped for a game that showed us how it all started. How this character was born. But this is not the case here. The creators prefered to choose to show us pieces of her past through the safer technique of those dreams. If the rest of the game is planned well however there will be no point in feeling any disappointed.
Good start. Few interesting characters introduced.
Well played so far.
Episode 2:
The story continues as we follow Michonne's steps to this adventure.
It is confirmed that the story follows the comics canon core and as I mentioned already, the developers follow the safe route of the flashbacks method in order to show glimpses of how it all started.
However I must admit i'm being left with a bit lack of satisfaction while playing this.
TellTale doesn't seem to care about you interacting with the environment at all.
We've seen how these games work so we know that if someone's life is saved by our choices they are bound to day anyway if the developers want to.
And most importantly, If you show mercy to someone who is a♥♥♥♥♥♥hoping to get a better outcome of him, he will still be a♥♥♥♥♥♥afterwards. like ALWAYS. In every single TellTale walking dead.
So all in all, thing are pretty narrow technically.
I do some choices to make myself feel good about them knowing that the result is going to be more or less the same.
So is there a reason for me to like this?
Well yes, the story is still nice and it's like watching a short movie.
But is there a way to make things even better than this?
Well yes again, because if you are going to give us the illusion of control over reality without actually having it you can do it in more interesting ways like many other adventure games do. Like for example give us reasons to "point and click" to more things. More environmental interactions. Find collective items. Hell even solving a puzzle every now and then adds to the fun.
A story is nice when you watch it. But it's even better when you interact with it.
So far things show that TellTale loves to keep things average by giving us strong story, good direction and amazing voice acting but completely lacking any fun interaction ideas.
Onward for Episode 3 and final verdict soon.
Episode 3:
Moving on to the final chapter the developers decide to use all their hidden cards on the table, bringing the best of their abilities to create a brilliant climax and a perfectly set conclusion to our story.
The story is eventually NOT focused on Michonne's adventure and meeting good and people no. It's focused on the mental torture of a person that has to go through the darkest corners of his/her consensus in order to deal with the best while reality becomes the surrounding.
Foreground and background switch places in a mindblowing turn of events. You experience a piece of art being evolved just like a painting showing you exactly where your eyes should be directed but at the same time having a background hiding the meaning of the whole picture.
That's how direction is being done people. It's not only about directing the resources of making a story. It's about directing the eyes and attention of the viewer/gamer.
Excellent work.
Final verdict:
It's a bit hard to decide to make an objective conclusion here. Because the first 2 episodes of this story seemed so too average and for a few moments too short or too boring, and then the third and final Episode takes your mind and blows all your feelings and thoughts up. The ending climax is satisfying and their staying true to the comics is really awesome.
On the other hand there are other elements I have to emphasize on.
Do choices REALLY matter in games like this?
Gameplay wise - you will eventually have the ending the developers want you to anyway. But the illusion that you can control the plot slowly becomes less and less strong. Take for example the achievement system for the past 2 Walking Dead games from TellTale. There are no missable achievements at all. In fact, they are not even "achievements", they are just flags poping up letting you know that you finished a chapter. There's no feeling of achieving something special any more. Point & Click doesn't motivate you to explore place or try new things. You are just left following a story, and if you find yourself too bored during a chapter of the story, you have one less reason to let's say go through the drawers and items you find yourself in but go straight to the NPC you need to talk to in order to go on with the story. You see what I'm talking about?
The game is a 7/10. Would had been a 6 - a slightly above average title, short, not sure if worthy a 15 buck release price.
But the story driven content is strong and the final chapter shows that the developers gave everything they got for it.
The game lacks the extra motivation some people might need to do extra exploring or replay chapters to see different outcomes.
We know TellTale can do better. They have shown us the potential.
I hope they bring us their best soon.

The game is advertised as you playing the *players* of people playing D&D. the gameplay honestly is just watered down D&D with the cast replaced by a table full of players though.
It's a cute game for a bit. It cameos or references various topical humor bits liek Gremlins, Scooby Doo, Star wars, TMNT, Short Circut (the list goes on amazingly and would probably be the main reason to keep playing when the gameplay starts being a bore: Just to see what else they show us).
But it doesn't really keep your interest too well as a game. The classes don't branch out or anything. Every class has the same 3 or 4 moves they started with. It also suffers from "FF7 status effect syndrome"; where only pure damage and buff moves matter as anytime a debuff would be theoretically useful the monster is immune to it anyway - usually a boss, but not always.
It's a cheap game though so you can't really go wrong if you just want to goof around and mess with something that doesn't take itself seriously. In small doses it's fun.

I just finished TBS, the first game I've finished in 2014. Helps that it was short, I'm thinking no more than 6-8 hours of actual, non-experimentation, non-reloading last checkpoint play time. This is one of the games I Kickstarted back when that was a thing (meaning before I figured out that it really wasn't worth it). No regrets through, well worth the KS$.
The game looks and sounds great. The visuals (Eyvind Earle-inspired) and music (Austin Wintory) are major parts of what drew me to TBS in the first place. The game universe, billed as a Viking fantasy, is competent. There's nothing groundbreaking about the story or characters, but they serve the purpose.
Gameplay is hit/miss. I'm a TBS (turn-based strategy of course) fan, but the oversimplified systems of TBS (The Banner Saga, of course) leave me wanting more options. Even the Gold Box TSR games had more combat choices than this. The initiative and action mechanisms leave a lot to be desired, as units don't have fixed speeds. It's always a he-goes-you-go deal, so if you mop up weak units early you're left with more powerful units acting more often. This leaves you with a counterintuitive strategy of weakening units without killing them. I'm also torn on the health-as-attack-power thing, but that much I can live with. Last glaring thing for me is the lack of any way to influence movement. Short of a couple of minor abilities that address threat, AI units can waltz around your melee units and go right for ranged. Nothing you can do to stop them.
The overland mechanisms are brutal, but if you've played King of Dragon Pass that's nothing new. The game has one currency, caller Renown, which is gained by killing enemies. Renown is used to level characters, buy items and buy supplies that keeps your army alive while travelling overland. You're probably not going to be able to afford any items, unless you're willing to lose people to starvation (events generally cost you supplies as you travel) or you're going to show restraint when levelling your characters (which can backfire if a toon you've invested a lot or resources in gets auto-killed in an event). Still, this is a thing you can get used to compared to the combat.
The save system can be confusing, but the game seems to save frequently on its own. You can't seem to manually save, but on hitting Load you can see that it's got three checkpoint saves. Not too bad. The system options are sparse for a PC game in 2014 - no volume controls, no graphics options. Again, nothing too bad. What I wanted most was Steam Cloud save capability, but it's not there. All mostly quality of life stuff here, which may be upgraded when the second chapter ships.
Word of warning - this is the first part of a planned trilogy, so the ending kind of feels exactly like that. There's a major event/battle, but a lot of loose ends remain to lead into chapter two. If you were ok with the ending of The Fellowship of the Ring (old school) or The Hunger Games (new school), you'll be fine. :)
Overall though I'm satisfied with the game. This is my third KS'd game to deliver (FTL and Shadowrun Returns were my first two) and so far all three are winners in my book. This actually kind of feels like Shadowrun Returns in terms of heft/depth/scope. I recommend TBS to anyone who's into the genre.
PS: Chapter 2 is out now so time to move on in this story!

Grim Dawn is a spectacular addition to the isometric ARPG family. Created by some of the team that brought you the timeless classic Titan Quest, strap up and delve into Cairn - a world in a 'victorian-esque' era that is experiencing the eradication of the human race.
At this time, this game is still a work in progress but it shows a ton of promise. Grim Dawn lives up to its name and paints a canvas of a harsh world where good help is hard to find, suvival isn't always guarenteed and death lurks around every corner. Accompanied by a fantastic soundtrack, I found this game sucked me into its world and I sunk tons of hours hacking and slashing my way to the finish of the current beta (Build 24).
If I had to compare it to other games of the genre, I'd say it has the grit and gore of Diablo 2/Path of Exile, mixed with the leveling system of Titan Quest and the fast combat of Torchlight 2. Grim Dawn introduces a variety of its own elements, such as the 'Constitution' health regeneration system, designed to reduce the number of trips to town and potions used so you spend more time in combat. The game also features a choice/consequence system where saving 'character A' means the death of 'character B' and a loss of trust from the faction character B is associated with. There is a ton of loot to reward you for your victories and a variety of options for crafting so customization is certainly an option for your gear.
Outside of expected and respected bug fixes, I would like to see: more voice acting for NPCs, more animations for skills and enemies, and hopefully another class (currently there are 5).
I highly recommend this game and I look forward to the completed product. Keep up the great work Crate Entertainment!

A very different tactical RPG that I have ever previously played. There were a few things that I did not like. The combat was fun, but I found it slightly unbalanced in favour to the enemies that you fought against. I also found the renown that you gain (XP, but used for buying items and supplies as well) was in short supply, and at end-game in my 1st playthrough I hadn't fully leveled up my characters. Finally, the game seemed pretty short for the $24.99 that I had to pay to play the game, especially considering the ending of the game  just seemed to be geared up for a sequel (there were a lot of unresolved plot issues).
All-in-all, I still found it to be a good game with great storyline and music. For people who like a story driven game, or tactical RPG's, I would recommend this game. Titan Quest lives again in this spiritual successor that expands upon ideas of loose quest progression and meaningfully-destructible environments which leads to a very open-world feel.
Secrets feel secret (reminiscent of old Gauntlet games) and items have fun and unique stats, often times granting cool new abilities.
For those left wanting with the somewhat shallow story of Path of Exile, they'll inhale this game's intriguing quest dialogs, flavor text, noteable NPCs, and lore drops throughout the game.

From the start you will find the progression of the game absolutley mesmerizing.  The amount of survival and how the beginning of the story progresses, will keep you begging for more.  The problem arrises with the game when the player becomes just too overpowered.  When you stop fearing anything and start acting like spiderman with a grap hook, the appeal wanes heavily.  The continuity of the game suffers a lot near the end.  The multiplayer aspect is very tight but has a few loose screws when it comes to Be The Zombie.
Overall I give this game a thumbs up but with some caution as playability and lack of good DLC content hold this game back a lot.

I could not get the bad taste out of my mouth after Dead Island for a few days on account of feeling like I was skating, no - floating, on ice and other engine-related allergies. But knowing that this game's main selling point was the parkour elements, I put these worries aside as it would be impossible to achieve that without fixing my previous woes.
Sure, the game does pander to the casual here and there. It does make me cringe somewhat that you're always being bombarded with overpowered weapons and rarely in the game feel like surviving is taking its toll at all. However, the game is so fun on account of the flow of moving from place to place that it becomes an objective unto itself to make perfect assaults and getaways rather than getting into sticky situations where outnumbered.
Also, difficulty increasing mods were some of the first to come out, and remain the most essential mods one can have today.
My biggest complaint about this game however is how early you master the movement. In Mirror's Edge, I found myself replaying the game because I wasn't satisfied with my mastery of the parkour when I completed the game. Not so for this game. In this game, it'll take less than 10 hours to reach perfection of your skills to move perfectly from place to place, and thus it becomes a bit repetitive near the end. It is simply too forgiving to be replayable.
But even my biggest complaint is minor, given that "AAA" these days have become synonymous with trash, and Dying Light came around and changed that for me. Or at least showed me a rare glimmer of hope.
The optimization problems at launch however do not paint these developers in a positive light, so while I can recommend this game now, I wouldn't recommend picking up anything fresh from this developer in the future until at least a couple of patches in.

If you enjoy Hack and Slash RPGs like Diablo, this game is for you.
I have played all the lastest H&S RPGs out there (Diablo 3, Torchlight2, Path of Exile, Marvel Heroes 2015), and none has attracted me as much as Grim Dawn.
The game has incredible physics, making it very fun to smash your weapons at your enemies and see them roll to the floor, fly back, or even explodein a gory way sometimes due to your Critical Hits.
The game has 6 classes so far, and there are more to come. The best part: You can combine them. Yes, you can make a Multiclass character, who is, for example, both an Arcanist and a Soldier. But you can stick to just one class if you prefer.
The enviorement is very gloomy, scary, dark, and grim, as the title suggests, and wich is awesome for us, Diablo 1 and 2 fans.
The story is actually interesting and creative.
Itemization is wonderful. You will slowly build up your character as you advance through the game.
The game is quite hard, wich makes it a challenge that never gets boring.
The music (BGM) is amazing. Pick Diablo 1 and 2 style of music, but instead of having an accoustic guitar, add an Electric Guitar.
The areas of the game are quite big, making it interesting to explore.
Lots of quests to do as well.
I strongly suggest this game for any fan of Action RPGs. Check the Steam Reviews and Metacritic Reviews if you are still in doubdt.

What Bioware couldn't achieve with Dragon Age series Original Sin has brought to us after so many years of waiting. Yes, they did it - CRPG in modern graphics and with sophisticated, yet easy to understand, game mechanics. Fallout (1&2)-esque combat system, Baldur's Gate exploration and story-telling mechanics and Divinity world that will make you come back again and again. Story is not as epic as you'd like but its execution brings satisfaction and fun. Battles are challenging and you'll have to implement a lot of tactics and preparation (nothing new for BG fans - you are going to LOVE the combat) but they will reward you appropriately - however, you must be aware of the level of your enemies - don't tread into locations with creatures that are 2-3 levels above you or you'll get owned (or not - the game actually lets you wander into such locations and if you are resourcefull enough, you may win those fights - but at a cost of money, resurrection, potions and patience). The only minor down-side of this marvel are a few bugs here and there but developers are getting rid of them as you are reading this - after all, they are nothing game breaking and even AAA titles are often buggy as hell shortly after the release. That's right,this is not an AAA title - it's a Kickstarter game and what a game it is! If Shadowrun was considered a success, this jewel is a miracle. Trully a MUST-HAVE for all RPG fans.

B-12 is a 1st/3rd person robot game that has action/shooter/platformer/light exploring elements. It's nice to switch between 1st and 3rd person view depending on the situation. There is the platforming and exploring/navigating when I prefer 3rd person and then there is the combat and narrow spaces when to switch to 1st person. Moving feels really good and weighty, you can feel the momentum. You have dashing, dash- and walljumping and a jetpac as a power-up to move around with. Shooting is somewhat reminescent of Mega Man, you can charge your shot (and you have a gun as your hand!). Another thing that this game made me think of for some reason is the Bugs Bunny/Duffy Duck/Marvin Martian episodes that take place in space, which is - let's face it - probably one of the best associations there is. The energy mechanic is also nice, makes you think a bit when to use your gun, jetpack, shield, etc.
Generally the game feels like it is made with heart, by which I mean that the dev has a vision of what the game should be like, what it should feel like, what kind of atmosphere it should have, and actually manages to capture this vision. I really like that you can see your body, arms and legs when in 1st person. I like that I can pick up destroyed enemy robot's hand (also weapons) only to whip up other robots with it. The enemy robots look nice and funny. Sounds & music fit well and compliment the atmosphere.
I wish there will be more exploring and secrets to find, maybe some sort of collectibles, items/non-talking or broken NPC robots/flora&fauna/art/something that hints about the lore for a carefully exploring player, generally I mean something little to fleshen out the game experience a bit, although I think this game doesn't need anything too complicated for the certain kind of simplicity is one of it's virtues (for example it's nice that it doesn't have any text).
I also encourage you to try the dev's other game, Hoverbike Joust (alpha), available at itch.io, really great fun.

I bought this game during the latest sale at the recommendation of one of my friends, but it was also on my wishlist to begin with.  If you'd like to see a video detailing everything I'm discussing here (review with a bit of humor), there's a link here for your viewing pleasure.
If that's not your style, here's the short version.  By the way, most of this will focus on Ys I.
YS I
For a remake of a game dating back to 1987 (and also remade before), Ys I remains a fun excursion.  It goes to show that some games can stand the test of time, even if their more current competitors are more high-toned and fancy.  For instance:
*The "bump" combat is a refreshingly simple system.  While appearing simple, it did have a considerable amount of minutiae to keep it engaging.
*The musical arrangements now come with three options and styles.  I personally chose to listen to the Chronicles version, and I enjoyed many of the songs.
However, there is a darker side to these same points.....
*At times it feels like the "bump" system relies a little too much on luck.  While it looks like you hit the enemy just to the side of head-on, the foe will still get a counter-attack in like you hit them head-on.  This is particularly concerning early on in the game while you are weaker than the enemies.
*Due to the limited programming options of the original release, there is not much variety with the music, which means you may get tired of hearing the same songs over and over again.
Other pros and cons to take into consideration are:
*Pro: The graphics look amazing, considering the source material.
*Con: At times the difficulty is low, and then suddenly there is something disproportionally challenging.
*Con: At times it can be difficult to figure out what you have to do, or there is a specific order that things must be completed in if you want to progress.
*Pro: While I had difficulty understanding some facets of what I had to do at times, there was a very rich backstory.
*Pro: The game's clarity improved over time.
Even with these flaws, I found myself enjoying the game considerably.  In addition, many of these issues are improved or corrected in Ys II.
YS II
Ys II is a lot like Ys I, except for several key facts:
*It's much clearer than its predecessor in terms of what to do.
*There's magic now, which offers a brand-new dimension and means by which to combat enemies.
These changes create a much easier to work with game, and I am enjoying it more than the first one.  However, something to keep in mind: the bosses can be INSANELY difficult.  Yet they are still really fun encounters.
So if you like action RPGs, I recommend taking a look at these classic Ys games, and have fun bumping off some foes.

I'm fairly well versed in Roguelikes, and while RoR is certainly difficult, the game isn't so much about skill as it's about getting extremely lucky.  The best strategy I've found involves sprinting through each level to the teleporter and cheesing the following fight as hard as you can to win.  This leads to the unfulfilling gameplay loop of "Did I get anything good, did I get close teleporters to the spawns, and did I get easy bosses in the first 2 stages?  If not, you're going to get 1 shot by something on the third level, restart."
I tried setting it down to Drizzle (easy) and the game became TOO easy.  While I was now able to fight things and buy everything I wanted, there's no interesting item combinations since you eventually collect everything, and none of them interact in interesting ways.  Combined with the fact that each level only has 1-2 variations, you'll see everything this game has to offer in about 2-3 playthroughs.
I like the graphics and the music, but the gameplay's just not fun.

A very different tactical RPG that I have ever previously played. The art, storytelling and music were things that I really did like, especially because the storyline choices that you make during the game could have consequences through-out the story (main characters can die!).  For people who have played Kingdom of Dragon Pass, the possible reward/atrocity depending on what you choose from that game is very similar to this one, at least in during the storyline portion of the game.
There were a few things that I did not like. The combat was fun, but I found it slightly unbalanced in favour to the enemies that you fought against. I also found the renown that you gain (XP, but used for buying items and supplies as well) was in short supply, and at end-game in my 1st playthrough I hadn't fully leveled up my characters. Finally, the game seemed pretty short for the $24.99 that I had to pay to play the game, especially considering the ending of the game  just seemed to be geared up for a sequel (there were a lot of unresolved plot issues).
All-in-all, I still found it to be a good game with great storyline and music. For people who like a story driven game, or tactical RPG's, I would recommend this game. However, I would recommend to pick it up on sale because the normal asking price is not worth it for such a short game... unless you are someone who likes multiple playthroughs with different stories each time. 7.5/10

This game is just... bad. There's no other way of describing it really. Nothing really works.
The story is hilariously mis-translated, but this is what I gathered from what I read: You and your soldier buddies were captured by Germany and are being kept in a castle named "Werewolf". Captives in said castle are being experimented on and are being turned into, if it weren't obvious enough, werewolves. Your character however doesn't plan on being experimented on, so he escapes his cell by walking straght through the unlocked door he was kept in. The actual story is pretty hard to interpret, so I could be very wrong, but that's what I got from reading the story in the Help menu, which was very obviously written by a Russian, much like the
on the Steam store page.
The music is all over the place, It's either (bad) DooM-style midis or (bad) dubstep midis, and there are only like 3 or 4 different songs, so they get old rather quickly. The sound design is laughable at best. It seems like whoever was in charge of getting gun sound effects just ripped some from different games and royalty free sites. Enemy sound effects are meh, not too bad but nothing to write home about. The ambiance sounds actually made me laugh pretty hard the first time I heard them, and by "ambiance" I mean the occasional wolf howl done by some guy first take with a LOT of white noise behind it.
The graphics are hard to look at, even for a retro-style shooter trying to replicate Wolfenstein 3D. The game is locked at 15 fps and the resolution of a whopping 480x360, which is a comedian's punchline in 2017. The poor frame-rate mixed with the rough graphics will most likely cause your head to ache, I know mine did within about 20 minutes of playtime. I know graphics shouldn't be a retro game's strongpoint, but Wolfenstein 3D did way better in
just by not being headache-inducing.
Believe it or not, the gameplay is pretty lame, too. Wolfenstein 3D, DooM, Duke Nukem, ANY DooM clone HAS to AT LEAST have good gunplay. The entire game revolves around you shooting enemies, so the guns have to at least sound and look dangerous to match their actual damage output. Make mowing down Nazis or any other type of enemy feel badass. That being said, this game's gunplay feels wimpy and half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. "Automatic" weapons like the SMG and the LMG are simply just semi-automatic weapons with sound effects simulating three round bursts, while only firing one bullet, which sounds kinda complicated now that I type it out, so just imagine pulling the trigger once, the gun shooting three times rapidly, but only one bullet comes out. Sometimes, pressing the fire button
. Gun design is just kinda weird. Your starting weapon is a metal fist for melee, then an old western-like revolver, then a more advanced looking SMG, followed by a dorky-looking double barrel shotgun, and finally an LMG that looks as if it were ripped straight from COD Black Ops. Keep in mind this is the WWII era, so it would've been extremely easy to just capitalize on the awesome weapons they had during that time.
If you want, just buy the game for the steam cards you get for playing it, then refund it, but other than that, stay far, FAR away from this garbage pile. Wolfenstein 3D browser version plays way better than this game, and if you want the real deal, the Steam version of Wolfenstein 3D is only 2 dollars more than this. Don't cheap out, seriously, you'll regret the choice.

It bums me out to give this a negative review, since I badly wanted it to be good and did enjoy some aspects of it.  The art and animation are stunning; it was very clearly made by a team of visual design veterans.  I applaud Stoic's attempt at breathing new life into tactical RPG battles by making it more akin to chess than say, FF Tactics.  Unfortunately, the system they came up with is easily exploited once you understand how it works.  Weaken (but don't kill!) lesser mobs so that they can't deal damage and continue to eat up turns for the enemy team, then focus on the heavy hitters.  After a while I started to dread fights because of how formulaic and boring they become.  No variation/advantages in terrain; just the same tired grid, battle after battle after battle.  The lore is excellent and well-formed, yet the story itself is unfocused and difficult to follow.  Even the score by Austin Wintory (whose soundtrack for indie darling Journey is amongst the greatest of all time) is forgettable.
I feel like there's a great game somewhere in here, but the pieces just haven't come together yet.  With any luck Stoic will raise enough funds to continue the saga and I'll give it another go to see if they resolve some of these issues.  Until then I can't bring myself to finish this first installment.  Too bad.
UPDATE: Ended up beating the game anyway since I was at the final boss.  Had to cheese my way through on easy thanks to an absurd upswing in difficulty for the second phase of the fight.  It did not improve my opinion of the game.

If you enjoy Hack and Slash RPGs like Diablo, this game is for you.
I have played all the lastest H&S RPGs out there (Diablo 3, Torchlight2, Path of Exile, Marvel Heroes 2015), and none has attracted me as much as Grim Dawn.

The game has 6 classes so far, and there are more to come. The best part: You can combine them. Yes, you can make a Multiclass character, who is, for example, both an Arcanist and a Soldier. But you can stick to just one class if you prefer.
The enviorement is very gloomy, scary, dark, and grim, as the title suggests, and wich is awesome for us, Diablo 1 and 2 fans.
The story is actually interesting and creative.
Itemization is wonderful. You will slowly build up your character as you advance through the game.
The game is quite hard, wich makes it a challenge that never gets boring.
The music (BGM) is amazing. Pick Diablo 1 and 2 style of music, but instead of having an accoustic guitar, add an Electric Guitar.
The areas of the game are quite big, making it interesting to explore.
Lots of quests to do as well.
I strongly suggest this game for any fan of Action RPGs. Check the Steam Reviews and Metacritic Reviews if you are still in doubdt.

The Banner Saga is a shiny red apple that looks delicious until you really bite into it and find it worm infested.  The art and music are very well done and bring a sure charm to the game that seems to have bedazzled a lot of reviewers.  My issues with the game didn't become aparent until well into it (more than a few hours).  The only important resource in the game is "renown", which you use to either level up your characters or to buy supplies so your "caravan" can eat.  There is so little renown in the game you generally have to choose to do either/or of these activities.  As a result you can either feed your people as a kind leader would and end up losing a lot of battles with a stagnant squad of low level guys or you can ignore your people, allow them to starve and die off, and level your squad of fighters to win battles.  Despite the fact that one of your two leaders you control has the occupation of "master hunter" there is no hunting in the game.  No way to procure food except for the occassional scripted even with a "King of Dragon Pass" choose your own adventure chance to get precious supplies.
It makes for a frustrating experience.  Perhaps the point is the force the player into being cold and heartless much the same way Fable 3 did.  That experience ended up being sub optimal as well.
For $30+ I wish there was more of a game here to go with the fantasy story.  It just as easily could have been an excellent interactive novel on an iPad.  Instead of playing to the strengths, the game is shackled like a mewing beast to lame "Oregon Trail" gameplay and a somewhat counter intuitive basic turn based tactical combat system.  There are D&D Goldbox games available online that were made twenty years ago with far more tactical depth than what this 2014 game offers.
On the upside, the game looks great (even on a Mac without a dedicated graphics card).  The music is decent if not a bit overly dramatic.  The characters are mostly interesting.
I haven't finished it.  I'm probably a little more than halfway.  Sadly, there are too many worms for me to finish this deceptive looking fruit.

Ah, Shadowgrounds. It's not the best top-down shooter I've ever played.
It's unbalanced, gives you at least twice as many guns as you actually need, it's a bit buggy and unpolished. It starts you off really slowly on the first few levels. The shotgun doesn't feel powerful at all even with burst fire, and the Electric Gun came far too late and ended up being pointless. The main character suffers from "gotta roll to go faster" syndrome. The boss in the Mines level is goddamn ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ as he's faster than you and you have no way to dodge him until he starts rolling and summoning enemies (fun fact, I lost a life). The final boss is disappointing and the ending is just awful. Co-op is local only. But perhaps worst of all, it's too damn short, clocking at a mere 6 hours, and with no reason whatsoever to replay it.
And yet, it's definitely one of the most enjoyable. The levels are built in a non-linear fashion and encourage exploration, and despite being somewhat repetitive at times, always come out with many varied challenges. Enemies manage to be varied, even requiring a different approach depending on your arsenal. Most weapons feel fantastic, especially when fully upgraded. The pistol, considering it's your backup infinite-ammo weapon, is goddamn amazing with the upgrades (though the secondary feels more like a passive skill, which was indeed the result in the sequel). Some of the effects and scenery are jaw-dropping, even today (♥♥♥♥ yeah particles). The soundtrack, especially in action sequences, really makes you pump adrenaline with all its awesomeness. It's jolly good fun.
Oh, and it's also absurdly cheap on sale, a mere 99 cents for the two games. So what the heck are you waiting for?

A review of Grim Dawn after beta develpment, testing and final release.
Grim Dawn is a traditional hack and slash Role Playing game written by the same development team (defunct Iron Lore Entertainment) who originally wrote Titan Quest and the expansion pack Immortal Throne, Having a near identical gaming mechanics, high resolution graphics and addictive game-play but instead of the Mythical Greek setting, Grim Dawn is set in a medieval environment with magic, gunpowder and mythical creatures galore. As in a similar vain to Diablo, Torchlight, and it's predecessor the players utilise the dual skill tree to build individual unique characters, through collecting a multitude of armour, weaponry, and miscellaneous items and gaining experience through killing or completing various quests. Although a linear storyline, there are a vast amount of quests to be completed which allows the players the freedom to roam the fantasy environment, and complete their tasks.
Since it's beta development, the programmers have refined and adding additional Acts and levels to the overall game. Also the developers have actively removed bugs, faults and improved the game-play. After completing the game with different characters and difficulty I can highly recommend Grim Damn as a great alternative for those seeking a similar game and genre to Diablo 3, or players who have enjoyed Titan Quest and Torchlight 2.
So for under a Tenner (£10) in the Steam or Humble Bundle (Monthly) sale the game is value for money, and highly recommended 85/100.

As someone who has played the original Ys games before they started gaining a following; I am satisfied with my purchase. Let me begin with saying that this collection is the ideal remake for a game. These two games are fairly close to the originals with the second game straying a little farther than the first. HOWEVER, if you do not like classic JRPG games the game might feel a little too simple for you. The bump battle system turns off a lot of people due to its' simplicity; it was implemented in a time where it had to deal with the limitations of the Sega Master System, and the Famicom. I suppose you could say this is one of the original ARPGs due to Ys' unique active battle system. Like most Falcom games the OST is pretty good so that shouldn't be an issue. If you want to take advantage of the replay value of these games; there is a Time Attack mode available for anyone who wants to speedrun the game. These games however are not difficult at all, and you can take advantage of the bump system VERY easily. You will be rewarded for grinding in this game, because a single level difference can make a big deal. To be more concise; this is a great collection of two JRPG classics, and I recommend them to anyone interested in the genre.

Of all the Telltale 'Walking Dead' games, this one falls rather short.
As one other reviewer pointed out, playing as Michonne eliminates some of the tension from the game - I already know she's going to survive all three episodes, so it's just a question of which of the minor characters die. It's also quite short when compared to other episodes from Season 1 & 2. There's a couple of interesting moments, but overall it feels rather flat as a story.
The brief 'combat' sections feel like they've been speeded up somewhat. I don't think I died more than a couple of times in Seasons 1 & 2 yet here it was far more frequent, and I felt that the designers had reduced the time available for key presses to make it feel more 'intense'. Still, it's just a case of learning the correct key sequence for any combat, which is very easy.
Much more concerning for me were the technical issues I encountered, which has never happened before whilst playing a Telltale game. I could not get the game to stay in 3400x1440 resolution at all. Some of the loading screens would be correct, but as soon as I went into the game proper it would revert to a lower resolution. About 40 mins of my 2 hour playtime was spent trying to fix this issue, before I gave up. There's also a long delay whilst loading each chapter, which I've never experienced before, and this doesn't help with the flow of the game at all.
The overall impression is that of a rushed game to hit a deadline. Even the icons for the Steam achievements are just numbers - Telltale haven't bothered with the small pictoral representations of each chapter from the previous games.

Pros
-Turn based combat with enviromental effects taken into consideration as well as enemies who will take advantage of said effects.
-Witty dialogue and banter from NPCs. Subtle is the way they deliver the clues.
-Challenging gameplay that forces you to think: This game won't hold your hand and paying attention to detail is the only way to solve quests. You do not have quest markers so those NPC dialogues and clues in books or parchment do matter. Certain puzzles and dialogue will require you to know the character you created by way of the choices you've made during your playthrough.
-World doesn't scale with player: If you're level 2 and decide to attack a group of level 5 mob then you're going to die very quickly. It's doable but you better have good tactics and a full group with a complement of skills and spells. You will actually see your character getting stronger.
-No grinding: Gold is not as essential as in most RPGs where vendors hold the best items. The game wants you to explore for XP and better gear. While gear helps, your tactics and skill levels matter more during combat.
-Traits and Skill matter: A high Perception character will gain access to certain areas, react to hidden switches and make progression easier. Those with Charisma can talk their way into a hostile village and instigate a fight between two hostile factions without having to resort to violence.
-Interactive enviroment: Use telekenesis to stack boxes for fun and glory, walk into a pool of poison and cast fire on it then explode into joy, run on a sheet of ice and introduce the back of your head to the ground, stand in water while casting area of effect lighting and watch as your enemies and yourself have a seizure for the ages, teleport enemies and be teleported in turn into lava and turn into ash and many more!
-Good waypoint system and the two main characters can travel to each other's location.
-Learn the greatest truth in the universe: "No-one has as many friends as the man with many cheeses"
(When you get to that area, you'll know. You will know)
Cons
-Crafting system needs better customization and variation. Sure it's fun mixing flour with water and makind dough but in the grand scheme of things it's not game changing.
-Vendors take forever to restock: As of now it seems they only do it when you level up. It's a pain trying to buy dyes because I do not enjoy running around in some purple armor I picked up.
-Storyline is decent but not the greatest and might detract the game's value for players who enjoy story driven games.
-Cheese Vendor might drive you loopy when shopping with the local enchantress for skill books. You'll know when get there.
Overall, the game requires you to pay attention because it will never hold your hand and assumes that the player is competent enough to decipher the various clues given. It definitely will require you to pay attention.
The combat is satisfying and can be quite punishing at times. Be careful who and how many you engage. Pick your battles.
Great game and well worth the full price if you enjoy turn based games, multiple ways to approach quests and interacting with the world around you.

8 out of 10.

I had about 30 of Paul's Goat Hooves (items that increase your hero's speed) and I walked into a wall and couldn't escape. I was stuck, and that was after about a 1 hour run. Other than this, very good.
8.5 out of 10.
Hopoo says that the randomly generated maps are great for replayability. I agree, to a certain extent. The maps, while having subtle differences every playthrough, are more or less the same. However, there are many different items to choose from, as well as many different heroes. This calls for many replays with different "builds", so to speak.

9 out of 10.
There really is not much of a story, and this really adds to the beauty of the game. They give you tidbits of information here and there, in things like the item and monster logs and the end game statement (dependent on the hero used). This leaves a lot to your imagination which I really love.
8.5 out of 10.
I have a soft spot in my heart for pixel graphics, growing up with a Super Nintendo. So, I may be a little biased here, but I really like the pixel graphics in this game. They give a good, dark atmosphere, and make it easier to feel immersed, as if YOU'RE the one who's ship crashed and left you on an alien world.
9.5 out of 10.
Oh my my, the soundtrack. One of the many high points of this game. Chris Christodoulou made songs that fit the stages nicely and add much to the aesthetics of the game. They all give you different feelings, as they're supposed to. The boss battle music is very intense, and the ambient wandering music is nice and calm, almost contributing to a feeling of eerieness.
8.5 out of 10.
This is a very good game with a not-too-steep learning curve. It sports a good amount of difficulty, seems pretty optimized, the bugs are practically nonexistent, and the replayability is high. BACKGROUND:
South Park: The Stick of Truth is an RPG developed by Obsidian Entertainment and published by Ubisoft. The game was written largely by the creators of the TV show, Trey Parker and Matt Stone. The game follows the life of a kid in the game simply referred to as "The New Kid" and his quest to help defend the titular Stick of Truth from the elves. As the game progresses, the New Kid realizes that he is not just fighting to save the Stick, but to save the world as well.
FACTORS AFFECTING MY REVIEW:
-I have seen the complete story through a Let's Play series on Youtube before I had bought and played this game and was well aware of the story and where I was to go.
-I am not a fan of South Park, yet I have seen a handful of episodes to have a basic idea of how some characters act.
-I played the game on normal settings.
REVIEW:
When South Park: The Stick of Truth came out, I was shocked at how successful it had become. Rarely in this day and age does a video game based on any movie or TV franchise ever leave an impression, but South Park managed to do just that. It's success is shocking as previous outings with the video game genre have been lackluster. South Park 64 was an abhorrent game that has lived on in infamy, but it served as an example as to what did not make a South Park game.
I bought this game a few weeks ago during the Steam Summer Sale. I had already saw the whole story and wanted to be able to play through it myself. As I first loaded the game, I was stunned to see just how well they made it look like the show. The environments and the characters feel like they just stepped of the TV screen and onto my computer screen. The whole game felt like I was playing through an episode of the show.
Although it is a good-looking game, the gameplay is a little hard to nail down. The farting mechanics (I wish I did not have to type that) are all shown how to do the same way, but it completely changes during the actual battles. Speaking of the battles, they are entirely too easy. I managed to get through the game without dying once in a battle and in some cases, I got to avoid some of them altogether. During the battles, most, if not all, attacks are followed by quick-time events that either boost your attack's damage or add specific effects. I, personally, found these quick-time events to be unnecessary and frustrating.
The comedy in this game is rather funny sometimes, but be sure to not be around any relatives or little children when it is expressed. The comedy is filled with vulgar language, crude humor, and disturbing images. This game actually depicts acts of sex and nudity right in front of your characters eyes. For the entirety of my gameplay sessions, I had to use headphones and lock my door because I was afraid of someone walking in on me during any of these foul actions.
To be honest, I was a little embarrased after having bought this game because I knew what it contained.

FINAL THOUGHTS:

Although it is not the greatest game I have ever played, South Park: The Stick of Truth is the ultimate love letter to South Park fans. If you are looking for a more investive RPG, this game is not for you. If you are a fan of the show and want something to make you feel like you are a part of it, I would recommend this game to you.
SCORE: 5.9/10

-=The Good=-
A throwback to the simpler days of the FPS genre
Interesting concept of werewolf Nazis
Decent character sprite designs
A couple of nice tunes
-=The Bad=-
Odd control setup
No key remapping
Too easy
Sluggish mouse movement
No map function
No difficulty selection
Art is inconsistent quality-wise
Rather short for the genre
Most levels could have been better designed
Some strange looking animations
Save system could have been more informative
Nazi werewolves concept not well utilized
-=The Details=-
Back in the 1990s, the First Person Shooter genre was in its infancy. We had classics like
,
,
and others that took us through violent worlds through the eyes of a protagonist. Since then, things have advanced a lot in terms of visuals, gameplay mechanics and so forth, but there's still a charm to some of those earlier games. And
tries to play off of those charms.
Using an engine that closely mirrors the one for
, the visuals are simplified with no floor or ceiling graphics. Only walls make up the environment, which consist of a lot of bricks that are dotted with the occasional emblem, wooden wall, door, locker row and such to break it up at times on each level. They look alright, but mostly just get the job done without much in the way of flair or inspired design. The enemy sprites themselves however, show more creativity than the wall types. While the human characters are generally cartoonish-looking German soldiers (save for the medieval armor-wearing soldiers that carry miniguns), the werewolves are more interesting in their appearance. Ranging from chest armor-wearing grunts to more mechanized super soldiers, they offer up the largest bit of creativity in the game. Sure, the animations for all of these sprites walking and attacking are pretty basic, but the era this game's mimicking was that way as well. So no real problem there.
The sound effects in the game are pretty straightforward. The different guns make solid sounds that fit pretty well for each one, the werewolves growl and howl, the human soldiers make short comments in German when they're triggered by seeing you, and your guy gives an “u-huh” when picking something up (sounds like he's clearing his throat, really). It all works without coming off poorly. The midi-like music that plays isn't too bad, but most of it (save for a track or two) has melodies that won't stick with you. Thankfully, none of the music is horrid or anything. So while it won't get you humming most of the tracks, they don't become annoying or grating either.
The gameplay in
is pretty much what you found in
. Walk around each map, grab ammo and health, shoot enemies, pick up treasures and find the occasional hidden section behind a wall. Your weapons range from an armored fist for punching, to several guns such as a pistol, two shotgun types, a machine gun and a minigun. You'll be using these weapons through 13 levels filled with human grunts, officers and armored soldiers, as well as several werewolf enemy types. The end result is a game that will feel very familiar to those who grew up with the genre's early entries, but one that also doesn't offer up much in the way of surprises.
So what does this game do wrong? Well, a fair number of things really. First off, the controls are rather cumbersome to use. W/A/S/D is for moving/strafing, but the left and right arrows allow you to turn in place. The up and down arrows can only be used for menu selection (you can't use W/S), while the mouse is what you use to fire and turn as you walk around. Oh, and the Space bar is for opening doors and checking walls for hidden passages. None of these keys can be remapped, which leaves you trying to come to grips with a setup that never feels natural or comfortable. Even the mouse doesn't feel right, as it moves too slow with no way to increase its sensitivity. And while I can't speak for all controllers, I know a wired 360 controller doesn't work with this game. So if you want to use it, you'll have to rely on a key-mapping program.
But the problems don't end there. The game is rather easy, with most of its difficulty coming from having to use the odd control setup. Also making the game feel too easy, is that most enemies are quick to die, even with the basic pistol. They can be readily outrun as well, with only the werwolves' up-close attack doing real damage. Heck, the game doesn't offer a noticeable challenge until the final map, where it gangs up on you by throwing everything it has at you on a straightforward, but good-sized map. Another issue is that the maps aren't very large or maze-like, so getting to the exit can be done pretty quickly for most of them. There are even a few maps that can be finished
quickly because they're so short. And though none of these maps are overly large, I still have to say that the lack of a mapping feature is missed. It's been a staple of the genre for decades and leaving it out feels like a lazy omission.
Other issues come in smaller, but numerous ways. The art style used for the title screen and between-levels isn't very appealing, with characters that are oddly drawn and shaded that end up looking like something done quickly in MS Paint. Next, the saving feature always displays everything as “file 1” to “file 4,” so you'll have to remember which one you saved to last due to the game giving you no clues as to what's on each save file. Then there's the issue of not having a difficulty selection, which means once you play through the game, there's nothing to go to that'll add a greater challenge. From there, we have levels that are pretty basic, with only a couple of them really feeling like they got more complicated in their layout toward the end of the game. Yet another problem is that the game isn't very long for a FPS entry, lasting only about an hour and a half. Next on the list is how some of the sprite animations are... odd. The werewolves don't look like they walk, but rather just kind of... well, tilt. You can see more animation if you look closely, but the jumpy slant simply looks strange and becomes the main thing you see. And lastly, the whole concept of werewolf Nazis is really underutilized. It's an idea that could have given the game its own identity with the settings, weapons, story, and all of that. Instead, all that's done with the concept is having three werewolf enemy types. Nothing else in the game reflects the idea, which just kills the novelty of it all.
So what can be said of
? It wears its inspiration right on its sleeve, and that means you know what you're getting. There is creativity in spots with this game via the music and the hulking werewolves, and really, the whole thing does function. It runs pretty smoothly, I encountered no crashes, key presses work... all of that. But when you look at the total package, it just doesn't really offer up enough to raise it above what could be considered someone's beginner
hack. The levels, the weapons, half of the enemies... they feel less like an homage to the old days and more like sprite edits mixed together with some original work. It's one thing to mimic a given game's look and technical capabilities/limitations, but there still has to be personality given to what's created in that vain. It has to have its own identity. And sadly, despite the interesting idea of Nazi werewolves, this game does little to distinguish itself from its id-made inspiration. So while it may not be a bad game per se, it's not one I can recommend due to it being all howl and no bite.

The Banner Saga is sure to entice you to visit its world through its early Disney-like artwork, but it is the game's melancholic universe along with its thoroughly thoughtful twist on tactical turn-based rpgs, accompanied by an outstanding soundtrack from the composer of the PS3 game Journey, that will keep those eyes locked to the screen.
Storywise, in short, The Banner Saga's story thrusts you into a norse-inspired world where the gods have died and the sun has stopped high in the sky. This has caused an old rock-like enemy of human and giant, the Dredge, to resurface and begin tearing a bloody swath across the land. Taking on multiple characters, you take to the road to either stop, understand, or escape this catastrophe.
The Banner Saga's gameplay is split into two portions: an Oregon Trail style caravan mangement system that puts you squarely in the shoes of quartermaster and a turn-based tactical RPG.
The former portion of the game may occasionaly have you gritting your teeth. The Banner Saga is a game that is committed to its themes of kinship, journey, and perseverance both through its story and gameplay. As such, you will not only be required to make diffcult choices through the story, but also on rationing a relatively limited single currency system that is used for purchasing items, upgrading characters, AND buying supplies for your caravan (without these, they will die of hunger). It is the managing of all these things, along with endeavoring to keep your caravan's moral high, that some may find unfair. I, on the other hand, find it exhilarating and refreshing that Stoic has enough faith in the player to acctually put them through the very challenges that characters suffers through. It will give you a sense of accomplishment for each passing day late in the game. If this kind of challenge is your thing, this game will be an excellent match for you.
If you're a fan of the combat in Final Fantasy Tactics or Fire Emblem (to a lesser degree of similarity) this will keep you excited to engage in every battle. The variation on characters losing health and armor directly tying into their strength in battle will provide you an interesting challenge. Also, there are plenty of characters and classes that bring their own unique stats and special abilities to the field that are sure to keep you devising new strategies with each new, powerful recruit. That is, if your choices do not get them killed!
Speaking of choice, certain events do feel scripted, or dare I say "linear". They are, however, judiciously mixed with tragedies that are completely avoideable. For this reason, Stoic has struck a balance between pushing forward a narrative that has an end and allowing the consquence of your choices to play out.
The game will ocassionally make you feel disheartened and it may even make you fruastrated over the difficulty of managing the caravan and party if that is not your thing, but it will challenge your sense of saftey in choice, tell you a bleak and whimsical epic, and provide you a incredibly fun tactical rpg.

The gameplay is fun and interesting. The story is epic. The characters are interesting and tend to cause you to get upset when bad things happen to them. The normal difficulty level is not harsh (no game overs) but not a breeze, either. Next playthrough I'll try on hard, and go for some more of the challenge achievements.
The combat mechanics resemble those from other turn-based tactics games. I appreciate that this game was tuned such that every single stat point matters, and such that all stats are equally important. There is no "never put points into that" stat, and your choices simply must reflect your strategy. The game also has a little bit of chess heritage in it.
In between battles, the game is a lot like Oregon Trail, and even has some easter-egg references to that. You encounter a variety of story events and have to decide how to handle each thing that comes up in your caravan. Depending on what you choose, you might gain or lose allies, fight extra battles or avoid them, acquire special items, gain or lose caravan population or morale, etc. I'm not sure what degree of randomness applies to these events after my first playthrough.
I found that I struggled with combat earlier in the game, despite already being familiar with the mechanics from
, but as I leveled my heroes and had more choices to fill my lineup with, things got easier on average. I managed to lose a couple of battles and was too weak to take on some of the optional ones, so next playthrough I'll have to be a bit more careful to unlock a few of the achievements. On the other hand, the caravan-management seemed overly easy-breezy at first, but then got very difficult towards the end. It was never clear to me whether or not I shoud stock up on supplies or if what I had was plenty to get me to the next place to buy some (or if they would be cheaper or more expensive). At any rate, I think I spent too much renown on supplies early on which cost me hero levels, and then didn't have any renown left to spend when the supplies were cheapest and then finally ran out in the final stretches of the journey, losing morale and most of the population of the caravan before the end. At that point in the game it wasn't clear whether it would have been advantageous to have an army with me or not, as those numbers didn't seem to come into play in the story events any more anyway.
Some of the events are "wars" where your caravan population are weighed against the hordes of dredge somehow, but I was never able to tell what effect these numbers had on the outcomes, or what the results would be of the various options for approach that you have to choose from. In my game, either I charged in with my team of heroes and fought a normal-looking battle against some dredge, or I chose some other option and we were defeated and lost population.

Grim Dawn is a definitely a fun game that should be played. It's a good middle ground between a regular hack and slash and Diablo; the game reminds me a lot of Titan Quest.
There's a lot of options with the "classes," none of them are the cliched "warrior, rogue, and mage" types where you are given either a sword, a bow, or a staff and stick with that the entire game. For example, you can play as what is essentially a demolitions expert that utilizes bombs and traps to damage groups and eliminate stronger enemies, or as a warrior-type class that focuses on passive and active skills and buffs and allows for many different types of weapon builds. I say "classes" in qoutation marks because you are not limited to one class, you can mix up the skills so you can be a mage that can go into stealth to get the drop on enemies or a warrior that can cripple enemies up close, then run back to take them out from afar with guns.
Due to some unknown reason Steam didn't log all the hours I played, I've played far more than under 2 hours, and I'm right around the middle of the game. The opening is slow, the first enemies are either way too easy or rush you in a gigantic group, and the jump into the first dungeon of the game is a gigantic leap in difficulty. I found it to balance out later in the game, but occasionally I will mop the floor with enemy mobs or get swarmed by enemies using ranged attacks that I can't deflect. There's a good loot system, with enchanted gear and a good variety weaponry, and you can seek out elite units of enemies to find components to upgrade gear. The combat is fun, and with the system of mixing and matching classes you can choose how the combat flows. The game plays as a straight up hack and slash if you go for the warrior-type class, a more strategic action game for the rogue and demolitionist class, and a WOW-style ability spam fest as a mage. Combat is always a blast to do.
The story is okay, nothing spectacular, you're dropped into the world with minimal background info, and it doesn't get any more deep than the usual "save the world by killing this evil monster with a weird sounding name." The choice aspect is interesting, but the choices themselves are presented way too quickly in each scenario for me as a player to care about the results. Overall it gets the job done, but its nothing groundbreaking.
Grim Dawn has some issues, but all in all it's a fun game that allows a variety of playstyles with its dual class system, and has many hours of enjoyable gameplay.

One of my all time absolute favorite games that I've put maaany hours into across multiple platforms and I'd recommend it to just about anyone. If you're the kind of person that enjoys a 'whole package' and can look past the few points where the gameplay is slightly lacking, you'll probably love this. The gameplay is great for the most part. It feels fluid and the controls are reasonably simple. As a huge fan of the game, even I'll say there are a few chapters where it's slightly lacking... mostly the 'forced' combat parts (note; you don't actually have to use combat at any point in the game, it's entirely possible to finish without ever fighting... that tends to be the more difficult option though).
But what the game does occasionally lack in gameplay, it 100% makes up for in its amazing art style, setting and score. The story is a bit short and cliché but it's definitely enjoyable and involving. The setting is stunning and the graphics hold up just fine even to todays standards, it's still one of the most beautiful games I've ever played. The soundtrack is also amazing. It fits every moment perfectly and completely matches the tone of the game. Every part of the game just comes together so well, it's a definite masterpiece.

A game about failure. Probably my favorite roguelike so far. Different ships have completely different characteristics and are fully customizable. It's definitely a challenge, though, and as a roguelike it's mostly based on chance. There are a few great mods out there that can significantly alter the gameplay as well. I'd recommend it on sale and I wouldn't pay more than 10 for it, but it's a good title to play around with and offers a very unique gameplay experience.

The Telltale formula is aging and it’s not doing so with a lot of grace. Given that this is the third The Walking Dead title under their belt it’s more egregious here than in other places. While their formula and business model are definitely working, it may be time to go and rework a bit of the foundations before they’re past the point where they’re just resting on their laurels. As a game, The Walking Dead Michonne is solid. Not terrible, not amazing, but solid. Decent. Serviceable. It does a competent job of building some interesting characters and delivering on a strong and I’d say compelling narrative, but falls short in terms of gameplay, simply because of how overused the formula is. A definite recommendation for Walking Dead fans hungry for more of the same, but maybe one of the surest signs in years that the time for Telltale Games to do something fresh is drawing close.

I love RPGs and have been playing them since the original Wizardry: Proving Grounds on the Apple II, and I have been playing paper and pencil DnD since Chainmail.
But this one is a hard one to rate because somehow it isn't my kind of game.  It is _terribly_ verbose, and you are forced to roleplay between party members.  I like a certain level of roleplay, hell it is in the name (rpg) right?  But there is a point where you spend _all_ your time talking and not doing anything.  That is _mind-numbing_, at least to me.
For those that like this sort of thing it looks to be a real gem, although it definitely has its share of issues.  Like in one particular quest you need a rain scroll which is said to have dropped nearby, but in five resets never did.  Lots of other stuff did, different each time I reloaded, but not the item I needed to complete the quest.  I eventually found someone who sold it so I was able to complete the quest, but what a _pain_!  Very unintuitive.
Also, there are lots of things lying around on the ground that you just cannot see.  I have a 70" monitor, I should be able to see most details, but many things are invisible it seems.  Fortunatly holding the <alt> key highlights a lot of them, but not all of them.  So you have to run around pressing <alt> a lot.
At the end of the day this is a Baldurs Gate clone, with really nice graphics.  I am really enjoying it for the most part, although I miss out on a lot of the story and plot because I just can't take all the damned talking!  Talk talk talk talk friggen TALK.  So I just madly click through it so I don't have to spend the majority of my play time wanting to gouge out my eyes.  So I am having fun with it now but I cannot see myself completing it.
There is role play and then there is just.. this.  Holy verbosity, Batman, were the writiers paid by the frigging word or something?!?
Anyway, if lots and lots and lots of talking is your thing, and you like the idea of role playing between characters (you have more than one active at a time, they like to talk to each other), this game really is good.
If you don't, then you might get carple tunnel just clicking through the dialog.  Oh, and choices seem to matter sometimes, so good luck with that.
So my recommendation is a good solid Maybe, based on which of the aforementioned groups you fall into.

Of all the Telltale 'Walking Dead' games, this one falls rather short.
As one other reviewer pointed out, playing as Michonne eliminates some of the tension from the game - I already know she's going to survive all three episodes, so it's just a question of which of the minor characters die. It's also quite short when compared to other episodes from Season 1 & 2. There's a couple of interesting moments, but overall it feels rather flat as a story.
The brief 'combat' sections feel like they've been speeded up somewhat. I don't think I died more than a couple of times in Seasons 1 & 2 yet here it was far more frequent, and I felt that the designers had reduced the time available for key presses to make it feel more 'intense'. Still, it's just a case of learning the correct key sequence for any combat, which is very easy.
Much more concerning for me were the technical issues I encountered, which has never happened before whilst playing a Telltale game. I could not get the game to stay in 3400x1440 resolution at all. Some of the loading screens would be correct, but as soon as I went into the game proper it would revert to a lower resolution. About 40 mins of my 2 hour playtime was spent trying to fix this issue, before I gave up. There's also a long delay whilst loading each chapter, which I've never experienced before, and this doesn't help with the flow of the game at all.
The overall impression is that of a rushed game to hit a deadline. Even the icons for the Steam achievements are just numbers - Telltale haven't bothered with the small pictoral representations of each chapter from the previous games.

I definitely recommend this game for any RPG fan, especially those who are fans of old-school cRPGs like Baldur's Gate. The game's very reminiscent of old-school RPGs where puzzles don't have obvious answers and you can get wrecked wandering in the wrong area at the wrong time.
Character customization is very extensive and every class has its own unique strengths that make them useful. Furthermore, you get to make two characters for double the fun. It's very easy to end up spending more than an hour deciding what to play. Even afterwards, it's possibly to level up any skill so if you want to play something else, you can easily do so. Later on, there's an option to respec your characters if you didn't invest stats properly.
In terms of combat, it's turn-based isometric; think Fallout 1/2 or Temple of Elemental Evil. However, it can be surprisingly fun even by modern standards. The game really forces you to think about where you should go and how to prepare for fights, whether that be taking advantage of narrow corriders, comboing spells to create environmental effects, or spamming oil barrels everywhere and cheesing the enemy.
Dialogue is typical of Larian (the developer); it's well-written and funny, but it can be pretty silly sometimes, so don't expect a serious game.  Your choices don't necessarily have a huge impact on the game events, but each choice you make affects your stats, so your characters end up developing a personality based on how you want to play them.
I've got 40 hours into this game and I'm probably only around 2/3 of the way through the game so far. If you're looking for a long well-crafted RPG, this is definitely what you want!

It's harder to recommend this than the other Ys games. It's a remake of a NES game that's so simple you don't even have an attack button, you just bump into the enemies at off-center angles to deal damage.
Ys 1 hasn't aged too gracefully, even with all the updates. The entire game is basically a fetch quest. Most of the boss fights are simple to the point of not being much fun and the game tries to compensate for its small world with constant backtracking. The power curve is also screwy since the max level is 10, so a boss will be impossible until you gain a level at which point it'll be a cakewalk. Funny enough it actually improves during the final dungeon which takes up half the length of the game.
Ys 2 is much better, the bumper combat has been improved so that it feels like less of a crapshoot, and the power curve is much smoother. The boss fights are still simple, but the new magic system makes them fun, and there's far less backtracking than in Ys 1. Both games are very uncaring towards the player. Ys 2 will let you kill yourself against a boss over and over again without telling you that you need to learn how to throw fireballs to damage it, it's usually not too hard to figure out you're missing something, but there's that.
The music for both games is pretty rad, you even get the choice betweeen the original PC soundtrack, the Chronicles soundtrack or the soundtrack from the 2001 port. It's a bit rough but still fun (mostly Ys 2). Oath and Origins are better though.
