"XCOM: Enemy Unknown" is an eligible descendant of a blockbuster strategy series "UFO". It responds to roots with piety and conscience. Yet, it's a completely different game - and I think I know the reason. It is a victim of new age in game design. A casualty of "fit to casuals" tendency.
If you want a clear picture, imagine a cute girl. She was born to sweet-hearted and smart parents. She is nice by nature, as they say. She has no problems with seducing almost every guy in her class. And then she goes to high school, where somebody occasionally points to our girl that she is too fat to be popular. Or too witty. Whatever. Our girl is too good to not abide those stupid marketing rules. And then comes diet. No fat. No protein. No books. Only to look "decent" compared to the so-called high school elite.
See, she's still real pretty. But very skinny too. And she never allows herself to be really clever. Never slips more-than-one-word-a-second from her mouth. She doesn't smile now.
Or maybe she doesn't smile just for me?
Let's take a closer look at her.
First thing we see is a very cunning make-up. Visuals and sounds are great, all those movie-type cut scenes in game are fascinating, and some of them bringing good memories for those who have seen the original UFO game.
Next thing we'll be involved is a sharp turn-based shootout with unknown lifeforms, rational and deadly. We gotta think tactical to overcome it, one wrong step and your soldier will die in vain, making others stunned and shocked, just to be shot in the next turn.
Those two parts, visuals and chess-like tactical shootouts are dominant. A primo. Sales hook. Love the game for those - and you won't be disappointed. But if you are a geek like myself or just remember good old UFO ... let's go further.
Next, we see a kind of a micromanagement system, a strategic part of game. There come the bad signs. See, economical part of "XCOM: enemy unknown" is anything but realistic. It's manageable, balanced... but dull and frustrating. Most players will spend more time personalizing suits of every soldier in squad than in "strategic" part of game.
Next… we see restrictions. The most powerful military alliance in the world have only one transport plane, for six soldiers maximum. So if aliens are striking in three places, we can secure only one of them. Two others will be infected. That’s cadaverous feature, reflecting to both size of invasion in contrast to human forces AND modern gamedev tendency to "make moral choices”. X-com organization can deploy only one aircraft at the time to shoot even a Battleship or Carrier type UFO. Only if it will be shot down, they let you send another… but even a heaviest UFO can outfly our interceptors. X-com can’t directly hire engineers and scientists – it relies on small grants from council from time to time. .. And so on, and so forth…
So. It can’t be compared with previous games ‘cause they're still way ahead in all terms, except for graphics quality.
But, returning to our girl portrait, maybe she still deserves to be loved, if only for small things? Not exactly. Her flaws are not brackets that can be turned down sometime. It’s in the thinking. A new age child, never heard of "Depeche Mode". 21st century big media project. That’s not something you'll want to spend life on. All she wants from you is a decent lunch in restaurant, sweet talk with her … and she’ll spend a night with you. Maybe even a week or month – she’s still a good girl from good parents, remember? But no love. No hard feelings. As SWAT says, “we move in, and we move out”.
It’s not a game “from fans to fans, 4 fun”. It’s a product. AAA Product. Fine by looks, working well for its price, engaging at multiplayer… but definitely not a sleep-taker. Not a masterpiece. Pompous and shiny money-taker, that’s my decision. 7.5 out of 10.

This ambitious Indy project stands above the rest with its beautiful, detailed artwork and amazing sound track. While its $25 price tag is a lot steeper than most Indy games, it boasts a deep and rich story inspired by Norse Mythology. It’s rather a nice take on fantasy and I have to say it was definitely worth the cost of admission.
It is difficult to describe exactly what kind of game The Banner Saga is. One part Tactical RPG, one part Oregon Trail, and one part choose your own adventure novel. And I mean novel, there’s a lot to read in this game. Much of the game is spent watching your caravan of warriors and/or refuges march across beautiful scenery as your supplies slowly dwindle. Occasionally there are encounters and fights mixed in here and there. Some are small scale that involve you and your band of heroes while others are large scale battles that involve your entire company. Intermixed between the travels are many encounter that make you take some excruciatingly tough decisions.
I mean really tough decisions. If I may give you an example: My ragtag group of villagers who have been fleeing from the Dredge, a giant group of evil black monsters that have pretty much annihilated everything in their path, have been walking through the wastes for more than a month now. We’ve been without food for several days and we come across a group of brigands holding up a group of peasants. The brigands offered me a bribe of food to just leave the peasants to their fate, the right thing might have been to save the peasants but then I would have even more mouths to feed and no food to feed them. I really did feel bad for taking the bribe but my people were starving to death!
The game is split up into two parties, one a group of Varl (giant) tax collectors who more or less raise a large army to confront (and eventually run away from) the Dredge. This party has a fairly straight forward and easy time of it without much problems in the ‘feeding all the mouths’ or ‘fighting big battles department’. The other party is made up of previously mentioned human refuges and they more or less are constantly on the verge of starvation and barely hold together. Even if you do get enough renown there might not even be enough food to buy at the few towns you come across and it proves to be quite the challenge to keep everyone alive and moral up during your journey.
The combat portion of the game is tactical turn based. It throws in a few interesting twists into your usual grid based combat by rotating turns between each side after each character action. Also the amount of damage a unit does is based upon their level of health so thanks to hints from a friend I’ve found in most fights the system can be exploited by weakening all enemies but not killing them. This strategy diverts significantly from most strategy type games I’ve played because it’s best to have a bunch of wounded, weak, units wasting your enemy’s turns. Combat both in the turn based portion and in the very vague ‘chose a strategy then go’ larger battles really feels like it could have come off a bit cleaner. Fighting isn’t *that* bad but it feels like it gets in the way of an amazing story rather than helping it.
And really, the story is the whole selling point of this game. It’s really quite impressive that an Indy studio pulled off an ambitious project such as this with it’s amazing musical score, deep story, and endless supply of beautiful artwork. This game is probably one of the first where the story makes everything else worth it. Even if you don’t like the trail bits or don’t really care for the combat system, if you like a good story then pick up this game. It’s deep, it’s rich, with great characters, and a dang good plot. Unfortunately it’s only Act 1 of a much larger story but from what I understand the developers didn’t have enough funds to completely finish the game and hope sales from this will help them finish the story. Since I want to experience the rest of the story, buy this game!

This is a game with the spirit of the classic RPGs but a modern design and technology. So far I love it and I highly recommend it.
Gameplay
This is where Divinity: Original Sin really shines the most, in my opinion.
There is a very interesting system that makes elements interact with each other. Is your character burning or reluctant to pass through a flake of poison? Cast a rain spell to dissipate these elements. But beware, everybody will become wet and thus will be more vulnerable to air and water spell. That means they can get frozen or electrified (stunned) more easily.
The engine also allows stuff like action happening in different places with different characters simultaneously. For example, you could split your party in two to attempt a flanking manoeuvre, or solve a puzzle that requires multiple actions at the same time.
Coop is great in this game. You can play with a friend, and not only you can take advantage of the two points aforementioned, but you also have a coop dialogue system. You and your friend (or stranger) play one of the two main characters, and you don't have to agree on everything. You can resolve conflicts with your charisma stat and a rock paper scissor game. Depending on the sentences you choose, you will get attributes points, like Compassionate or Heartless, which will give you opposite bonuses. So choose well.
Graphics
The game is quite sexy and is above the average for such RPGs. You can zoom and tumble the camera to see it better, and apart from a few blurry rock textures here and there, I have nothing to criticize. The effects of the elements in combat are quite beautiful, for instance the reflections when a surface is frozen. But don't get too distracted or you might slip on the ice.
Sound
The music is generally good, sometimes original and the themes are quite memorable. I can remember some of the tunes when not playing the game.There are voice overs and they are of good quality as well (can't say for other languages though). The sounds effects are good to very good. The ambient sounds really help to bring you more immersion.
Story / Writing
Although English is not my native language, I can say that the writing is really good. The language there is quite elevated, and it's pleasant to read.
There is a lot of humor, and characters have some depth, even the cheese merchant with his cheesy pick up lines :)
The Story is good so far, although not super original (you're gonna save the world once again). But the quests and dialogues, coupled with the graphics, sound and gameplay, are good enough to guaranty a total immersion and many hours of enjoyable gameplay (even more if you can bring a friend along).
There is also a level editor shipping with the game, so keep an eye for (potentially awesome) player content in the future.

This game is amazing. Can't stop playing it. I've played over thirty hours without finishing it because I can't stop chasing down all the different  effects your choices make over the long run. Will you let the protagonist's daughter shame him into acting against everyone's best interest or will you plunder the countryside to keep your people safe and fed? Characters will question your leadership and your motivation, and when your people are starving while they struggle against the odds you will question your leadership as well. Different play styles will have very different experiences so ymmv, but I really appreciated the minimalistic dialogue and narrative. I am tired of the walls of text or the overlong cutscenes that fantasy games throw at us  because of genre expectations. Instead of reading or hearing about what is happening in the game world with info dumps, you are there fighting the battles and influencing the decisions that are shaping the future destiny of the world's inhabitants. Finally, the painstaking attention to detail of systems you might never use like the map or the sidequests you might never explore or the complexity of strategic combinations in combat are evidence that the games was a labor of love for its creators. I hope they get to finish their trilogy. I would have happily paid more for this experience.

FTL: Faster Than Light is a really interesting game. It manages to combine space exploration, adventure game elements, and roguelike gameplay. Its randomly generated maps give a new experience each time you play, and depending on certain upgrades or members your ship has, you are able to do hidden actions in some of the game's many events, giving it even more replay value.
Slowly, it does begin to get repetitive, and the randomly generated maps can create some false difficulty depending on what may have appeared. However, its clever events, multiple achievements, and various ship layouts breathe life into the game, as does its fanbase and available mods.
Overall, it's a very great game that can keep you entertained for hours and keep you coming back, but it does have its limit in just how much you can play.
Ten dollars for a game that can easily last you 36+ hours is a fairly good deal, and adding on mods once you finish can give it even more possibilities.

The game features fully animated leaders interacting with players from a screen-filling diplomatic scene and speaking in their native language for the first time. Wars between empires feel massive as armies dominate the landscape, and combat is more exciting and intense than ever before. The addition of ranged bombardment allows players to fire weapons from behind the front lines, challenging players to develop clever strategies to guarantee victory on the battlefield. In addition, an extensive suite of community, modding and multiplayer elements also make an appearance.

This is a great game with a very interesting combination of genres. It has elements that remind me a lot of games like Oregon Trail, Walking Dead Game, Heroes of Might & Magic/King's Bounty, and FTL.
It has the wagon-train travel aspects of Oregon Trail where you have to travel unerringly in a straight line from one destination to the next, managing supplies along the way. The decision making and roleplaying situations that occur along the way invoke the Walking Dead game, where you have to choose your allies and the choices you make can come back to haunt you. The tough, tactical, turn-based combat is reminiscent of the fights from Heroes/KB. Mix all this in with risk/reward events that pop up during your journey that will have you celebrating when something goes right or crying when it doesn't, ala FTL.
Just note that this is the first chapter of a series, so it has a bit of an abrupt ending just when things start getting really interesting.

I have got to express my deep love for this game. Going back to the troop levelling, everything seems so polished and thought through, typical of a Firaxis game. You will begin to feel really attached to your troops and your prized squad of elites, and the pain of one of them dying can be horrible. The AI is also extremely challenging, and you will find yourself playing through the campaign, having to try about 3 times before you can get to see the ending. Overall, I rate this game 8/10 on its own, and 9.5/10 with the enemy within DLC, which adds mechs, maps, and terrorists (lol).

Until this game, I never felt the need to get every achievement just to eek out more playtime, but this game was good enough that I did so. Not bad, for half a game. It does well to recapture some of the frustration of playing the original, and yet improves on the experience. I have to admit, I do miss being able to target a wall and create my own doorways, I also miss setting fire to the fields in order to wipeout aliens hiding in the long grass. By the time you finish Enemy Uknown, you will feel like something is missing, and it is, the other half of the game. The developers decided to remove half the game, and sell it to you later. Once you also purchase Enemy within, and finish the game, it feels complete, like how the game should have been in the first place.
I do like the addition of council missions, it helps break up the monotony of abduction/terror sites, and shot down ufos. The game (when veiwed as a whole, including the DLC and Enemy Within expansion) expands on the original adding more content that the original missed, like augmenting soldiers both genetically and mechanically. However the lack of a ranged stun option like the original becomes a little tedious when having to expose your soldiers over and over again to try and capture an alien.
Overall I think this game is faster paced than UFO defense, and not having to explore every inch of a map in order to find that last alien hiding from your squad is a relief. I was not fussed on the financial system in game, and preferred the economy of the original more. I was also a little disappointed that I was restricted to only 6 units for my squad. Perhaps if they seek to do a sequal the squad size may increase. I think the multiplayer is lacking, as all the aliens seem underpowered. The game is geared to being overwhelemed by underpowered aliens, yet in the multiplayer you simply cannot create a comparable alien race team to take on a human soldier team asboth sides are limited to 6 units. I enjoyed playing this game, but in the end, it still kinda made me just wanna play UFO Defense again...

The Banner Saga is such a refreshing game on so many levels, the influences are very noticable, but it all feels remarably fresh. There are no dwarves, elves or other things you might expect from the 'fantasy' genre, but rather something entirely new. Gameplay to me was the weakest part, it is engaging and fun to play, and weak for this game is still very strong, but I felt myself wanting to finish a battle quick just to see where the story went. It's very easy to sink many hours into this game. Be warned though while it clocks in at around a 10 hour or so play through, this is the first part of a larger series, so don't expect a full conclusion. There is only one major issue I had and that was that I wish more of it was voice acted, most of the cutscenes are, but the rest is just text. Even though I got over that very quickly, it would have added so much to the game in my personal opinion. If you are like me and have always wanted a hand drawn Disney style Viking themed dark fantasy RPG that plays like the love child of Fire Emblem and The Organ Trail, then this game is for you.

"BEGIN." -Super Hexagon
This game is definitely a step up from its predecessor, Hexagon. Sure, Hexagon was an incredible game in and of itself, but Super Hexagon stepped up from that.
In my opinion, I don't really care about having to redo levels from the beginning each time. Games like that challenge you to go further. Hexagon did the same thing, but that was only one level. And by level I mean the succession of stage after stage, from point to hexagon.
Here's a little guide for the "Hexagon" level: The point stage is always the easiest to do. I had a bit of trouble at first on each of the levels, but it's still manageable. The line stage is a bit harder, and I've only gotten it in the "Hexagon" level (at the time I am posting this). The triangle stage was also a step up, but not due to speed. The difficulty was due to the decrease of shape sides. Usually, it went from a hexagon to a pentagon in this stage. At the square difficulty, it would either go back to a hexagon (not very likely), or become a square (more likely, and harder). Pentagon and hexagon stages are both either sped up, or there is a change in shape in one of them. After getting to the hexagon stage, the level enteres "hyper mode," and the hyper mode versions of the level will be available, unless you are playing in Arcade Mode, which unlocks all the levels for you. All of the levels increase in difficulty, from hard to hardest, and beyond.
If you do manage to complete all of the levels, then be glad that you can finally watch the ending to this rage-enducing game.
A few warnings: This game includes flashing lights, spinning objects, and rage-enducing qualities. If you suffer from any conditions in which this will trigger something, then please don't put your life at risk, and don't buy this game.
Other than that, you're good to go.

Summary: A remake of a short action-RPG with gameplay elements similar to The Legend of Zelda, Ys I is challenging and will easily frustrate the average gamer. The game is largely unforgiving and boss fights will make you want to tear your hair out as they rely more on luck and chance than actual skill. When starting the game for the first time, I highly recommend normal difficulty and secondly, to save often as there is no automatic save feature. All in all, the game is a 3.5/5.
Originally for the PC-Engine, Ys was released in 1987 and received critical and commercial acclaim. It paved the way for Ys being a flagship RPG title in Japan and with localizations in the US. Interestingly enough, the story may have roots in the mythical city of Ys (Is) that was built off of the coast of Brittany in northwestern France, a city that had befallen the same plight as Sodom and Gomorrah and due to the sinfulness of its' inhabitants found itself swallowed up by the sea. The world of the game Ys however, takes place on an island called Esteria, where the ancient kingdom of Ys once stood. A young adventurer named Adol Christin decides to cross the Stormfront, a massive seastorm isolating Esteria, and finds himself shipwrecked and rescued. Nursed back, Adol adventures through the land and a seer named Sara guides him into collecting the books of Ys. Six books that tell of the history and downfall of the ancient kingdom of Ys. As Adol goes forth to collect these books, he will meet a host of characters that shape and guide his adventure until the fateful encounter on top of Darm Tower.
Plot-wise and of course understanding that this is a remake, I found no real issues, things generally made sense and where I needed to go next was generally not a problem. There are only a few characters that you will meet reoccuringly, but given that the game is roughly 5-6 hours long, you won't develop any strong bonds with any supporting characters.
The gameplay probably needs the biggest explanation as it really doesn't fit nicely into any game I've played. Sure, the easiest way to explain it is, "it's like The Legend of Zelda," but even then there are some big differences. You don't control any type of attack animation, to attack an enemy target you simply move Adol into them. If you're offset, or hit them from the side or behind, you do damage and avoid damage to Adol. This can be frustrating sometimes, find enemies in a narrow corridor and your options are limited, enemies move at the last moment and you get damaged. Just remember that saving often is imperative in this game, there is no auto-save and you will die alot...ALOT. Just the first few battle sequences are challenging and once you start your first boss battle it will be harsh and unforgiving. Adol does level up with each monster he defeats, but there is a cap at Level 10, which you will probably have by mid-game. You can't simply farm yourself or strongarm yourself through the game, and being anything less than level 10 by the time you tackle Darm Tower is suicide.
There are some bosses that will just make you livid and frustrate you. The final boss is the perfect example, because it's simply a matter of luck and chance rather than skill that will carry you to win. The first boss can also frustrate new players because of how unforgiving one wrong move can be, but remember to save before each boss battle and to just keep trying. It took me about 40 tries to get the final boss, and the more you play it the easier it will become to predict his pathway.
The graphics is so-so, it's a remake but obviously there are limitations in how much could be changed without alientating the fans. The music is fantastic in some levels, especially when you start up Darm Tower, and although I never played the original, I'm guessing that they are remakes from the original PC-Engine tunes.
Overall, if you want a quick but challenging action-RPG, I would recommend Ys I. I'm planning on playing the second game, and with everything I've read it should improve on everything from the first game. 3.5/5

So this finally went on sale enough on another site where I felt like I could finally quit being such a cheapskate and buy this game that I've wanted for a long time now.  I've got to say that it would have been more than worth it at full price.
The graphics are great.  The game looks beautiful and exploring the city is a blast.  The parkour system where you're running and jumping and flying through the air is way more fun than I ever thought it could be.  Unlocking the grappling hook just makes it that much more enjoyable and you whizz along even faster than before.  I absolutely love digging through abandoned houses, climbing through windows, garage doors, and holes in the roof.  Picking locks on doors, chests, and lockers to find all sorts of goodies left abandoned by their owners.
The entire atmosphere of the game is just excellent.  Combat is fun and, for me at least, I find myself almost exclusively relying on melee weapons and very rarely using firearms.  (Except in a few fights against a few specific zombie / human types.)  If I had to give the game a knock it would be the story.  You're not going to find anything earth shatteringly compelling or original here.  A secret agent dropped into a land ravaged by zombies and you need to recover those secret agency files that you secret leadership happened to leave there that was stolen by bad guy.
It's not that the story is bad it's just that it's not what it could be.
I highly recommend leaving your games public, both so that others can join them and for Night Invasions.  For me the first day I was playing some guy that had months into the game joined mine to play along.  He threw me weapons that I really shouldn't have had and I was suddenly running around killing everything that moved with one shot.  As fun and as awesome as it was it did break the game for a little while.  Any sense of danger was gone as I could two shot even the big goons.  Eventually they broke though and I was back to my usual stuff.
While Dying Light can be tense and scary during the day Night takes it to a whole 'nother level.  Night Invasions, like I mentioned before, are crazy.  It's when another person joins your game and plays as this special infected zombie.  They have infinite lives (with a longer respawn timer than you) and five "nests" that they need to protect.  The humans get 10 lives with the goal to destroy those nests.  Kill all the nests before you run out of lives and you win.  It can be incredibly challenging and incredibly fun.  I highly recommend not just sleeping through every night time.  No matter how scary it can be!
A definite buy.  I love Dying Light.

Ys Chronicles+ is a decent two-for-one package, though mostly only for the second of the two games provided.
was originally developed in the 80's as one of Falcom's first games, and its age clearly shows. Normal enemies are all incapable of anything but walking in the four cardinal directions and attempting to ram your character for damage, with the only difference between enemies being the damage they deal, the amount of hits it takes to kill them, and the speed at which they move. It ends up making for pretty dull, repetitive combat once you get the handle of the bump combat system. This is slightly broken up by the boss fights, but sadly boss design typically only falls into one of two categories: Ridiculously easy, or obnoxiously random/luck based.
Money and exp distribution in
is somewhat unbalanced as well. You'll most likely reach the low level cap well before even starting the final dungeon (which makes up about half the game). You'll also get tons of money drops in the final dungeon, all of which is completely useless since you can't backtrack out of the last dungeon to buy more items. There is a positive side to this, however, as it does mean you can bypass late-game enemies without worrying about missing out on anything (unless you're an achievement completionist).
does have a few redeeming traits, though. There's a wide selection of difficulty levels to accomodate any player. The combat system is extremely simple and easy to pick up, and as a whole, the game is short enough for the combat to avoid getting
tedious and repetitive. The story is decent with a fairly wide variety of characters. The updated visuals look nice, and the rearranged rock soundtrack is absolutely kickass.
Overall,
is not
bad of a game, but its age clearly shows. I would only recommend
to players who are already fans of the Ys franchise. For those just looking to get into the Ys universe, I'd instead recommend starting with this game's prequel,
.
Now this is a massive step up from before.
pretty much addresses everything that was wrong with
fantastically.
Combat is
more engaging. Basic enemies can now move in more than the basic four directions, and have varying traits beyond boasting different strength, HP, and speed values. Some enemies are immune to certain types of damage, some have projectile attacks, and some have much more erratic movement patterns than others. Boss design is much stronger in this game as well. Successfully taking one down feels like a good accomplishment, rather than being a free victory or a matter of getting a good dice roll.
Another big change is the introduction of a magic system. This allows for alternative combat options to the old bump system. You can use fire magic to attack at a range, time magic to freeze enemies and make them easier to kill, or alter magic to turn yourself into a demon and avoid enemies altogether. The amount of detail put into the alter magic is impressive; every single enemy spawn in the game has unique dialogue that you can trigger while in demon form.
The level system is now broken up from a short 10 level system to a more game-length-appropriate 55 level system. This allows for more consistent growth throughout the game with level-ups occurring at a fairly frequent pace. There is also a significantly higher amount of items for purchase throughout the game, ensuring that gold keeps its value throughout the duration of the game without abruptly becoming totally useless halfway through.
The strong traits from
are also present here: Good variety of difficulty levels, strong storyline and cast of characters, nice visuals, and a robust modernized rock soundtrack. The game is somewhat longer than
, but thanks to all the fixes to the problems mentioned above, that instead simply amounts to there being more of a good thing.
Overall,
manages to take the same formula from
and turn it into something pretty impressive, especially considering its age. It still stands up remarkably well today, and it's a game I would not hesitate to recommend to anyone who is interested in a more old-school action RPG.

As far as remakes go, this isn't half bad. It suffers from many of the same problems the original did, like confusing dungeon layouts and an occasionally directionless objective. The Ys I ending/Ys II intro cutscene also doesn't make a whole lot of sense compared to previous versions, It feels a lot more rushed. The addition of new escort missions is also somewhat aggravating.
That being said, the originals were great games and the Chronicles+ remakes are no exception. The dialogue has been touched up and it makes the story a lot easier to follow.
The improved graphics are great, although a part of me misses the brighter colors of the originals. But by far the biggest improvement is the gameplay. The addition of 360 degree movement really takes away the frustrating aspects of the originals, especially during boss fights.
The ability to choose between different versions of the soundtracks released throughout the years is a nice bonus (although an option for the Turbografx-CD music would've been nice)
Overall, if you've never played Ys I & II before, or if you have and just want to re-experience them, this is a perfectly fine way to play them.

This is the review for the first episode of the game.
I'm going to try to keep it fairly short. I completed the first episode about 5 minutes ago, and was overall pretty impressed with the game. It isn't as emotion-filled, story heavy, or decisive as the "canon," (Season 1, 2) games, but is unique, and good in it's own way. The game starts off promising, and then declines for a little while. There is *SEMI SPOILER* a flashback in the beginning of the game, that has some QTEs and is very, "cool," to say the least. */SEMI SPOILER* After this, the game seems a little boring as it's mostly just dialogue. However, once you essentially leave the area you were just in, it is easy to see the potential in this mini-series. First of all, this game is littered with QTEs, which is not a bad thing because they are fun, use the same couple buttons (Q, E, WASD) and give you enough time to react. This connects into this games next unique feature; it's violence. You kill quite alot of zombies within the first few minutes to say the least, and while it dies down a little after that, the killing is still present. Right now, I don't want to spoil anything else, so I'll end this review in the next few sentences, but alot of other things are present in this game, that aren't in the other TWD games, but if I were to mention them, it'd ruin the fun. Anyways, the last thing for now that I adore in this game, is that just like in the comics and show, Michonne is a very independent, quiet, and brave character. In the previous games, you were usually narrowed down dialogue-wise with a nice option, neutral option,or sarcastic/anry option. Michonne however is very open-minded, and says what she thinks. You can be more straight forward and honest, you can "distract" the person you're talking to, you can share your mind on what someone should do, and you can just be alot more straightforward. You don't have to be the nice guy Lee was, or the sweet yet sarcastic girl Clem was. You can actually choose how Michonne is, and you can help her getover her past, or struggle for a possible "solution." She can help other, or focus on herself, and that is pretty much the focus of this game, or episode at least. I do not know if it is worth $15 at the moment, but if that includes all 3 episodes, or I can get the other 2 for around $5, then it is definitley worth it. This game is really good, it's just not quite the same game as the other TWD games, or other Telltale games.
Props to Telltale though- try to keep the episodes coming out pretty quick.
And don't forget, this isn't an excuse to release season 3 later, so get to it.

Let's get this out of the way, is this game worth buying even in Early Access? Yes.
Why? Well, first of all, it's further along than most early access games. I've already put over 40 hours into the game and still haven't seen most of chapter 2. The amount of content is huge.
But while content is king, gameplay is God for most. The easiest way to describe the game is to compare it to Titan's Quest, but improved. It makes sense since Crate Entertainment is made up of some of the same people who worked on Titan's Quest. It's also built on the same engine, though that's been improved too. The art style is more how I wanted Diablo 3 to look, and I absolutely love it.
Unlike Diablo 3, in Grim Dawn you can have two skillsets or you can just stick with one, but each level only gives you three points to spread over the skillsets, so you have to choose. You also are able to choose your attribute points, though there are only three choices. It's simplified, but not to the point of Diablo 3.
The game has a faction system that looks like it could be promising later on, but at the moment it's simple and mostly meaningless. You gain fame and reputation through killing big bosses and monsters which can open up other side quests, but you'll usually open these up just from playing normally and not paying attention to your fame stats.
I dropped $58 on this game during its kickstarter, it was money I had saved for Diablo 3. I don't regret a penny, and after picking up Diablo 3 on sale, I think I made the right choice.
But, it is in early access so there are chances for bugs. I haven't ran into any since they've released  Act 2, but keep in mind it's still a work in progress, but even then it's better in my opinion than some full release games.
If you love ARPGs then you owe it to yourself to pick up this game, especially when it's only $25.

Orcs Must Die! is yet another take on the now ubiquitous action-tower defense genre. In many ways, it's similar to Dungeon Defenders (see previous review), but you play as only one character and there is no customization, other than what traps you decide to use on each level. That doesn't make it bad, however. In fact, it's a real plus in the game's favor... as the main character is, well, quite a character! I guarantee his goofy lines will bring a smile to your face. Gameplay is standard fare for the genre - progress through a series of levels in which you must set up traps and defend your magic rift from hordes of orcs. Every new level completed adds a new trap or ally to your arsenal, making for a smooth progression (though nothing is ever really a cakewalk). You will be challenged, for sure... especially on later levels. If you're looking for a new tower defense game (or maybe looking to try one for the first time), Orcs Must Die is about as solid as they come. Give it a look!

The Banner Saga is made up of three parts:
(a)
-- You assume the roles of fixed characters and guide them through the story, in a choose-your-own-adventure style, albeit in a relatively linear way.
(b)
-- You manage a viking caravan that's almost always in peril, with enemies constantly on its heels.
(c)
-- You assemble your heroes (1-6 of them) and fight against various enemies on a grid-board. This part of the game is probably the one you'll spend more time with.
The first thing you've probably noticed about The Banner Saga is the uniquely
. Just look, if you haven't. What you can't actually "experience", unless you actually play the game, is the excellent bonding of the
with the visuals and the atmosphere it creates. That's also unique and powerful, worth another thumbs up. Now, lets get to the main course, the
. If you've played Factions, the free-to-play offspring release in March 2013, you know what I'm talking about. The combat mechanics are very sharp and allow for great simplicity and remarkable strategy depth, at the same time! It's the paragon of the "easy to learn but hard to master" type of game. Finally, the last merit I'm gonna give to the game is the marvelous lore and deeply detailed
they have created. It takes a lot off of the viking/Norse history, but it also blends-in many fantasy themes in a very successful way.
OK, enough with the good stuff. Lets see the bad ones. Actually, what hurts most about this game is its own extremely high potential. I mean, it offers so much potential that seeing it come short of that is enough to let you down. For me, the biggest problem about the game is that the final product feels a little
, kinda unfinished in the sense of
. There aren't big flaws in the core mechanics of the game, but it could use a lot more polishing. I'm gonna bring up some specific issues so that you understand what I mean:
-- Caravan/Survival balancing issues : Sometimes the game feels too hard for its own sake. I mean, it's supposed to be hard, about survival and all, but at some points it just feels wrong and falls out of perspective.
This was addressed, to some extent, by the first patch. Chapter 6 is now kinda easier, but there's still no incentive to try to keep your clansmen alive, or have more join you...
-- Language & Localizations: In my opinion, the language used is often too "casual American" styled, something that hits bad with respect to the viking theme of the world. Also, the quality of some localizations was sub-standard, according to native speakers.
-- Inconsistencies and awkward "story delivery" : The game is all about a branching story line, where each choice you make has consequences. That's fine. Problem is that it feels like some story parts don't quite glue together, or the pacing of the story changes from Chapter to Chapter sometimes putting you off. That's more noticeable near the end of the game, where the pace dramatically picks up, and you are bombarded by a lot events all at once, that you barely have time to digest. Also, I could argue that the ending sequence, despite its emotional strength, is a little wanting in view of the climax that precedes it. Finally, it's quite evident that the game is just the first part of the proclaimed trilogy, so it leaves a lot of unanswered questions. It's not a cliffhanger per se, but close enough.
To conclude, I'm giving it the thumbs up because it's a beauty to behold and has
(visuals, music, battle system, theme/lore). Also, I believe that most of the problems I found can be easily addressed with patches without meaning that the game is "bad" in its release state. I'll say it once more --

This is pretty much everything I could have wanted in a Baldur's Gate-style RPG.
You can steal pretty much everything that isn't nailed down, but you can't do it when anyone is watching, lest they alert the guards. You can bash doors and chests open if you don't have a thief in your party.
There are a number of classes in addition to the classic 4 (Fighter, Mage, Cleric, Thief), but you can customize them to however you'd like them if you don't like what Larian offers.
Turn based combat where the environment affects your spells (Shocking a nearby enemy while it's raining may have the desired effect of stunning them, but it may also arc and stun yourself too!)
Quests have multiple ways to solve them, which is sort of necessary, as you're limited to two party members.
Oh, and when two different people play the two characters? You can argue about the actions you take and your dialog choices can affect how other NPCs react to you and how well you can persuade them to do things they may not want to, via Intimidation, Charm, and appealing to Reason.
I think my only real critique is that in combat, it's super easy to accidentally target something you didn't mean to and thus waste a turn, possibly to lethal outcomes.
Overall, it's a fantastically fun game that takes the best parts of Planescape: Torment and Fallout 2. The competitive co-op is just icing on the cake.

This game captures the spirit of Baldurs Gate perfectly!

Graphics are really good and it runs flawless on my machine. The music is not superepic but fits in nicely in all the areas.
Although there is almost no voice-acting the dialogues are well written and there is plenty to explore if you are interested in the lore!
Where the game REALLY shines is the tactical combat. It starts out very good and gets better and better and better.
At level 10 you have so many spells and skills and every single one is usable either with the enviorment or works as a catalyst with other spells - this is the best tactical combat I have EVER experienced!
I don't know how huge D:OS is. The world just invites me to explore (no quest markers, no quest compass - you have to THINK!) and I cannot remember the last time a game has hooked me in that level. After 22 hours I finished everything around the first village - and that is when the story begins!
The quests have a wide reach from funny to creative to combat to explore.
And the best thing : If you think of a creative way to solve quests or riddle-situations (there are a lot!) - it usually works!
I did not experience a single situation in which I thought "damn, this HAD to work now, but it didn't!"
And it gets better and better : This game is actually playable in coop from start to finish! Hell, it is MEANT to be played cooperatively!
In addition to the 2 main characters you can recruit 2 more heros. The downside is that these are not customizeable but there are so many options to choose from that it does not really matter, because you can branch them out any way you like anyway.
There are no classes in this game, so feel free to experiment. I would even recommend to do so. For example one of my characters started out as a healer and is now a 2hand-tank-cleric-witch and extremely powerfull! This game rewards you to play a hybrid, not like other games! Even with just 1 point in witchcraft (for example) you can use a high-lvl witchcraft spell, but have to pay more action-points to use it in combat. This is just an awesome system!
Every npc you meet - and sometimes enemies as well - want to trade stuff with you!
If you have a rogue in your party (which I also recommend!) you will spend hours and hours to steal all the good stuff from the nice people in the towns ^^ But beware - if you get cought, you will have to fight. I would recommend loading a quicksave if that happens.
Oh, and have you ever been angry about doors in other games? Or chests that you do not have a key for?
In D:OS everything works as it logically should : burn down a door with mighty fire-spells, break a chest with your sword or even put a chest in your inventory for later, if you hope to find a key! That is just PURE AWESOMENESS!
You can even teleport things like barrels and crates around! Block enemys with them, put an oil-barrel from your inventory next to a boss, ignite the oil and then cast a rain-spell to transform the burning field into a steamcloud followed by a lightning strike that will stun all the wet enemies at once! But beware - such a reaction can hit your party too, with your OWN spells! So always pay attention to positioning!
I could go on and on and on, this game had me hooked from the start and I did not have it in my "interesting game"-list.
Check it out, play it, you won't regret it!

If I had to sum up the experience of Ys I & II in one word it would be "Charming".
Both games are very short compared to your average jRPG and the stories fit together really well, so that it's like playing two halves of the same great title. The sprite and character portrait artwork, whether you choose the older or newer style for portraits, is beautiful. As are the soundtracks. Likewise the bump combat system is fun and fast once you get into it (I highly recommend using a controller) and the magic system mixes things up a bit for boss battles in Y II.
While I don't think there's a bad song in either game, they do suffer a bit from a shortage of tracks. Most areas have only one song, and some songs are spread out over several areas. This problem is alleviated somewhat by the ability to change which version of the soundtrack you're listening to on the fly. Tired of the Chronicles orchestration? Switch to the Complete edition's midi rendition, tired of that? Switch to the original PC-88 version. You can do the same for character portrait style if you want to change that at any point in the game.
Probably the biggest problem with this package is the bosses for Y I, in that they're all terrible and mostly very easy. The Ys I end boss battle is especially bad because it hinges a great deal on luck. But don't let these minor annoyances stop you from enjoying two beautiful and surprisingly touching classics of the jRPG genre. Playing them it's not hard to see why they spawned such an enduring franchise. And honestly how many games let you turn into a kangaroo monster and go back to speak to every non-boss enemy in the game if you want to?

At the time of posting I have exactly 100 games on steam, and because of my limited time most of them are untouched. Yet somehow FTL still has over forty hours logged on it, with countless epic games engraved in my memory even though I've only actually beaten it twice. Lots of games claim to do a lot with a little, but this game has you attaching personality and sentiment to the little clusters of pixels that serve as your crew just by giving them a name and the ability to walk around.
By the end of a long game, I feel like I've written--no LIVED--a novel about a hardbitten crew plying their way in an unforgiving galaxy. This game is the perfect example of situationally dependent strategy.
It is a fantastic single player experience, but still long for one thing: head-to-head combat. Picture this, you and an opponent spawn at mega-store with a certain amount of scrap to kit your ships out, and then you jump into battle with each other, seeing each other for the first time. The pausing issue could be solved by just making pause time limited, or nonexistent for a real hectic challenge.
+++EDIT+++
The Advanced Edition content is absolutely fantastic. The new ships and lore in the form of the Lanius are an absolute joy, but veteran players will appreciate the more subtle changes. The ability to rename crew, even found crew, mid-voyage is awesome, and the ability to save crew positions and send them back there with a single click is handy as well.

I don't have the best internet but I deserve to play the game I bought damn it. I shouldn't have to find a hack to a game I own so I can run it offline... (End edit.)
Start game = Start Uplay a few times before the game will ever begin to start starting.
Once in you start on top of a slope ready 2 shred. Unless you're like me in which case it's straight to the settings to make it stop playing at 800x600 on your 4k display.
Most people I've seen have been comparing this to Skate and I can see why. The game feels very much like that emptyish world made just for you to play in. However Skates controls and mechanics were tight and responsive. ♥♥♥♥ing up meant you did a bad not the game.
This game has none of that. It's the kind of thing where when pushing entirely left or right theres only a chance your character will listen. Nothing you do matters because at any point in time your character may just decide he likes that tree/rock.
In the looks department this game is glory. It shines and damn near makes up for the♥♥♥♥♥♥ Half of the time I would end up focusing more on the environment than I did the player model because trying to land tricks is just such a hassle. Though I do definitely feel like if you spent to long playing everything would probably start pretty samey, due in part to the somewhat small(er than you'd expect) map.
All in all the game is ok. It's the kind of thing where if you can push past the ♥♥♥♥ awful controls I'm sure you could have a nice time. But at the same time be very ready to occasionally get stuck and unable to turn your board.
Also similar to how the other three sports feel I'm gonna tack this last bit on. The skiing, paragliding, and squirrel suit are all pretty lack luster and control just as lame. Paragliding though? I don't even know how to get points! The tricks seemed mostly like swinging so??? I guess?
Tl;Dr If you want to enjoy some pretty good views, don't care about Uplay, don't mind having little to no control at many many points, and really enjoy tiny snowballs flicking up from your board to tumble through the snow (don't worry I love it too) go for it on sale. You're relaxing in the lounge of your spaceship when the bucket list app on your phone alerts you to the fact that there is something you still have not yet done in life: cliff dive into the deepest caverns on alien planets. So you grab your A.I. companion drone, wing suit and rocket boots and get ready to jump!
Planet diver is a different take on the minimalist "runner" style of games. You're on a non-stop collision course with the finish line (unless you're in a survival mode where you just keep falling), your weapon is either your limited dash or your companion (depending on upgrades), and your job is to avoid or destroy obstacles in your path while gathering "starstuff" to buy new upgrades/costumes/music.
Controls are very simple: left and right or A and D to move left and right along your track, down or S to perform a dash attack and increase your speed, and W or up to perform a dual purpose "evade-brake" that both evades obstacles and drops your speed to the lowest rate.
Each fall (run) takes place in a semi-randomly generated pit divided into invisible lanes, littered with a variety of enemies, obstacles, and starstuff. Enemies and mobile obstacles, such as boulders, can be evaded or destroyed, while immobile obstacles, such as protruting walls, separated walls and flame geysers, must be avoided entirely. falling through starstuff collects it to be used at the shop between falls, with your current speed acting as a collection modifier: the faster you are, the more you get per collection.
The character has two gauges: Health and Dash. Depending on upgrades, the character han have 1-3 health and 1-4 dashes. Striking any obstacles take away one health, which is restored by collecting starstuff or destroying enemies; striking an obstacle while at less than one helth ends the run. Each time a dash it performed, one point of the dash gauge is consumed; dashes regenerate over time and by evade-braking.
Beyond regular gameplay, there are also per-level missions, a speed run timer, and planetary bosses. Level missions are objectives attached to each level, such as "kill X bats" or "keep an average speed rating of X", that award starstuff and rating stars upon completion. The speed run gauge tracks how quickly you complete a fall and is purely competitive. At the end of each planet is a boss with its own mechanics to beat; defeat each boss to unlock the next planet and ultimately complete story mode.
While I have some personal qualms over the dialogue character design, overall the game is
. I highly recommend this game to any reflex gamer or anybody loooking for a "coffee break" game, and hope to see great things in the future If this is the expected quality of this developer,

I'm surprised at just how much of a blast I'm having playing this game!  I mean, when Janelle recommended it to me it sounded cool -- "two-player Neverwinter Nights" is enough of a recommendation -- but after playing it for an hour or two we couldn't stop.  There's a murder mystery to solve right off the bat in which the culprit isn't obvious and you have to use your own wits to track down leads -- no blinking "the evidence is right here" quest arrow.
In amongst that, you get to run around fighting monsters in a truly fun strategy RPG type system.  It works a lot like X-COM or Wasteland 2 (Action Points and all that) but with some almost puzzle-like additions.  For instance, if you break open a water barrel it will create a puddle over a wide area; then you can shoot the puddle with a fire arrow to make it into a steam cloud that hides you from archers, or shoot it with a lightning arrow to electrify it and stun all enemies standing in it, or shoot it with an ice arrow to freeze it and make enemies that run across it fall down.  And of course the abilities you've chosen for your character change your options a ton -- teleport behind that guy and back-stab him, make yourself immune to flames and cause a poison gas explosion...
It's also quite a challenge (but not TOO hard)... we have to try two or three times to succeed at most encounters.  A couple of them it's been more like a dozen times, but there are so many ways to approach each one that even trying again and again doesn't get old.  (Of course, we could turn down the difficulty, but...)
Anyway, just a lot of fun.

Fun game remniscent of Ultima/Divinity/etc, where there is plenty of nooks and corners to explore, but like in Dragon Age origins, you need to upgrade your arsenal a bit before you head into combat. If you rush in, prepare for trouble. But make it double. MEOWTH, That's right! When i played the beta, it revolved around a center town hub, where the main quest seems to play out around that area, but it goes into alot of depth as you continue, without spoiling anything, don't expect a large open world, but more of a purposeful community, where every crate can help you out, literally. Besides the loot inside, you can drag crates ontop of mines to detonate them. Please don't teamkill... not like in magicka where it is funny, it is hard to get res scrolls, but play however you want.
Mages start off with less actions and later on you can buy summon scrolls and upgrade your actions at lvl 7 to double with glass cannon talent. The ice elemental is viciously powerful and now comes with piercing shard, useable at lvl 7 with enough points in hydrosophist ability. but make sure to buy new skills for any class you want to use as your main, you aren't tied down to a class, but mages are already high in INT so they would work best for healers and casters. You can mix and match any class with any skills you desire, but without the corresponding attribute raised, there might be a reduction in effectiveness, for ex: Trying to cast a buff with low int  might give you -20% chance to succeed.
AP is what makes the turn based combat quite unique. Many factors affect AP utilization. Constitution affects max HP but also max AP limit (max of 20)
Perception includes starting battle with higher AP
Speed is how much AP you recover at end of turn (Glass cannon talent doubles this but halves HP)
Any attribute you excel at like INT for a mage, reduces AP usage for corresponding skills/abilities.
In the beginning you might need 5 AP for a beginner spell, but as you add INT it might go down to 3...
You should generously use the F5 quicksave function especially before big battles, so you can get the drop on enemies, such as putting down oil slicks on the ground or tossing a boulder onto group of enemies, or buffing your teammate/ summoning to give you slight advantage going into combat, wildfire will haste you and should be used in beginning or right before combat, especially without the glass cannon talent. You can summon an elemental and fortify it on your first turn in battle, so it becomes armored... Tons of freedom in combat and selecting skills. You can even carry around equipment like +1 blacksmithing to only equip when you need to repair to save your skillpoints for more useful ones.
The game is tough in the beginning, because you have no good equipment, armor, or skills. Just start stealing paintings, light gold cups, and you will soon be reeling in the big ones. (Cough, try cecil's house directly above the market in town hall, you can steal many paintings as long as you sneak and quicksave often)
Synergy is something to consider when building a team. If you think you can handle two lone wolf characters (I recommend this for a challenge and for less hectic experience) You need to compliment your teammates well such as buffing damage or defense of teammates and teleporting enemies to areas where your warrior can give them a good run for their money.
The game is de-leveled meaning that anything you kill is gone forever, and also don't really change in level but skills and items do scale as you go on, including what merchants sell, so don't be discouraged if you only see low level spellbooks as a low level character yourself... Reload quicksaves infront of chests (Especially ornate chests) As this randomizes the contents every time, and try to find +1 armors or good weapons. I suggest +1 constitution or +1speed/ crafting skills so you can toggle them in/out to save on actually spending points into them.
If you are still reading this you care too much about little details or you are trying to figure out how to play correctly. If you are dying often, it is because you can't beat them yet, sell some stolen paintings , explore different areas like the cemetary early game with a shovel, and start talking up the town, but don't kill gaurds or else the whole game will become hostile to you including the gatekeeper of spoiler.
Just save alot and don't get mad if you die because it means you aren't ready or you aren't using the right tactics for your arsenal. Skills and AP are your best friend in the game, and it is always always always good to have a heal skill for your team, cure wounds has long cooldown in manatarms tree, while Hydrosophist has a short cool down recommended skill for the job... Out of battle always heal up! K! Have fun!

Pros
The story/journey is phenomenal
The decision making (while forcing you down a linear path to your next main progression point) is often weighty and mentally taxing.  If you let yourself get immersed, you will be rewarded.
The combat itself is quite fun, though it has a few drawbacks.  You never get the opportunity to truly play around with the systems/characters/strategy side of things.  This is largely tied to.....
Cons
Renown.  It is used for supplies, character upgrades and items.  While it serves its purpose of "hard decisions", it simply isn't fun. Once upon a time, they used to make role playing games for computers.   They weren't strategy/action/shooter hybrids. They weren't massively multiplayer.  They were just RPGs -- no hypens, no prefixes.  They had titles like Ultima, Baldur's Gate, Icewind Dale, Fallout (1 & 2), Neverwinter Nights, Arcanum, Dragon Age: Origins.  These were awesome games and a lot of people loved them, but game publishers decided that they weren't generating enough revenue so they stopped making them.
Larian has successfully revived a dead genre and updated it in a meaningful way.  And they somehow managed it without a publisher and the compromises that come along with them.  I could list the reasons why I love this game, but I really want to get back to playing.  So all I'll say is this:  if you've ever enjoyed a real computer RPG, get this game.  If you're sick of gear grinding, F2P schemes, and consolization, buy this game.  Don't wait for a sale.  Just click the button and buy it.  You can thank me later.

So this finally went on sale enough on another site where I felt like I could finally quit being such a cheapskate and buy this game that I've wanted for a long time now.  I've got to say that it would have been more than worth it at full price.
The graphics are great.  The game looks beautiful and exploring the city is a blast.  The parkour system where you're running and jumping and flying through the air is way more fun than I ever thought it could be.  Unlocking the grappling hook just makes it that much more enjoyable and you whizz along even faster than before.  I absolutely love digging through abandoned houses, climbing through windows, garage doors, and holes in the roof.  Picking locks on doors, chests, and lockers to find all sorts of goodies left abandoned by their owners.
The entire atmosphere of the game is just excellent.  Combat is fun and, for me at least, I find myself almost exclusively relying on melee weapons and very rarely using firearms.  (Except in a few fights against a few specific zombie / human types.)  If I had to give the game a knock it would be the story.  You're not going to find anything earth shatteringly compelling or original here.  A secret agent dropped into a land ravaged by zombies and you need to recover those secret agency files that you secret leadership happened to leave there that was stolen by bad guy.
It's not that the story is bad it's just that it's not what it could be.
I highly recommend leaving your games public, both so that others can join them and for Night Invasions.  For me the first day I was playing some guy that had months into the game joined mine to play along.  He threw me weapons that I really shouldn't have had and I was suddenly running around killing everything that moved with one shot.  As fun and as awesome as it was it did break the game for a little while.  Any sense of danger was gone as I could two shot even the big goons.  Eventually they broke though and I was back to my usual stuff.
While Dying Light can be tense and scary during the day Night takes it to a whole 'nother level.  Night Invasions, like I mentioned before, are crazy.  It's when another person joins your game and plays as this special infected zombie.  They have infinite lives (with a longer respawn timer than you) and five "nests" that they need to protect.  The humans get 10 lives with the goal to destroy those nests.  Kill all the nests before you run out of lives and you win.  It can be incredibly challenging and incredibly fun.  I highly recommend not just sleeping through every night time.  No matter how scary it can be!
A definite buy.  I love Dying Light.

First of all, this game is easily the best zombie game in existence.  The parkour is phenomenal, and it complements the combat very well.  The fighting is as fun as the running, but don't expect to be a ninja at the beginning of the game.  The protagonist, Kyle Crane, hasn't much stamina, so the game has a slow start during which one needs to focus on survival; on finding enough weapons.  Durability is a huge aspect of this game.  Things break, and, once things break, they don't return.  Minecraft style.  The game doesn't take long to speed up, though.  Before you know it, your stats will be maxed out, and you'll be rolling your eyes at an inventory that's stuffed with weapons.  If the beginning is too slow for you, I find it necessary to tell you that there is a New Game Plus option.  You keep your inventory and your abilities.  Meanwhile, you enjoy the game, again.  Definitely don't worry about replayability.

Whereas games like Super Mario Brothers complicated gameplay by requiring you to jump atop the heads of foes, Ys requires that you merely bump into them, and it is wonderful!
For a game that can be played largely by only ever touching the directional pad and using a few buttons to navigate menus, I found the gameplay to be incredibly enjoyable. It's a top down adventure RPG, with elements of Metroidvania - lots of backtracking and puzzle solving, finding items, finding uses for items that open new paths. Plenty of NPCs to talk to. The game manages to make some challenging boss fights with incredibly simple mechanics.
The visual style is incredibly pleasing to look at, the music was beyond surprising - it sounds almost piece for piece like something from Castlevania: Order of Ecclesia, and the pace of the music suits the breezy combat well!
All in all, I wasn't expecting to even play the game - I picked it up incredibly cheap off a Steam sale. Instead, I've been incredibly surprised with a delightful game with superb presentation and classic gameplay that left me with nothing but good feelings. And I've only finished Ys 1, the first game of the pack.

Add some very nice music and voicework, and you get one of the definitive games of 2011.

Steep is a weird game. A love letter to exploring the picturesque Swiss Alps by way of extreme sports, it toes the line between realism and Red Bull guzzling, MTV goofiness. It's built for scale and spectacle, but digging deeper to actually play the game can feel like you're on a team of beta testers, sharing challenges you pulled out of your♥♥♥♥♥and turning a blind eye to the glaring glitches and rough edges. It suffers from an identity crisis; one minute you'll be paragliding peacefully above a glacier while your avatar narrates a somber diary of conquering the wilderness, fighting oxygen deprivation and dehydration. Then you'll be following a literal ghost rider through the mouths of Ubisoft's Raving Rabbids mascots or being lectured by a stereotypical New York agent for not hitting enough “sick” kickflips. Or a mountain will try to intimidate you, reciting some Robert Frost style poetry. Steep is best played with an open mind. A really open mind...
 
  The game can be stunningly gorgeous; the scale of the mountain range is very impressive and boasts some of the most realistic looking representation of snow I've seen. The glittering of the sun off of fresh powder in particular is approaching levels of photorealism. The detail of your character is quite sharp as well, especially considering the vast amount of unlockable accessories available to outfit him/her in. Traversing the frozen environment also leaves convincing tracks as you sink into the drifts, climbing steep slopes to reach points of interest. An applaudable amount of work and artistry went into the snow, but some of the elements surrounding it look out of place. Rocky surfaces can look like smears painted with a broad brush, often visibly, hastily thrown together at artificially rough angles and clipping through each other. Trees and glaciers are carbon copies of each other, leading to stretches of boring, repeating terrain. But the large scale picture is the reason for playing, and these are the compromises of a completely open, load-free playground.
 
  You have five modes of transport at your disposal: skiing, snowboarding, paragliding, wing gliding, and walking. Skiing and snowboarding are similar and the challenges that feature them are interchangeable. You have very simple controls with these two: steer with the left stick, the right stick cuts sharply, you hold and release jump to ollie, and from there you can spin and grab. For the most part, though, you're at the mercy of the mountain; it's incredibly difficult to make quick adjustments and it can be a struggle to get your avatar to do what you want to do without serious effort. You have no control over the camera, and that becomes an adversary; jamming to the right trying to hit a checkpoint can easily be undermined by a wild, uncontrollable swing or zoom because the game felt like it. You certainly don't have Tony Hawk/SSX levels of control, which is fine, but what's in Steep is better described as “loose” than simulation. After about twenty hours of playing I felt adjusted to the game's quirks, but more often than not trying to get your rider to generally perform something specific still comes down to trial and error, combating the controls, and a good amount of luck. You're provided with a G-meter that is supposed to track how much punishment you can take before you spill, but in practice the game just does what it wants; a ten second free fall onto solid rock might be okay, but hitting what appears to be a pebble may or may not send you into a knockout faceplant.
 
  Wing gliding is the highlight. Flying inches above the ground, weaving around snow covered trees and sharp rocks is exhilarating and it controls responsively. Most of the challenges in the wing suit revolve around passing through rings and gives a serious Pilotwings vibe. Paragliding is more relaxed and is the preferred method for exploring the Alps, allowing you to cover large swaths of land and soak in the sights while you're at it. You're given a very generous updraft system: get close and kinda/sorta perpendicular to a mountainside and there will always be uplift, essentially allowing you to glide endlessly. I'm pretty sure that's not how wind works, but whatever. Walking is where you put one foot in front of the other to initiate locomotion, and while on foot you can use binoculars to spot drop zones and places of interest.
 
  The scale and freeform exploration is great, but the “game” part of the game, the challenges, are all over the place. These events are scattered all over the mountains and they're generally races against the clock or score based affairs. They are categorized into Easy, Medium, and Hard difficulties, and you can earn bronze, silver, or gold medals depending on your performance, which awards XP to level up to unlock drop zones and currency to buy cosmetic items. The open nature of the game itself wrecks havoc with any scoring conventions; a single, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t trick pulled out of your♥♥♥♥♥can destroy a gold medal challenge in seconds. Alternatively, a glitchy camera can be a repeatable bane to finishing a race without ragdolling down a cliff face, and the difference between a gold medal or complete failure can either be a matter of minutes or seconds. There's very little consistency between which challenges will be a fun exercise in sharpening your skills or controller throwing frustration.
 
  And that's Steep broadly speaking. It demands to be enjoyed with a relaxed demeanor and forgiving nature from a zoomed out perspective. If you can find that zen state it's one of the best extreme sports games that's released in years. Just don't look at it too closely.

Steep. The game to fill the hole in my heart that skate has left me since I switched to PC gaming so many years ago.
This game is not something most people will want to play each and every day like they would play dota2 or counter strike. It's not a game about completing all the challenges or getting the level cap as fast as possible. it's a game about snowboarding, skiing, paragliding and flying with your wingsuit. Your playground is a huge place with various mountains. the game leaves you on your own and you can do whatever the hell you want.
The challenges are all awesome and it feels to me that every single race is polished and balanced. I can't comprehend how much work it must have taken to build a world like this and make it feel consistently awesome.
Anyway, it's not ultra-super-amazing realistic. It certainly looks like it would be, but there's some arcade mechanics worked into how the game plays, and in my opinion that's exactly how it should be! It's still a game people, if you had a ultra-realistic snowboarding game you would fall every 7 seconds.
To conclude my review, I don't think I'll ever get enough of Steep. It fills my times of boredom and gives me an opportunity to just hang back and chill out. I recommend it!

I have mixed feelings about this game, but am glad I got it for under $1.00 due to a Black Friday sale.  I would not pay $9.99 for this game.
I enjoy the concept of an FPS that involves fighting demons in an evil castle.  However, the game's mechanics were very buggy, in my opinion.  All I had to do was walk incorrectly off of the last step on a set of stairs and my guy screams in agony from a broken leg.  While this normally doesn't happen, it happened enough to annoy me a lot.
In the game menu, my mouse appeared to have a mind of its own.
Also, one of the biggest issues I had was with my flintlock weapons.  There's a pistol and a rifle, which I would always check to make sure were loaded.  I would usually have my flintlock rifle out and would quickly select the flintlock pistol if I missed with the rifle, since they were such powerful weapons.  Unfortunately, most of the time, my pistol would suddenly be empty, even after I had reloaded it.  This would always occur at the most dire moment when a large demon is attacking me.  I tested it; check that it's loaded, fire, reload, switch weapons and check that it's still loaded.  Success.  Then, this would happen:
*demonic scream*
*fires rifle and misses*
Me (to myself): "Crap."
*switch to pistol*
*click*
Me: "Are you serious??"
*receive colossal amounts of facial deconstructive surgery from screaming demon*
Some people might consider this to be a minor bug.  However, I was incredibly irritated by it after only a few times.  I eventually gave up on using the flintlock pistol as a backup weapon.  To me, this should not happen at all.  I feel like a game that came out 5+ years after the first Half-Life should have been better developed than this.
The fact that the castle was randomized made it very enjoyable, though.  You could never predict when a demon would come out, or what kind it would be.  Likewise, you could never memorize the locations of your relatives, as they were usually never found in the same places.
TL;DR
Alright game.  Randomization of castle is good.  Bugs are annoying.  Would recommend to anyone as long as it's on sale.  Do not pay full price.

Mirror's Edge, I'm sure, is going to stay one of my all time favorite games. The graphics are beautiful, the soundtrack is relaxing, and the parkour is very fluid. This is the game I play when I get frustrated with CS:GO (I'm not the best). It does have its faults however. It will require you to pick up a fallen enemy's firearm every so often, and the gunplay is less than desireable, which is surprising coming from the creators of Battlefield (DICE). Aside from the poor gunplay, the levels sometimes incorporate live, die, repeat, Super Mario Bros-esque jumps that make the game feel almost unfair, but when you finally do make it (usually by utilizing some aspect of the environment that was previously overlooked), the rush of victory and accomplishment feels great.
The game makes you play through it on easy or normal difficulty the first time, which means Runner Vision is enabled. Runner Vision highlights different objects that can be used to navigate to your destination, which I find can be immersion breaking. Hard mode is unlocked after your first playthrough. It increases the combat difficulty and has Runner Vision permanently disabled.
I recommend this game to everyone especially when it goes on sale for $5. You have no reason to pass this up. The story isn't memorable, but the relaxing, detailed atmosphere and simple, fluid parkour controls make this game a must have.

This is a first person game. It's a parkour game where you manuever around building tops mostly and inside the building.
Controls:
The controls aren't that bad. The movements aren't bad, but there are times where it feels like the game misinterprets what you try to do.
Example - you run parallel to the wall and then try to wall run and then jump to the obstacle top on the opposite side of where you are wall-running to, but if it doesn't stick, or just bad timing, you will fall on your back.
When it works, it's great and fun, but on situations where you are being chased, this can be a problem.
Combat:
There is not much an emphasis on combat control. You basically slide-kick into or jump kick into the enemies and then follow it up with your punch combo. If they are near the ledge, the kick can usually knock them off, killing them, removing the need for your punch combos.
The disarm timings are a little difficult and require a lot of timing practice with the heavy units, as the lightly armored units swing at a pace where you can see when to disarm them. BTW, when you disarm your opponent, you also knock them out at the same time, so it's a good thing I guess. But you are not invulnerable when you are disarming. There are no invulnerability frames, as far as what I've seen. You can pick up the guns that enemies have and use it, but you can't reload because the main focus of this game is parkouring.
Story:
You are kind of thrown into the story. You are given slight clues as to what's going on in the game by your surroundings and when you pay attention a little to the character dialogues (Really pay attention to it, to catch a little bit of what's going on in that time period of the game). The game is pretty short and so it doesn't really explain everything in the game.
Overall Rating: 6/10
It's not a bad game. The graphics and style of the game is interesting and new when the game came out. The combat was pretty bad though. It wasn't as smooth as I would have hoped, especially since the parkouring was smooth (when everything goes right). The movements aren't bad but could be a little better.
But all in all, I'd still recommend this game. Although, if you want, wait for a sale or discount before buying because why not save when you can?
