TBS core is its gameplay. It is fun and challanging and the combination of Strength and Health in one Stat makes the fighting pretty complex. Each unit also has an Armor Stat. Damage equals your Strength minus the enemys Armor, as you take damage you loose Strength and by this you do less damage on your next move. So you have always to decide if you weaken an enemy by attaking his Strength directly or if you lower his Armor so that another unit can deal mor damage.
TBS offers a nice range of different classes for your units, each with his own special ablility. The classes are ranging from tanks to fast and versatile units to archers.
The heart of TBS is its story. You are provided with a huge Universe overflowing with lore. Each of your characters has its own backstory and motives and I enjoyed their interaction quite a lot. At its core TBS story is about Family and the ones your are responsible for and how far you are willing to go for them. It is about concequences of choice and dealing with loose.
As you progress through the Story you are faced with decisions and your choice will affect your experience.
The Soul of TBS is its presantation. The artstyle andt the animation is gourgues and the Soundtrack is fantastic. It is just to sad that there are quite a few passages where no music at all is used.
All in all as said above TBS is a very good game! It is a bit minimalistic in some places (cutscenes and story presantation) but in a good way, resampling the charme of oldschool videogames

Easily one of my all-time favorite RPG franchises, this is where it all started. Chronicles revives the vision Masaya Hashimoto had by introducing a re-vamped soundtrack, art, sprites and general configuration that supports modern systems and resolutions. The Ys Vanished saga is included in two parts, each one being a seperate game, and both games also enable the option of experiencing the game with PC-88 art/music, as well as the 2001 variant officially known as Complete.
Simply put, if you are looking for a somewhat minimal action-rpg that has an engrossing plot, varied landscapes and engaging boss fights, then this is the game you're looking for. Seriously, you WILL have fun if you enjoy fast-paced action-RPGs. There are obviously a few flaws to the game such as an awkward leveling system (only in the first one), and inconsistent difficulty between bosses (also more prevalent in the first one), but the pros definitely outperform the cons for this fantastic epic.
Also as a side remainder, there is a heavy lack of jRPG ports on PC from Japan to America. This is indeed a very sad, but real problem that we have had for the past many years now. XSEED is famous for making ports like these a reality for many of us niche players, as well as other rpg-gamers who enjoy these sort of games. This is why I urge anyone who actually enjoys jRPGs and especially the Ys franchise to support XSEED and purchase all 4 Ys games they've published so far (Ys I and II are packed, so it's 3 in the store along with Oath and Origins). With continued support we can expect XSEED to translate and pot even more jRPGs in the future, and that's the kind of thing that I could only dream of for so long up until now.
So please, I know many people tend to pirate games since money is indeed a hard thing to come by, but make an exception to this great franchise, especially since it tends to go on sale once in a while for 75% off. It's how we can secure a good future for the ported/translated pc jRPG market.

Before anything else, for anything under $45, this game is worth it hands down. After a few days of playing (26h) I beat all sidequests and the main story, but there's still tons of challenges to do.
Let's run a pros and cons list
Pros
+Good crafting system.
+Great freerunning. Movement just feels right.
+Good environment that never felt old.
+Still afraid to go out at night.
+The developers are pretty good people #drinkrightdyinglight
+Doesn't rely on too many jump scares, although some are present.
+Brutal kill sequences are pretty satisfying on zombies.
+Interiors are intense and scary.
There may be more cons than pros since I have some specific grievances but don't let that detract from an amazing world.
Cons
-The story was eh
-There's an enemy that blows up when it gets close to you. It can sense you through walls. It is often located just out of sight around a cornor. A bunch of unavoidable instadeaths is never a good idea Techland.
-The grappling hook could be a little glitchy, but in fairness, it's a big world and that had to be difficult to get to work as much as it does.
-It is incredibly difficult to climb downwards. Falling or climbing up? Smooth as silk.
-The final boss is just a quicktime event. Very anticlimactic.
-While there is a fast travel port between two areas located in the two major bases of the game, nobody tells you that, and it's very easy to miss.
-Had some mild issues with some flickering with crossfired 7770s, but I could easily play through.
-There were a few issues with slopes and some ledges being unclimbable, but it's understandable with an open world. Plus you get a sense of what you can and can't climb very quickly.
-A lot of buildings had no interior, which is to be expected and is not dissapointing in itself, but it's difficult to see which ones do have interiors when out gathering supplies.
-None of the characters stood out.
Overall this game gets a solid 8/10 from me, despite the issues listed, because I bought this game to run around like an idiot killing zombies. The world itself was rich and well designed, which made even random errands fun.

Review for Ys I: Game starts off pretty well. Loved the art style and music. I grew up on classic consoles and that's where this came from. It's simple to get into. You attack by running into enemies. There's no loot, no stats to allocate, and a short storyline. The combat isn't bad normally.
But the end will leave you very frustrated. The story frequently leaves you with no indicator of where to go to progress. You end up wasting time or googling it instead and there's too much backtracking at the end. The difficulty of the bosses at the end will leave you frustrated and looking for strategies. The final boss will frequently kill you in 1 hit. The saving grace is that reloading saved games is instant so you can replay those boss fights immediately until you get it right (and you will be doing this if you buy this game!).

The only game where consequences actually matter. Other games claim they do. They're all pretenders.
Nosferatu centers around rescuing your family from an evil Count before they are murdered. This all goes on in a horror atmosphere that still scares even while looking dated.
The game is running on a timer in the form of a clock. As it gets later into the night, relatives will die if you don't rescue them in time. Why does it matter? The more that die, the harder the end of the game will be. Not only that, if you save them you get powerful items that give you great advantages. The pressure is on right out of the literal gate. Saving them has a direct and major impact on your game. Not only does this give us a rare game where consequences really do matter, it enhances the horror atmosphere by making you care. The pressure doesn't end there. There are other reasons why you need to be as fast as you can...
The castle interior and placement of people and items is randomised each time you play, so there's replay value here.
The first person combat is a mixture of melee, ranged, conventional and holy weapons. Some enemies are only affected by certain weapons. See a supernatural foe? Try holy water or the crucifix. It's a good system and very responsive but there is one major flaw.
Your fists. Don't ruin this wonderful game and use your fists. They're more effective than your bloody sword! They are fast, powerful and stunlock enemies until they die. Totally ruins the game. If you're disciplined and don't use them the game is fun. Simple as that.
There are several other annoying bugs and escorting family members to safety can be a pain but I never encountered anything game breaking.
Nosferatu has aged very well. Unique with real 'consequences matter' gameplay (which isn't even highlighted on the store page) and still scary in 2017.
Headphones, a dark room and spare underwear recommended.

After a long journey, you have arrived. The castle where your sister's wedding is to take place towers over you, an imposing edifice obscuring the night sky. You have not yet had the pleasure of meeting your soon to be brother-in-law, but it is clear he is a man of means. Your pulse quickens as you anticipate the welcoming arms of your family. Having been delayed, you are arriving a day behind everyone else. The curse of being a bureaucrat in parliament. Your body weary from traveling, you yearn to enjoy the warmth of family and the feast that must certainly await you. Dismounting the carriage, you approach the gate to the hilltop monolith, its doors aged and adorned haphazardly with crucifixes of varying size and construction. "Where is the gatekeeper" you think to yourself. "Surely a family of such wealth would have someone to mind comings and goings." Pushing aside the large doors, you enter the castle. The moonlight shines blue on the ancient hand hewn stones of the courtyard; an eerie silence looms in the air. "Where is everyone, were they not expecting my arrival? Even still, the night is young; someone must be up and about?" Just then, you notice luggage and suitcases carelessly strewn about the entrance way. In the light of a nearby lamp, you see your father's traveling case, its lid ajar. You walk over and open it, examining its contents. Gleaming in the lamplight, you see your father's cane sword, a handsome weapon fashioned by the best craftsmen in London. Grasping the sword in your hand, you rise to your feet. "Something is clearly off." You walk towards the east wing and open the heavy wooden door. The air emanating from inside is musty and thick. You venture into the dim half-light, unsure of what you might find. After walking a few paces, you hear a strange gurgling noise ahead and come to a full stop. Straining your eyes against the darkness you see a shuffling figure at the end of the corridor. Suddenly you are struck from behind and thrown to the floor, your back aching, torn open by an unseen force. Clambering to defend yourself, you ignore the searing pain and roll onto your back. What you see causes your whole being to recoil. Something that can only be described as a demon stands over you. It looks down on you with its gaunt and eyeless face. Before you can blink it lunges, mouth agape, at your unguarded throat. Welcome, the wedding party awaits…

Planet Diver is an infinite runner (or rather and infinite faller) from Fabraz. You take on the role of an adrenaline junkie who's decided that the latest kick is to dive down very deep holes on alien planets. Dragging your AI robot cube 'Buddy' along for the ride you leap headfirst to the centre of a planet and whatever awaits you (Spoiler: Something not too friendly)
Diving is simple you progressively fall towards the planets centre moving left or right to avoid rocks, enemies, fire etc. Along with this you also have down, which acts as a speed boost and initially as an attack, and up, which slows you and allows you to pass through falling objects. You have a limited number of dashes which you can recharge by breaking, star bit collectables are worth more the faster you travel so you need to balance risk vs reward.
So far so standard. Where Planet Diver stands out is in its selection of mods and outfits. The currency you collect whilst falling allows you to buy a bunch of interesting items. Whilst outfits just change your look and your dashing animation (for example the 'Bounty Hunter' which turns you into a morph ball whilst dashing) the mods can completely change the way you play. Maybe you'll pick up the 'Gunslinger Mod' that means your dash is no longer an attack but instead when you break you release a wave of damaging beams. Or maybe the 'No Manual Mod' is more to your liking, you gain an additional health bar and dash bar but you lose the UI! Each of the mods really changes up the way you play the game and means there's lots of variety.
In terms of game modes there is a story of 75 different missions each with differing goals spread out across the three planets. When you get through each planet you unlock the next one not only in the story but also in the arcade mode which acts as your infinite level generator.
Planet Diver has been released on Steam and  IOS/Andriod whilst this is often a black mark against a game in this case it doesn't seem to have made much of a difference other than the relatively simple controls. The steam version has the micro transactions removed and whilst I haven't tried the mobile version reviews seem to be positive.
Whilst the infinite runner style game can get very dull very fast planet diver has plenty of features to give you good value for your money.  With all of the different mods and a few surprises that I won't spoil the game is a lot of fun. The game also comes with a fantastic soundtrack, one of the best I've listened to in a long time. Whilst it's not going to be anyone's game of the year Planet diver is a great fun and is probably a really good pick up.

If you ever wanted to play a vampire hunter, look no further than this interactive bloodsucker-murder-sim. This game has all the tricks of the trade that you could want: a crucifix, wooden stakes, garlic, a sword, flintlock weapons, even a revolver and machine gun later on. Not to mention appropriate enemies to use 'em on: hounds of hell, various ghouls, bats, evil henchmen and of course your titular vampires. It also never loses its sense of dread and forces you to stay careful; these monsters are scary, because they'll murder you if you leave your guard down for even a second. It's also short and sweet, and can be beaten in just five hours. Randomly generated rooms up the replayability factor, and it keeps a near-perfect sense of progression; as you unlock more powerful weaponry, your enemies become exponentially tougher. Small hickups with the AI are few and far between, and not at all enough to detract from the overall experience. If you can live with the graphics, maybe you can live through Nosferatu: The Wrath of Malachi. Highly recommended.

Nosferatu: The Wrath of Malachi starts as you arrive at a ridiculously spooky castle in Transylvania where your sister is set to marry a count, and to everyone's shock, he's a vampire and the castle is chock full of vampires and other horrors. 15 of your family members and the family dog have been taken hostage, and at various set times throughout the night, each non-canine family member will be sacrificed, unless you can save them. After resolving this, you will be set to take on the count himself and Malachi, which is some nasty thingy the count is summoning using the sacrifices. Can you defeat them and achieve victory and an undoubtedly inadequate ending will play, followed by credits? Or will you and your family succumb to the vampiric threat (oh and peasants will eat your dog)? This game is a roller coaster of likes and dislikes for me, though, and I'd like to go over what I enjoyed and did not here.
I find the randomization of things in this games actually to be a rather fun element in general. For instance, when I play some games, I know what is on the other side of the next door, but in Nosferatu: The Wrath of Malachi, I typically have no idea. Monsters are random, the room layout of the castle is random in each wing, the relatives are in random rooms much of the time, and even the chests on the ground have random items in them (except for a few very specific, scripted chests). Quick-saving and quick-loading can net you better ammo or health as needed if you want to save-scum like crazy (good times!).
This game's graphics, though very, very dated, had nice light ray effects (considering the tech), nice enemy design and art style, and the interesting "film" filter over the screen (kinda making it resemble a movie playing on a projector) were nice touches. The sound design plays scary music jingles to let you know one or more enemies are around. In some games, it takes away from the scare or the terror, but in this game, I actually jumped pretty bad at some of the scares thanks to the sound and music cues. The ambient noises are also creepy. At one point, I was charging my headphones and they were off, and I found the game far less scary without them...you'll just take a few more hits as a result of not knowing an enemy is around.
With that in mind, it should be no surprise that the game's atmosphere is excellent. The castle is very creepy, and the sights and sounds all resonate to make it memorable and relevant. As you rescue each relative, it nets you a reward, sometimes in the form of a new item. I hadn't found a revolver yet, rescued my character's aunt, and received a revolver. I'd already been stocking up, so then I was ready to shoot some hell-spawn, and it was quite nice.
This vampire game actually lets you repel vampires and hell-spawn with a crucifix and kill vampires with wooden stakes. Yes, you read that right! Although vampires are somewhat rare in the game, you can walk into a random room with a coffin. In it lays a vampire woman (I thought she was kinda hawt :D). You have a few seconds to stake her! If you don't, you will have to fight her by conventional means (or stake her repeately once she gets out of the coffin). I didn't get it, but there is apparently garlic which will automatically repel the enemies without having to equip it like you have to with the crucifix. This is so cool. I loved watching monster movies as a kid, and I never got to stake a vampire in a coffin except for in King's Quest II until this game! I wish more games would do this.
Enemy respawns were a bit of a mixed bag for me...normally I dislike them when there is a finite amount of ammo in a game, but I didn't really seem to need ammunition. However, not needing ammo leads me into what I did not like about the game...
Ammunition was irrelevant in my time with the game. At some point, I'm sure that I'll need guns, but in the few hours I played, the best weapon in the game by far is...your bare fists. No, they're not blessed (that we know of). They're not covered in holy water. You're not playing as a prize fighter (that we know of). You aren't a "chosen one" legendary hero. You're not a mutant or a superhero. You're human, and a gentleman. Your fists are deadlier than your cane sword. Yes, you have a cane sword, which sounds cool, but using it will get you hurt badly. The fists, on the other hand, will stun-lock the living daylights out of almost any enemy I encountered, and anything I couldn't fist to death could be trashed using the crucifix. This is hilarious but annoying, because I tend to prefer good game design, and this is a clear example of horrible balance. The cane sword may as well not exist. Its range is irrelevant since I was still taking hits, because it does not stun the enemy like the fists do.
There is a stamina bar which fills (instead of consuming) and makes you attack slower once it is full. This didn't bother me much but is a little annoying. Stamina bars are rarely a good thing. No, using the cane sword is not the solution, because you will need to run away more since you're going to be likely to get hit. Fisting your enemy is almost always the answer here.
This is a minor gripe, but an annoyance all the same: the number "5" is always displayed backwards on your health, your ammo, the time, your entire UI. It's not cool or even stylistic, because there is no justification I can find for doing it in the game...unless "because pentagrams!" is someone's best effort at explaining this absurd display of a number.
The game does not have a map at all. You get a compass, but it's literally a N, S, E, W, etc. compass, with no other information. It's rarely of any use, and when the game randomly generates the entire castle from playthrough to playthrough, and many of the rooms look identical, that's a recipe for disaster. Although I have a poor natural sense of direction, this could easily also be an issue for someone with a good sense of direction. There's often no logical flow to the rooms, and with quite a few of them looking the same, it's very easy to get turned around or lost, and wander around bored for a bit. No walkthrough will help you, either, because the map is random. I got lost a few times but managed to find my way around enough to take out two bosses. Although I managed, much of my time was just spent wandering around backtracking, asking myself "Wait, did I go here? Oh, yeah, I did...hmm" and not really challenged with combat, because you just fist all the non-vampire/non-boss enemies to death without any real effort.
I am supposed to care about my relatives, but the game never has me meet a single relative until their lives are already in danger. This is a terrible emotional stimulant. The right way to handle this in a short timeframe is to do what the Tomb Raider reboot did: flashbacks and brief scenes with people your character knows, then have their life in danger. It's not a guarantee that you'll care if they die, but at least it's something. Here, you get a page of photographs and names. One has large breasts, and I'm pretty sure it's because they tried to make players care about her the most since character development, personality, and character introductions aren't things things you will encounter in this game.
I also dislike the escort missions and timer. Some relatives are found deep inside the castle and you have to perform an escort mission with every one of them, all the way back to where you started the game, making sure they don't randomly stop following you or wildly run in circles forever. If 7 relatives die, you lose the entire game, and since their lives end on a timer and you just fist everything to death, the game feels like one big maze on a timer, and nothing more. It has nice window dressing,but putting a game-ending timer on the whole experience is the kiss of death for me.

The Banner Saga while beautiful to watch delivers a grim story full of painful scenarios that create a bleak and melancholy world in which your caravan travels. The scenarios that come up frequently throughout your journey often leave you regretting your decisions and praying for reprieve. With that being said though the story and gameplay drives you to continue your journey; from managing your armies, keeping track of supplies to keep you going through the days and the constant brutality that is the decision making.
The Banner Saga is brought to life with a gorgeous art style and illustrations. The character interaction and story gives a great depth to the world you are traversing with constant threat of war and death. The combat is a well-structured machine that relies both on the strategy in combat and the logistics outside of combat. Through that combat and the scenarios users are presented with, you gain a currency known as renown which gives you the caravan leader the duty of managing the resources and where they're spent. Should you buy more supplies for your armies to sustain themselves on their journey? Should you spend your renown purchasing trinkets and weapons for your people from the markets you come across? Or should you spend that renown promoting your units so they last longer in combat? It all comes down to human choice and well human error...
Battle on through the realm and lead your caravan on a journey of discovery... and... pray that you don't kill off your trusted companion while trying to save a supply wagon.

Planet Diver is an action game about diving through planets using a wing suit. Diving through these planets will be dangerous and you’ll find many obstacles in your way but fear not, for you have Buddy with you! Buddy is your robotic companion of amusement and will be of use to you on your perilous adventure.
Planet Diver’s graphical style is quite hard to describe, it’s almost as if it’s being displayed on a relatively old analogue TV, well not really but you get the idea. Anyway, this graphical style not only fits the game well but also looks damn good! While fairly simple, all of the models in game look great, particularly some of the more colourful enemies you’ll face.
Taking place on three planets each with three different biomes, Planet Diver’s 75 missions is reasonably varied and with an endless arcade mode too there’s a good amount of bang for your buck. The core mechanics of the game are incredibly simple. The levels have different lanes your character can travel in. As well as having the ability to move left or right into a new lane you can also speed up or slow down (the speeds and number of speed levels vary depending on what Buddy mods you have but the default is three different levels of speed). Speeding up (boosting) just before hitting an enemy will allow you to fly through them, i.e. kill them. Slowing down (braking) is used as a way to dodge as well as a way to recharge your boosts (default number of charges is three).
Okay so it’s not quite that simple. For a start you have two health bars, meaning you can take three hits before it’s game over. A health bar is depleted whenever you hit or get hit by something without dodging or boosting. For example if you fly straight into one of the many unfriendly creatures found in the game you’ll lose one health bar. But fear not! Health bars can be recharged by killing creatures or by collecting star stuff. Star stuff is a resource found throughout the game, the amount found depends on your speed and how far into the level you are, the more you collect the more your health bar is recharged. Star stuff is also the game’s currency and can be used to purchase new skins, Buddy mods and soundtracks. As well as all of this the tunnel you fly through isn’t smooth with nothing in it, there are often obstacles in the level which you’ll need to dodge if you want to survive.
Back to those pesky creatures I mentioned earlier. There are some. You’ll find them throughout each level and more often than not they’ll do their damn best to make your life a misery. What they do, of course, varies with each critter. Some of them will follow you and then dive bomb into you while others will sit on the wall of the level and shoot webs that slow you down at you. As well as these, you’ll find yourself in boss fights at certain points in the game. The bosses are damn well challenging I’ll tell you that, even the best Planet Divers will struggle a little here.
The last thing worth mentioning about the gameplay is the fact that each level has a challenge you have to complete in order to progress with each challenge having three levels: bronze (the minimum needed to unlock the next level), silver and gold. Generally these are relatively easy to do without going too far out of your way in any given level though some of them are rather challenging. While I did like these challenges I did feel as though some of them were a little too harsh considering the fact you can’t progress without completing them. For example the first boss fight’s challenge is to only get hit three times for bronze, something that’s incredibly hard to achieve. Now you can of course avoid the challenges thanks to something I’ll mention in the next section but I didn’t want to take the easy way out and I imagine most people won’t.

Planet Diver is a fun and often challenging action game where you’ll plunge through narrow levels using your wing suit. The graphics are nice and the gameplay is relatively simple but very entertaining.

Disclaimer, This is my first review.
First and foremost, I was highly skeptical about this game before I bought it. I saw it and thought "Re-skin of Titan Quest." I am happy to see the spirit of TQ perserved while establishing itself as it's own Intellectual Property and its take on Action Role Playing Games.
I was let down by the charactor creation (I spend a lot of time on charactor creation in games like Saints Row 3, 4 and Skyrim etc) and thusly wasn't able to creat a persona that felt like mine. However I've come to expect this from ARPGs so I wasn't to let down.
After playing Diablo 3 from launch and being terribly dissapointed by it's lacklustre story I was impressed by how fast I took to the setting and story being told here. In a nutshell you are a "Taken" and about to be hung. Once the game began I noticed zombies assaulting the town and was actually excited to get into the swing of things. 5 hours later, my wife is giving me the stare and the fog clears. This is the first ARPG to legit suck me into the zone. Story wise there are genuine choices to be had and content "can be skipped" (Zones have a minimum monster level however).
Gameplay wise I've only played as a Demolistionist/Occultist but the skills are rewarding and the weapons have an oomph. One gripe i have is being unable to undo mastery points (Something I learned a little late) full on respecs should be a thing.
Graphically the game looks well, the setting and the monsters fit in and match the games tone.
I highly suggest this game to any ARPG lover.

Saints Row IV contiunues where Saints Row The 3rd leaves off, now you play as the president of the USA, facing an intergalactic alien menace. You spend most of your time in a simulated computer version of Earth causing all sorts of problems. Imagine Grandtheft Auto and The Matrix combined into a "kind of" sandbox styled game and you'll get the general idea of what it's like.
It's everything you've come to expect from the Saints Row franchise, all of it's rude, crude and raunchy humor is still in tact. When first playing the game, you'll enjoy what they have to offer, but after a few hours of it, you'll soon learn that the majority of the game has nothing new to offer.
What it boils down to is "events" you have to complete in order to cause chaos in the simulated Earth. As you complete more of these events, you take more control of the alien computer system. Unfortunately that's really all there is to the game, it all boils down to just a series of mini games tacked together in a very loose version of Saints Row.
It's an okay game, but feels like a grind after a few hours. It won't offer you anything beyond what you've alreaqdy seen, it's much better with co-op and friends. I do not recommend getting it unless it's on sale, $50.00 is too much to ask for a series of mini games.

Ys is, so far, an old JRPG. You've got your maps that are too large, you've got your 90s anime character art, you've got your grinding, and you've got your barely-held-together plot.
That said, it's a remarkably enjoyable game. The combat is an interesting system that if anything allows you to run through earlier areas cleaving everything that gets in your way, and otherwise makes the boss battles quite difficult and rewarding. The plot, if loose, is good, telling the story of a boy attempting to solve both the mystery of the island and the mystery of the civilization that came before.
It also lets you switch between the "Chronicles" and "Complete" versions of the character art and music, with even the original game's music as an option, which is a nice touch.
All in all, a classic JRPG. Us PC gamers could certainly use more of them.

Having played YS oath of felghana and YS ark of napishtim and YS Seven on PS2 and PSP respectively; i was not sure what to expect from Ys 1+2 and i am overjoyed to say it is the same fantastic top down action RPG / with fantastic NPC's and a simplistic yet enjoyable plot. I highly reccomend this game to anyone that are fans of RPG,s / action titles.
I have yet to start YS 2, but YS 1 truly hooks you right away with a great style of presentation that the series is known for, although a little on the short side [10-15 hours or so] thats only the first title of the game. It intially threw me off guard that you need to run into enemies to do damage but that quickly subsides after an hour or so. Ys games are well known for their difficulty and amazing music and boss fights and this game does not dissapoint in the slightest. The soundtrack is fantastic and always fit the mood/setting perfectly. it is just pure joy to hack and slash dozens of monsters while exploring this intriguing envronment.  the boss fights are also challenging and on thing i love about the game is it does not hold your hand, you are free to explore wherever you will even if that means multple deaths trying to reach that elusive chest or just testing the waters in a new area, that lack of linearity is something i love about the YS games and this is no exception.
A simple yet dynamic equipment system, a great bestiary and plenty of personality in the NPC's is something i love about the YS titles and this one delivers in that regard yet again. this game came out quite long ago [1997 or so] and i can definitely say it has stood the test of time as it is very enjoyable which is an impressive feat in itself.
Honestly, i reccomend this game to its fullest extent. the YS series is one of the most unique and under appreciated RPG series out there and it deserves much more recognition. With the new YS game on PSP Vita just coming out, im hoping this series continues to excel at what it does best. Amazing soundtrack, Fun hack and slash elements, fantastic NPC's,  great sense of exploration, and a simplistic yet great plot are thing you will find in Ys 1+2.
I sincerely reccomend it!

After taking a break from playing Enemy Unknown, I picked up the expansion on sale and jumped back in to see how things changed. It is immediately apparent that many aspects that were annoying and slightly lacking in the original are either solved outright or solved with improvements to the mechanics. I won't spoil any aspects of the game or story changes, but I will say that almost every one of them is a welcome improvement.
If you haven't played the original or the expansion, I would highly reccommend getting them together and playing it this way. In the original, your soldiers were almost completely useless, missing even perfectly set up and close range shotgun attacks, or losing their cool and panicking. While they didn't remove these effects in the expansion, it feels more realistic when these events occur, and add the right amount of tension to the experience without the additional annoyance. TL:DR you won't rage quit the level anymore.
I know there are those people who do not like turn based gaming. I liken this game to chess. You have your resources and they have theirs. You will be at a disadvantage most of the time, but you will receive a great sense of satisfaction from adapting and overcoming the enemy.
I'll end with a quote from Benjamin Franklin.
"The game of Chess is not merely an idle amusement. Several very valuable qualities of the mind, useful in the course of human life, are to be acquired or strengthened by it, so as to become habits, ready on all occasions . . . we learn by Chess the habit of not being discouraged by present bad appearances in the state of our affairs, the habit of hoping for a favorable change, and that of persevering in the search of resources." —Benjamin Franklin, “The Morals of Chess”

Only played Ys I, so this will just be covering that. As spoiler-free as possible. It started out pretty straightforward, and once I accidentally discovered some game mechanics which for some reason weren't mentioned in game at all, it wasn't too challenging early on (which it shouldn't be anyway, on Normal).
Later on, there didn't seem to be much direction whatsoever, and I eventually just got into the habit of checking a walkthrough every step of the way just because I wanted to finish it. Half the time after following the directions I just laughed, thinking "how the hell was I supposed to know to do that?". There is vague direction, but it's mostly trial and error if you're trying to move on with only the information the game gives you. I don't know if it's supposed to be like that, maybe figuring out the randomest things imaginable is supposed to be the actual challenge of the game. The challenge certainly isn't from the bosses, those are either pathetically easy or laughably luck-based. I liked the easy ones more.
The final boss is just the worst, without spoiling things, I can only say that it has absolutely nothing done right about it. It's flat-out horrible in terms of story, gameplay, and, well... The music isn't that bad actually, the first few times. Unfortunately if you can't get the luck you need to beat him early, you may wind up listening to the same music for hours.
That's generally how the music in this game is, throughout the whole game. The game doesn't really have any bad music, but most of it is heard for too long, making it tedious, and it gets annoying after a while. If you want to simulate the experience without playing the game, look up one of the songs on YouTube or something, listen to it once. It's pretty good, right? Now listen to it again, for about an hour, and see if it's still good. One positive thing is that there are three different versions of music you can choose from, one from what I assume was the original version of the game, one from this modern version, and one from in between. I often found myself switching between the three because just listening to one was painful.

South Park: The Stick of Truth is a turn-based roleplaying videogames developed by Obsidian Entertainment and takes place in the South Park setting: your character is a new kid just arrived in town who gets immediately involved into a large-scale LARP organized by the series' protagonist. Predictably, the game soon gets out of hand as increasingly gross and dangerous events start plaguing South Park.
As the New Kid, a male kid whose apparel you can completely customize, you can choose between four classes: wizard, thief, warrior or jew (a special class specialized in debuff and who gets stronger as he gets debuffed in return). The class of choice only determines the kind of abilities you can unleash on your enemies, as gear and weapons are completely class-free. On top of your set of abilities, you will learn special magic moves (farts) as the story progresses, as well as one-per-day summons. Weapons and pieces of armor can also be "enchanted" by applying different stickers to them, which grant the Kid special passive effects. While levelling up allows you to unlock new class abilities or empower the ones you already posses, unlocking perks (special passive skills) requires you to befriend people (and creatures) around the town: the more you befriend, the sooner you get new perks. You can carry with you a single additional party member, choosing from the members of the main cast: each as his own abilities and special skills for you to use.
The combat of South Park: The Stick of Truth doesn't differ that much from your typical turn-based RPG. In order to truly master it you'll have to get savvy about:
- Defending yourself and dish out your attacks, which is done with button prompts
- The status effect you can inflict upon your foes: burning, freezing, bleeding, screwed (dead in a certain number of turns) and grossed-out (a poisoned status that will sometimes prevent an enemy from acting), which are something vital to break someone's defense.
The strongest suit of The Stick of Truth is of course is extreme adherence to the show itself, something that was helped by both Trey Parker and Matt Stone working on the project: the town of South Park you get to explore is extremely faithful, the graphic engine makes you feel like you are moving through an actual episode and the various characters react and talk as you'd expect them to. If you are a fan of the show you'll recognize several characters and places (some you'll even get to interact to) and appreciate how far this videogame goes, sometimes even beyond the show itself.
Gameplay-wise, though, South Park: The Stick of Truth suffers from two significant shortcoming:
1) For a roleplaying videogame, it can be beaten fairly quickly (between nine and ten hours, on an average), even considering the optional side quests and extra objective you can entertain yourself with. This however could be tied to the game shifting publiusher (from THQ to Ubisoft)
2) The combat starts off as reasonable in difficulty, with no strong challenge curve progression afterwards, and becomes drammatically easy and mindless halfway through till the very end. This is due to the general generosity of the game when it comes to gear and weapons, the extremely low level cap (15), every class getting at the very least one or two abilities they can use to whipe the floor with even the largest pack of mooks and your health and mana being refilled completely after each fight.
Still, South Park: The Stick of Truth is basically a must-have for the fan of the show proper and a very unique, solid, satyrical and entertaining turn-based roleplaying videogame for everyone else. Just don't come in and expect a very hard challenge

Nosferatu is, has been, and always will be one of the true go-to mental images whenever somebody mentions those classic horror monsters, vampires. Despite not having the most solid reputation in recent years, vampires are very much still badass and sometimes scary as hell. To know something immortal, thirsty for your blood, and a master manipulator can unnerve you quite easily if you think hard enough about it. Or you watch/read the right bit of vampiric fiction that's out there.
Games of all kinds are certainly no stranger to the vampire. From the very rad table-top RPG Vampire: The Masquerade to the long-running classic video game series Castlevania, the more suave side of the undead have had ample time to branch out across the interactive medium and make themselves comfy. The results have been... varied, sure, but with the Castlevania series still kicking around and the popularity of horror games in recent years skyrocketing thanks to Youtube Let's Players, we could most likely continue to see vampires in games for a long, long time.
Nosferatu: The Wrath of Malachi does something unique and has a lot of good ideas. Unfortunately the end result is less-than-stellar. It's a mix of rogue-like dungeon crawling and Victorian vampire mythos using the legendary original screen vampire Nosferatu as it's main hook. Released back in 2003 by a Swedish developer called Idol FX, N:TWOM falls short of being a truly original gaming experience. Which is too bad, because there's a lot to like about it.
The pitch is a bit strange: you are a aristocrat in Victorian England tasked with rescuing your family from vampires and other dwellers of the night. Your battleground is a castle that, while on the outside looks similar everytime you boot up the game, is randomly generated upon every new game that's started. This alone is awesome, a first-person roguelike was enough to peak my interest at first. And the fact that you have to drive stakes into vampires' chests while fending off troll-looking creatures and hellhounds is pretty kickass if you ask me. You're also given a timelimit of ninety minutes to save your family from ol' Count Orlok.
Have I peaked your interest? Good, because that's kinda where the pros stop. The game has a lot of flaws that pretty much makes the act of playing it infuriating. The game gives you no sense of direction, making you rely solely on exploration. And I know that's a basic element of roguelike, but here it can be difficult to keep a grasp on where you are in the castle. Don't get me wrong, I like roguelikes, and the original NetHack is one of my favourite games ever. But here, the exploration is a bit... lacking. Now, while the graphics are dated, that's not something I have a problem with. But I do have a problem with the combat. My god, regardless of what weapon you choose to dispose baddies with, you'll have a ♥♥♥♥♥ of a time trying to slay trolls with your cane sword. The combat is wonky, indirect, and unsatisfying. The random generation is pretty cool, but it's hard to also tell when something is different from the last time you played. The variety is lacking, rooms look the same, and enemies seem like they can hit you way more easily than you can hit them.
I know this sounds like ♥♥♥♥♥ing. Maybe I'm just not the kind of person to play this game, that might be true. But what really kills me about this game in the end is the wasted potential. This idea is badass, I cannot tell you how cool I thought this concept for a game was. I genuinely tried to get invested in it, and I tried to forgive all the aforementioned flaws, but as I kept replaying, the law of diminishing returns came a-crashing down.
Folks, if any of this sounds tolerable for you, go for it. But I can't recommend it in the end.

Banner Saga is a real treat from former Bioware employees and the writing, tough decisions, and attachment to the story / characters is on par with earlier Bioware titles (KOTOR, Dragon Age: Origins). The game is a mash-up of Bioware storytelling, Oregon Trail-like treks, and fairly deep turn-based rpg combat (Final Fantasy Tactics, Disgaea). The treks transverse a fantasy nordic realm and you have to deal with having enough food for your soldiers / civilians, encountering hazards, and sometimes deviating from the "main" route. Visually they were inspired by Disney's Sleeping Beauty and the nordic soundtrack compliments the awesome landscapes and story well. There is some voice-over work, but nearly all the dialog is text.
I backed this game on Kickstarter and I'm happy to say the game has surpassed my expectations. To be clear, this is Chapter 1 of a trilogy Stoic has planned and additional chapters will not be free. My first playthrough lasted a little over 14 hours and I felt the journey was fulfilling and satisfying, while still wanting to continue the narrative. I can see myself replaying the story once or twice again, since there were numerous choices I'd like to see pan out differently.
There is also a free-to-play multiplayer client, The Banner Saga: Factions, which features this game's combat and is worth a try imo.

YAY's:
- Great combat mechanics; emphasis on abilities and terrain/objects interaction.
- Beautiful graphics engine; vivid colors and nice particle effects.
- Good lengthy storyline/dialog with a quirky sense of humor.
- Excellent music, sound effects, and character voice-overs.
- Hot-join 2-player coop; party members can be reassigned.
- Dev studio that listens to the community and quickly patches.
- Toolkit to develop your own mods.
- Very limited player hand-holding (challenging enemies, no quest markers, no auto-crafting); may be a NAY for some?
NAY's:
- Interface (inventory management, spell bar, party grouping) is clunky.
- Character and weapon/armor aesthetics are lacking in variety.
- Requires a larger amount of customizable hotkeys.
Divinity: Original Sin is a love letter to earlier cRPGs like Ultima 7 or Baldur's Gate. Player characters are completely customizable, not pigeon-holed to a specific class. You can build whatever combination you desire, though some builds may be more effective than others. Combat is turn-based and individual battles may take as long as 20 minutes to finish. Battles are tough as you will typically be outnumbered. However, taking time to learn the mechanics is very rewarding and you will finish each battle feeling like a tactical genius. The game can be played single-player but the coop experience is where the game really shines. A friend can join your game at any point and control any character(s) that you assign to him/her. Larian Studios have been really stellar in quickly releasing patches and hotfixes post-release. This developer deserves your money. Buy this game.

Mirror's Edge is a very interesting game that while flawed in many fields still stands as a very colorful and unique title among many first person games. Now obviously there are many more reviews besides mine that will explain the gameplay, story, graphics, etc. I'll just tell you what I felt about the game. Personally the game is very nice to look at, its colorful in a seamingless empty city with mysteries behind every skyscraper, the city is a place in which I would greatly live in disregarding the politics and conflict that the game vaguely presents. Now I knew what most of the major events in the game where going to be due to spoiler game videos on YouTube which, I can admit, ruined the experience for me.
Gameplay sides is a game about free running/parkour, the movement mechanics are excelently well done and is very satisfying, the problem that I had with the running was the fact that the running feels slow when it should be fast and a continuos flow of movement. In Mirror's Edge you will die, a lot, mostly from minor mistakes or just being plain bad at the game in some parts (like me), that and falling off of things, and you will fall off a lot of things. What's interesting as well is that this game really caters to those who can play the game very well, it's fun when you are good but not so much fun when you are bad at it.
Besides that I recommend Mirror's Edge but what ever you do, buy it from a sale, the game is not worth purchasing at its current retail price of $20 with the game length spanning about 4-6 hours, yes its that short. As of writing this review being the 13th of June, 2015, I want to reflect on this game and it's upcoming sequel Nirror's Edge 2 which more will be revealed in the following E3 2015 event starting tomorrow. To me Mirror's Edge is more of a prototype/tech demo, a simple gameplay experiment to try something completely different that DICE (the developers) have never done before with a studio predominately known for making military shooters. It's the exact same thing with Portal, it was short, not so high of quality and try's to do something new, years later we get Portal 2 which expands everything from the first game, makes the game longer, fleshes out the story and increases the overall quality of the last and adds a bunch new things making the game more worthy of a $40 -$60 purchase. The same will happen with Mirror's Edge 2 with it being the Portal 2 of Mirror's Edge with better(should I say AMAZING)graphics, better gameplay, higher overall quality, much more fleshed out story and plot and a bunch more features added making the game worthy of a high price for purchase.

Quick Impressions (3 hours in):
This game is incredibly polished compared to most other games I've played recently.  It was developed on Kickstarter and the extra time and support the fan base's commitment to the developers has been Well rewarded with this creation.
I've played through the tutorial 'dungeon' and starting area, and got a pretty good feel for the mechanics, combat, and overall feel of the game.  If this game is as large as I've read it is, and if the detail and entertainment value hold up as highly as the first few hours have, this is going to be an instant classic.
Let's start off with what I liked most:
Graphics.   I have a pretty powerful pc, but have still had a few hitches on some recent games.  Not a single one on D:OS.  With the graphics cranked up to ultra the game is absolutely beautiful.  With spell effects and weather effects going off, everything runs smooth as silk, not a single stutter or slowdown.  The level of detail is very good, terrain, textures, animation, all excellent.  And the Attention to detail is also obvious.  You'll see exactly what I mean the first time you attempt to 'sneak' with one of your characters, LOL.
Sound.  Captivating musical score, excellent voice acting that actually sounds professionally produced and directed!   I've read elsewhere that not all interactions are voice-acted, but given how large a game this promises to be, I'm willing to forgive that.   The environmental ambient sounds add well to immersion.  Combat sounds are also good; solid and realistic.
Combat.  This is turn-based and right up my alley.  I've always preferred using tactics during combat and enjoy having the freedom to plan out my moves, rather than engaging in a mindless clickfest or spamming hotkeys until they cooldown.  While games like Diablo and Path of Exile have their merits,  it's refresing to discover that true turn based tactical combat models are still alive and kicking.
Character Development.  There are more classes to choose from starting out than most other rpgs offer, and one quickly discovers that these are really just starting templates,  as you have the option to fully customize any character into exactly the model you desire.  Some combinations will work better than others and discovering these can be a lot of fun.  In any case, many recent rpgs (especially mmos) have fallen into the trap of trying to 'balance' every character class, which only results in classes that are merely clones with minor asthetical differences.
Inventory and Crafting.  It's clear even from the start that there will be a Ton of options and items to collect and create while one travels through this game.  And it's also quite refreshing to play a game that doesn't throw too much 'uber' at you at once.   I compare this to Diablo 3, a game I really do enjoy, but whose loot system still feels broken and overpowered well after the lauded expansion.
And a few things I Did find fault with:
The User Interface is good for the most part, pretty standard fare, as you can see from the screenshots on the store page.  Menus and popups aren't difficult to navigate, but I did have some trouble with inventory management.  Nothing severe, just some issues with moving items from one character to another, finding particular books and recipes, that sort of thing.  It may just take some getting used to, but I was hoping for something a little more streamlined.
Camera controls:  Movement is acceptable, being basically a left click to move the selected character.   My main complaint is with the camera rotation.  Unless I'm missing something, it appears that the player is locked into a 90 degree arc that limits the actual ability to 'look around'.  The camera will only shift from Northwest to Northeast.  With occlusion in the dungeons and behind walls, this gets to be a little annoying.  Occluding terrain will turn transparent to show your your characters but objects and interactible characters can still be hidden sometimes until you move to and rotate the camera just right.  I have to wonder why they didn't just go with 360 rotation..
Those minor concerns aside, I still Highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys CRPGs.  The pluses far outweigh the negatives and the price is absolutely right ($40 is a Bargain for a quality game these days!).  If you'd like to engage in some good old school fantasy roleplaying that channels the pen & paper spirit of Baldur's Gate, mixes in some epic gameplay ala Diablo 3 and tops it all off with the high level tactical combat of XCOM and Jagged Alliance, do yourself a favor and buy this game.

Quick summary if you don't want to read a review- it's up to par with the other Walking Dead games, but it's not the best one by any means.
Pros:
1.) It's Michonne. This is more of a personal bias, but I just absolutely love Michonne as a character in the comics. And they did the character justice. I prefer keeping her silent through the game, as plenty of characters can take her silent gestures as a response. A+.
2.) The QTE system is new and improved. While it's really only a minor change, the black bars added to the action sequences help the player prepare for a quick response rather than catching them off guard leading to a cheap death. This doesn't mean the QTEs have gotten easier, though. The direction and button prompts on the screen have definitely gotten more thematic.
3.) The action sequences have only gotten more badass. Fitting, since the main character is Michonne, but in the past, TWD's action has been somewhat lame in my opinion. The opening sequence is a glorious use of hallucinations and flashbacks in action, and it actually even develops Michonne's character. Take notes, David Cage!
Cons:
1.) Some of the new characters' voice acting is somewhat lackluster to say the least. For instance,
, and Sam appears to be doing her best Mark Wahlberg from The Happening impression. While Michonne's voice acting is EXACTLY how I envisioned, the other characters' voice acting is still not up to par with some of the supreme voice acting of the previous seasons.
2.) The story is weak. Think of every trope you could find in a zombie story, and throw it in. Tyrannical leader with a false dichotomy of morals? Check! Poor, helpless stragglers? Checkerooni. Pointless undeveloped character death? Absolutely check that box. Disappointing for a game from Telltale, the new adventure game pioneers.
3.) Lack of any character development, as previously stated. You learn nothing about any of the characters EXCEPT Michonne, which I guess is better but my motivations were solely based on Michonne and how it would be best for her to just get out of the situation and head home. And even the character development for Michonne is somewhat weak, given that the very first choice, while harrowing, is utterly meaningless.
In conclusion, I would recommend this to fans of the previous TWD games. However, if you're a new player, go back and play the first two seasons and 400 Days first. It's up to par by TTG's standards, but I had so much more in mind. I suppose we'll have to wait for that ultimate TWD quality until Season 3.

Before anything else, for anything under $45, this game is worth it hands down. After a few days of playing (26h) I beat all sidequests and the main story, but there's still tons of challenges to do.
Let's run a pros and cons list
Pros
+Good crafting system.
+Great freerunning. Movement just feels right.
+Good environment that never felt old.
+Still afraid to go out at night.
+The developers are pretty good people #drinkrightdyinglight
+Doesn't rely on too many jump scares, although some are present.
+Brutal kill sequences are pretty satisfying on zombies.
+Interiors are intense and scary.
There may be more cons than pros since I have some specific grievances but don't let that detract from an amazing world.
Cons
-The story was eh
-There's an enemy that blows up when it gets close to you. It can sense you through walls. It is often located just out of sight around a cornor. A bunch of unavoidable instadeaths is never a good idea Techland.
-The grappling hook could be a little glitchy, but in fairness, it's a big world and that had to be difficult to get to work as much as it does.
-It is incredibly difficult to climb downwards. Falling or climbing up? Smooth as silk.
-The final boss is just a quicktime event. Very anticlimactic.
-While there is a fast travel port between two areas located in the two major bases of the game, nobody tells you that, and it's very easy to miss.
-Had some mild issues with some flickering with crossfired 7770s, but I could easily play through.
-There were a few issues with slopes and some ledges being unclimbable, but it's understandable with an open world. Plus you get a sense of what you can and can't climb very quickly.
-A lot of buildings had no interior, which is to be expected and is not dissapointing in itself, but it's difficult to see which ones do have interiors when out gathering supplies.
-None of the characters stood out.
Overall this game gets a solid 8/10 from me, despite the issues listed, because I bought this game to run around like an idiot killing zombies. The world itself was rich and well designed, which made even random errands fun.
Incredibly fun and casual. Highly recommend for everyone.

Probably my favourite puzzle game ever.
What's so special about the game is that it actually messes with your mind, rather than only trying to do so.
The puzzles are incredibly well designed and never feel unfair, while they are still challenging.
Whenever you get stuck at a certain puzzle, you can take a step back and try clearing another room.
Essentially this means it is unlikely to really get stuck somewhere, because you can simply walk away.
This pretty much keeps the game at a reasonably high pace, at least for what it is.
The only downside in my opinion, is that the final series of rooms get incredibly easy once you have unlocked the red gun.
This made the final parts feel a bit anticlimactic, rather than a puzzle in which all your gained knowledge has to be used.
All things considered, I would give this game 9/10.
If you are at least mildly interested after watching the trailer, you won't be disappointed.

In my opinion Antichamber deserves the same level of recognition that heavy hitters like The Talos Principle and the Portal franchise have achieved and it is well worth a play if you are fans of those games.

XCOM: Enemy Unknown is a Turn-Based Strategy game centering on squad-level tactics. You are in command of XCOM, an organization devoted to fighting off the threat of alien invaders. Your mission is to protect the Earth from this invasion, stopping alien abductions, terror attacks on population centers, and otherwise keeping everyone from panicking and defunding your project, gradually accumulating superior weapons and technology from the aliens so that you have a fighting chance.
Overall, the game is quite strong; the macro-level stuff is fairly addictive in its skinner-box techniques as there is always something new which is going to come just around the corner, and the combat-level stuff works well enough, though it is not perfect either. On the whole, it really makes you want to play through the whole game, though at the very end of the game it may end up feeling a bit strange; there comes a point at which you are really in control of the situation and the earlier desperation goes away, and about that same point the research starts really drying up, meaning that if you take too long to finish the game, it could potentially get a bit dry; the last couple missions before I beat the game were the weakest in the game simply because I had figured it out and there was little threat from the game at that point.
Still, I played through and beat the game in three or four sittings, which is always a sign that a game has you hooked.

A modernized Planescape:Torment retaining morally ambiguous problems/solutions, but opting for the tried-and-true save-the-world plot and a more classic setting populated by familiar fantasy races. It has a creative co-op implementation and turn based combat.
Two main player characters (PCs) are created to be dual protagonists in the story. Naturally, others can be recruited in-game. The PCs may occupy one party and even have player guided/role-played disputes with one another. Or during co-op, each player controlling one protagonist, they may choose to embark in separate parties and, if there are disputes, they are handed with rock/paper/scissors where relevant PC skills weight the balance. This mechanic makes the the game seamless between single/multi player and is fun both ways! Plus the game supports LAN, Steam and direct cross-platform IP connections for multiplayer. They also seem to have designed it to be user friendly for custom made campaigns.
Combat proceeds one actor at a time, with stats dictating the order. Action points, also calculated from stats, restrict what you may do in any one turn. My twohander wielding knight is a front line powerhouse and is backed up by my mage/wizard. Skill selection is completely free (no classes restrict your point allocations) but you should pay attention to the many synergies between skills. For instance, I can summon an oil slick to slow down enemies with my geomancer spell and then set it on fire with my pyromancer spell. The flare spell can also dry off an actor that was wet, preventing them from being frozen by a chill status effect, or it can detonate volatile environmental hazards. Many other interactions are also possible, both with the environment and tactics with party members, during and outside of battle. It seems that every obstacle can be handled in many different ways, diplomatically, or just simply killing or avoiding it, if you're charismatic, strong or witty enough... Except when you wander into an area far outside your level, despite the warnings against doing so--then you just get slaughtered.
The story progresses through myriad dialogues and choices during interactions with non PCs. This means lots of reading and, since there are no hand-holding quest markers, it also means paying attention and making notes on your map. There is some voice acting, but it's mostly for setting atmosphere and if an NPC repeats his line once too often for the nerves, just turn down the voices in the options. The writing is sober or sophisticated or silly or clever or funny depending on the encounter. But sometimes the encounters don't update to reflect the order things were done in--the doctor was still explaining to me how I might help his assistant, when only a moment before I had completed the task, as was reported by lightning bolts and fireworks in the next room; you'd think that would have tipped him off. But to expect Larian to account for every possible nuance like this in the text may be expecting too much. Though, Torment managed that very well, which is still something hard to believe. Maybe I'm just not remembering its incongruities through a veil of nostalgia?
I was a tiny bit disappointed that I had to dial back the graphics settings to get a smooth experience on my, admittedly old, i5+Radeon5830 laptop, but I can still play in a nice 1600x900 resolution, and fonts seemed to scale to be easily readable at any resolution. In any case, it looks great, is well executed and is extremely fun. I'm looking forward to playing much more of it!

A gorgeous art style, witty dialogue, and some solid mechanics help make the Banner Saga something to sink hours on end into. The Banner Saga is a beautiful story-driven turn-based strategy game/RPG lasting about 8-12 hours. Overall, I thought it was a great experience and would recommend it to anyone who enjoys tactical strategy games like Fire Emblem and XCOM. Its major strengths are its fantastic art, reminiscent of classic Disney or Don Bluth animated films, good soundtrack, and relatively challenging and compelling battles. My primary complaint with the game is that its story is told in a bit of an exhausting way with a ton of dialogue that's not easy to care about, and I was really ready for the game to end a few hours before it actually did. Also, the game feels episodic and I'd imagine more content is on the horizon. If that's the case, I really feel like the experience didn't need to be as padded out with so many seemingly same-y towns and encounters. Still, The Banner Saga is a really ambitious title and one of the better strategy games I've played in recent memory (and certainly the most visually striking).

Episode 1 PROS:

The tension is still there and Michonne is a really cool character. She seems so hardened by life but there are brief moments where she is a bit less so. I have no context for her outside of this game but I'm really liking her so far.
Episode 1 CONS:
The game ran slightly less than perfect for me but I am running this on my laptop (my desktop is out of commission for the moment) so it could just be that. I have a Win7 i3 with 8gb Ram and the intel integrated graphics. Its not great for gaming by any means but I've played FF6,7, Shovel Knight, Bastion, and Flame in the Flood on this laptop without a hitch. So what issues did I have exactly? I had occasional framerate problems where it would stutter and voices did not match the lips. Nothing game breaking but it did pull me out of the game whenever it happend which was occassionally or less.
Verdict:
I would recommend Episode 1 but ideally on a better system than my laptop, perferably one with a dedicated graphics card.

A very good and entertaining episode that helps add some backstory to one of the best Walking Dead characters. Whilst still very familiar to anyone who has played a Telltale game before, this episode has done a great job improving the animations and overall visual quality of the game, which has been one of my main issues with previous games these developers have made.  Whilst the story is very familiar and isn't very long for a first episode, it has a few intense scenes and choices, and Michonne's character makes every minute of it really enjoyable.
If you're a fan of the Walking Dead or other Telltale games (their previous Walking Dead games in particular) you should really consider giving this one a try.

I'm going to say first and foremost: that the music, atmosphere and carefully crafted scapes are immediately engrossing.  Within a short time of learning the basics and running through the tutorial,  The game compels a very nuanced degree of giddy adnventure and stark contrast of savagery against a simple but gorgeous dated animation-syle. I found the frosty environs of the detailed backgrounds and low-tones of overtures welling a sense of frigid cold and prideful bitterness in me.  A stoutness that has driven me to delve further into the story.  I love this game ...
Let's just get the nit-picks out of the way.  Though I am immediately smitten with the game, I stumble through the text-dialogue at times, as it lacks a consistent flow.  Strange wording and grammer choices throw me around every now and then.  This tends to break immersion, but given that, I'm still logging hours in the title.  As for the interface, it can be mildly to moderately frustrating.  My frustrations seem to mount over extended play until a boiling point is achieved.  I often find myself struggling to direct the mouse over the proper tile, or scrmabling to click the proper reticule.  If the game wasn't turn-based or included timing-based elements, I'd probably drive my head into the edge of a counter-top to relieve the strain.  The animated sequences of story are too far apart, which is a shame given that the flowing sequences are abso-goddamn-lutely beautiful.  All-in-all, that's not even close to enough to really knock the game over.
Aside from quibbles with the controls, I am completely stricken dumb by the gameplay.  The inventory and class structures are simplistic, almost minimalist, but in a diversity of classes and materials the game shines.  The battles aren't sweeping thrash-metal explosions, but cruciall and hard engagements of suffering the betweens of a rock and a hard-place.  Some stages leave me swelling with a barbaric sense of superiority as I lay waste to my opposition, but frequently and easily the game pushes the player into almost feeling helpless at points.  The tiny combinations of the limited characters, items and promotions lends to the strategy of the engagements in the campaign.  I'm pressed between the smallest of choices, that often spell grand victory or horrific disaster for my party and its individuals.  An affair I'm not well-adjusted to, as over the years the shellshock of skill-trees, upgrades and endless xp grinds found in other titles I am too busy managing unlocks and minutia rather than focusing on the deciding battles of the storyline.  The Banner Saga excels in forcing my attentions elsewhere with its minimalist approach and striking visuals.  A fact that I am grateful for, the change in pace, environments and stylization is a welcomed experience.

UPDATED FOR EPISODE 2
AS OF EPISODE 1
The Walking Dead: Michonne is yet another great Telltale Game. It isn't perfect, and isn't the best, but for those who love Telltale like I do, I'm sure you'll enjoy it. NOTE: I have beat it twice to experience both sides (Good/Evil/Alternate).
PROS:
-More Walking Dead: If you liked The Walking Dead, I guarantee you will like this game. It feels just like the others and is another thrill ride.
-Michonne: They freaking nail Michonne. Telltale has done it again, delving deep into the beloved character and keeping her fresh and exciting.
-The intro sequence: Just play it. It's fantastic.
CONS:
-Story: Now what In Too Deep really messed up on was it's antagonists. While retaining some originality, TWD: Michonne steps dangerously close to previous WD plotlines, and I know a lot of people were disappointed. In my opinion, I didn't think it was that bad, but it COULD get worse in future episodes.
-Cloud Save: As of 2/24/16, cloud save is not functioning, and won't save progress once the game shuts down.
Final Score: 7/10 - Good
AS OF EPISODE 2
Episode 2 comes back fierce in a fantastic penultimate episode. Improving upon In Too Deep's flaws, Give No Shelter is a great second part. NOTE: I have beat it twice to experience both sides (Good/Evil/Alternate)
PROS:
-Michonne: Michonne's character development is absolutely fantastic. Diving more into Michonne's past and her inner feelings is a thrill the entire way through.
-Choice Diversity: The further in this game, the more different it gets. You can choose whether multiple people live or die, who comes with you, and all bear different dialogue and changes with them. Your choices legitimately feel yours.
-Story: I was completely engaged the entire episode. Unlike the similarities E1 had with S2, this episode manages to hold its own gloriously.
-Flashback Scene: More insight on Michonne's past and people she knew. It was great.
(Also Cloud Save is fixed. Hooray.)
CONS:
-Length: This episode is only an hour long. Though I'd like to have more, I'm generally unfazed. You know what they say, quality over quantity.
Final Score: 9/10 - Amazing

Might this be a zombie-game worth buying you might be thinking. If you like zombies, the answer is probably yes. Zombies has always been my favourite genre in videogames and about half of my games sets me in the apocalypse. This game however offered me an experience other zombiegames failed to deliver. MOTHER♥♥♥♥♥♥ DROPKICKING FROM A ROOF!
Zombies, and parkour is a quite unique combination but works very well. The designers has achieved a great balance between kick♥♥♥♥♥zombie action and a very smooth parkour system which supports every move you make. That is probably the best thing about this game. The movement is so accurate. I will now try my best to summarize my thoughts in an original pros and cons list:
Pros
+Amazing parkour system which is difficult to find on the same level in other similar games. 9/10
+Good variety between the different zombies you will have to deal with throughout the game. You will find anything from sneaky little ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s hunting you down from afar to tanky, clumpsy giants ready to smash you down. This dissables your ability to adapt and learn about the enemy as they all behave differently. Even though there is a variety, I feel like most of the ideas are very straight on copied from other developers. 7/10
+Great graphics, of course. But I have seen better. Honestly, in this type of game there should be alot more focus on gameplay, which they have succeeded with. 7/10
+Loot system is also something quite different here. I love how you have to take the risk of going out of the safesone just to get to that airdrop or that crate you spotted earlier. It makes you feel independent, and by that I mean you have to make choices, and not as the character you are playing as but yourself. Great job. 9/10
+Story is ok I guess. I haven't made it very far into the game yet (but sure do I enjoy it) and there doesn't seem to be a very deep telling about how the world got to this..♥♥♥♥♥♥ The story is more like thrilling, which they paired perfectly with the rest of the game. If you want a game where you look at the credits and think about the characters decisions, you are at the wrong store page. 6/10
Cons
-Takes a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of processing power. Do note that this is nothing the developers made a bad job with. It means that if you don't have a good pc enough, playing this game will become very difficult.
-Overall bad planning with the weapons. The fact that your weapon will do up to 60% less damage (I'm guessing) when overused. It gets passively annoying when you have to look for metal parts instead of bashing some zombies. This feature is being brought from Dead Island which even there made me grouchy.
-In my opion unclear where you find your equipment. You can access five different menus just to equip some damn firecrackers. Two menus would have been enough. One for weapons, and one for items.
Overall feeling
Once again, beutifully done with the parkour system. If you don't like zombie games, you might still enjoy the freerunning, which is packed with a ton of action. Another thing you realise in this game is that you are bound to "the tower". This is your base, your safezone and your home. Leaving it is something that is risky, but necessary. Enjoy the zombie splatting at daytime and look out the window for a minute at night, while feeling safe. Ready to go out the next day.
I recommend this game for sure. Also, excuse me for most inappropriate mis-use of the English language, for my tounge is not well suited for this type of writtenl expression :-). Thank you for reading my rewiew

What an unbeliveably bad game. I bought this for around three euros in the sales and I still feel short-changed.
It's one of those games that's difficult simply for the sake of being difficult. You can tell that the designers just ran out of ideas on how to make the game properly challenging and just jacked the difficulty curve up. This game is set up to annoy and frustrate the player, the random teleporting suicide squads who came out of no-where (from no ship) were a prime example of this.
It's a game for those who think that difficulty is the same as (or a good substitute for) a challenging task, in other words, morons. It was pitched to me by a friend who said: "You can play it perfectly and STILL lose!", when I asked him how on earth that could constitute into a good game he just told me "I didn't get it", and he's right I don't get the whole "Dying the part of the fun!" bit. No; Dying is not fun in a game! Especially not when I've been playing for a good hour and It gets dropped on me that I've to kill the final boss three times! (or more, i don't know, as I'm not bothering with this crap anymore)
It's a game that encourages you to grind through the levels (their words exactly) even though the constant dying means any items you get will be gone at the restart. There very little variety in the action, after a few hours you'll have encountered most of the scenarios you're ever going to. It VERY quickly gets really boring. Soon you'll be able to spot the points where you know you don't have a chance if the game progresses and you'll end up just hitting restart rather then try and grind a decent item for the next half hour only to just die anyway.
What really annoys me is that this game really could've been great, if they'd just added more variety and toned down the stupid difficulty level. This really could've one of those games that takes years off your life and you loving it.
If you are one of those weirdos who loved Dark Souls simply because the game was impossible to beat and that's what kept you grinding through it like water torture then this is the game for you. If you're sane and/or have taste save yourself time and use the money to buy a girl you like a coffee. Even if you crash and burn it'll give you more of a thrill than this game.....
