Original review:
Demon Peak is a faithful-to-SNES-capabilities Metroidvania-style game where you play a nameless demon samurai journeying to the top of, well, Demon Peak. Honestly there's not a lot of story to be had in the game and that's fine, because it would probably be dumb and just get in the way anyway.
Let me start out by saying that the game is significantly flawed. In fact, before I get into the meat of the issues let me note that this game is not at this time marked as Early Access. It really, really should be. I soft-locked the game twice, and  I actually found a marker in a secret area that seemed to be a reminder for the developer to add a shop in that area. Overall, the quality of things is a little inconsistent, and the game is sorely lacking a final polish pass.
Some of that lack of polish might be due to the game's almost-slavish faithfulness to the capabilities of 16-bit game console hardware, though. The music is straight out of an SNES game, SPC700-style. The visuals are pixel art but the sprites are on the whole fantastic, and the environment detail work ranges from competent to excellent. The environments themselves could use some work; it's a bit strange how most of the time, so much of the screen is taken up by empty black void outside of the play area. Some more intelligent viewport control could have helped with that.
The consistency issues extend into the gameplay. Sometimes you can attack faster than other times and it's not always clear why. Some enemies can be dashed through, while others can't. Sometimes a given enemy will kill you almost instantaneously, while other times it will only slightly damage you. I fought a major boss (bosses have a big red lifebar at the bottom of the screen) and sometimes I could stand inside it and whack away, while other times touching any part of it killed me almost instantly. It's not a constant problem, but when these issues crop up they can be pretty frustrating.
While I'm talking about the game's flaws, let me bring up the biggest one: the movement. The player character in Demon Peak runs fast. Very fast. Sonic the Hedgehog fast. This is awesome when it's working for you, because it feels great in combat and in some areas. Much of the game is fairly precise platforming, though, and there's a sort of simulated inertia to the movement that doesn't feel like inertia, it feels like you're constantly in an ice level. The game is slippy and it's hard to move with precision. I've taken ten seconds just to exit a save room because I can't get positioned in front of the door.
So that's a lot of issues, but don't let the above scare you off. The movement can be mastered with a little effort and the rest of the controls are really solid. The combat is fluid and precise, and surprisingly technical. Attacks can be high or low, like a fighting game, as can your (and enemies'!) guard, which reminded me of Zelda II. You end up with a fair range of options, and you can blend light sword attacks and heavy hammer attacks without having to swap weapons. Shortly after the beginning of the game, you get a shield, and you can use it to block or parry enemy blows.
You don't change weapons or equipment, or anything like that, though. This game is much shallower than say, Symphony of the Night or Valdis Story: Abyssal City. In fact, comparing it to those games is sort of unfair because it's just not the same kind of game really. It's a simpler title that yearns for an earlier era.
The title I can most readily compare it to is Super Metroid, although it's deeper than that game by a fair whack. There are also comparisons to be made to Dark Souls, as it clearly draws inspiration from that title in many elements. The theming, the overall structure, and the "you will die a thousand deaths" difficulty all remind of From Software's dark fantasy epic. As I mentioned above, it lacks the RPG mechanics and equipment of that game, and eschews them for a Metroid-style powerup hunt with open exploration and reasons to re-visit past areas. I wish there were more to the game, but then, it was only $4. (Regular price $5.)
The price is ultimately why I'm giving this game a thumbs-up. It is not a great game, it's not even really a good game. But it's definitely not a BAD game, and it has some aspects (like the sprite art) that are really outstanding. The developers say they're going to keep working on it too, so hopefully it will improve into something really great.
In short, if you like 2D action games like classic Ninja Gaiden, Shinobi, and Castlevania titles, pick up Demon Peak and give it a shot. Here's a few tips:
—Try backdashing while attacking, instead of blocking or just tanking the hits. This is especially useful against the little beast enemies that bum rush you.
—You can "just guard" or "parry" enemy attacks using the shield with good timing. This even works on things you wouldn't necessarily expect to be able to parry. Parrying ranged attacks sends them back at the attacker!
—The spear is a utility tool, and has limited use as a weapon. You can stand on it after you stick it in the wall.
—Don't be afraid to just leap over an enemy, instead of trying to fight it straight up.
—Enemies can damage each other! Bait the mage enemies' magic blasts into their friends.

can be a serviceable Metroidvania game but I would recommend waiting for few patches to get the optimal experience. Right now the game has a lot of glitches and developers seem to have forgotten to put items in some of the hidden chests. I actually killed the first boss with 1 hit (probably not intended). Most of the problems are easy fixes so I'll give the developers a chance to address it before I burn them with fire. Once you unlock couple powers the combat feels enjoyable enough but I think the biggest concern here is the amount of content. The game is 4-5 hours (much of it is backtracking) although you can also play New Game+ that has your stats carried over.
(I replayed the game in Patch 1.1 and 90% of the glitches are fixed. Not gona rewrite the whole review but the game is in decent state. Win7 x64)
The character starts with few moves which makes  a bad first impression .However, like with most games in this genre, you will find a lot more powers and upgrades overtime. Most of them are new moves and not just stat increases.Default dash controls are a little awkward but you can switch them in options to a more common set up. I think it plays fluidly once you get use to timing special skills .Most of the enemies can be beaten tactically if you know their weakness. There is only one enemy that just shreds HP bar regardless of how you play so developers will need to fix that.
There are 4 bosses and 3 of them were very disappointing. I just did not feel like I had to use strategy for them. Perhaps developers need to rethink the hitboxes and balancing so I am not potion chugging for the win.
Well, you start with only a jump & dash which is limiting. You will eventually find double-jump and few other mobility moves like fly-kick that will improve gameplay. I really like that you can get a spear-shoot power and then use the spear as a step. It certainly opens some interesting puzzle scenarios. Platforming gameplay was alright but they could have done a lot more with the idea.
I got to say that environments and stage design are mostly generic. It is just a couple caves with few different colors and little detail. I kinda assumed that caves were the first area of a bigger world but that was the whole game. Out of the few Metroidvania games that I played this might actually be the worst one in stage variety. There are some secrets around the map that have items and shrines that increase stats or give new powers.

The soundtrack was hit and miss for me. I liked a few songs and few other were just kinda there to fill in the gaps. You could argue that it does not fit the tone of the game. Also, it feels like the game does not have enough sound effects. Definitely not remarkable as a whole. As far as pixel art I have no problem with animation of the character or enemies. I just wish  the environment had more detail.
Demon Peak seems very promising in the first few hours until you realize it's all you get. Overall it was not great but I enjoyed my time with it. The core gameplay is decent enough to expand so it all depends on how far developers will take it. Patch 1.1 fixed most of the problems so I bumped score from 6 to 7.

Saints Row has progressed a lot from the days of the first Saints Row when it was an unabashed GTA clone. Okay, to start, I did mostly enjoy playing this game... but there are some things that need to be discussed and reasons I wouldn't recommend this to a friend. To summarize, the game is not ready to be released. There are a plethora of bugs that are nearly inexcusable when selling a "completed" game. Not only bugs, but also game design decisions. I'll make this a simple pro/con list. (Although it says 8 hours played, I beat the game in less than 5. At least 3 hours were AFK in menus).
Pros:
+ Very nostalgic Castlevania feel
+ Good art
+ Multiple usable items/skills that can be unlocked
+ Good enemy variety
Cons:
- Some chests (the "rare" ones) are empty. You will not be rewarded for finding some of the rarest chests in the game.
- Incorrect map programming. There will be multiple zones of the map where you exit a room and end up 2 rooms away instead of the correct room.
- Missing/Poor textures. Some platforms don't have textures yet and hidden walls underwater have a very awkward texture that makes them stick out like a sore thumb.
- The weakest enemies in the game are some of the strongest and will make the first few minutes very frustrating.
- Bosses are way too easy... I beat the final boss without much of a problem while only having beaten one other boss (I didn't even need this). When I beat the boss, I only had like one health upgrade and one stamina upgrade.
- Although there are many skills, your main auto attack, double-jumping (unlocked) and health potions are all you need to beat the game. Literally.
- Enemies don't have anything to fight against your "cheese". Almost every enemy in the game can be "cheesed"... except for the first/weakest mob in the game and their upgraded counterpart. They are the only difficult enemies because of their extreme speed, damage, and inability to be read.
- There appears to actually be "debug" stuff left in the game. Invisible portals, "notes" for where merchants should be... not sure if these were debug tools, but they didn't add anything to the game.
- There's actually a point in the game where you can soft lock by getting stuck in a room if you don't have the ground smash yet. You'll have to quit the game and load back in to your last save.
- The soundtrack. I muted the music in the first 5 minutes and played my own music. The music does not fit the game at all. If there are better songs later in the game... then that might be nice. But I doubt it.
So, if the game actually required me to defeat all of the sub-bosses before the final boss, that'd make the game much more enjoyable. If all the bugs I mentioned were fixed, that'd also help. If the  last boss required anything more than the main auto attack, double jump, and health potions... that'd also be nice.

SAINTS ROW IV is the greatest alternative to seriousness. It stands directly in opposition to "serious games" that cover "serious issues," principally GRAND THEFT AUTO and the MASS EFFECT franchise. Lovingly, it reminds you how fun videogames can be, and loving takes potshots at its more serious peers. It's a love letter to videogames, written on stationary covered in farts and purple ♥♥♥♥♥♥.
The plot is utter nonsense, but the game commits to that nonsense so earnestly that it drags you in and makes you want to go along for the ride.
Like all long-running franchises, SAINTS ROW IV is an ensemble piece. It surrounds you with memorable characters who may not mean as much to you as Garrus or Bonnie MacFarlene, but Kinzie, Ben King, Vice President Keith David, and the rest are a constant and consistent source of laughter, and when their lives are put in Jeopardy, it matters to you, because you really don't want your good times to end.
SAINTS ROW IV leaves me with high hopes for whatever future there is for the franchise (and there almost certainly will be a future with those sales numbers). At this point, there are infinite possiblities for where we could go and what we could do. No longer a gangster game, SAINTS ROW IV embraces its anything goes nature, Dubstep gun clutched in hand, and has cemented its place in videogaming as the best damn time you're liable to have.

The Gods are Dead.
The lands of The Banner Saga are desolate and barren, the sun hang motionless in the sky, men speak of the end of days as death marches from the north. Stoic has made a game that is just like the land it is based in, stark, cold and beautiful.
That beauty is the very first thing you will see when you begin your march in the banner saga. Half the time I was playing The Banner Saga I could not believe what I was looking at, the hand drawn feel and look of classic Disney or the better bits of ‘80s animation.  The aesthetic plays into gameplay as well, with the banner over your party getting bigger as your caravan gets bigger and as you accomplish what you can along your very hard journey. Characters and character classes have distinct looks which helps keep the many characters straight and to pick out what type of enemy you were fighting.
The only place that the art slightly falls down is in the arenas that you spend a good chunk of your time in over the course of the game. They are simple grids, sometimes in interesting locations, other times in just fields of snow. There is no topography to the maps, which is good for keeping battles from getting too complex, but doesn’t help with battle variety.
Tactical RPG battles are only part of the experience, but are quite important to the experience as a whole. The system brings some interesting mechanics to the tRPG genre while dropping some others. The central mechanic is built around managing two stats on both friends and foe over the course of a battle, Armor and Strength. Strength is interesting in that, it is both your health and how hard a character can hit. The more damage done to a character the less damage they can deal. That is where armor becomes important, blocking damage to strength and allowing characters to stay in battle. Being smart with how you balance your approach to the many fights that the game puts in your path will make impossible seeming battles, just barely winnable.

Unit selection also plays a major role in The Banner Saga with not just character class mattering, but also character race. The game has two playable races, humans and Varl. Varl are half man half animal giants that take up four squares on the battle grid instead of one, they hit harder, but are far less mobile. Humans are smaller and can take less hits, but can pester enemies and make it possible to chase certain types of enemies down.
Unlike some other games in the genre such as XCOM The Banner Saga does not feature permadeath in battles, but instead characters can be lost in a much more interesting way, your choices outside of battle.
Story in The Banner Saga is second only to its art. The story is told from multiple perspectives, as characters deal with a world descending into chaos as an old enemy “the Dredge” a race of obsidian creatures invades from the north. The perspective shifts between an Varl Army and refugees fleeing from the dredge. I loved the contrast of the campaign trail  of the well stocked army of Varl Warriors as it marches home with the prince of man to solidify a long held treaty. You are never short on supplies or warriors and, while a few characters can die, you will mostly be losing faceless stats of Varl and human warriors.
In contrast Rook the main character of the refugee campaign, and the main focus of the games story, has a much harder story, that is also full of much more interesting choices. Every choice you make is a pyrrhic victory, either making life harder for yourself or the caravan. On the run from “the dredge” you never feel like you have enough supplies to make it to the next town, which may not even be there anymore, or may be hostile to outsiders. Choices made early in the story, may crop up later as double crosses and or loss of supplies or even characters that you have invested a lot of time and resources on.
Almost not choices that you have to make as Rook are easy, even small choices may have big consequences.  Even the meta game choices when you stop in town may effect the over all game for you, for example: the main resource in the game is renown, you gain renown from battle and certain actions outside of battle. Renown is treated as both a currency and experience for your party members, leaving you with the choice of feeding your caravan, so that you have enough men to make it to the next town, or leveling up your party so that you have a chance of surviving the next encounter.  And the game is ready to knock you down emotionally Game of Thrones style by having smaller seeming choices cost you a fully leveled character, just remember, be careful of who you trust.
Overall The Banner Saga is a beautiful game that has a few issues in gameplay, but most of that is  settled out by having some the most accessible gameplay in the genre. Its story is dark, and leaves you with choices that are as interesting and difficult as choice made in any game before. I want the next chapter and I want it now after the dark and stark ending of the first chapter of this saga.

Steam has dropped it's quality control over the past months and again this game is a clear proof of that. Nyctophobia offers little to nothing to my personal interest while poorly taking elements from other similar games in the same genre. The game uses Unity, so graphics-wise you can't expect anything very pretty. Length wise it lasts about 30 minutes, which has an annoying perma-death throughout most of the game. Does it make it challenging? Yes. Is it entertaining? No.
The only difficulty in this game is literally finding batteries which last about 30 seconds. The mechanics are complete nonsense. Honestly I can't even call this a horror game. The only horror element is darkness, therefore you have a flashlight. There's no jumpscares, there's barely any creatures at all to scare you. All you get is a shadow thing that doesn't appear until the end section who calls himself the Keeper, you get a weird zombie sitting on a table who gets an epileptic attack when you enter said house, also he doesn't attack you. Oh and who could forget the skeleton on the end of the boat section that is downright laughable. I'm usually very sensible to horror and find myself getting scared with the most little things even in the worst games, but this one had absolutely nothing, honestly it doesn't even try to scare you.
I feel like this game is also missing any sense of proportion at all. Sometimes things like ladders are just too big, it feels like the game character is a midget sometimes. As I've stated, the main game last 30 minutes at most, the story makes no sense but since it's a horror game that's totally okay. The sound effects and soundtrack are so out of place, sometimes there's a music building up to... nothing.
There's also another game mode that you get after beating the main one, it's called Own the Night. It adds about more 10 minutes of gameplay where you turn on some lights and kill zombies with the lights. The zombies (which are just a person fully painted in black with a worker jacket) sounds make the worst zombie sound I've ever heard in a game, ever. They literally sound like ghosts effects from a children's movie or something.
The negatives obviously beat the positives in this game, if you get Nyctophobia for free, try it out and get some laughs of it, but don't think about spending money on this game. 2/10.

Episode One of The Walking Dead: Michonne is brutal from the start. It's a short time from booting the game to curb stomping walkers into fires and quick-timing your way to gory decapitations. The action sequences are stylishly letterboxed, and even go into John Woo slow motion at times to highlight the deadly efficiency of the title character. This is Michonne after all; one of the most badass characters this side of a Segio Leone film, and the game admirably does her justice for the most part.
Aside from some flashbacks and hallucinations alluding to her past, you're thrust aboard a ship with little explanation or backstory, surrounded by characters you (as a player) don't really know. The game takes place during a certain time period in the comic books I'm not too familiar with, so the tie-ins/fan service were lost on me. But that's fine, as I was more than willing to just enjoy the journey the game wanted me to take. The story starts as a simple scavenging/rescue mission at a beached ferry, where you uncover some unsettling signs of nefarious♥♥♥♥♥♥going down. It's not long before you're predictably captured and taken to a Walking Dead signature settlement lead by a larger-than-life personality. And, rather predictably again, you're singled out and taken to have a face-to-face confrontation with said leader in a dialogue driven “boss battle”.
Yeah, Michonne can be structurally formulaic at times. If you're completely burnt out on the Telltale style of games this probably isn't the one to get you back on board. The same can be said about the graphics, as well: yep, it's still the same engine, and it can still get janky at times. Gripes aside, I think it still works incredibly well for this comic book style presentation. When it works it can look stunning, and when it breaks it's usually pretty minor. There's certainly more creativity and style here than the previous Walking Dead seasons, with some unconventional camera angles and an opening with some Wolf Among Us inspirations.
Playing as an emotionally unstable character leads to some noteworthy moments. I played Machonne as a strong, silent type... because she's Machonne and that seemed like the thing to do. As the brief, pre-outbreak flashbacks allude to her familial downfall without bogging the game down in exposition that can gleamed elsewhere, you're also treated to a few mental breakdowns and moments of emotional emptiness that are quite effective. When Machonne says, “I've got nothing to lose” you know it's true and it makes her that much more dangerous and badass. When you're tasked with giving a♥♥♥♥♥♥about some of the supporting cast, however, the writing doesn't fare as well. The swelling music and story beats might be telling you to care about a heavy, dramatic moment involving some characters you just met a few minutes ago... but you won't. Same for the cartoon villains who may or may not be what the script and acting is strongly hinting towards... but it's quite heavy handed regardless.
“In Too Deep” is a great first chapter to what hopefully turns out to be a memorable game. If the forthcoming chapters take a nose dive it will be a damn shame. Because Machonne is a badass.

Not sure how to classify FTL in terms of genre or playstyle, as it's pretty unique. It's a roguelike space simulator where you control your crew and ship as you race through various solar systems towards the end game. An individual game maybe lasts an hour or two or until you die (can be much sooner), but while winning is the goal, trying out new tactics and combinations of weapons is the fun part of the game.
You control a few crew members in a ship with various parts. You can assign a crewman to pilot the ship, one to control the ship's shields, and have a third crew rotate between manning the weapons systems and doing ship repairs. When you get into a fight, your ship takes localized damage that interferes with your ship's functions in every way. Thus, combat is a game of maintaining your ship and taking out the enemy as quickly as possible to minimize the mayhem they cause. Sometimes your ship will be boarded and you'll have to determine how to kill the enemy crew who are breaking stuff and attacking your own crew while trying to destroy an enemy ship that is likely still shooting you. The game has a million tactical possibilities every playthrough and is wildly popular.
It's cheap, and if you've got enough patience to play a game where the journey is the enjoyment, not the ending, you'll probably like FTL.

Old but gold. Nosferatu is one of those horror games where you'll be walking in constant stress, checking and over-checking what's behind your back over and over again. It's the game where even the "easy" game difficulty might be over-the-head-hard for some of the new casual-breeded gamers. Where you can die from one hit and even just from too strong blood pressure! Yeah, there is a game mechanic which follows your stress level along with depleted stamina from sprint runs and melee fights. And you have to run, there is a timer ticking, with less than 2 hours to save your people from the overmighty vampires.. With all said, I'd like to highlight it again - it is the type of horror game where you can strike back. And if you're skillful enough, you can kill all the demons and save all the people, which, ultimately, makes you a hero. Not the start of the game makes you a hero, no, oh, Lord! Only your success!
Technically, the game aged fairly, but not perfectly. Yeah, the resolution is quite low. The visuals are obviously bad, you'll not find there any of all those flashy things gamedevs are using to earn people's attention by the book of Crytek, EA and other game producers who are all about money soaking. What's still there is just a solid gameplay of overcome-the-horror type. There are not so many good games in that sub-genre, and Nosferatu: the wrath of Malachi is still one of the best. So, I'd like to recommend this game to all people above the age of 12, who can bear the sword and the crucifix and overcome monsters lurking in the dark and always spawning on your back...
My mark is 8.2/10. Game's not perfect, sure, but it is still rock hard.

I think this is currently the best open world Skiing/Snowboarding Game out there.
Traverse a large mountain terrain and explore to your hearts content. If you can see it you can walk to it, you can ski on it or you can fly over it.
The visuals are amazing, excellent graphics. Decent music/sound effects. Gameplay can be either immensely challenging or soothingly chill as you carve up the slopes pulling off insane tricks or just exploring the vast and beautiful environment.
Most of the challenges arent too hard, but there are a few that will have you raging hard to beat them. It was personally pretty satsifying to overcome these, but they are mostly the higher level challenges.
The biggest complaint I have seen is about the price tag. Is it worth $60? .. maybe, it is for me personally as I intend to be playing it often just to relax and explore and remind myself of Skiing. This means I will eventually sink at least 80 to 100 hours into the game easily, thus making it a solid investment. If you're looking for something more than that, then maybe perhaps wait for the price to come down a bit to around $40.
After about 20 hours of gameplay I have hit max level and unlocked all the mountains, but there is still tonnes of challenges left that I haven't yet gotten gold on and plenty of drop-points/points of interest still left to find.
IMO: If you want a Skiing Game that focuses primarily on exploration, then I would say that this is worth getting it for the full price. If you are looking for anything else, wait for a sale.

Fans of Castlevania or other "Metroidvania" style titles will probably find some enjoyment from this title. The game takes place thus far in a dark medieval fantasy setting akin to Castlevania or Dark Souls, with a variety of enemies from hulking monstrosities to creeping little skulls taking place in a variety of locations including underground tunnels and decrepit monasteries.
The game's biggest problem that turned me off initially while playing (I'm using an Xbox One USB controller) is that the platforming feels somewhat imprecise and a bit like your character's speed builds momentum too fast, it feels a bit like you have to press jump a couple steps before you're about to reach the end of some of the game's smaller platforms. I'm more used to it now but it took a fair amount of getting used to.  The combat as well seems to resemble more of a mash fest versus certain enemies but there is precise timing involved as well. You have a back and forward dash with LB and RB and you also pick up a shield which can block damage.What is there can range in feeling from a mash fest DPS race versus certain enemies (with your default abilities, anyway...) to precise dodges required to defeat bosses. I haven't unlocked a double-jump yet, or another item to unlock something on the ground, so more player abilities will probably add to the player's feeling of mobility and fluidity that may be lacking in the early sections of the game. You can tell early on while exploring the levels whether it be a platform ~just~ out of reach or a strange looking wall that you'll be retreading areas (for better of for worse, I don't mind) with new abilities to unlock the next part of the story once you can "use the mist."
Speaking of the story, it seems very minimal at this point, which I don't mind ambiguity in a game's storyline, but you're pretty much just thrown in to explore without much incentive beyond seeing the new areas and enemies. The game graphically looks great and runs fine, with well-done pixel art for your main character, bosses, enemies, and attacks. The levels have a good variety of where they take place -I just arrived to a Monastery section- but how they take place on some of the platforming sequences do feel a bit uninspired/limited (i.e. I have to jump to how many of these moss platforms before I see something new in the background?) that being said, I imagine a variety of traversal options will speed the pace up quite a bit (double-jump, etc...) The music and sound effects are all really well-done as well.
It's a really good game overall, but its at times imprecise-feeling platforming controls and at times "frantic" feeling combat versus certain enemies can be annoying.

Ys I & II Chronicles plus is a remake of the first Ys games from '87 and '88, offering some old school fun for fans of the Ys series who want to see how the story started or to relive the old times.
For those familiar with the other games of the Ys series, like Ys Origins on Steam, this game is more like older 2D Zelda games. It features a "Bump combat system" which makes combat simplier (You only need to hit enemies from corner without pressing a button, this doesn't apply for bosses however) and a magic system on Ys 2, but this doesn't make things less fun: You'll be fighting tough, fast paced enemies and bosses like usual, rocking to a great soundtrack!
While simplier than the newer games, these games offer a good look to how the series started with beautiful 2D graphics, 3  soundtracks to choose from for those who want those old chip-tune sounds or modern studio performance music and a well done english translation.
If you love old style 2D action games or want to see how the Ys series started, I highly recommend this game: It'll give you your money worth of old school goodness!

If you're picky like me and don't like image filtering, I recommend using the 4:3 aspect ratio mode (Complete) as opposed to 30:17 (Chronicles, which is secretly 16:9, and shall be referred to as such from here on). Using the 16:9 aspect ratio will cause the game to pan out during boss fights. To do this without staying pixel perfect, it filters the image and it becomes really blurry. You can also see more in 4:3.
It's a lot of fun, rather challenging at times (it certainly won't be holding your hand at all), and has fantastic art and music. Highly recommended.

It's a fun tower defense game, similar to Plants vs. Zombies.
Basically you have to set up various kinds of towers and traps to defend against various kinds of Martian invaders.
Early in the game you get a "zapper" which lets you attack the Martians directly, or overcharge your towers, or respond to various obstacles that will pop up. For example on the winter levels your towers will slowly start to freeze which will cause them to shut down. So you have to take your zapper and periodically knock the ice off them to keep them functional.
So the zapper actually makes this game superior to tower defense games in which you only have towers -- like iBomber defense. In iBomber Defense there are times when you're just sitting around with nothing to do after you've set up all your towers. In this game there are constant threats that need to be handled with your zapper, so there are no "boring" lets-wait-for-this-wave-to-finish sections.

TWD:Michonne isn't in ANY WAY affiliated with Telltale's The Walking Dead Season 1 nor 2, so you don't have to own either seasons to understand anything, and although it helps if you've read the comics/watched the show, you aren't required to know A SINGLE BIT of TWD to understand the story and or plot in the game. There are characters who appear in the comics that are familiar to someone who has read them, but it doesn't make much of a difference if you have/haven't read the comics.
The game has also had such pretty visuals to accompany it. Although I cought A♥♥♥♥♥♥TON of reused models from TWD Season 1 and 2, lots of textures were polished on reused walkers, so although they were reused, they looked VERY nice. Models such as Jane's hunting knife and Arvo's revolver are seen throughout the game, but if you aren't a die hard fan of the game, you MOST LIKELY won't notice them (same with the walker models being reused). With these new and updated textures comes a beautifully created landscape and f ucking beautiful atmosphere. The aquatic area that is shown to us
looks absolutely gorgeous, especially accompanied by the horizon in the distance.

Not sure how to classify FTL in terms of genre or playstyle, as it's pretty unique. It's a roguelike space simulator where you control your crew and ship as you race through various solar systems towards the end game. An individual game maybe lasts an hour or two or until you die (can be much sooner), but while winning is the goal, trying out new tactics and combinations of weapons is the fun part of the game.
You control a few crew members in a ship with various parts. You can assign a crewman to pilot the ship, one to control the ship's shields, and have a third crew rotate between manning the weapons systems and doing ship repairs. When you get into a fight, your ship takes localized damage that interferes with your ship's functions in every way. Thus, combat is a game of maintaining your ship and taking out the enemy as quickly as possible to minimize the mayhem they cause. Sometimes your ship will be boarded and you'll have to determine how to kill the enemy crew who are breaking stuff and attacking your own crew while trying to destroy an enemy ship that is likely still shooting you. The game has a million tactical possibilities every playthrough and is wildly popular.
It's cheap, and if you've got enough patience to play a game where the journey is the enjoyment, not the ending, you'll probably like FTL.

Steep™  is an open-world extreme sports game that can cover your EA Skate 3 itch that you have been holding for years! You can do up 4 different sports in this game that fits your style of gameplay. There is Snowboarding, Skiing, Wingsuits, and even paragliding. It holds many challenges to do for each sport and you can even make your own for your friends to beat.
If you are not big on the challenge thing, there is much exploration you can do. The map is very big and cut into sections of a couple different mountains. You can just ride or fly your way down with a breathtaking view of the whole mountain. There are areas called "Points of Interest" throughout each mountain that you can find while exploring the vast areas of the map.
The physics in this game, in my opinion, might need some touch up on but it's not too bad honestly. there are sometimes where you'll just randomly get pulled to the ground when going over a hump of snow. Other times it's just completely fine. There is a G-Force feature put into the game so if you hit the ground too hard or hit too many things at a time you will crash which helps with the realism of the game and can prevent big trick spams.
Lastly, there is character customization, it's not a lot but it's enough to show your personality of what you would want. There are premade characters of professional athletes you may or may not know, but you can buy different boards, skis, wingsuits, parachutes, clothes, etc. for your characters of choice.
I might have only 20hrs of gameplay when I made this review, but I can see myself playing it for much more in the future since not many good extreme sports game are made often.
Overall I give Steep™ a solid 9.5/10
All it needs is a couple bug fixes and maybe some more songs for the gameplay if you're into music like I am.

At the moment it is impossible to give this game a positive rating due to numerous issues.
On a technical standpoint, game is not optimized and stuttering a lot even on high end rigs; devs explained there was room for optimization which has not yet taken place. For a year a vast majority of anti-virus reported a trojan in the main EXE and the answer from DEVs was, "this is a false report". As a result I couldn't play the game for a year and was invited to remove the anti-virus which of course I wouldn't recommend to anybody having a minimum common sense.
The graphics are pretty attractive and detailed and 3D Vision generally gives good results except on fire and a few other light effects.
The game offers a pretty rich content and has an interesting universe but lacks a good plot. Bear in mind that it is very repetitive which is inherent to this type of game. Don't expect strategy here, it is a pure hack & slash, and the required player IQ is the same as the zombie ennemies you will face at the beginning of the game. After some time, this game becomes pretty boring and I'm not clear about how it expects to be better than commercial and even free alternatives. In a sense it compares to the Titan serie which I started with a lot of enthusiasm but never could finish due to interest lost (while I finished the Diablo serie as well as POE).

So, I rolled a fresh character after the announcement that it was content complete, as of this review I finished my first playthrough of the entire story (normal diff). I can't say enough positive things about this game, so here's a short list of my impressions:
1) The overall story has an excellent pace, it doesn't feel rushed and there's plenty of side content.

2) The Devotion system is a fantastic mechanism that adds a lot of flavor to your build and play style.
3) There's a great balance of challenge acheived with combat. At level 50 I felt like I could walk over certain packs of mobs only to find some creature around the corner that would gladly treat me like a pinata. I'll also add that I've started a new game with the same character on Elite, and so far in Act 1 it has continued to present a satisfying challenge.
4) Skills to pay the...Blacksmith? A couple things I'd like to note. The refinement of the skills, and dual class system, has only gotten better since Early Access. Compared to other games in the genre I am really pleased with the fact that the success of your progression feels more deeply routed in skill choice and not primarily driven by gear choice. Your gear is important, but it feels more like an augment to your class and not how your class gets defined.
In the same hand, this impacts crafting and in a great way. There's a lot of incentive to craft different items as you learn new patterns, but it's not going to make or break your build. I appreciate that because there's a certain level satisfaction that keeps coming back every time you get a new piece of gear that's an upgrade, and it may not even be that big of an upgrade.
5) Grim Dawn reminds me of what originally drew me into this genre, and refines it to make it fresh and enjoyable. I'll clocking a lot more hours with different classes and I'm definitely looking forward to future content.
Lastly: With voice overs, I'm even more convinced, if the opportunity presented itself, I would follow Captain Bourbon into the depths of the void to rescue his brother Scotch (future content idea?)

DEMON PEAK REVIEW
Having played around an hour and a half of DEMON PEAK I can tell I'm in for a real journey. If you're like me and have a taste for the nostalgic days of Castlevania, Mega Man, Metroid, with a hint of (NES)Ninja Gaiden thrown in for flavor, you're in for a treat.
LEVEL DESIGN
Let me start the review by comlementing the art of the game - the levels are absolutely stunning with sprites you can tell were hand crafted with the utmost care. When I came upon an ancient ruin with a waterfall pouring over the delapitated stonework it nearly took my breath away. It's one thing to make a game that harkens back to the graphics of old, but to actually take those styles and vastly improve upon them creates a true work of art. The whole world makes me want to explore deeper into the darkness, with many different paths to take I feel like I'm constantly finding something new.
MUSIC
The music and sound effects are top of their class and blend perfectly with the world. It's hard to deside what my favorite song is so far, but I really love Rainy Ridge's theme - those horns are amazing and the whole song gets you pumped. I've found myself rushing to keep up with the tempo, dashing past enemies and closer to the next boss fight.
Truely a perfect mix of old and new, hints of east asia, western riffs and european orchestras that blend together to form the sounds of the world around you.
SOUND EFFECTS
You can tell each sound effect was built for a specific purpose, nothing feels repetitive or recycled - giving you audio cues as to what enemy you're up against. The sound of rushing waterfalls, growling demons, massive stomping bosses with hulking hammers the size of your entire body bring the chaotic and dangerous world around you to life.  Each action, each power or item, all seem to have their own sound to them creating a lot of diversity. Everything sounds so organic and real, in fact so real I wonder if they were hand sampled then digitized.
GAMEPLAY
The game can be played at whatever pace you would like, but I for one see it as an excellent speed running candidate. The mechanics involved in dashing and jumping can become quite complex as you progress through the game. Perfect timing is important when dealing with multiple enemies while assending platforms, some with highly lethal ranged attakcs  others charging you with melee attacks, while also dodging spinning blades attached to some of the platforms.
It all creates a pretty pulse punding experience and while at times I was having difficulty passing an area it was usually due to my own horrible timing and/or understanding of new/different enemies. Thankfully a save area is never TOO far away and I always found my way back into the fight quickly enough, but not so close as that I didn't feel rewarded for finding the next save zone.
That's something I noticed right off the bat over all, I feel rewarded for progressing in this game where other titles have lacked that same feeling for many years. I remember when games were difficult not for the sake of being difficult, they were challenging to give a sense of accoplishment once you had progressed past a hard boss/platforming area, found the next save, or held onto just enough health to get you there.
END THOUGHTS
DEMON PEAK is going to be quite a ride, I can tell. I'm not a skilled platformer these days, and haven't played a 2D side scroller very seriously in years, but this one has me pulled in and I'm loving it. From the absolutely amazing music and sound effects to the art and design of the levels, this game oozes passion from the developers. It all has a very unique but somehow familiar vibe to it that brings about the feeling of discovery as well as nosalgia.
While I did find a few minor bugs through the hour and a half I played, I can see that the developers have put a lot of love and time into the game and are sticking with it by rolling out patches as quickly as possible. I've seen them personally address multiple issues people have had and have immence respect that - so many "AAA" games or even other indie titles hardly communicate with their community - especially when there is something wrong.  I have faith after theses initial hiccups it'll be smooth sailing from here on out.
PROS & CONS (TLDR)
Pro
(+)Soundtrack
(+)Sound FX
(+)Graphics
(+)Level Design
(+)Different bosses, powers to absorbe
(+)Pacing is as slow or fast as you like it, but excellent for speed runs
(+)Many different enemies
(+)Advanced movement mechanics
(+)Difficult with worth while rewards
Cons
(-)Some glitches, nothing major

Ten classes (unforgivably called "Perks") that you can level up by playing as (or simply using their weapons as a different class) to level 25. Each gains ~unique stat increases on leveling, but every five levels they will unlock the choice of two perks (I don't know what the game calls them - skills?) for that level tier, so five by level 25. You can switch between them at any time, ie go from +75% health to +2hp regen and increased move speed as berserker. This makes the game for me.
Similar concept to L4D2 gameplay wise, playing the same maps (though there's a decent amount in KF2, and 4 difficulties) over and over killing zombies ("zeds" this time around - technologically enhanced zombie-like creatures) with whatever weapons you choose. Except this time it's.. better.. uh, this time you get to grind for EXP while doing it! So it's L4D2 with ten classes and a lot more weapons and a leveling mechanic that grants slight stats and perks (or "skills", whatever, calling classes perks is my only real grievance with the game).
Expensive when not on sale ($30 USD), but not completely unreasonable. Great value at 50% off though, if you have any interest in this sort of thing it could definitely end up with hundreds of hours' playtime.

A very hard call to make here. On the one hand, I want to respect Mirror's Edge; it's well-programmed (no glitches that I've encountered and it's only frozen once), it looks and sounds fairly good, and it's really, really impressive when you think of how difficult it was to make, to program a proper parkour game, with all the wall-running and jumping and sliding and rolling. It's one of those games where you feel like, everyone needs to see this. At least play it once.
The problem is, everything else sucks. The world-building is terrible; it's a dystopia, because, uh, the game says it is. You are a runner, who transports sensitive info, except you never do this, and your group apparently has the capability to hack into virtually anything in real-time, so why can't we just encrypt emails? Your activities are allegedly in a legal grey area, but cops also seem to shoot at you all the time, and while I can accept the Master Chief surviving all these shots, I don't buy a 110 pound asian girl in gym clothes doing it, no matter how amazingly tough she must be to do what she does. The story is just thrown at you, with no real establishment of, well, anything. It's like Portal, except that game didn't pretend to have a real narrative.
Gameplay wise, there's alot of stupid things wrong with it. First off, you are expected to fight, a little bit. Every mechanic involved sucks. Which is the point, I guess, because you are supposed to just run away, but then why make mandatory combat parts? You occasionally have to just run straight for a cop, wait for him to try and pistol whip you, disarm him, and then use his gun to shoot everyone else. A gun you can't see the ammo count for, can't reload, can't aim down the sights with, etc, and that you have to drop if you want to parkour some more. Second, despite how good the programming mostly is, it's still got stupid parts; you will look around a room and know immediately how to solve the puzzle of getting over to the exit, but you won't be able to do it for like 15 minutes, because it doesn't want to work, or you are barely grazing, mid-jump, a single polygon, and so you plummet to your death. Or you will find a solution, but it won't work, because while this thing over here CAN be grabbed onto and jumped off of, this identical one over there can't be, but you have no way of knowing that. This is compounded by the very weird control scheme, and of course, the first-person perspective.
Yeah, it's a short review, but I still don't know how to rate this game. It's amazing for what it manages to actually do, and yet, it's really not that good of a GAME. It's gameplay is interrupted by terrible story, and then again by repeated deaths because of bad controls or silly hang-ups. It reminds me of alot of other action-adventure type games, like superhero games, where the thing you really want to do is just not deep and well-developed enough, and they keep interrupting you with frustrating nonsense, like random enemy immunity.

Let me start this review with one, very, very important note: you need to add zip-ties to your list of 'top ten items to pack for a zombie apocalypse'. Do it. Do it NOW!
So here's the deal. There will be people around telling you this episode is way too short; that there's not enough time to connect to characters or to really feel the weigh of your choices. There will probably be some hardcore fans telling you that they didn't get some stuff 'right' from the comics or that there's just 'sooo many' references you can't understand. They are probably all right in their own way, but let's get down to the important stuff.
Will you enjoy this game if you're not familiar with the comics and haven't ever played telltale's TWD's games? I'm not sure. If you're part of the group that played the games before though then I'll suspect that, just like me, you'll be fairly happy able to return to the universe of walkers, QTE events and choices you kind of don't really want to make.
However, is this as good as that very first season that made you feel your heartbeat in your throat and shed a tear? Nope, probably not, but what it does achieve is reintroducing that much loved world to you in a way that you know what to expect, attempt to 'read' inbetween the lines and make an effort to give yourself the best experience.
If you're sitting there just waiting for S3 then The Walking Dead: Michonne is not a bad way to get that little, extra fix to remember why on earth you loved this game series in the first place. Can you survive without it? Well, that's up to you. Just don't forget the bloody zip-ties!

I'm not a huge fan of walking simulators, so let's get that out of the way first. Cause that's basically what this game is: a timed walking simulator.
The game requires you to find randomized checkpoints in the form of batteries to stay alive. Your only clues on where to go are based on question marks on the map that you have to manually go find to look at. If you go off exploring too much, you can easily die due to there not being any battery packs in that area.
I highly recommend using the guide.
Sounds: In terms of sound, the game is pretty boring. There were a couple of sounds that felt right, but overall the sounds felt a bit forced. There is no depth of sound either. In Own the Night mode, it doesn't matter if a zombie is 1 foot from you, or 20 feet from you, the sound level is the same. No volume scaling based on distance at all.
Issues with Clipping: Clipping occurs often during this game, so when you try to enter certain areas, you may not be able to without wiggling your way in, which makes absolutely no sense. Further, as you're walking along, random things can catch you, and you might slow down for no apparent reason.
Graphics: Visually the graphics are low quality, but I don't think that was the main goal of the designers.
Controls: If you use two monitors, I would highly recommend disabling the second monitor during play, because the game gets confused when your mouse leaves the window/fullscreen area of its existence. I was often walking in strange directions or having the screen flip and move around due to mouse position on the other monitor. It was rather frustrating.
Interface: While the game says its supports inverted mouse control on the y-axis, whenever I tried to select "yes" the game just laughed at me and did nothing. I could also select no, and the same thing happened. Nothing. When you want to access the menu, you press escape.... often I'd have to press it twice to bring it up, but not always. Something weird was going on there.
Story: Fairly weak, as the premise itself is obviously flawed. You have a deep terrifying fear of the night, and yet for some reason you've decided to go out for a drive in the middle of no where, at night. Whatever. While the game attempts to piece together some sort of semblence of a story, it just seems a bit forced as if they came up with a game mechanic and designed something around it.
Overall: Fairly boring, but easy to 100%. The most exciting times playing will be when you've wandered off too far from places you are supposed to be and are desparately running to a battery pack watching your battery drain down. Then just before it's completely empty and it looks like it has 15% left, you'll have 0% and die and that will surprise you.
Two dollars is too much for this game. I'd pick it up in a bundle, if at all.
Rating: 3/10

I'm going to review the first and second chapters separately since they were originally separate games. First though, the things the two games have in common, like the combat system, which to some may be a turn-off since it uses the "bump" system to attack rather than the traditional "push button to attack". Personally I didn't find it to be a problem - in fact, it makes the game even more action-packed this way. The two games also sport absolutely phenomenal music - some of the best I've ever heard. Ys I though is very archaic in its design - it's easy to get lost, and the game doesn't give you enough clues to tell you what to do next. The map is confusing. The game also doesn't have much variety - just ram into enemies and talk to villagers. Ys II, on the other hand, corrects all the problems of Ys I. The inclusion of magic makes the combat significantly more fun, and the game now has a ton of variety of scenarios - my favorite is disguising as Roos. Ys II is just pure, unadulterated fun. Ys I - 6/10, Ys II - 9/10.

This is a great old-school rpg that, surprisingly, becomes much more fun when played with a friend. While most people will be content leading their parties of four on their own, the game opens up when you split the group and let someone else control a pair of characters. This seems like a scary prospect at first, but thankfully D:OS deftly avoids most co-op/multiplayer rpg annoyances. Any character can receive or turn in a quest on the party's behalf. Swapping loot between characters is a breeze (no more dropping items on the ground). The already tactical turn-based combat becomes even more complex and gratifying when you and a friend can each take a pair of characters, discuss your plan of attack, and watch the sparks, steel, fire, poison, and ice fly.
Speaking of combat...well, I could talk about the combat all day. Each character takes a turn to move or perform an action, and everything that a character does costs action points (including changing gear in the middle of a battle). Unused action points can be carried over into the next turn if saved, which allows you to bank points for more expensive skills or certain sequences of actions. The various skills in D:OS come with surprising amounts of pros and cons. Your piercing ice attack may  shoot through and freeze multiple enemies, but anyone killed by the attack leaves behind an icy surface that will cause anyone who walks over it to slip and fall for several turns. Your fire attacks can trigger explosives or ignite clouds of poison, creating massive conflagrations in the blink of an eye; however, if you're not careful, you may end up seriously hurting your melee characters in the process. Rain spells will put out fires on the ground and on characters but will also leave everything on the screen more vulnerable to ice and lightning attacks.
I don't really have many complaints about this game. There is a lot to discover in the land of Cyseal, and the game does not hold your hand outside of a few UI and gameplay tooltips here and there. Quests will not be marked on your map. You will have to carefully read npc dialogue and review the entries added to your journal in order to know where to complete and turn in quests. Your characters will frequently discuss things among themselves, and you are able to role-play their responses  in order to affect their dispositions towards each other, actions taken by the group, and even certain ideas (two of the companions you can pick up early on are very vocal about hating certain things). If you want to venture out into the wilderness and fight fire skeletons that are two levels above your characters, you are free to do so. You may be victorious, or your party might be reduced to four piles of ash within a turn. Everything is up to you, and at the end of the day, that is precisely what an rpg should be about.

Released too early, and perhaps never should have been in it current state.  Controls are terrible still, even after all of the complaints.  The camera is an extraordinarily poor performer and the engine isn't capable of handling the data thrown at it.  This is not a hardware issue.  Even on a current Alienware laptop, overstepping the FOW halts advancement to a slow chug, whether you're actually stepping or just edge sliding (accidentally, happens often due to lag).  And this is all in SP mode.  The direction is, well, directionless.  Hapless and lackluster, even the very minimal voice acting is annoying.  And, honestly, in this day and age, if you're going to make me read the story, you'd best make it book quality otherwise, well, I'll just read a book and avoid the annoyance of my map flying 5 miles off target because the game engine was slogged down.  It *might* be a different story without the substantial (so far crashless, thankfully) performance issues, the addition of a fully functional camera, and bound tolerance around enemies for ranged combat.  But with the schizophrenic level design and bland to poor story, probably not.  I really wanted to like this one, and it's a shame because the game mechanics and art are solid, items and crafting are interesting, and so on.  It's a shame because someone made the decision to ignore the game engine and story in favor of everything else and those are the two cornerstones of any fine game.  At best, in its current state, being, for me, annoyingly unplayable when competing games are clearly better performers, I rate this a 4/10, 5 being average.

This is totally not my type of game, but the demo was so entertaining that I just had to put it on my wishlist, and then get it when I saw it on sale for 1.99 euro. It's well worth more than that (and I'm stingy). The graphics and humour hits the right spot for me.
It was great fun until I tried to get those stupid achievements, then it turned into frustrating no fun on the Veteran play through of Winter level 5. After far too many attempts on the previous levels each time until I got lucky, too. (Achievements only ever get in the way of enjoying a game for me, and this game was where I finally decided to say 'screw them all'. I'd really like a button in Steam to turn them all off.)
Back to just playing for the fun (screw veteran), it's entertaining me still, replaying the levels in order and the challenge and bonus ones I like.
There are plenty of levels, hours upon hours of play time! The progression is good, starts easy and gets slowly more difficult.
There are some different types of challenge levels throughout the Story mode, where I would like to just skip the one that I find no fun at all (Maid Raid), and get more of the one I like best (Back to Basics). They each unlock a few more levels of the same type once you've beaten the one in the Story mode, which is nice. There are also bonus levels where the aliens and playing area look different, and some have somewhat different special abilities (with no way that I know to read up details about them, unfortunately).
I'd have liked a way to re-check the aliens while playing in a normal level, too. My memory isn't the best anymore.
And I'd have liked a way to go to the next level in a second play through, rather than having to go back to the main menu and pick a previously played level just to get to the one after the one I just played.
And I'd much prefer the game to remember that I unticked Fullscreen, rather than having to do it again every time I launch it.
But overall, great fun. Try the free demo, it has 7 or so levels from different spots in the story mode, so you get to see easy and somewhat tougher levels in shorter time, giving you a good idea of what to expect in the full version.

The first 30 minutes or so of this game are a little slow, as you have yet to make any decisions of consequence. The travelling/story sections of the game truly get you into the game, and the decisions you make within those sections both matter AND feel difficult. Can you afford to welcome more travellers in your band? What if you don't have enough food? What if they turn on your later? Truly amazing. Would buy again at twice the price.

I really wanted to like Demon Peak. The art looked amazing, and gameplay videos I saw looked promising. Unfortunately, there were too many issues to consider this a game worth purchasing.
The controls aren't tight, and I often had trouble making basic jumps I can easily make in other games.
Enemies are far too aggressive at the beginning of the game. There's one enemy that constantly chases you and lunges after you; I didn't even bother fighting it and just jumped over it or ran away. It's the beginning of the game, where players are just getting used to the controls and mechanics. They shouldn't be thrown in to the deep end that quickly.
The shield feels like it's supposed to combat the archer enemies, but it doesn't really do much to succeed in this. The dash feels pretty restricted as well.
The music felt unfitting to the game world.
Overall, I can not recommend this game in its current state. I hope that the developers take these criticisms into account to offer a higher quality experience in the future. I don't want to give up on Demon Peak, but I simply can't enjoy it as it currently is.

I'm not sure I've ever felt as vulnerable in a video game as in The Banner Saga. In most tactical RPGs, the barrier to difficulty can simply be hurdled by a spot of grinding. Here, there's no such opportunity. At every stage of the game you are hounded, chased from one location to another, the weight of the enemy always at your back, with hard decisions (which often only make you weaker) stacking up as you move along. There's no chance to pause and grind the game's singular currency - renown - which leaves it always scarce in quantity. This forces you to choose between purchasing supplies for your caravan, strengthening your warriors, or purchasing a shiny item to give you a small power boost, and it never feels like enough. At no point in my playthrough did I feel overpowered. Even my strongest warriors could be felled in one blow if I made a bad tactical decision. At the start of each encounter, there was always the sense of, "I don't know how I'll make it through this one," and following each battle, "I can't believe I made it out of there alive." And that's only the combat. The game also constantly forces you to make difficult decisions throughout, which frequently lead to the death of your party members. It's not always obvious, either, and since the game has no manual saves - only a handful of sporadic auto-saves - you can only change your mind so often. Sometimes, a decision you made hours ago will come back to haunt you much later, wreaking havoc on your party. So yes - in this game, there isn't just the illusion that your choices matter - they do, and you're bound to make some bad ones along the way. It's a bleak game, and feels like Game of Thrones meets The Walking Dead in terms of tone, and hope (or lack thereof). Luckily, it's also a gorgeous game, with a hand drawn aesthetic that looks quite unlike anything else out there. The combat system is interesting, but not nearly as varied as Japanese TRPGs like FF: Tactics, or the Disgaea series. By the end of the game, the mechanics do feel like a bit of a slog - but then, it suits the game's mood perfectly. To come out as some super charged badass capable of leveling a whole army isn't the point here, and wouldn't suit the story. Here, the core is survival, and the grim likelihood that at any moment, any one of your party might not make it to see the next day.

This was a fascinating and captivating look into eSports, specifically the first Dota 2 International Tournament ("The International") that took place in Cologne, Germany at Gamescom from August 17–21, 2011. The tournament was funded by Valve, including the $1 million USD grand prize, with Nvidia supplying the hardware.
The film not only covers the tournament progression. It also explores the lives of three of the players from different parts of the world, letting us see the "human" side of some of the professional gamers. We learn about some of their background, how gaming has affected their lives leading up to the tournament, and more. I could almost feel the emotion seeping out of it.
Valve did an excellent job with this. It's an all-around quality production, including design, filming, editing, and sound. I enjoyed the whole film. I watched it with Closed Captioning turned on along with Dendi's commentary since he was in the winning team, Na'Vi (Natus Vincere). The extras also include a Q&A with players.
The actual size of the downloaded version is 7.36GB. The soundtrack is an additional 68MB, which I also recommend. The 3GB mentioned in the details is for the streaming bandwidth.

. It includes all sorts of information about the tournament since its inception.

Ten classes (unforgivably called "Perks") that you can level up by playing as (or simply using their weapons as a different class) to level 25. Each gains ~unique stat increases on leveling, but every five levels they will unlock the choice of two perks (I don't know what the game calls them - skills?) for that level tier, so five by level 25. You can switch between them at any time, ie go from +75% health to +2hp regen and increased move speed as berserker. This makes the game for me.
Similar concept to L4D2 gameplay wise, playing the same maps (though there's a decent amount in KF2, and 4 difficulties) over and over killing zombies ("zeds" this time around - technologically enhanced zombie-like creatures) with whatever weapons you choose. Except this time it's.. better.. uh, this time you get to grind for EXP while doing it! So it's L4D2 with ten classes and a lot more weapons and a leveling mechanic that grants slight stats and perks (or "skills", whatever, calling classes perks is my only real grievance with the game).
Expensive when not on sale ($30 USD), but not completely unreasonable. Great value at 50% off though, if you have any interest in this sort of thing it could definitely end up with hundreds of hours' playtime.

[Partial Review based on 60+ hours in the game and being in the 2nd act (of 4/5 acts?) of the game]
They say time flies when you're having fun, and boy, has time been flying. Really glad I backed this game on Kickstarter, and the released product doesn't fail to live up to expectations.
That's not to say the game at release isn't perfect - there are a couple of crashing bugs here and there but Larian is patching them fast (releasing micro-patches on a daily basis). There are also some bugs/polish issues and areas that could use refinement, particularly with the henchman system - although a part of the problem is a side effect of having much of the henchman being designed by Kickstarter backers before Larian changed the skills/talent tree substantially late in beta. And boy the present (limited) companions in this game at the moment are nothing like the many memorable companions of Bioware RPGs (here, they're pretty much one-dimensional, extremeist, dislikeable) but at the end of the day there are a ton MORE things that this game does right than wrong and it all comes together to equate tons of fun. And FWIW all the major systems do work well.
Note that combat can be quite hard if you're not used to turn-based tactical combat, but once you figure out various game mechanics (via making lots of mistakes at first and possibly dying), things become managable even while challenging. Boss battles are immensely satisfying too (the first act's final boss makes you go "WTF!!" with all the thing it throws at you (literally lol) but I got this immense sense of satisfaction when I finally emerged out of that battle with 0 deaths on my first attempt).
I expect this game to only get better overtime as Larian continues to support this post-game.
Overall: Strongly recommend particularly if you like cRPGs, exploration, and/or turn-based tactical combat.

Nosferatu: The Wrath of Malachi is a survival horror first-person shooter.
Your family is being held hostage by vampires and will be sacrificed to resurrect Lord Malachi.
You explore the castle fighting enemies such as dogs, gypsies, ghouls, vampires, bats, etc
And occasionally a boss.
You have a variety of weapons such as pistols, sword, fists, musket, stakes, and holy weapons like a crucifix and holy water. These are not automatic weapons and are slow to reload which really makes this a survival horror game. You do eventually get a great weapon but thats near the end.
You find your family members (aswell as friends, priests and pets) one by one within a time limit. And have to escort them back to safety and can get a reward from them.
Finding them in time might not be easy though. Their locations are a bit random. And since the graphics are old many areas look the same. Dont expect the first playthrough to be perfect. The game gets better when you start to understand the mechanics and the castle's layout.
Their AI is not great. You have to constantly keep an eye on them to make sure they are still following. They stop following when an enemy appears. They may get stuck on various objects or glitch through walls and disappear. You constantly have to go back to them which just wastes time. And if you try to escort 5 at a time...then may God have mercy on your soul.
You have 8 manual save slots. 1 quicksave slot. Saves can be overwritten. Its a matter of saving often but also saving smartly. You dont want to lose too much progress, but you also dont want the manual saves too close to each other.
Flaws:
-Lack of/not working game settings. Fixed by creating a reg file and by downloading an exe.
-No official or unofficial patches. This game needs support.
-The game doesnt explain how the time limit works
-Bad AI
-Getting through doors can be a pain since they tend to close behind you and enemies hide behind doors in the corner of rooms. They also seem to sometimes respawn when i leave and enter despite already clearing the room.
-There is a certain character in the game that is made almost impossible to save sometimes unless you retry over and over. So it becomes a frustrating game of rushing, dying and retrying.
-Not to mention a scripted death if you rescue the 14th person without the 15th. They need to be rescued together.
-The game emphasis saving your family within a certain time limit. But at the end the game just says ♥♥♥♥ it and jumps time anyways. I think its a cheap move to pull on the player changing the rules like that.

This is a great game with a few issues.  Even with my negative points below I still recommend it for people who like RPG+Turn based battles, if you liked games like Baldur’s Gate series then you will likely enjoy this game.
Good:
+Great Graphics.
+Moody atmosphere for dungeons.
+Talk/trade with almost every neutral NPC.
+Developers are listening to players and updates/patches are coming out frequently.
Not so Good:
-Inventory management is clunky.  Yes you can use "Send to Homestead" but I would love to see an option to access it from anywhere as well as quick transfer, say CTRL+left click to transfer to Homestead.
-Enemy visual range is so large that often you’re in battle before you can even see them.  Once in battle you often have to move the map around just to spot the enemy, since they are so spread out.
-Quest tracking.  I know this was their intent but the lack of any visual clues and limited suggestions in quest log can make questing painful and slow.  I’ve spend a large amount of my time running between people in town asking the same questions and hoping for a different answer or quest update.  If there were better visual clues (pointer) or more details in quest log on what is expected next I wouldn’t feel some much like I’m wasting time running around.

-So far with my limited play it seems like the enemy count is too low on the maps, i.e. only one or two groups of enemies per map area.

Despite being in beta (early access) the game is very well fleshed out up to level 40. I've only encountered a couple bugs. Gameplay wise I find it just as fun - if not more-so - than Path of Exile (PoE). Both Grim Dawn and PoE borrow heavily from other games in terms of character progression. Grim Dawn from Titan Quest, and PoE from Final Fantasy 7 and 10.
Grim Dawn isn't an always-online game like PoE however can be played multi-player online or locally. It also allows you to circle the camera around to get a full look at the environment, which Path doesn't. My main gripes with this game is its continued use of Diablo-style isometric gameplay (instead of straight 3D 3rd person action RPG), lack of multi-character control and unoriginality in terms of character progression.
That said isometric "Diablo-style" Action RPGs are still one of my favorite genres and it's way worth the buy, even in beta.

+ Intense and satisfying gameplay
When you kill a vampire, you can't help but feel proud of yourself. And given all the adrenaline this game pumps into you, you'd be on your toes alot, watching your back for any vampires or monsters hunting you.
- Minor glitches
You might get stuck in some areas.

One of the biggest pains in gaming and it's what you have to do to improve your chances and get new weapons. I hate escorts in videogames, but seeing the benefits, mildly softens the blow.
- Graphics can be a little distracting an hard to look at
- I really wish they gave this game a map system instead of following a glowing green light. It would be especially welcome, seeing how the castle ALWAYS changing when you start a new game.
All in all, intense and creepy game that you'd best NOT play alone. 8/10 with a seal of approval.

Long story short: If you like Action RPGs with a dark atmosphere, then give Grim Dawn a try. I did, and I am enjoying it.
If you're like me and you want an ARPG that isn't cartoonish and bright or colorful, your options are pretty much Path of Exile, The Adventures of Van Helsing, and Grim Dawn. Having played the former two first, I can't help but compare Grim Dawn to them, but this is actually in this game's favor.
Van Helsing, in my opinion, is plagued both by a poorly made skill tree with few viable builds, limiting replayability, and also by the  fact that the game just feels small; it's short, and the lack of customization in appearance and build limit the time one is willing to invest. PoE goes to the other extreme. The passive tree is so massive and branching that countless viable builds are possible, but the result is that leveling up is a bit tedious, with little sense of progression some times. Grinding for x hours just to get what feels like +1 strength is not always fun. It pays off in the end, but the going is rough.
Grim Dawn hits a great middle ground. Though you only get enough skill points to focus on 1-2 skills, with a few one-point wonders if you like, those skills generally have several passives that can totally alter gameplay, and you feel the change as you level them. There are many ways to build each class alone, and you're also given the option to dual class. This gives quite a bit of customization, without being dauntingly complex.
The Game looks great, and the sound is executed quite well, particularly with melee attacks. I found myself not quite minding missing my target because of the satisfying metallic sound of a sword slicing air, only matched by the lovely sound of a club smashing flesh. The pacing of the combat is slower than a game like Path of Exile, but the sound of the heavy hits gives more of a sense of stength and impact, so I didn't really mind. The music sounds great, and while I'm probably not going to be whistling any of the tunes any time soon, it does a fair job of keeping me immersed.
Probably my only warnings are that the game is not perfectly optimized (yet; this is early access). My computer is able to play PoE, which has better graphics, on middling settings at high fps, but I had to turn down all this games settings to the lowest and lower the resolution or else my character would attack or move a full 1-2 seconds after I click. The game isn't complete yet, but it does seem that the developers are working well on it, so I look forward to what the future holds and can comfortably recommend this game.
