I love snowboarding and this is my dream open world snowboarding game.
Steep is a fantastic sports game in many ways.
Its open world is vast, fun to explore, and filled with challenges to complete.
The game plays great
The controls are tight and responsive and it is satisfying as hell to pull off tricks and death defying feats in all the sports. Especially in the wingsuit.
The audio is fantastic
I love the sound of snow crunching and this game does it well. You also hear your gear hit different surfaces. I'm basically trying to say the game is an ear gasm. The music is also great. I listened to the Rock playlist and turned on copyrighted music. There are some good songs. They're also not obnoxiously loud. Songs stay quiet until you begin to snowboard, ski, etc.
But I have some gripes.
1. The challenges are repetitive, mainly for snowboarding/skiing.
The vast majority of challenges are doing tricks before you reach the finish line, and it doesn't play to Steep's strength of its environment. There are some cross-country challenges, where you have to reach a certain point in a given amount of time. These were my favorite because you get to explore the environment more and work your way around it rather than short jumping paths to do another flip or spin. There are also mountain missions that have you follow another rider, discover places, and more. They're fantastic and goofy at times. I found them more memorable than the races and trick challenges.
2. There is no custom character.
You do get A LOT of clothing options, but you don't get to create your own custom rider. I found this odd because of the crazy amount of clothing items. Balaclavas are included too, thankfully.
3. The world feels unpopulated.
This is a constant online game, and you will run into other players, but the actual map itself is devoid of life. I'd like to maybe see some NPC's Snowboarding, Skiing, Gliding, etc. Or maybe some avalanches? Wildlife?

Jumping:
It's REALLY inconsistent. This is probably realistic, but in my honest opinion it's not fun to play. G-Meter:

The screen goes black and white and you want to avoid doing any tricks or jumping until it recharges (NO MATTER HOW SMOOTH AND SKILLFUL THE LANDING YOU WILL CRASH). It's horribly inconsistent. Sometimes you'll lose all your health on small things or lose nothing at all.
It should also be mentioned that there are times when the physics will ♥♥♥♥ YOU. Sometimes if you hit a hill at an angle you'll be sling shot backwards or if you "try again" you may spawn in the ground.

Super Hexagon doesn't have leveling, tech trees, or experience points.  It's simply a challenge where you compete against yourself - or your friends - to get the highest score.  This simplicity is what makes the game.  We find then when you strip away all the fluff of modern gaming and distill it down to its main gameplay, games manage to still be fun.
For instance, when you finally beat the first level, it's not because you bought enough upgrades to get there, or reached a high enough level; it's because you as the player have gained enough experience to finally succeed.  Focusing on skill of the player, and not their character, gives us a sense of motivation to succeed because we want to, and not to get the next level up.
You don't even need to complete a level to see yourself improving.  Simply getting 5 more seconds than your last run can be motivating.  Somehow a game with technically only 6 minutes of unique gameplay kept me engaged for over 30 hours, and I still come back and revisit it frequently.

There is something to this game that really speaks to people, the free-running first person parkour, when it works, is absolutely amazing.
Unfortunately, there's a whole lot of stuff getting in the way of your fun.
It's not the plot, the plot is perfectly serviceable. Sure, it starts with your sister being framed for a murder and returns to that big bag of clichés for every new twist and development, but it wasn't bad and the little animated cutscenes did their job (...of masking loading screens, but they're neat too).
No, what breaks this game is the lack of polish that was applied to it. The finishing touches. There are many small gripes to be had here (lack of non-hostile characters within levels, level design not making sense from a functional perspective, big bulkhead doors that take half a minute to open, no subtitles for ambient speech like overheard conversations and announcements, shoddy and partially missing directions) but the two main ones are:
For DICE, a studio that was at that point best known for its Battlefield series, this was a huge and impressive step towards something more creative. A first person game built around avoiding fights, with a kick♥♥♥♥♥female protagonist.
For Electronic Arts, a publisher known at that point for buying up smaller development studios and turning them into faceless drones that will never make another fun game in their life this was a great moment to show the world they could do something special, something different. Unfortunately, they did not.
With an extra 6 months of development and a whole lot more play-testing and polishing this could have been an absolute gem and must-play.
As it stands it is a 5-hour eulogy for what could have been.
Do not get this game, and be careful with the upcoming sequel, it might have similar problems.

Free to Play is a unique perspective at the first look most outside of Valve ever got at Dota 2; the first tournament ever played on Dota 2; and the very first Valve International championship held for Dota 2 at Gamescom. As such, it\'s got incredible historical value both for veterans and newcomers.
It\'s also a terrific way to understand Dota if you\'re someone who\'s never played it before and is interested in understanding what makes it tick and what makes it so popular. It even explains Dota itself, along with the background leading up to the first International and focuses on the stories of three players from totally different parts of the world; all carefully approached with a remarkably generous scope and a keen eye for cultural perspectives.
The narrative builds up to the tournament, sure, but the narrative is much more than just match recaps, which I think is terrific. Filmography and sound design are great and the editing and design of the in-game Dota scenes is absolutely brilliant and something we ought to see more of in films that focus on gaming.
Overall you can tell Valve put a lot of effort, resources and time into this. It\'s free, it\'s amazing, and it\'s undoubtedly worth watching. Highly recommended.

Ys I & II use a different combat system than the newer games in that you only have to walk into enemies to attack them and the direction that you walk into them determines if you will take damage.  In Ys II you do get some direct magical attacks, though they are mostly useful for boss fights.  It keeps the pace of combat pretty quick and really almost relaxing.
The storylines aren't bad for a JRPG, the music is really high quality and the games aren't all that long assuming you don't try to be more comprehensive with achievements and such.  The games are designed to encourage grinding before boss fights, but I never had to spend unbearable lengths of time doing so in order to progress. There are sections of both games that can be a bit convoluted or would require a bit of running around/backtracking to figure out and find missable or hidden items, so I would suggest using walkthroughs for a number of areas in the interest of time.
The only bug I encountered was with the final boss of Ys I, where running the game in fullscreen causes him to spam projectiles at insane speeds, so change it to windowed mode before then and then back to fullscreen before the ending if you prefer.  Might only occur on 120hz displays.
Both games come with a launcher that lets you set the visual mode to Chronicles+, which gives you a better fullscreen view without all of the fluff around the edges, adds improved art and I think more cinematics as well.  Definitely turn that on, as I don't think it is by default.
In the end, if older JRPG games appeal to you then these are great quality PC releases.  I wanted to go through them to get some context before playing Ys: The Oath in Felghana which is the remake of Ys III.

I never have any doubts when I start to play some old game I never played before and still, somehow I installed Nosferatu: The Wrath of Malachi around half of year ago and played it just now. Why? Maybe because I thought it will be simply FPS with tons of vampires to kill. How wrong I was.
Before I can call this game a FPS, I must say it's more of horror game. No, not only because there are vampires and game's main stage is big castle, it's of this horror climate. I mean, so many things are happening in this game. From the very start as you pass the gate there are some strange and "omg, what was that" moments, filled on places where you can't access on start yet you can wander around to see where you might be going later. Places where many dangerous things are waiting for you and you don't know what will happen after you open another set of doors. It's a game from 13 year ago and it have random generated levels. It is something to be surprised about? Probably no, but it's still impresive to game like that. The moment when I saved my game, went to the room, met one of friends which needed to be rescued, failed to survive and loaded my last state was the one that made me feel like I'm playing something really good. Upon loading my save and going to the same room, there was nobody... that felt like a really good horror. What's even more amazing is set of weapons: Crucifix, chalice filled up with Holy Water - you don't see stuff like that in horror, fps or any other games.
Nosferatu: The Wrath of Malachi might have really outdated graphics but it builds really nice atmosphere. And music, it fits fantastic and doesn't make you feel like you are safe at some times. If there is anything in this game I can complain about it's game's physics and level design. What about physics? It's really... strange. When you open chests when standing on it, it will launch you like catapult. When you run down from stairs you not only can, but I'm sure you it will happen at least few times, hurt yourself while going down. You just make some strange big moves which deals you fall damage. And what about level design? Like half of rooms looks... same. I mean, maybe it's made this way because it's old castle, but it made me really confused. I was playing here and asking myself many times "is it new place or maybe I was here before? It looks same...".
I can't be the only person who doesn't like all those screaming and jump scaries horror games. If you are looking for horror which is great fused with FPS genre, and is scary in different way, Nosferatu: The Wrath of Malachi is one of best you can get. Maybe it's not really long game but for few nights it should deliver great fun. At sales it's going mostly 90% off main price so get it then, you won't regret it.

Divinity: Original Sin is very well made modern RPG. However, in my personal opinion the claim that this game was "modern Baldur's Gate" is not entirely true.
Few years ago games like Project Eternity, Wasteland 2 and DIvinity: Original Sin popped up in Kickstarter and got funded, clearly demonstrating that the consumers want to see games like the old isometric legends such as Baldur's Gate series, Icewind Dale series, Planescape Torment, Fallout 1-2, Temple of Elemental Evil, etc.
As such, D:OS does make good job at being modern isometric RPG (you can even zoom and pan the camera). The game is fun and challenging, and each deadly encounter could very well be the end of your two Source Hunters and their companions.
The turn-based combat system itself is solid, and more often than not, coordination and tactics win fights over brute force. Spells, enviroment and effects can be combo'ed in many different ways, and battlefield control is crucial for success.
Even if you play with just the two Source Hunters, even the deadliest fight can be overcome with the use of skillful tactics, right spells and crowd control. Understanding the action point system is crucial, and planning your moves few rounds ahead of your current turn helps a ton.
Each of the class archetypes (warrior, rogue, mage) excell on their playing field, but you can freely customize the starting abilities, talents, traits and skills, and mix-and-match your character the way you want. The ability and skill system is also easy to understand, though at current some of the traits do seem largely overpowered (such as Leech).
Of course, the combat (and the game in general) is of course twice as fun in the Co-op mode.
Still, almost every fight the game throws at you is a challenge, something that I like - even if I had to reload the game 20 times to clear that one encounter. It should be noted though, that the enemies do not scale with player levels, so that a fight that was challenging early on might be a lot easier with a few level ups.
Randomization plays a huge part in D:OS. All the loot is randomly generated. Each chest, corpse, boss loot, even vendor's stock, are all randomly generated. A minor dissatisfaction I have with the current system is that it's possible to save the game while fighting a Boss monster so that the Boss will die from next hit - kill the boss, check the loot -> reload -> rinse & repeat until you get the best possible drops you want.
Itemization is vast and robust. The crafting system is different than one might expect, but it encourages trial and error (perhaps even frustration?). There are some goofy things you can craft, but once you understand the system, it is quite self-explanatory. You can also dye most items you find, if you are not entirely sold on those charming pink sandals you found.
Graphically the game looks good. Animations are for the larger part very well made, with many different death animations added depending on the manner the character dies.
The dialogue is for the most part good, especially the banter between the two Source Hunters is very well done. However, the game does seem to lack
dialogue options (at least if compared to games like Baldur's Gate). Nonetheless, the game features a ton of dialogue, but it's a personal matter if one likes the slightly comedic and over-the-top general tone of it. At some points, the dialogue might even seem childish.
However, one area of the game which could really use some updating is the User Interface and inventory / skill management.
As it stands, each character has a skill-bar of 10 slots with 2 additional bars you can scroll up to. As the skill-bars get filled, it quickly becomes a chore to switch between the different bars for each different situation. Likewise, inventory space can become cluttered in a matter of minutes or hours, depending on if you pick up everything you find. Occasionally, you do find extra backbags to which you can store (and you should!) crafting materials, skillbooks, scrolls, etc. However, to use such items from inside the backbag, you first need to unpack them.
First you open your inventory, then you open a backbag, you want to stash something into the bag, so you grab that item from the inventory window, only to see that the inventory window now overlays the backbag interface, meaning you have manually adjust the two screens from under each other. Inconveniences related to GUI such as these are somewhat common, unfortunately.
Of course, there are minor bugs and glitches. For my game, I had my entirely Cyseal map revealed to me through what I suspect is a bug. Also after this revelation, all monsters I encountered had 50% health remaining.
Still, the game is enjoyable and it has its moments. It is very similiar to Divine Divinity, but I wouldn't compare it to Baldur's Gate - at least in the sense of story and mood.

You're no longer fighting with the mountain the second you decide to race down the mountain, it's a breeze to your rider that shrugs off even the worst bumps now. An overhaul of the controls and feel this big should at least have a test phase or opt-in/out feature. I can't enjoy the game in it's current state, a game I adored through the beta and completely loved after the initial launch.
This is where I'd make a joke about Steep being like dating someone and falling out of love quickly. But it's more like, at the 3rd or 4th date your drink is suddenly roofied, after which you wake up with an empty wallet and a disgusting feeling of being very unclean.
I ain't even exaggerating.
===========================ORIGINAL REVIEW BELOW=========================
Roughly 30 hours playtime.
I've reached level cap and maxed all different riding disciplines, earning myself legendary status.
And you know what?
It's just the beginning.
I bet I'll be spending hundreds of hours on this digital vacation this game has taken me since release.
There's so much to love in this game, and I'll be completely upfront; this isn't a objective opinion at all.
You like starting off on a sunny hill filled with deep powder, and leisurely ski downhill, enjoing the weather, listening to some chill music? The game lets you do that, and rewards you for it.
Want to jump off the most fearsome looking mountain, skydiving past rocky outcroppings that look like hell on earth, adrenaline making your hands shaky? The game lets you do that, and rewards you for it.
My only nagging points are minor.
The "level cap" at 25 is... Odd. I liked doing the different disciplines so much that I capped out quickly, but kept at it anyway.
Sometimes, the control system and physics engine doesn't make any sense at all, and other days it's smoother than butter on a hot pan.
I'm a little worried at longevity, but Ubisoft has lately had a trend with updating their games with both free and paid content that holds a decent standard. Might return to redact this in case things change.
TL;DR:
If you liked SSX or any similar game/series, but felt like you never had real freedom - here it is. Enjoy.

An amazing strategy RPG in the same vein as Fallout 1 & 2 and Baldur's Gate and Icewind Dale. If you like party-based RPGs with turn-based combat, this game is a modern re-imaginging of everything that made those games great. The story can be completed in multiple ways, so you don't have to worry about pigeon-holing yourself because you happened to get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at one NPC and murdered their whole family violently in a fit of rage.
Perhaps the best part of the whole combat is that elements come into play with status effects like warm, wet, chilled, etc. When your character is effected by these, you can use the elements to your advantage. For example, if you have a group of enemies standing in a low-lying spot, you can have a Hydrosophist in your party use the rain spell to cause a puddle of water to appear underneath them, then use the lightning bolt spell on the puddle to stun everyone standing in the puddle. Elemental combinations like this make the battlefield an amazingly fun place to be.
Pick this game up, you won't regret it. Larian has done an amazing job on creating this experience with the help of Kickstarter and it has very few problems thanks to that extended beta test, unlike their previous releases.

Long story short: If you like Action RPGs with a dark atmosphere, then give Grim Dawn a try. I did, and I am enjoying it.
If you're like me and you want an ARPG that isn't cartoonish and bright or colorful, your options are pretty much Path of Exile, The Adventures of Van Helsing, and Grim Dawn. Having played the former two first, I can't help but compare Grim Dawn to them, but this is actually in this game's favor.
Van Helsing, in my opinion, is plagued both by a poorly made skill tree with few viable builds, limiting replayability, and also by the  fact that the game just feels small; it's short, and the lack of customization in appearance and build limit the time one is willing to invest. PoE goes to the other extreme. The passive tree is so massive and branching that countless viable builds are possible, but the result is that leveling up is a bit tedious, with little sense of progression some times. Grinding for x hours just to get what feels like +1 strength is not always fun. It pays off in the end, but the going is rough.
Grim Dawn hits a great middle ground. Though you only get enough skill points to focus on 1-2 skills, with a few one-point wonders if you like, those skills generally have several passives that can totally alter gameplay, and you feel the change as you level them. There are many ways to build each class alone, and you're also given the option to dual class. This gives quite a bit of customization, without being dauntingly complex.
The Game looks great, and the sound is executed quite well, particularly with melee attacks. I found myself not quite minding missing my target because of the satisfying metallic sound of a sword slicing air, only matched by the lovely sound of a club smashing flesh. The pacing of the combat is slower than a game like Path of Exile, but the sound of the heavy hits gives more of a sense of stength and impact, so I didn't really mind. The music sounds great, and while I'm probably not going to be whistling any of the tunes any time soon, it does a fair job of keeping me immersed.
Probably my only warnings are that the game is not perfectly optimized (yet; this is early access). My computer is able to play PoE, which has better graphics, on middling settings at high fps, but I had to turn down all this games settings to the lowest and lower the resolution or else my character would attack or move a full 1-2 seconds after I click. The game isn't complete yet, but it does seem that the developers are working well on it, so I look forward to what the future holds and can comfortably recommend this game.

I own this game since it's release and i can proudly tell, how i promote this game to everyone i know as one of the best games i have ever had in the world of gaming and i have been around in that world quite the time.
The level design is stunning and quite nostalgic, a lot of parallax scrolling going on and very nice love to the detail of the world. Keeping it simple while still enhancing the whole thing with little contrast in the back- and foreground.
The color palette is a quite brave choice, because there is a great deal of contrast in this game, from the muddy purple worlds, through a contrasted cavern onto a totally brightened up temple-like area. Every map has it's own unique approach on the atmosphere which is enhanced by the amazing choice of soundtrack. And the soundtrack really does it in this game.
The character choices are somewhat interesting if you are into  platformers, due to the fact that you are somehow supposed to play this cooperatively. From the overly mobile characters with movement skills, to the immobile guards you want to see in a game where everybody can fullfill an important role in the teamplay. The characters are very diverse as well, simple in design, yet with neat details.
Let's get to the bare bones of this piece of art, the gameplay.
It strictly reminds me of Capcom's Megaman series.
The hitboxes and the movement is just on point, like in a real platformer.
The growing strength of your character of choice, is direct and you are able to feel it.
Yet you have many options to get another experience with every playthrough, thanks to the fact that you never get the same maps, same enemies, nor the same items and not even the bosses are fixed in any level, except for the endboss of course.
The enemies are diverse as well, from melee to range, from slow walking to fast teleporting, from usual to special.
Even the bosses are able to spawn in as a rare version of itself, which mostly means a more difficult and engaging fight, which needs you to rethink your approach onto beating the boss.
The unlocking system is, except for one thing i really am bad at, a very nice thing, because it achieves you more possible drops in a vanilla playthrough, via using everything the characters have to offer in a playthrough.
Also every playthrough lets you achieve the so called artifacts, modifiers which enhance the game, sometimes, to your advantage.
A specific combination of artifacts, lets you run this game in easy mode, even at the highest difficulty settings, but it doesn't get tedious, it's getting ridiculous. Once you have a certain level of godlike strength, you can not be stopped to just keep on playing because it is hilarious what the items have to offer in combination and you finally have the same exact effect i remember from the Megaman games after getting the Z-saber or the Hadouken, or the golden Armor.
You reached the level of power which mostly seemed unreachable, but that's where the fun really starts. It delivers the feeling of true power after you experienced near death experiences around every corner otherwise.
The fact that you can re-run after you've beaten the fourth level, is also a thing which some people consider a weak point of this game, but they better rethink that, because even if you want to have a 2 hour round of grinding the first four stages over and over, they do not repeat in the same order you started, they still have the roguelike promise right in them, you basically can discover every possible map spawn in one playthrough, while grinding for the most unnecessary amount of items.
Long story short, this game offers it all.
Nice music, nice design, spot on hitboxes and movement, support for controllers, support for multiplayer, even in shared-screen. Nice enemy design, a very nice way of telling the story, with neat extras in the menus to find out what the hell you even are killing the whole time. A whole bunch of different items, from mayimum destruction onto maximum defense, up to the damn meteor that let's you kill all your friends.
Definitely one the best games ever made.

I have never ran into such an issue with the card on any other games, most of which are newly realeased / high-end games. Keep an eye on your hardware temps with this one, just in case. To remedy this I moved one of my many case fans to get better air-flow to the GPU, you can also try leaving your case door off / open. This may also have been due to hot weather however it still didn't happen with other games that day. Just a heads up for anyone else on a possible issue!
Anyway, I would give this game a solid 7 / 10 - loses points for being a bit over-priced and having that ♥♥♥♥ing stupid GoPro Karma drone in it, ♥♥♥♥ing worst drone ever released.. And loses points for some bad hardware compatibility. I kind of just bought this on a whim hoping that it would work for me. Luckily, it works fantastically. It has steam integration, all your steam games are detected automatically, and you can also add non-steam games. DO NOT EXPECT FPS GAINS OF 20-30, most cases will not have such an improvement. In most games i only get a ~5 fps increase but when you're just 5 fps from being at stable 60/144 frames then i think it's very worth it. Don't know what more to ask for from an app like this not to mention the Dev is very active with his/her community and constantly updating the app. Works great, just as advertised. I would recommend this to any friend looking to get a little more juice out of an aging set up, ESPECIALLY if you can manage to find the product on sale.

I backed the Kickstarter, donating twice the value of the retail game (fifty dollars), because even at that early stage it was clear that this was a game with two of the ingredients required for greatness: a story worth telling and the people capable of telling it. All they lacked were the funds to bring it into being.
So, what did I get for my money? Was it worth paying double? In a word, yes. The Banner Saga is clearly influenced by Bioware's golden age of games in the social aspects with your followers (Knights of the Old Republic, Mass Effect), as well as the Oregon Trail, oddly enough,  but for the most part it is its own being. The art and music are achingly beautiful. The characters are written robustly, so that we get to know them slowly, over this chapter of the saga. I was actually surprised at how much I cared about them, and how much more I wanted to know.
The combat, once you get the hang of it (I jumped right in since I played a lot of the multiplayer) is fun, and the addition of magic items that allow you to tweak your characters is welcome. The choices you make along the journey, whether to rout or regroup, how much food to buy, when to train your followers, have definite consequences, made all the more dear by the fact that you cannot jump back to old saves if something goes disasterously wrong.
Having already finished the game on normal nut the climax on easy, I am now going to play it again, which is, you'll agree, the test of great game. I want more! The developers have created a new world of in gaming, populated with their own unique population of giants, men, and magic. I very much hope that this is the first of many chapters in the Banner Saga, and that future iterations with expand and enrich the spectacle and vibrance of the world they have created with voice actors and longer sagas.

> "And it also said I only have 1 core when I infact have 2"
Are you sure you don't actually have 1 core but hyper-threading enabled? Try running this command on your pc from a command prompt:
wmic cpu get name, NumberOfCores, NumberOfLogicalProcessors /Format:List
This will show how many FULL, REAL cores you have, and how many virtual/non-full cores you have. For example, AMD Bulldozers have 2 core modules, whereas the module has 1 REAL core and 1 SHARED core (aka non-full core).
I suggest going to
and using those settings BUT making this tweak:
Then go to CPUCores -> Advanced -> Constrain Web Browsers and enable that.
UNSELECT the "Isolate OS" option and "Game on dedicated" option.
I hope you can take a peek at the settings and see if things can work and then hopefully feel positive enough to take that into account for your review.
Happy gaming and I wish you well :)

Killing Floor 2 is a good game, unfortunately the Floor is not what's trying to
you, (yes, they always try to trick you with fancy names and give you something completely unrelated...) it will be Zeds trying to
kill you.
The game itself is remarkably different from its predecessor, Killing Floor 2 has changed game mechanics and (if you're a KF veteran) you might feel more... enclosured, let's say. The fact that you can sprint whereas in the first game you'd have to pull out your knife and walk hilariously makes this second part feel like spaces are smaller and that you get pinned down way faster and with an entirely more graphic picture of what dismemberment means.
There are other areas I'd like to mention, for instance:
Where the hell are the sexual innuendos from the Trader? No, really, this was a big deal in Killing Floor 1, we all got tired of the same stupid puns from one of the ugliest NPCs ever, but it was an inherent part of the game, now we have someone who managed to take one step further into the whole "being annoying" matter. Want my opinion? I'd rather have someone asking me if I like the Big Ones rather than a French-accented invisible bossy ♥♥♥♥♥.
Now the guns, we may not have as many guns as we were used to, but we have enough (though I really miss my old STG-44). All well balanced (more or less) and with a very good work on the modeling and the reloading technique. Having a cool variety of knives is something interesting but perhaps not worth saying here (I did it anyway, didn't I?). We were also given the chance to push enemies away by punching/hitting them with the stock; this was genious and surely we applaud it, how many times have you, KF veteran, been chewed off by clots before, while a bloat puked on you
while a scrake did you some surgery? That's it.
Now the perks is something I like to see growing. In Killing Floor 1 you would take lots of time to level one perk to the maximum, while in Killing Floor 2 you can do as much in a single day (if you have nothing else to do, not like it is
easy. Most of the perks remained essentially the same although some of them... I'll just explain it:
In my humble opinion; Sharpshooter and Commando from Killing Floor 1 have branched out into Gunslinger + Sharpshooter and SWAT + Commando respectively. This gives you more to do in the game, and better technique with weapons you would have used in the same perk before. I can't really say I enjoy being Sharpshooter as much as I did in the first version but… I accept the mutability of life and go with the flow.
It's also an important part of the changed perk system that every five levels there is a booster, which compels us to level up before moving into higher diffilculties. It is no longer the cost of guns, the initial weapon for levels five to six in KF1 or the slight improvements what keeps people out from the Hell on Earth servers.
Bosses are still challenging, some things never change (too much).
The Community is very decent, most of the time, and honestly agreeable but you know, there's always that one ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ whose efforts are directly focused towards being a pain in your♥♥♥♥♥ >shrugs< There are lots of maps, servers, and well, I have read a lot about people having issues with high pings... I guess it all depends on who's server you join and it is fairly easy to make your own server, where people will probably join when they see how low the latency is.
Of course, not everything is good, there are some glitches and physics-defying events, so if you like your shooting straight and precise, try not to fight anything around stairs. But if you like to see bloats being literally catapulted into you while puking because the script couldn't be properly read, hey, it's your call, your tastes and your life. >shrugs even harder< I can't think of anything else I'd really like to complain about in the game, perhaps that it gets repetitive at some point (no♥♥♥♥♥♥Sherlock) and that you want to murder the Trader and you are not given the chance. (By the way, Micro-transactions suck).
The game overall is fun, you have a laugh at the beautifully British-accented characters (German-accented if you love Anton Strasser) saying random stuff and the possibility of personalizing your character (although we no longer have 10249123.62 characters any more, no Chickenator, no Grim Reaper and no Mrs. Foster among others).
Welp, to finish this and let you go and play... the game is good, not the best game ever made, but pick five friends, play, hunt achievements and you will have the feeling that you invested your money properly (Avoid. Micro. Transactions.) Don't feel like you're changing Killing Floor 1 for Killing Floor 2 (assuming you have played it, I pretty much wrote this whole damn review for people who played the first part so it's not like I'm switching now). Killing Floor 1 and 2 are very different games that require different skill. All this said...

It's been a few years since this movie was made, but it's still good to watch. eSports back in the day is non-existent. Heck, eSports at that time might be even just for bragging rights and such. Also, video games as a career is shunned by many, as a job even. Because people generally had taught that games are just games. Simple as that. Games are just for recreation, not as a means of garnering profit.
But, how times have changed! eSports then started to come into the fray of profit. First, it likely had hundreds of dollars as prize money. Then, it became hundreds; then thousands; then hundred thousands! Now, with the big games out there: League of Legends, CS:GO, Overwatch, Heroes of the Storm, Battleborn, and now DOTA 2, the prize money goes beyond what people had normally expected on video games.
At the present, it has now attracted so many aspiring to enter the eSports Scene, hoping to gain some easy profit. But life is not as easy as pushing the power button of a CPU; it requires you to pour dedication and focus into what you are doing. Hell, even making many sacrifices just to achieve what you want to achieve. This Free to Play documentary movie made by Valve shows what sacrifices are made and how those who have been successful (and not so successful) managed to be on the top. The eSports Scene is a high risk-high reward opportunity. Many have tried to gamble but failed, and those who managed to accomplish that hurdle came rolling down instantly. Another hardship of eSports is that you have to be relevant to stay in the Big League; for example, people are who considered beasts or legends in DotA (or Dota 1) tried to transition into DOTA 2, but failed miserably. That's one of the many examples of people who got on the top, and fell from grace. All-in-all, eSports is a cutthroat battle, where everyone is constantly against each other's throats.
A good point resides in the movie that eSports, while not really considered a sport, is not to be taken lightly. It does give large money. In fact, most eSports' prize pools have overtaken some of the prize pools or real sports! Still, the prize pool of eSports favor those who come on top only, and that's the sole reason why people are still hesitant to delve deeper into it. However, eSports grows exponentially year by year. I hope to see more in how eSports grows.
Even if you don't have the general knowledge of DotA, or DOTA 2, Free to Play is still nice to watch. It gives you a simple explanation of what is DOTA 2 and how professional gamers play the game. But that's not the main point of Free to Play, rather, it revolves around three prominent players in that time, and what are their tribulations and efforts done along the way to glory.
- You can watch it in Valve Video Streaming for free, or download it to watch the deleted and extra scenes, commentary, and Q&A of the players in the documentary movie, which also nets you free achievements.
- Solid transition of camera angles. It captures the faces and emotions of the person talking. Kudos to Valve!
- Excellent music! Keep in mind that most of the music are in the DOTA 2 game already.
- Good summarization of what is DOTA 2, and how players generally play it.
- And most of all, it explains how eSports generally started as a newborn and how it grew into what it is now.
- Though clear and can be heard, I wish people who are native-English speakers (ie Fear talking) should also have subtitles. Non-fluent English speakers have subtitles when speaking so you can understand them. I just wished the same goes for native speakers as well. People might not understand their accent and all. That's my two cents.
- This might be my only problem, but sometimes Steam crashes and leaves the Free to Play movie open. When I tried to upload the screenshots I made during that, it leads to an error and I have to exit Free to Play before I can upload screenshots again.
Overall, it's a great movie. I definitely recommend people to watch this free movie, along with other free and good movies in Steam.
So, hop in. It's Free to Play, after all!

Nosferatu The Wrath Of Malachi is a good but flawed game. Despite its age, it actually does a good job at combining FPS gameplay with survival horror. This game shows that even games that were made in the early 2000’s were able to be creepy and scary. The game provides something a little different in the sense that what you’re trying to do is find your family members within the castle and escort them to safety outside. And you have a time limit that you have to try to do it in. Each family member that you successfully rescue gives you a special item or weapon to help you as you continue. The game has interesting enemies and monsters. It also has some boss battles too. The game has a well done look to it that works very well at keeping the tension and scare factor high from start to finish. The music is one of the game’s biggest strengths. The game’s creepy music is just fantastic for a horror game. And it has some good and creepy sound effects too. The game has some randomization to it as well which helps with its replay value. Every time you play a new game, the item locations, item spawns, enemy spawns, and the locations of your family members inside the castle, are all randomized. So you never really know when or where enemies are going to show up. And you also don’t know what particular enemies they will be either. The randomization elements of this game add to its horror very well. Now, the game does have bugs and flaws. It’s unlikely that any of them will get fixed being that the game is pretty old and it was abandoned by the developers a long time ago. If you have trouble getting the game to work properly, there are third party tools available for getting the game to work properly and let you play it in a widescreen format on current Windows computers if needed. It’s as easy as just replacing the default Nosferatu.exe file that comes with the game with a third party version of that file that was made for current Windows computers (you should back up the default Nosferatu.exe file before replacing it with a third party version just in case). The third party fixes are available here:
. This game is very deserving of an HD remake, or a sequel, or at the bare minimum, an official update that fixes the bugs and flaws of the game. Despite its bugs and flaws, this game is still worth playing. It is a good combination of FPS gameplay and survival horror. I do recommend Nosferatu The Wrath Of Malachi

Note: The last time I played this, you couldn't play this through the Steam launcher, you had to start it from its installation folder. It seems to have been fixed at the time of this writing.
While at times very reminiscent of the original Doom games in its simplicity and fun factor, it's initially difficult to understand some of the goals and peculiarities of this game, and this and its incredible glitchiness lend it a similarity to the much more recent indie fangame SCP Containment Breach. Both Nosferatu and SCP are riddled with bugs, and from the very start throw at you gimmicky enemies that at first seem implacable without the right tools to surpass them. Both of these frequently use random gen to surprise you and keep the game flowing, and while it works here, you will encounter many samey rooms and enemies and will get lost which can make your experience tedious. You can walk down one corridor in these mazes, double back and find a few enemies waiting for you in rooms you just cleared, and again and again keep seeing the same enemies recycled as you figure out where to go which just makes it harder to advance. Areas like these are linked to places like the entryway courtyard, present in every playthrough, that seem to have set places for certain objects that you need. Those places are obvious from their uniqueness and greater scale and it's easy to remember them, making it easier to progress, however it still takes real effort (or virtual if you want to get pedantic) to make it through this game and the mazes.
It's best to keep multiple saves every playthrough if you want to beat it, even if you want to play it like a roguelite; you can get stuck in scaffolding or walls at the worst times. It's so half-done there are actually even random glitches that give you positive effects, for example your flintlock pistol gaining infinite ammo which can be really nice when you get swarmed by demons.
The AI is decent for people that are used to playing old Doom clones, but nothing to write home about. Enemies can jump over obstacles in a creepy weightless way, like marionettes, and sometimes fly. I don't recall anything special. Eerie music cues are tied into the supernatural creatures' appearances and can help you avoid an annoying death, because even though they are simplistic they are quick and often unexpected. AI of the human enemies is lacking in particular, such as the snipers which are fixed in place and can't turn, no matter how long you stand behind them. It's just another sign of the real problem with this game, that they simply didn't care enough to polish it. Back then in the early 2000s, games like Timesplitters 1 and 2 did have this exact issue with their sniper enemies, and no one complained as far as I know. In a game as buggy as Nosferatu: The Wrath of Malachi, any old defect can take you out of the experience and make you forget it's not some low poly alternate universe nightmare you were experiencing.
What keeps people from passing over titles like this (referring back to SCP) is their thrilling atmosphere that isn't often matched, not even by bigger budget horror games, although that of course is subjective and this particular game is not for everyone. Especially this game, mind you, not for its music and ambiance which lends your quest (rescuing your family from a certain Count) an immediately unsettling vibe that can make you quite nervous if you let it, just the bugs.
It's worth buying when it gets on sale, there's too much wrong with it to pretend it's great.

Great Remake of the Cult Classic!
When I heard of the remake of XCOM I was both thrilled and worried all at the same time.
I was thrilled because I LOVED this game when I was younger. Played it for hours, upon days on end. The idea of a remake with today's graphics and user interfaces intrigued me. However, I was worried because many game makers today (looking at your FPS's) focus entirely on the graphics and not enough on the story. The original XCOM graphics were somewhat lacking (even by the standards of that day), however the game play was awesome. Just when you thought you had built or researched it all, you got a new alien or artifact which unlocked even more stuff.I was pleasantly surprised to find the remake of XCOM has both graphics and a in-depth story line. The story is even better if you add the expansion pack: Enemy Within.

Once you beat the game you open the Second Wave Options. This allow you to drastically change the way the game behaves and the strategies you will need to use in order to win the next time. This offers a very nice re-play ability you rarely see today.
The only negative, is there are some issues with the Percentage Chance to hit when taking a shot. You 90% chance to hit the Alien with a 75% chance of a Critical Hit and your Sniper COMPLETELY misses, not even close to the target and the Alien is out in the open.  Yet the Aliens will shoot you from across the map, around a corner while you are in full cover and get a kill shot every time. Other than the frustration of that...it is a great game.
Kudos to you 2k this is a well thought out game.... XCOM: The Bureau however is another review....

Well, what can I say?
This game is brilliant. It may not be the most in depth game, or have the best graphics, but it dosen't need to have these. FTL has to be one of the most addictive games I have played, you soon start to get into the role of a ship commander, and it's great fun.
The combat sections are solid and well balanced, being as close as as 2D game could get to space ship combat, I especially love how you can target the different sections of the enemy ships. I also love the versatile and different races you can get as ship members, it really makes the gameplay interesting. I also love the thought put into the background of all the groups you will meet.
However, one thing I did notice is that although you can easily make it to the last sections, in my opinion, unless you have played a game like this before, you will be facing some lerning curve here. Whenever I get to the last section, I never seem to have enough fuel or resources, having been pressured to move on in previous sections (which can be taken as a plus by some), I just feel it is a little too difficult to complete for first time players, or people new to these types of games. I also feel that the prices of items within the game are steep, considering the rewards you get from various events and battles throughout your playthrough.
Despite this, it is a good game that, if you can get over the initial learning curve, you will enjoy until completion.
Summary
+ Addictive, yet still enjoyable gameplay
+ In depth characters and backstories
+ Balanced and varied characters and races
- Steep learning curve for new players (to complete)
- Short play time, can complete in minutes, and there isn't much motivation other than badges to carry on.
7/10

Now THIS, this is a really addictive game!
FTL, which stands for Faster Than Light, is a rouge-like, spaceship command action simulator (or something like that).
You are in command of a spaceship that is being pursued by the hostile Rebel fleet, seeking to destroy you because you carry vital information for the Federation fleet, that you seek to aid.
You take control of the ship, rerouting power between necessary sub-systems to shield yourself from enemy attacks and destroy their ships.
The game does a great job at getting you involved in what is actually happening with your ship during your flight from the rebels and before you know it you get really sentimental whenever one of your crewmembers dies.
The balance in the game is great, and even though the "luck-factor" may be a tiny bit unfair, the game in itself never fails to entertain (and you could probably guess that after my 80+ hours of play).
Just remeber though, if you don't like dying and restarting a lot (A LOT!), this is not a game for you. If you do however, you will LOVE this one!

Really just an excellently done game, and incredible how all the different parts come together. There's nothing else quite like it.

I got it just to see if the reviews were being honest or if it was just blowing smoke. Mind you, all of my hardware uses Skylakes and Kabylakes. Having said that however Cities: Skylines can still wreck a computer on that initial load-screen.
I've seen positive results from using this program with Cities: Skylines, Fallout 4, some of the MMO's I play, and other games that I keep on a 6TB HDD drive so that they don't take up space on the much smaller SSD and M.2 SSD drives.
What this app WILL do is give you some performance increase in everything you can apply it successfully to. It has for me so far and I've just been sitting here the last few minutes punting it through all of my load-heavy portions of games I know to be load-heavy on the CPU. Is it going to give you a 90% increase on a game? Idk, that depends on your hardware. Even high end stuff like mine is receiving a small boost which I honestly appreciate since I was annoyed that I still have to use an HDD in this day and age at all. Especially for a Windows 10 user where random crap is always running in my background no matter how hard I try to make it not do that, this little app is a nice helper.
What this app will NOT do is give you a miracle. It's more or less telling Windows to shut up and sit down during game time as opposed to Microsoft's absolutely atrocious current methods which suck down resources for absolutely NO decent reason. It is NOT going to magically enable you to go from running Witcher 3 on minimum settings, to running Witcher 3 and Fallout 4 at the same time on Ultra-settings with a load of graphics mods. From what I can see so far it HELPS though.
Overall I'd say if you're on the fence about it, try it during a sale or even try it at full price. Your mileage will vary depending on your hardware but all of my hardware on both my laptop and my desktop is really high-end Intel & NVidea stuff and I'm still seeing some noticeable increases. It's a good little complimentary app to get Windows to behave like a HELPFUL OS instead of a big fat pig.

I backed this, during its Kickstarter run, primarily because of the art style. I'm very, very happy with the end result. The visual style in-game is amazing. The vista while the caravan is travelling is just a treat to see, and there are so many portions which could stand alone as works of art in themselves.
The character designs and combat animations are all great, IMHO. The only thing that could, perhaps, make it "better", would be if they had millions of dollars to spend on full animation and voiced dialogue...but from what I've seen and played through, that wouldn't really be necessary, and may even detract from the experience.
It took me around 12 hours to finish. Normal Difficulty.
I enjoyed the gameplay, overall, particularly the story choices (and, well, the story itself). The management of the "resource" you can earn and spend, Renown, keeps things interesting: do I use it to level up my characters? to buy my characters items to buff them? or do I spend it all on supplies for my caravan?
Combat itself is quite well done. It seems relatively simple, at first glance, but turn order, unit placement (both during setup and combat) and target prioritization soon become quite important and can make for some very engaging and even stressful fights.
The armor and strength stats mechanic is also an interesting feature: Each character has an armor and strength value, with armor reducing damage, and strength acting as both health and damage capability, with the latter decreasing as strength is damaged.
Taking all that into account, along with each combatant's innate/passive ability plus their activated abilities, along with the willpower mechanic (which boosts damage, or movement, or pays for ability use)...and it may not seem so simple anymore. Which isn't a bad thing. :)
The soundtrack's great. I loved Austin Wintory's work on "Journey" (I wish it'd get ported to PC; I'd gladly buy it a second time if it came out for PC). From the softer, somber tones of some of the caravan marching tracks, to the faster and heavy beats of the combat track...all great. I love the tracks with the strong vocals in them, and the last piece in the game was amazing (the credits song/music, too). I'd definitely recommend getting the Soundtrack.
Bugs? Glitches? I had one freeze after several hours of play, but I was alt+tab'ing a lot and had stuff running in the background. I also had one combat glitch that required me to load a game, but it was a one time thing.
Complaints?
There's only one save "track". If you start a new game, it'll overwrite your previous saves.
It's an autosave system that saves at key points (like entering/leaving a town, after an encounter, etc.), which may also be a problem for some. I'm fine with it being autosave-only (since it keeps every autosave point), but the lack of extra save "tracks" or profiles is kinda annoying, esp. since I'm now thinking of a new playthrough and, this being the 1st chapter (of an intended trilogy? still fuzzy on that. I should re-read my backer emails...), saves could carry over and other stuff like that.
Volume control. There isn't one. It's either you have music/sounds on, or you have them off.
There are also no subtitles. It's not really that important, as the voiceover parts are few, but it'd still be nice to have 'em.
TL;DR:
I loved the game. I'm looking forward to the next installment. Amazing art (waiting for my digital art book) and soundtrack (if you're going to get it: get the one w/ the Soundtrack), and engaging combat and gameplay. I'm very glad that I backed this game's Kickstarter. :)

Nosferatu: The Wrath of Malachi. Not a great many games fill me with as much dread as this one. I remember my very first playthrough terrifying me to the point where I had to step away from my computer for awhile, and I had issues getting to sleep for the next few days after. That says something about this game, as only one other game in all the years since then has managed to ♥♥♥♥ with me so badly (Not even Amnesia gets me that bad)
It's a vampire thriller game, made in the classic style of Vampires
The story goes that your sister Rebecca is being married to the son of a wealthy Count. You show up late, the last of your family to arrive, only to find out that you and your family are now trapped in a randomly generated castle, filled to the brim with Vampires and zombies, among others. Your goal is simple: Rescue your family and friends from the clutches of Evil in a set real-time limit of 1 hour and 30 minutes. You need to hurry, as your family members WILL die if you don't.
Visually, it's not the sharpest tool in the shed. It was released in 2003 and it sure looks like it. That being said, maybe it's just me, but it has quite a bit of charm to it.
Gameplay wise, it's a first person game. I'm hesitant to call it a shooter, because while you do get Guns from certain family members if you rescue them and get them back to the Sanctuary in one piece, you also get your classic vampire hunting affair; Wooden Stakes that can be used to stake vampires or used as torches. A crucifix which can be used to repel vampires and kill ghosts, and a chalice that you can find and put water in with, then bless it with the crucifix to make holy water to kill monsters instantly.
The game is truely an experience, if you're the type that understands graphics aren't the most important thing. In fact, if you can get past them, it's atmosphere and soundtrack alone make it better than most dreck put out today that people just eat up for some reason.
Now pardon me while I go and further ruin my chances of sleeping well this week.
tl;dr The visuals may be outdated, but the gameplay, the story, the sounds and music, and just the sheer atmosphere of the game make it absolutely worth it.
If you like PvZ do yourself a favor and try the demo at least. This game is fun

The world of indie gaming will never cease to amaze me. Just like the world of triple A title, it is crowded with cheap knock-off and copycats. Who thought that making a Slender clone without Slender would be a good idea?
In Nyctophobia the real threat is not an entity but your own fear of the dark. In order to survive you must pick up batteries floating around the map since your flashlight can't last more than 1 minute. If you don't do that darkness will overwhelm you and you will be greeted with a game over screen. That's some lazy game design, isn't it? Not to mention the minefield that stands between you and the gas can that you must pick up to progress. It just feels out of place.
At the end of the game a silly looking shadow chases you and the only thing you have to do to survive this encounter is to make your way to the safety zone before it gets you.
The only positive thing about the game is its ambiant sound effects which gave me the chills at some moments but that's all.
To summarize, Nyctophobia is absolutely not worth a buy. Wait for someone to gift it to you instead. It takes no more than 20 minutes to beat the game on the first playthrough.

XCOM is a fantastic turn-based strategy game.  I didn't play the original XCOM from way back when so I can't compare the two, but this one has a great balance of weapons, unit types, and gameplay that has brought me back for multiple playthroughs.  It isn't perfect with some rather annoying technical glitches on occasion during the combat, but they're rare enough that they don't detract too much from the enjoyment of the game.  The base management is also well balanced requiring you to make tough choices as to what you are going to purchase/upgrade/build when you are funded each month.  You never quite feel fully in control of the situation as your lack of resources requires you to not attend certain situations, which merely emphasizes the feeling of urgency you have as you play.
I would highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys turn-based strategy.

I got it just to see if the reviews were being honest or if it was just blowing smoke. Mind you, all of my hardware uses Skylakes and Kabylakes. Having said that however Cities: Skylines can still wreck a computer on that initial load-screen.
I've seen positive results from using this program with Cities: Skylines, Fallout 4, some of the MMO's I play, and other games that I keep on a 6TB HDD drive so that they don't take up space on the much smaller SSD and M.2 SSD drives.
What this app WILL do is give you some performance increase in everything you can apply it successfully to. It has for me so far and I've just been sitting here the last few minutes punting it through all of my load-heavy portions of games I know to be load-heavy on the CPU. Is it going to give you a 90% increase on a game? Idk, that depends on your hardware. Even high end stuff like mine is receiving a small boost which I honestly appreciate since I was annoyed that I still have to use an HDD in this day and age at all. Especially for a Windows 10 user where random crap is always running in my background no matter how hard I try to make it not do that, this little app is a nice helper.
What this app will NOT do is give you a miracle. It's more or less telling Windows to shut up and sit down during game time as opposed to Microsoft's absolutely atrocious current methods which suck down resources for absolutely NO decent reason. It is NOT going to magically enable you to go from running Witcher 3 on minimum settings, to running Witcher 3 and Fallout 4 at the same time on Ultra-settings with a load of graphics mods. From what I can see so far it HELPS though.
Overall I'd say if you're on the fence about it, try it during a sale or even try it at full price. Your mileage will vary depending on your hardware but all of my hardware on both my laptop and my desktop is really high-end Intel & NVidea stuff and I'm still seeing some noticeable increases. It's a good little complimentary app to get Windows to behave like a HELPFUL OS instead of a big fat pig.

Brilliantly done open world extreme sports game. It's like if Skate was a snowboarding game where you could also ride skis, and also fly around in wing suits and with a paraglider. The gameplay is perhaps a bit on the simplistic side, but on the flipside it makes it so its very easy to pick up and play while allowing the game to throw some truly outrageous challenges at you later, where winning those are all about skill rather than memory of systems.
The game is the sort of thing that is best enjoyed over time I feel. Its a massive world with tons and tons of different missions and events, and trying to grind all of it could be overwhelming. Instead, the game seems to want you to treat it like going on a mountain trip, where its awesome to pick up if you feel like rushing down some hills or relaxing and exploring the snowy landscape someday.
If you're a fan of games like Skate, 1080 Avalanche or just the idea of a huge open world that is built for sports and exploration rather than combat and collectibles I highly recommend it. Having tons of fun with it and I feel its the sort of game I will keep coming back to regularly.

I love this game. The Banner Saga is like people always describe women they are in love with, beautiful inside and out.
The art animations and overall feel of this game is stunning. I'm not exaggerating when I say that. I just stopped and stared at the main menu for bit when I first loaded the game. The gorgeous art is also put to good use by the caravan marching motif that dominates the gameplay when not in combat. And the music and sound design subtley accent the whole feel of the thing.
The combat mechanics are simple yet incredibly deep. Which is the hallmark of great game design.
The balance of breaking your enemies armor or trying to punch through it to damage his health, and thus reduce the damage he can do to your people, is the core of the design. It is a brilliant one. And every design decision accents that concept. Combat is almost entirely skill based, and so it feels like chess. It is extremely rewarding when you start to learn how to really play. And the game let's you learn easily, by doing training battles in camp against randomly generated enemies matched to your party's level.
However, this game is also incredibly punishing to mistakes. something as simple moving an ally incorrectly so they cannot attack that turn can lose an entire battle. If an ally goes down they will be at reduced power/health until they can rest, costing valuable supplies to feed your caravan. Being aggresive in major battles can save your troops lives but take party members out of action when you need them most. Being defensive makes combat easier for your party but can cost troops. And troops have to eat so the more you have the more supplys you need to keep them going. And the wrong choice in a dialogue can send a maxed out, and extremely useful, party member off on a tanrum that gets him killed.
Long story short: Even on medium this game feels like dancing on a razor's edge. And I love that too, maybe most of all.
It is not without it's flaws however. The game only has autosave and it does so constantly. Which sucks when you mis-click. I clicked leave about 30 "days" in just as I saw there was one of the unique side conversations that I'd missed. I went to load and, of course, it had saved right after I left. So I loaded the save right before that, played the one battle to get to where I could do this elusive conversation, and realized that the incredibly awesome items that I'd bought before were replaced by crappy ones in the store. And no, I couldn't just load the later save and not have the conversation because it overwrote that one. Also, and more important in the grand scheme if less personally frustrating, The items, which are a very key component in advancing your parties power, are all over the place in power and usefulness and thier level is not always commensurate. Sometimes that is because of clever use by the player, giving them to the character that can best exploit it's effects... and sometimes not.
In summary, this game is beautiful in both it's art and mechanics. If Viking Turn-Based Tactical RPG sounds like something you could ever enjoy, I strongly recommend this game.

All three episodes of TWD: Michonne have now been released. I had high hopes for the series back when it was first announced, but after playing the first episode, I was left severely disappointed. When the second episode rolled around in late March, my faith was restored. The episode was short, but had many great moments, plus a very intense ending with one of the tougher choices I've had to make in a TellTale game.
Unfortunately, after playing through the finale in April, the series took a nosedive right down into mediocrity again. Episode 2 had a great setup for Episode 3, but the finale just does not live up to what Episode 2 made it out to be.
And here is the main problem with TWD:Mihconne. The setup for a good story is there, but the narrative doesn't deliver. The first episode has a great sense of gray morality. Without saying too much, you are held captive by another group of survivors. These guys don't seem immedeately like bad people, you might even feel sympathy for them. You don't even know much about your "partners in crime" and whose side to take is really up to you.
Until episodes two and three come around and try to force you into hating the "villains" eventhough you might not want to.
There's also this underlying narrative with Michonne's daughters, whom keep appearing in front of Michonne as hallucinations. They were kind of novel and exciting in Episode 1 and 2, but it gets really overdone and obnoxious by the time you play Episode 3, and you just end up wishing it wasn't there at all. The series ends with the stupidest binary choice of all time, as evidenced by the endgame stats, which showed a 93%/7% split.
And I haven't even mentioned the myriad of technical problems yet:
Choppy animation, bad framerate, and long load times all drag down the experience even further. I don't understand why this happens, Seasons 1 and 2 ran like a charm on my system, as did other TellTale titles, so I'm forced to conclude, that TWD:Michonne is just really poorly optimized.
As a TellTale fan and The Walking Dead fan, I can't help but feel disappointed in this miniseries. Here's to hoping Season 3 will bring back what made TellTale's The Waling Dead great.

This story has a habit of kicking you while you're down, and then delivering a few more swift kicks for good measure. It is not your typical role-playing game, nor strictly a turn-based strategy; it is more of a choose your own adventure story. And you have distinct honour of having to pick your own poison. No one is holding your hand throughout the story, and the friends you meet along the way may become your enemy in due time. This game is not meant for everyone. It does not aim to please everyone. On the contrary, you will be cursing the Gods for the cruel fate that destiny has entwined for your past deeds and decisions. But no one is listening. Didn’t you know, the Gods are dead.
--
EDIT: I decided that I should also include the negatives of this game, to ensure people know what they are buying into, I wouldn't feel right recommending a game to a friend or even a stranger without the entire picture. With that said, you should know that it is the first chapter in a three-chapter story.
The negatives: The entire story you are met with problem after problem, and at the end (which was abrupt and unexpected) you feel like you haven't solved any of them at all, leaving the player with more questions than answers. The problem is that this story doesnt stand on its own feet, since it is one part of a planned trilogy. Although it does a good job of introducing the characters, world and the problems they face, it does not do much past that. I am sure the game will stand better alongside its other two counterparts, but I cannot recommend this to anyone looking for a self-contained story, since this is just the first chapter; it feels more like an introduction to the world of Varl, dredge and men. You will want to get the second and third chapter to get the full experience of the Banner Saga, but this is a series that will be well worth the investment. The first chapter is one piece of what looks to be a great pie, but you are not given a vertical slice; you are given a horizontal one, and tasting only the crust of the entire story you are left wanting more.
After all is said and done, I am sure it is going to be a masterpiece of a trilogy. I would recommend this if you can take it for what it is, the first part of a three-part series.

Be warned—these aren't complete reinventions like Oath of Felghana was to Ys III, but updated versions of the original games.  Both have somewhat redesigned maps, a little bit of additional items and playable content, unlockable boss rush modes, and (most significantly) the ability to move diagonally, but these are both still essentially the same games as the originals.
There are some elements of the games that haven't aged well, notably some inscrutable puzzles (save yourself hours of confusion and just look at a guide once you get the hammer in Ys I), mandatory level grinding, and plenty of backtracking through large, mazelike dungeons.  That said, these are still charming action RPGs with a fun and unique battle system, well-designed bosses, and what are still some of the best soundtracks in the history of video games—and you get three versions of them!
Ys I & II Chronicles is too similar to earlier versions of the games for me to highly recommend it to people who have already played them, yet different enough that I can't quite call it the definitive version.  If you have a Wii, you might want to download the Turbo CD version (Ys Book I & II) instead—it was one of the earliest CD games and is really interesting from a historical perspective.  Either way, these are games that deserve to be played.

“Another tower defense game,” I thought to myself. I will at least give it a shot.
My low expectations were blown out of the water after playing the demo. I grabbed the game at full price, which is something I very rarely do, and have now beaten it and all the bonus levels. If Plants versus Zombies and Defense Grid had a love child, this is that game. Do not let the cute graphics fool you, the aliens will hand you your butt on a platter if you do not plan carefully. I have played and beaten a variety of tower defense games, but this one still challenged me.
On top of actually requiring you to use deft strategy, you are never left sitting and watching the screen as your towers do everything for you. Early in the game, you are given a zapper gun that you must use to help fight off the aliens. If you do no use it, the aliens WILL beat you. Unlike other tower defense games you have to actively participate the in the action every second of the stages. The aliens can disable your towers, get rid of your traps, and even destroy your defenses if you do not use the zapper wisely to counter their offensive.
The only thing that holds the game back from getting a perfect score from me is that there are a slew of game closing bugs during the extra missions.  There are also a couple of sections (particularly with the Maid challenge they throw at you) that take the game from being challenged to downright frustrating since you have to feel out the strategy that the developers want you to use through trial and error rather than make one of your own.
I have to give this game 4.5 out of 5.

This is the best horror game I have ever played. I have played this game a few times each year since 2003 and it still brings new experiences every time I play it. The basis of this game is that you must rescue you'r family whom have been kidnapped by vampires.
These family members can be found semi random in the semi randomly generated castle.
This is a FPS in which you can use a multitude of weapons and you need to figure out what weapons work best on which enemies.
The game is really hard so I suggest you start off at easy difficulty.
What sets this game apart from other horror games is its semi randomly generated castle.
You never know what will be in your path. You can have terrible luck and get no ammo and surrounded by enemies in the first few rooms in the game. Since you are in a race against the clock you have to keep the pace and can't be overly causious of enemies. Enemies can respawn in rooms you have already been too which will suprise you in the moment you are running away from harder enemies. There are small glitches in the game, but they make the game more fun and random. Enemies can become invisible, attack you outside of melee range and sometimes teleport. While this does not happen frequently it will scare the crap out of you when it does. The game has a lot of speed running potential, but working with your AI family members can be a pain.
There is a few things which are nice to know when you start off:
- there is a sword in your trunk
- the key to enter the castle is randomly located in the inner yard
- the crusifix can kill shadow vampires
- holy water is the most powerfull weapon in the game
- vampires need to be staked in order to kill them
- all family members will die after there timer expires.
- there is a revolver located on top of a wooden construction to your right when you first enter the castle
- you can have ans switch between multiple weapons of the same type
- reloading does not save ammo that is still in your clip
Overall I hope you guys give this game a shot.

This review will be divided into parts that describe each feature of the game as I experienced it.
GUNPLAY
Gunplay in Saints Row IV is fairly standard for an open world game, but without the fine tuning of some similar titles. It leaves something to be desired at first, but soon you'll find it doesn't get in the way of enjoying the game.
DRIVING
The physics are far from realistic and some vehicles are very hard to control.  Due to this and an overall lack of driving in the game, the missions that include driving can be somewhat jarring for your gameplay experience.
STORY
Let's get this out of the way: This is a cynical, satirical, hilarious game. It is not a dark, gritty, serious tale of life in a gang. The story matches the game well.  Certainly not one of the best stories in open world gaming, but at no point was I bothered by its delivery.
POWERS
I played through the game on Hardcore, and I feel that the powers were balanced for this difficulty. You progress slowly, and each new power, along with their upgrades and elements, adds new potential to your gameplay experience. The system was well designed and well implemented. My only complaint is that you get too strong too soon (under two hours into the game and I abandoned cars forever)
ENEMY AI
What AI? They walk towards you with raised guns and try to kill you. In a game like this, that's just fine.
OVERALL
Saints Row IV will not be remembered for being a classic with a great story.  It will  be remembered for being one of the best virtual playgrounds that you can find.  My complaints about this game are few and small.  This is simply one of those games that is -FUN- to play. Isn't that why you're browsing through Steam looking for something to dump money on?

Ys Chronicles+ is everything you could want from the classic Ys I & II. If you're like me and got into the game at Complete, then having the music from both that version, and the PC-88 will make you feel happily nostalgic. The translation is beautifully done, and while I dislike some of the changes from the Complete translation Deuce originally released (Rance being Lance makes sense but I dislike it, Zeptic being Zepic just doesn't sound as good, etc) it corrects some that were... bothersome... (Lair was the original translation for Reah, afterall!)
If this is your first time playing an older Ys game, it will feel primative. It came before Zelda, before Hydlide, from the game makers that set standards to be improved upon by themselves and others. Bump combat is archaic in many ways, but can be so much fun. Ys II's addition of magic gives you more tools to work with, but most of the games your combat is about aligning properly with an enemy, and bashing them as hard as you can with Adol's body. This is easier in Ys II as the enemies gain attack animations and diagonal becomes more of an effective tactic.
For completionists theres plenty to do, people to meet in a rich world where everyone has a house to live in and feels like it could actually work within the rules of its own universe, and there are plenty of easter eggs to find. As a 100%er myself, I loved the achievements they added to the games to give you more reason to play.
Boss Rush in these games is also different from later games, in that if you die its game over. You can't just retry. Boss Rush for Ys I suffers in this regard I find, because Vagulion (the bat boss) is frustrating to fight repeatedly just to get the chance to die against Dark Fact. But it is so satisfying when you succeed!
If you like Zelda, and want to be drawn into a world that has more of a focus on combat, no confusing timelines, and amazing rockin' soundtracks, this is your game. When I first played Ys I Complete years ago it made me need to play Ys II, Felghana, Mask of the Sun, Kefin, Napishtim, and Origin as quickly as I could. While it may not be for everyone, I think this game is a must try.
If playing this game feels dissappointing due to its age, I reccomend giving Ys Origin or Ys Felghana a try, as they are much more modern but keep all of the other important aspects alive.
