Nosferatu: The Wrath of Malachi is the sort of game that feels like it's flying apart as you play.  It's an authentically janky experience, filled with rough visuals, rough AI, and rough edges of all sorts... but a surprisingly playable, unique, charming, and fun "janky experience."
At heart it's actually a fairly simple FPS--traditional, even, with its backtracking and weapon inventory and twitchy gunplay.  You're tasked with exploring a pseudo-random castle to rescue various family members and deal with the local vampire population.  "Deal with" in this case meaning "slaughter."
The arsenal provided for this job is surprisingly unique and varied.  You begin with only a cane sword and your fists, neither of which are particularly effective and lead to a rather difficult initial experience.  Soon however, you're able to find a flintlock pistol and rifle, both of which provide enormous firepower but must be slowly reloaded after every shot.  The revolver is weaker but can of course fire multiple times before needing to be reloaded, and also features a surprisingly powerful alternate melee attack.  The crucifix has limited offensive use, but can be used both to keep weaker vampire creatures at bay and to turn basins of regular water into powerful holy water.  Said holy water can be carried in a holy chalice and will cause massive damage to most enemies, including bosses.  Stakes are a decent melee alternative to your sword/fists and can be used as torches for some extra light, but more importantly are the only way to kill vampires.  Finally, a good old machine gun does machine gun stuff, mowing through enemies and ammunition alike.
The combat itself is workable, if somewhat clunky.  My biggest complaint is that enemy attacks tend to knock your view around (similar to Clive Barker's Undying) and it's quite difficult to get your own hits in at close range.  As a result the beginning melee-focused  areas of the game are easily the most difficult and offputting.  Even when firearms come into play, combat is really a matter of "hit them before they hit you" rather than any sort of give and take.  Still, the emphasis on non-traditional weapons is interesting, and outside of melee fights seldom feel unfair or frustrating.
Enemies aren't the only threat, however.  The castle itself is labrinthine at best and downright overwhelming at worst, and the randomized nature of its layout means navigation can be challenging in and of itself.  And yes, sometimes frustrating as well.  That said, I found that after an hour or so I'd gotten used to the game's maze-like logic, and actually had very little trouble finding my way around or figuring out what to do next.  I even started to enjoy the "exploration zen" of having to keep track of where I'd been and where I had left to explore.
I mean... there's a story too, but it's far from the main event.  Perhaps less "story" and more "setup" for the gameplay: you're trapped in a castle, Count Nosferatu is using your family members to summon something even more evil.  Go stop him.  The cutscenes and NPC dialogue are delightfully cheesy however, and a joy to listen to if you're into that sort of thing.
Overall, this is a game for people who a) love vampire films, b) love janky shooters with interesting ideas, or c) both.  If you're going to get wrapped up in production values or polish, or don't have the patience for dealing with some quirks, Nosferatu: The Wrath of Malachi is not for you.  But if you're looking for a flawed-but-charming little budget FPS with some unique weapons and a cool horror atmosphere, it's honestly a pretty good choice.

XCOM is a fantastic turn-based strategy game.  I didn't play the original XCOM from way back when so I can't compare the two, but this one has a great balance of weapons, unit types, and gameplay that has brought me back for multiple playthroughs. NOTE: This is more of a bug log as well as an overview of things that I believe should be added/improved/fixed.
Some issues I noticed:
- Frontend UI needs a lot of work, it feels really rough right now. I'd suggest splitting the Controls screen off into its own page with its own button.
- In the "How to Play" page, the way the text and graphics are laid out make it extremely difficult to be able to comprehend what I'm supposed to do. I mocked up a quick wireframe of how I'd recommend you do it:
Note: The images of the battery meter should be small enough so they're no taller than the height of the line of text they're inserted into.
- Typo in "How to Play" page: "acess" should be spelled "access".
- There's virtually zero payoff for dying. A black screen saying "you died" without the player ever even seeing the monster (unless I guess the monster is darkness itself?) isn't exactly horrifying. Modern horror typically demands a build of tension with some sort of payoff or release. Extra Credits has an excellent video on this:
- When the player spawns, I don't think you should have the player character directly talk about the battery indicator at the top of the screen. Instead, I think you should have them say something like, "My flashlight's batteries are limited, so I should do my best to make sure that they don't run out."
- I highly recommend that you don't use icons in the pause menu, I'd use normal buttons with text instead. Or, what you could do is when the mouse hovers over a button, have text appear under the button that says what it does.
- There should be some sort of confirmation message for restarting the game when I press the button to do so, as well as for when I press the button that takes me back to the main menu.
- Kevin MacLeod's music isn't being credited correctly. Here's how he requests it be done:

- The footstep sounds should be quieter.
Overall, I like the atmosphere you've created - it has a very nice aesthetic, despite its jarring lack of polish, but there remains a lot of work to be done overall. Giving this a thumbs down for the time being, at least until most of these are addressed in some form.

No Government, No Taxes, and a Bunch of Drunken Monkeys
Donald Trump's plan for America?  Maybe.  The problem with Civ5?  Definitely.
Let me explain.  I love Civ and have put in an embarrassing number of hours since the first version and every version since.  Civ5 is a beautiful and fun game.  I have put in many hours and expect to put in many more.  But it has two critical flaws that keep it from being a truly great GAME (no matter how good it looks and feels).
The first problem is something everybody talks about: the AI isn't very good.  None of the other civs ever really seem to have a coherent strategy, and in battle they are inept at using the one-unit-per-tile mechanics.  They stumble around (figuratively and literally) and you can usually count on the AI's poor decisions to save you from any onslaught, even at the hardest difficulties.
There are a number of good mods that attempt to address this, but they tend to focus on improving AI tactics – how troops move, what buildings to build first, what techs to research.  None that I’ve tested really give the AI a coherent game strategy.  Things like alliances, city placement, trade deals, and a real plan to achieve a victory condition.  There’s more to the game than just spamming troops or spamming culture.
The second problem took me a lot longer to wrap my head around, and I have not seen anybody else talking about it.  It's what I call "Levers of Power".  Civ5 has lots of great advancements in the form of social policies, ideologies, and religious tenants, but all of them are (more or less) permanent and additive.  You build up bonuses, but you never want to change course.  Unlike Civ4 with its rich array of civics, you never change policies in Civ5.  You never throw your economy into a recession and adopt a military government to take on a sudden enemy.  You never change governments, for that matter, because there are no governments.  And what is Civ without governments?
Similarly, there is no tax slider, which is traditionally the main way you balance money, science, and culture (plus things like espionage). Yeah, you can assign your workers to different tiles, but it’s not the same, and you can’t do that at a global scale.  You can change tile improvements, but that’s not the same thing either.  Some people may hate that tax slider (or consider it archaic) but it represents the basic “guns or butter” dilemma, and nothing in Civ5 really takes its place.
Instead, we’re left with a beautiful and glorious system of +1s. As in, “select this policy for +1 production, or that policy for +1 faith.”  You keep building up your +1s following a certain strategy and hopefully you choose wisely and never need to change because you can’t.
And for me, that changing is at the heart of what Civ should be about: Throwing the tiller hard to port, making a sudden change to adapt to new challenges, hoping you can pull it off before you crash your economy, break out in riots, or are overrun by the angry hordes at your borders.
So that’s my problem with Civ5: No Government, No Taxes, and you’re playing against a bunch of drunken moneys.

This is a game I could see my older brother playing as I grew up, but now I have the chance to appreciate it for myself.
I cannot recommend this game enough.  If the latest 3D-rendered actionfest is taking its toll on you and/or your system, give this a shot.

Steep is a game that I had high expectations for. As a kid I loved to ski and still do, nothing beats looking down a snowy white mountain with snow hitting your face. The feeling is like nothing else in the world, a feeling like at any point everything can go wrong but it doesn't. When you go down the mountain your making art, your trail is your trail and can never be fully replicated. Steep nails this feeling perfectly. The world is beautiful and gives you the freedom of creating your own lines and doesn't force you on a set pathway. The ski/snowboard physics are very good and but there is one gripe I have with them and thats the way they interact when on rocks. The game plays it off as it being impossible to have control on any rock surface which can really ruin a great run. The challanges themselves are all very fun except for the paragliding ones. I rarely got frustrated while playing except when I had to paraglide up the Matterhorn. Even though I still got Gold it was one of the few times during the game where I didn't want to continue, ddn't want to explore the next slope or challange ahead of me. Some say this game is light on content but I truely dissagree. On paper this isn't on $60 dollar game but when you break it down and actually understand the range of things you can do it's unbeliable. The soundtrack is amazing at times and irritating occasionally as well but I found that most songs were enjoyable to listen to even though they are almost all liscenced music. A common misconception with this game is that it's the next SFX or tony hawk pro skater with a snowboard. That's not true, it's more of a mix of a simmulator and if Skate was a winter sports game. I very much do recomend Steep at it's launch price tag since it's a game that has more under the initial layer that you just need to find. Find the perfect slope and racing down wiith friends or other online players is insanely fun. I expect to continue playing this for a while and I can't wait to see what more it has in store.

There also seems to be a few issues with inviting friends, but I cannot comment on that due to no-one else playing this.
Overall, I'd wait for a price drop or more content before pulling the trigger. It's rare enough for games like this to come out on the platform, and Steep certainly is worth trying, outside of a few questionable design choices.

FULL DISCLOSURE:  I backed this on Kickstarter.  They put me in the credits!
DOUBLE FULL: This is a first impressions review.
ALSO GOOD TO KNOW:  This game is part one of a planned trilogy.
TBS is a beautifully illustrated tactics game that explores the grey areas of leadership.  There are no do-overs - each interaction is final and moves the story forward.  This means that when you play, you should try to get into your character's head as much as possible, rather than speculating about the other possible outcomes.
I found myself liking the challenging dialogue choices quite a bit.  The theme of "there are no good decisions" comes up often.  One interesting thing is that losing a battle does NOT mean game over, so don't despair.  Your caravan will drag you out so you can lick your wounds and hopefully improve for the next fight.  A training mode is always available, so you can try different scenarios without getting your characters hurt or advancing the story.
I'm excited to play deeper into the game and find out what's in store for everybody, and see more of this lovingly crafted world.  If you're not sure about buying it right now, you can also check out the free PvP battle version called Banner Saga: Factions.  That will get you used to the chess/Advance Wars style of play.
EDIT:  I have finished it.  Conclusion - the drawn art, gorgeous music and detailed writing combine to make this a deeply affecting game.  The battles are exciting and fit into the story well.  I can't wait to play the next installment!
EDIT:  regarding music...
The music in this game keep evolving. The themes get more complex as your road takes you into greater confrontations. Listening to the soundtrack on Bandcamp is nice, but it becomes richer once you've played the whole game (I heartily recommend playing it first).
When I heard the first version of the title theme in Banner Saga: Factions, I thought it was kinda evocative, but strangely loose and unfocused. I can say without a doubt that as I played through the campaign it was this very theme that pulled me headlong into the vibrant, crumbling world of Iver, Rook and Alette. The horns tightened and twisted, grew deeper and more resonant. As I was playing I realized I had been transported emotionally to somewhere unfamiliar - a place of sorrow, regret and grim resolve. Far beyond the threshold of "enjoying" a game - I fell in love...and, well, I've gotta lot of heart-pieces to clean up now. How often can you say that?
Hats off to Stoic, Mr. Wintory, The Dallas Winds and all the other lovely contributors. And hats off you you lot, for funding and playing this game!

If you aren't quite sure what this is, the gameplay is basically a grid/turn based battle system like you'd see in Final Fantasy Tactics. It's over head though, not 3D (no screen rotating, height variations, etc).
The character development and story progression is a lot like XCOM. Your characters have different classes, advance slowly (at first), they can be injured and have to rest after battle before they are usable again and naturally - strategy plays a huge part, in both development and battles.
Furthermore, you are constantly making meaningful decisions. Again, it's like XCOM. You'll get a request to help a small village under attack. If you deny it, some of your followers may get upset and leave. If you agree, you might gain some resources or even a new item or character. However this always comes at a cost. After a battle you'll be forced to camp out and rest, which uses up your valuable supplies.
If anyone is still reading, ill drop some simple Pros and Cons based on my first few hours with the game.
+Beautiful artwork and Soundtrack (Yup, just like everyone else is saying)
+Familiar, yet inventive battle system. Refreshing and surprising to someone like me, who has played dozens of SRPGs.
+The story keeps you involved. It's not just paragraph after paragraph. You're constantly making decisions and they tend to be rather blunt about most scenarios. There isn't a whole lot of filler but it still remains engaging.
+So far I've played with about 7-8 different classes. They seem pretty similar at first, but youll quickly learn their differences on the battlefield.
+Just flat out fun. Frankly, im pretty surprised to play a game like this on the PC. It seems more like a console game... and there's nothing wrong with that.
-ONLY AUTOSAVES, no manual! I kind of get why they did this, but it doesn't negate how glaringly absent it is. A prime example: I decided to raid a village that had been invaded. I fought a tough battle and won. Immediately after, I was given the option to finish off any other enemies and possibly gain some loot or to let them get away. Naturally, I chose the loot.... and died. Being the treasure hog that I am, I knew that I wanted to reload and try again. However I was given no such option. I ended the scene and had to rest a few days to let me heroes recover. I went to go and manually load -- but the autosave was for when I finished the battle, the only other option was to reload the chapter (which would have meant replaying about 45mins of gameplay).
-Pretty bland tutorial. It does the job, but trust me, youll find yourself saying 'wait, what just happened' fairly often. Just be prepared, it's kind of trial and error for a little while.
-The first 4 hours have been pretty confusing and a little overwhelming. You basically play the story from 2 different perspectives and have to switch back and forth between two armies. It works, but don't be surprised if you find yourself in some training battles just to get used to all the new characters they throw at you.
A final note, the preorder character was absolutely worth the preorder. He's my favorite character so far and hes actually pretty damn good in battle. I'd suggest picking him up if they release DLC down the road.

Amazing game. It's like a cross between a turn-based tactical RPG like Final Fantasy Tactics or Shining Force, and King of the Dragon Pass. It's not flawless, though: while some of those flaws (like lack of full voice acting) are completely understandable, given Stoic's small size, others (like the lack of subtitles, or being forced to replay the last five hours of gameplay due to some decision you took waaaay back that now means game over for you) are not.
But even with these flaws the game is still a gem, totally worth the two years Stoic took to develop it since the game's Kickstarter campaign was funded in 2012.

TL;DR: Rather simple cartoonish inoffensive tower defense game. Martians are coming and you must use a bunch of mechanical contraptions (fridges, grills, ...) to stop them from abducting the cows.
I've played this game for about 14 zones in Veteran mode (Summer, invasion 4).
BPE takes some cues from Plants vs Zombies: having to click currency icons to collect them (cogs in BPE), cartoonish visual style with rather silly enemies (Martian maids, crazy scientists, ninjas, ...), pre-mission selection of towers, no tower upgrades, a chance to look at the enemies in the incoming wave...
The biggest difference is that the Martians move along a single route, from the crop circle to collect the cows at the pasture, after which they will haul the cows to the circle to be abducted. In this sense, it's a bit like Defense Grid: dropped cows will (slowly) walk back to the pasture.
With no actual tower upgrades, after placing the towers the player ends up mostly using a ray gun to cause additional damage to the enemies. There are some enemies that actually need player input to defeat (energy shields, ninja Martians who replaced themselves with logs, undercover Martians), but together with the "need to click the cogs to collect them" mechanic feels a bit like a means to give the player something to do. There hasn't been a chance of designing the enemy path (mazeing) either.
It's inoffensive, but nothing spectacular. Just get Plants vs Zombies or Defense Grid instead.

Oh my. I didn't think I would enjoy this game as much as I did.
The story is pretty basic. You arrive at Castle
Malachi to celebrate your sister's wedding, just to realize that all your relatives are going to be used as sacrifices to summon the evil Malachi.
The game also doesn't look that great. The graphics are pretty dated, although I thought the short cut scenes actually looked alright. Something which was great was that there is a filter on the screen which makes the game look and feel like the old Nosferatu movie. The soundtrack also fits the game really well, with creepy songs and sounds, although the voices of the characters could have been done a bit better. Then again, a bit of camp just adds to the charm of the game.
What makes this game so great is the gameplay.
- You have to rescue your family members in time or they will die. They can also die while you are escorting them out of the castle. If they die, they will not be able to assist you, which will make the game harder.
- The game has a good and a "bad" ending. If you are not able to rescue all of your relatives you will not be able to see the good ending. I played on easy mode, but I still failed to save one of the family members, and even let the dog, Buster, die.
- I only played through the game once, which took me about 4-5 hours, but since the castle is randomly generated when you start a new game I will definitely return to the castle at some point, playing on hard mode and aiming for a happy ending.
- There are various enemies, some that need to be killed in a certain way (or with a certain weapon). A sword, a crucifix, various guns, holy water, and of course the most powerful weapon of all - your fists - are all useful in some way or the other. And just to be clear: Killing a vampire is not enough. You need to find their chest and drive a stake through their heart.
- Another thing which makes this game really good is that it sometimes surprises you. At one point I noticed that somehow I had dropped my crucifix, which you need to create holy water. After checking online I learned that apparently bats can knock your weapon out of your hands, so I had to retrace my steps just to get my crucifix back.
- Also, there is no map available. You
get lost.
As for the downsides, as I mentioned the game doesn't look that great. It is also fairly short, but then again the replay value is high, so that is not really a big minus. I also encountered a few bugs while playing. Dying just as I was saving a family member caused the game to crash. Sometimes the AI family members would do stupid things like walk off the edge of a tower. Still, these are minor things, and all things that I can live with.
This game goes on sale all the time, and it is
worth it. It might even be worth it at full price, as long as you don't mind the dated graphics and short length.

This review will be divided into parts that describe each feature of the game as I experienced it.
GUNPLAY
Gunplay in Saints Row IV is fairly standard for an open world game, but without the fine tuning of some similar titles. It leaves something to be desired at first, but soon you'll find it doesn't get in the way of enjoying the game.
DRIVING
The physics are far from realistic and some vehicles are very hard to control.  Due to this and an overall lack of driving in the game, the missions that include driving can be somewhat jarring for your gameplay experience.
STORY
Let's get this out of the way: This is a cynical, satirical, hilarious game. It is not a dark, gritty, serious tale of life in a gang. The story matches the game well.  Certainly not one of the best stories in open world gaming, but at no point was I bothered by its delivery.
POWERS
I played through the game on Hardcore, and I feel that the powers were balanced for this difficulty. You progress slowly, and each new power, along with their upgrades and elements, adds new potential to your gameplay experience. The system was well designed and well implemented. My only complaint is that you get too strong too soon (under two hours into the game and I abandoned cars forever)
ENEMY AI
What AI? They walk towards you with raised guns and try to kill you. In a game like this, that's just fine.
OVERALL
Saints Row IV will not be remembered for being a classic with a great story.  It will  be remembered for being one of the best virtual playgrounds that you can find.  My complaints about this game are few and small.  This is simply one of those games that is -FUN- to play. Isn't that why you're browsing through Steam looking for something to dump money on?

In the grim, dark, grim darkness of Grim Dawn, you will slaughter enemies in their hundreds and thousands with chainaxes and semi-automatic muskets until you get eaten by a boss monster.
If that sounds negative, it isn't. The folks behind Grim Dawn also produced Titan Quest almost a decade ago- anybody who plays both of them will see obvious parallels, right down to individual powers and skills- and know exactly what they want to offer. This is a straightforward hack'n'slash: you see something moving that isn't you, you click on it and hit hotkeys (and occasionally run away until you can drink another health potion) until the critter dies in a spray of bloody gibs, then you rinse and repeat. The formula's as old as the original Diablo, but Grim Dawn provides enough character-building options that it feels fresh. Monsters are fairly straightforward- you've got slow melee, fast melee, shooters, shooters with some area effect, some immobilization, boss versions of each type, etc. They're mixed together enough to provide some interesting tactical challenges.
What else? As mentioned above, the setting employs copious amounts of Grimdark(TM): 19th Century weaponry made out of junkyard materials, armour alternatively borrowed from The Road Warrior and a Victorian costume shop, abandoned and burnt-out buildings, spiky axes made for a steampunk serial killer, you get the idea. Goes well with the gameplay. Buy it and kill stuff, or don't buy it and don't kill stuff (unless you're playing another game that also entails killing stuff.)

I haven't had as much fun playing an RPG since Chrono Trigger. In fact, within the various quests of Divinity: Original Sin, there exists somewhat of an homage to Chrono Trigger.
The very first major quest of the game involves the investigation of a murder. This quest culminates in an epic boss battle that will really test the player's skill (even on normal difficulty).
There are very many puzzles to decipher while the story unfolds. Many of which include fail conditions that will leave you wondering if you should load your auto/quick save just so that you can try again.
Speaking of choices, the dynamic dialog system offers rewards based upon how the player chooses to react to situations within the gameplay. Are you heartless or compassionate? Bold or cautious? You will find out.
The variety of skill choices and combinations is quite impressive. Also, the way that skills/abilities interact makes for an overall amazing experience. Sometimes, it can be quite overwhelming as to how potent these interactions can be!
Given that there are so many abilities and combos based on them, monster encounters are quite entertaining and require some careful planning to emerge victorious. Hostile NPC's do adhere to common archetypes throughout much of the first main quest, but since the abilities are numerous and varied, the encounters don't feel stale. Rewards for difficult encounters feel worthy of the action.
Although it is a bit difficult to figure out, the crafting system can be rather in depth. A player can still choose to ignore it all together and remain successful. I highly recommend trying it out. It can be very beneficial to craft weaponry and the system will be very very helpful for archer types.
The economy of the game is also quite solid. Having completed the first main quest and having moved on to the second area of the game, I have had just enough gold and a little extra at all times. Keep in mind that this is including having stolen every painting and golden goblet in town! Hey, Source Hunters have gotta pay the bills somehow... I would venture to say that managing items and gold in the game is a game all on it's own.
Fans of RPG's like Chrono Trigger, Final Fantasy, Diablo, and other such games like The Secret of Mana will find a refreshing experience while playing Divinity: Original Sin. I feel like this game is a slight departure from it's roots in the franchise. There are many aspects that can remind the player of other Divinity games, but there are enough new additions to give Original Sin it's own identity.
TL:DR *thumbs up*
P.S. I should mention that upon writing this review, I have played 31 hours and I am only mid-way through level 8. There is a lot of game here. (Estimated level 20 by end-game.)

Don't be fooled by all those colours: there is actually quite a bit of depth poured into the gameplay, and the zapper makes sure you basically never sit idle (on the contrary, you must constantly decide if/what to boost or explode), and that's where it differs from many other TD's (and from PvZ, specifically): apart from building towers and picking up ressources, you are always active with what is basically a multi-tool, there's not much waiting involved.
Veteran mode is also quite handy, and I'd recommand tower denfense... veterans ^^ to actually enable it. I'd even say it's worth to turn it on from start. You won't get to make many mistakes and get away with it, but the difficulty isn't offputting either, and as long as your strategy is sound, you shouldn't get stuck wondering what went wrong. "Normal" difficulty I didn't try so I can't really comment, but it sounds nice to be able to play with less focus, or to enable less-hardcore players to fully enjoy the game I guess. Plus, you can always switch between Normal/Vet with the flick of a button apparently.
There's a whole bunch of animations, graphics, easter eggs, you name it. You get everything from ninjas, to secret agents reading news papers unsuspectingly, to Martian ladies filing their nails and cleaning up the alleys :D
Gameplay wise, there's something I found rather odd at first for a TD: compared to mostly every other TD I ever played, the maps are rather small, and towers have very limited range (basically just 3 squares). I was afraid of that at first, but it turns out that it just makes you think about placement and synergy even more, instead of just spamming long ranged OP towers everywhere like in some other TDs. Speaking of which : the game starts slow, but it's kind of a tutorial even though it doesn't officially says so. You gotta hang in there for the first 4 or 5 levels, but after that you get the zapper and get to occupy yourself with it, and start seeing more diversity towers-wise.
All in all, much more fun that some random movie, at the price of a movie theater ticket ;p

At first the game starts pretty slow, but the pace really cranks up a notch after the "tutorial" levels. Everything's explained in great detail (maybe too much for some people?), but after those explanations, the fun really begins and boy does it get hectic at times!
The main originality is the "zapper" (a raygun you get at level 6 I think), and it's used pretty much everywhere: you can shoot down creeps with it (although it's quite weak compared to your actual towers and traps, and it breaks down if it overheats, so you have to manage that too), and you have lots of interactions. For example, quite early in the game, you have G-men like martians that your towers can't detect until you blow his cover with the raygun. You can also zap away the forcefields the mad scientists cast around other martians.
It really adds a great deal of action to the game, it's unlike any other tower defense game I've played so far (in which you basically deploy your towers and wait for them to do the job until you get enough money to put some more).
The graphics are cute and really fun and the music is cool too. It look like PopCap's "Plants versus Zombies" and is every bit as good (although quite different when you get far enough in the game).
The demo is good but don't be fooled: the learning/difficulty curve is actually smoother in the game (although the beginning is still quite slow). Oh also, you have two difficulty modes: normal and veteran. Normal is pretty easy, Veteran is the opposite and will have you yell at your computer, only to come back for more right away :p

To me, it's hard to make a 2D Cartoony style like this entertaining, and honestly I laughed a lot as I discovered the cows along the seasons, the aliens' animations, and of course, Barney ! This toilets cabin makes him so alive, and yet we never see the guy ! Now, imagine that all the 'towers' you put in the fields are alive too... Man, this ambiance is soooo fun ! It's actually a part of the machine, but it's also its eyes. It's a vent, but it's also its mouth. Just love the design of these characters/machines ! Mobs have suits, costumes, cohesive animations, and their abilities are related to their appearance. You could guess what it can or cannot do by just looking at them. It's very pleasant and made me feel like I was watching a good old cartoon from Tex Avery/Hanna Barbera. So alive !
Then came the game... I really don't like Tower Defense game type. BPE is the first one I DO want to complete ! God, I felt entertained all time long ! The first levels were clearly designed as tutorials. That's why all the people who got used to play TDs may be bored, but I think their experience will allow them to complete these levels very fast, to finally get to...
... THE ZAPPER !
Here is how you can turn a simple TD into a frenetic game experience : developpers managed to give you this intense feeling of being overwhelmed, without simply adding mobs, and mobs, and a new wave of mobs... The ZAPPER ! They also played on mobs' resistance, and finally managed to balance mobs' speed, defense, zapper's power, machines' utility and player's actions so that you have a lot of things to setup, manage and use... but in a very effective way ! Everything is damn simple to understand and use, and provides a lot of fun ! Don't... forget... to use... the ZAPPER ! It's your best ally all game long !
And finally, a new dimension came to my attention: mobs' transformations ! You think you killed it, it turns into something else ! Hard Rockers turn into "Berserk Hard Rockers", Zombies turn into graves, where new smaller zombies emerge, ... but I won't spoil everything ^_^ I found these game mechanics very inventive !
A lot of TDs should take example on this game. It's simple, yet effective and terribly addictive, fun and easy to play, and includes a very well balanced challenge.
I should have given feedback on the 'charismatic' fields, or on the growing number of aliens' spawn points as you progress in the game, or maybe on the evolutive environment (mushrooms and their spores, ice forming on your machines during winter and the zapper's utility at this moment of the game,...), and maybe I should have told you about the bosses, the drill, the gears or the cow bell... but I really have nothing to say about it, because everything was part of the fun, and very well thought !
Play this game, it really worths its price !

So heres the obligatory pros and cons list
Pros:
1. Graphics are very nice and detailed. Much detail went into a lot of the textures, and environmental effects to enhance the feeling of the zone you are in. Also the granularity and amount of settings to tweek would make any enthusiast gamer smile.
2. Skills are almost ripped right out of titan quest. Mix and match up to two different skill trees to form your own classes!
3. The current story is rather intriguing, and for a game genre not typically inundated with dialogue, it offers nice story depth, and "bioware-esque" branching diologue.
4. The sounds and music are very well created to the atmospheres you travel around to.
5. Closest thing I've ever come across to an open world ARPG. It gives a general direction to head in, and several winding paths and side dungeons to explore, making the map feel massive in scale.
6. Fledgling ( Currently ) crafting system which uses upgrades as a currency for crafting multitudes of items. Very exciting to see where they take it from here.
7. Offline and Online multiplayer, currently up to 4 players.
8. Heres a unique one, The game doesnt treat you like a child, and hold your hand. It gives you the option for pop up tutorials if thats your thing, but after that, it doesnt spoonfeed you easy enemies and a straight path. It tends to let you wander and choose many different ways to get to your goal. Some more painful than others.
9. The combat feels punchy and rewarding if you can get the hang of how the A.I. functions and your mastery of the controls.
10. THE ABILITY TO MOVE YOUR CAMERA, and to zoom out. These simple buttons make all the world personally. You can view everything in any angle you choose!
Cons:
1. The graphics / engine. The game is, albeit, an alpha, however it suffers from extreme frame dips, chops, stutters, and minor freezes. It is generally playable, yet sometimes it randomly dips to near unplayable frame rates for no apparent reason, causing many a player to drop their settings.
2. The current amount of skill trees feel rather limited to the basics, and it feels rather cramped in comparison to Titan Quest.
3. The multiplayer is glitchy, and crahses for reasons unknown more often then appreciated.
4. Information on some quests and most items and crafting is very scarce due to the new-ness of the game, which sometimes causes confusion.
5. No voice overs on the main bulk of dialogue causes a small feeling of disconnect from the story.
In summary, the game will steal many an hour from your spare time if you let it, and they are very well deserved and spent hours, based on the amount of money they are currently asking. The game is in no way finished yet, and there are extremely exciting features coming soon, such as Factions, and hopefully more crafting.

description of game:
Risk of rain is a one man 2D run&gun game, where you pick a character who's ship got hijacked by evilmcbaddude Providince. You crash land on a "desolate" planet, shooting the faces off various enemies. Killing enemies gives exp and gold which is automatically collected after a few seconds. Gain enough exp to level up, and your abilities will be upgraded and your character will get more health. Use gold to unlock chests that will give you items that will aid in your quest to kill evilmcbaddude Providince. Once you've done everything in one area, you go to the teleporter, which is so interesting looking you won't be able to miss it. Activate the teleporter and you will get a 90 second bum rush of enemies. a boss or 2 are thrown in too. (The time the bum rush takes is dependant on game difficulty). Once the bum rush is over, you can teleport to the next area. Rinse and repeat until evilmcbaddude Providince is dead. Every 15 minutes, you can hear a bell in the background, this means that the difficulty rises. Enemies get tougher, and can be variant. (they get buff) This difficulty meter maxes out when you've played for around 90 minutes, where the difficulty will be set to HAHAHAHAHAHAHAHA and by now you probably have enough items where its no biggie. Alot of stages will have a secret area where a relic can be found. These are basically hax. These include but are not limited to: Glass-deal 5x more damage, but have 1/10 health. Command- Pick the items you get from chests. Spirit-Everything runs sanic fast when almost dead. and much more.

I am biased as this is the first game primarily made by Ubisoft Annecy, my hometown. It is not one of the best in tricks-based snowboarding, especially compared to SSX. It is more of a pure winter sports/mountaineering game. Playing steep brings back memories of my own skiing, obviously not completely true to life, but containing enough little touches you can really feel there at times. The chalets are convincing, as are the pine forests, and the crunch of the snow when you're on foot is perfect when you're stuck in a snowless piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥city and longing for the mountains of home.
I realize I am getting tacky and dramatic, but Steep put me in the mood for that. See, above all, though, it is a gushing love letter to the mountains and winter sports, and it is impossible not to like it when you're a boy of these regions.
Is the midnight ride with a personnification of the Pointe Percée chanting the wonders of the mountains a bit tacky ? Yes. But tacky and overly passionate is a rarity in current year's video games. It's made by mountaineers, for mountaineers, and it shows.
It is not exempt of faults by a long shot. The physics are often pretty ♥♥♥♥ed, there are no goddamn ski lifts when they should be shaping the landscape, the places named in reference to the real Alps have pretty much nothing to do with reality (though in regards of the refuge de leschaux, putting a traditional chalet was more tasteful than the real thing), the tricks system is awkward and a bit too restrictive, and the snowing effects are tame. No Government, No Taxes, and a Bunch of Drunken Monkeys
Donald Trump's plan for America?  Maybe.  The problem with Civ5?  Definitely.
Let me explain.  I love Civ and have put in an embarrassing number of hours since the first version and every version since.  Civ5 is a beautiful and fun game.  I have put in many hours and expect to put in many more.  But it has two critical flaws that keep it from being a truly great GAME (no matter how good it looks and feels).
The first problem is something everybody talks about: the AI isn't very good.  None of the other civs ever really seem to have a coherent strategy, and in battle they are inept at using the one-unit-per-tile mechanics.  They stumble around (figuratively and literally) and you can usually count on the AI's poor decisions to save you from any onslaught, even at the hardest difficulties.
There are a number of good mods that attempt to address this, but they tend to focus on improving AI tactics – how troops move, what buildings to build first, what techs to research.  None that I’ve tested really give the AI a coherent game strategy.  Things like alliances, city placement, trade deals, and a real plan to achieve a victory condition.  There’s more to the game than just spamming troops or spamming culture.
The second problem took me a lot longer to wrap my head around, and I have not seen anybody else talking about it.  It's what I call "Levers of Power".  Civ5 has lots of great advancements in the form of social policies, ideologies, and religious tenants, but all of them are (more or less) permanent and additive.  You build up bonuses, but you never want to change course.  Unlike Civ4 with its rich array of civics, you never change policies in Civ5.  You never throw your economy into a recession and adopt a military government to take on a sudden enemy.  You never change governments, for that matter, because there are no governments.  And what is Civ without governments?
Similarly, there is no tax slider, which is traditionally the main way you balance money, science, and culture (plus things like espionage). Yeah, you can assign your workers to different tiles, but it’s not the same, and you can’t do that at a global scale.  You can change tile improvements, but that’s not the same thing either.  Some people may hate that tax slider (or consider it archaic) but it represents the basic “guns or butter” dilemma, and nothing in Civ5 really takes its place.
Instead, we’re left with a beautiful and glorious system of +1s. As in, “select this policy for +1 production, or that policy for +1 faith.”  You keep building up your +1s following a certain strategy and hopefully you choose wisely and never need to change because you can’t.
And for me, that changing is at the heart of what Civ should be about: Throwing the tiller hard to port, making a sudden change to adapt to new challenges, hoping you can pull it off before you crash your economy, break out in riots, or are overrun by the angry hordes at your borders.
So that’s my problem with Civ5: No Government, No Taxes, and you’re playing against a bunch of drunken moneys.

Antichamber is a game developed by Alexander Bruce and published by Demruth. Antichamber is a first person puzzle game wherein you move from chamber to chamber, equipped with a puzzle gun which interacts with the environment
Antichamber is a game which aims to subvert your expectations about how a puzzle should fundamentally work. It makes you question the unspoken rules that video games abide by. Frequently, it is simply brilliant and mind blowing, though occasionally it’s too obscure or random for its own good (especially nearing the end of the game)
There’s no real story to speak of in Antichamber, but the entire experience is expertly accented in a very sterile atmosphere and minimal graphics. Sound design is also minimal, but well done. Certain audio cues can give you hints to where you are in the world, and the simple tick-tock of a clock can become a fixture of an entire portion of the game. It’s definitely a polished game which looks and feels nice
Of course, the real meat of Antichamber is the puzzles, and it’s hard to say much about them without revealing part of what makes this game special. For the most part, especially in early parts of the game, Antichamber does an excellent job of staying consistent and teaching you the ways of its mind-melting world
However later on in the game, you will be bound to run into situations where a puzzle solution will feel almost entirely arbitrary. Frustration will set in, and occasionally solutions don’t have the satisfying payoff they were designed for
Overall, Antichamber is a smart and incredible puzzle game. It occasionally missteps and frustration just leads to greater frustration, but it’s easy to forgive when so much of the game is so good

Super Hexagon,
A game which is great
It is great because of its simplicity.
It features great gameplay, great controls, a great interface and a great story
Yes, you heard me... a great story.
"But Nick", you may complain, "this game neither has a campaign nor a story". "Well shut up" I reply "and listen to the greatest stories never told, the one of your own"
While playing Super Hexagon for about 2 years now (mostly on phone) you venture through a series of phases you encounter while playing this game. You start with the beginning just thinking "Wow this game is fast and complicated". You may get to 10 seconds on the first level if you're lucky. Then out of sheer interest, you try out the other levels and notice how hard they are and see that there are three more locked ones. You wonder how much harder those are, but quickly return to the first one and try to get better.
In the beginning, nobody would expect this game to be life changing. "It's just a game" you say, yeah well, of course, it's just a game when you die after 10 seconds, but try to stay calm when you reach 59 seconds and die milliseconds before you reach the goal of every level: the 60-second mark. Because, you know, Hexagon, 6 sides, and 60 seconds.. you get what I mean.
But here we are at the main emotion this game will cause: anger. Next to frustration and the will to kill yourself, one of the most common feeling after a few hours into the game. See, I never got how people got so angry at games like Fifa or Dark Souls to a point where they would throw their controllers at the screen. After destroying 2 keyboards and nearly my phone several times I now see the point in getting angry at a game or yourself.
It will most likely end like this: You die a couple of times, get a little angry, but calm down as you now finally reach 30 seconds, then die, get frustrated, die again, get more frustrated, die even earlier, get to a point where you have nearly beaten your record, you start to concentrate real hard, time stops around you, you start to sweat on your hands and your forehead and then, finally, after so many times of trying, the game voice says "excellent" and a second later you die.
Suddenly all that frustration, built up to nearly being happy and the voice mocking you again with "Game over" explodes into a rage you've never seen before. After that sudden explosion of a mixture of violence and swear words you realize what you have done... you got angry... really angry... at a game... because you lost.
There will be much more moments like this. Those moments will surely make you think about yourself and the way you think. In my case I got less angry in general because it made me realize that it is a stupid emotion, one, that should never be let out onto a person. It gave me the ability to really concentrate on certain tasks because I learned how to do it with the game itself.
That's why I think that I can only recommend this game, it will surely tell you a lot about yourself.
Oh, and it's fun I guess.

If your a glutton for punishment then this is the game for you. Whether its hard tactical battles or just waiting for your caravan to get to the end of the screen this game punishes you in so many ways that you keep coming back for more. There are 2 main parts of gameplay to The Banner Saga, the first is obviously the Turn Base Tactical Strategy where your units and the computer take turns pummeling each other. The concept is actually very simple, your STR determines both your health and attack power,  while your ARM determines your resistance to damage by either deflecting, avoiding or minimizing the damage. Your units can choose which type to deal damage in but mostly you need to keep on chipping a unit's ARM away before you can do some real damage to the STR and kill the unit off. Unfortunately most of the enemies you'll encounter have high stats on both and you have to really be tactical on placing your units and how what type of damage you deal. Often you'll find yourself down to just 1 last unit trying to last a war of attrition. The second part of the gameplay is the punishing choices you make, every choice has an impact either immediate or later in the game. The game tries very hard to be real and often the heroic choices lead to a lot of people getting hurt or killed. The game also has some minor managing of your caravan on whether to spend your resource on travelling supplies to get to the next area safely or buy stronger equipment or even use that resource to power up your unit, however the resources you get are sparse and it really forces you to make a choice on whether you let your caravan starve to death to prepare for a hard tactical battle or buy enough food but risk getting a whooping on the next fight. The presentation of the game is simply amazing from the audio down to the design of the characters which tries very hard to be authentic and not your usual rpg tones of half naked girls wearing bikini armour that doesn't even make sense. There's a lot of replay value on this game as you can keep replaying it to see the what ifs of your choices and with only one save slot to use you'd really have to start fresh every time. My only gripe is after your first play through you'd start wanting for a bit of fastforward on some events especially when your caravan is travelling and your really just waiting for the game's event to trigger. Other than that an excellent game to waste your time on and worth a couple of hours of entertaiment before you move on to your next fix.

I have not yet played very far into this game, but I assure you I am enjoying it immensely.
This game feels like a quake-style shooter, doom or wolfenstien gameplay in 3D, but has many quirks and features that make it stand out on it's own.
Nosferatu, The Wrath of Malachi, puts you as the sole able body in a huge family who have gone to a castle in transylvania to marry your sister to a powerful figure, who, of course, is not what he seems.
The castle is filled with demons, from vampires to zombies to imps to spectres, and you must make your way through saving family and friends one by one. Each person saved grants you a new perk at the entrance, from new weapons to the ability to heal there. Your family members CAN DIE, and the enemies WILL GO NUTS ON THEM, so escorting family out of the castle can be a real horror fest. The game is also TIME LIMIT BASED, meaning if you dont book it, people start dying, so do you take old aunt whats-her-name deeper into the east wing to find the rest of the people trapped there, risking her life, or do you escort her out, wasting time backtracking and getting lost, and putting those still in the castle in greater danger?
Rescource management is an important part of this game, you are given a supply of stakes and can find more, and you have to choose "do i use this to make a torch, or save it for a vampire" that kinda thing. You also start with a Crucifix which can ward off some enemies and even damage them, but does not work on all of them. All in all, the weapons in this game are surprisingly fun and satisfying to use, its hard not to feel like van helsing when throwing holy water on a demon. Some enemies require specific tactics to take down, such as the shadow vampire, a creepy thing that comes out of dark corners to rip you to shreds, can only be killed by the Crucifix.
As a horror game, this game does a pretty good job of freaking the player out. Theres no huge jumpscares, but the environment and music can scare the crap out of you if you arent ready for it. Coming from a peaceful dungeon style room right into a hell portal room, the music suddenly goes full blown horror strings and you panic as demons flood out of the portal, in this way, this game fulfills the audio side of horror unlike any other ive played.
The random generation gives it some replayability, but isnt anything groundbreaking. (Though keep in mind this game came out in 2003, long before random generation was a big deal in games)
The pitfalls in this game are the shoddy pathfinding of your friends and the enemies, who get stuck on things often, and a few bugs. If you reload while already full on ammo, the animation plays and consumes a round of ammo, for instance.
I heavily recommend playing on EASY the first time as this game starts off difficult and progressively gets easier, but on your first playthrough getting past the beginning can be hard. Save often.

Superb game from Techland. Mixing the fluid parkour of Mirror's Edge with the up and personal brutality of Dead Rising is simply fun. It is Dying Light's gameplay that really shines above everything else. You can feel yourself becoming immersed in the map, believing yourself to be scavaging around for supplies whilst continually watching your back for the undead.
Your skill tree adds to the experience as I often found myself fussing over which upgrade to go for next. Haven't had this much enjoyment with a grapple hook since Just Cause 2.
Modding your weapons with various elemental qualities is extremely rewarding as you end up slicing your way through your foes like a hot knife through butter.
This game hits another level however when night time falls. The tension increases and suddenly, instead of running amok through the streets, you need to keep back and choose your moves carefully. There's nothing like being camped out in a bus in pitch black as you wait for your chance to escape!
I have forty plus hours spent in this game. The side quests feel like mini missions and every bit integral to the game as the story missions.
Anything negative to say? Not much. There could have been more night based missions. The voice acting was, well, not great. All of this doesn't matter though because the game will surely end up in many people's lists of top games in 2015.

Ok, I've put a little time into this game. Enough to where I can start to form an opinion on it. First off, let me precede this with a disclaimer. The game is currently in Early Access so parts may change once it hits the final build.
This game does have a dark atmosphere similar to Diablo series of old. I've played around with several different builds to date and they all offer something different. However, the true magic happens once you can combine 2 professions to make your own hybrid class(think Titan Quest and you'll completely understand what I'm talking about). If you enjoy that idea and don't mind some occasional weirdness occuring during gameplay, then this game belongs in your library.
Here is where I explain the weirdness I spoke of earlier. Controls can be a little wonky(there have been times that I've selected the enemy that I wanted to attack and my character simply ran over to stand next to them). You will occasionally come across an area that you should be able to reach but an invisible wall will prevent you(to date, I have only seen this a small handful of times and is nothing too major). Also, there is some popup issues where I had to be actively running to have an object appear in front of me.
If the Early Access thing worries you, then I would state that they appear to give regular updates on the game. I'm unsure if they are planning a final pass once they finish the primary development of the title but since they are apparently trying to create themselves and have shown an openess to the community, I cannot see that they will leave issues remaining in the game.
I currently cannot comment on the co-op as I have not yet experienced it other than saying that the game does offer LAN and Online modes.
If you enjoy ARPG's of old and want to experience something both new and old at the same time, I would recommend this. If you are looking for a graphical masterpiece, then hold off. For myself, I fully intend on grabbing a few copies for friends once it is finished so we can all have a grand old time loot grinding.

This a really helpful app.  I had been manually adjusting CPU Affinity and Priorities for years and now all that and more is automated by this app.
Games that this impacts the most positively include Dovetail Games' Train Simulator 2017 and earlier, which depends heavily on CPU for graphics rendering (doesn't matter how good your graphics card is on that game).  Other games that benefit are MAME and other emulators (restrict them to a dedicated core).
Also, if you are cursed with Intel Hyper-Threading, you can turn it off.  H-T is one of the biggest scams out there since it only benefits running many things at a time poorly rather than running a few things excellently.  Anyone who has used Amazon Web Services knows that a 1 vCPU VM is barely 1/2 of a real CPU so don't make this false economy affect your gaming experience at home.

One of my favorite strategy games to spend hours of my life playing.  There really aren't any other strategy games with Civ5's level of depth and diversity.
Each game, you pick a civilization with a unique bonus that somewhat directs the style of gameplay for that civilization.  You start with no vision of the world and slowly venture out to unveil the map.  Depending on how you want to play your game, you can build a bunch of military units and expand your empire by conquering neutral city-states or other civilizations, or you can focus on building your civilization's culture and technology.  Of course, the game is more complicated than that and often ends up being a mixture of the two.
It takes a few games of trial and error before you really start to 'get' the game, at which point you will be obsessed with it.  There's a feeling of wonder you get whenever you start a new game.  There are so many paths you can take to win, if you even get that far.  I personally love playing on the largest maps and spending days upon days building my cities, whereas some people prefer smaller maps that force you to fight the AI.
After a while (and I mean a few hundred hours of gameplay when I say a while), you might find Civ5 to get stale, at which point I would recommend getting the expansion packs.  Brave New World and Gods and Kings really bring new levels of gameplay to Civ5, plus a bunch of new civilizations to choose from and new maps.
Fans of the turn-based strategy genre would love this game (it pretty much defines the genre).  It takes some getting used to, and a bunch of patience, but it is very rewarding and stimulating.

Gorgeous artwork. I've never seen a game that looked this lovely. Honestly, the art alone is worth the purchase price. It combines delightfully with the world building, which is also wonderful.
The gameplay is some of the most chess-like turn-based-tactics gameplay I've ever seen. I say "chess-like" because it relies heavily on formations and using a small number of rules and abilities in different ways to win, rather than, say, Disgaea's approach where you have hundreds of abilities, with elemental affinities that beat each other in a rock > paper > scissors way. In The Banner Saga there's no simple "Fire beats Ice", you have roughly the same skills and abilities as your opponents and the way to win is to outsmart and out-maneuver them, not out-gun.
Outside of combat the game is very much like a visual novel with a survival-game twist: Every decision you make will either help or hinder you (with many more hinderances or pyrrhic victories than clear wins) and this re-enforces the overarching bleakness and sense of desperate struggle.
Highly recommended game, but only if you're fine losing at combat until you get the knack.

The Banner Saga is a tactical turn-based strategy RPG that thrusts you into the position of chieftain of a band of norsemen.  You must lead your clan through starvation and war to the safety of the capital Groffheim, and discover the reasonings behind a grim invasion of the feifs of man and varl.
So, TBS.  The game is a linear progression of fights and encounters as your caravan wends its slow way down the Wandering Road to safety.  You have to manage your food stores, as well as the morale of your clansmen and the size of your army.  The controls and interface are minimalistic - You either travel down the road, or you stop for the night.  Once you have set up camp or reach a settlement, you have access to a number of other screens and options, from the Market, to Training, checking the world Map, Resting, or managing your Heroes.  The camp and town screens are all very beautifully depicted, and all of the towns are unique.  The Map, in particular, is wonderfully drawn and practically every single feature on it has an information and lore window.
Combat is fairly standard for Turn Based Strategy games.  You choose your party from your cast of available Heroes, each with their own special ability.  Fights take place on a grid, and you move and act in alternating sequence with your foes.  Character progression is dictated by kills, and gaining at least one or two levels on all of your characters is very important.  If a Hero is defeated in battle, they will be Injured and suffer a penalty to their Strength stat until a certain number of days have passed.  Like the other features of this game, the combat system is minimalistic in form but quite servicable in function.  I found combats to be interesting and challenging, with the many different class combination of your Heroes providing many tactical options.  The characters, backgrounds, and animations are all wonderfully vibrant and fluid.
If you like TBS games and Vikings, this is the game for you!

This game steps out of the box and grabs hold of you, refusing to let go. Not because it is addictive in its mechanics, not because it has flashy AAA graphics, and not because of gratitious violence or other cheap thrills. Because it has soul, and plenty of it. Stoic dared to go their own way an create something that is not only beautiful, but also enthralling and evocative in its simplicity.
The mechanics for individual parts of the game are not amazing: the caravan mechanic has been over-simplified and sometimes the dialogues feel a bit rushed. The combat is engaging and has strategic depth but has a tad too much repetition to it. Yet the combination of the different parts makes the game special. Together they create a feeling that sticks with you long after you have quit the game.
The magic is created by a combination of stunningly beautiful visuals, a haunting soundtrack that adapts to the story and a feeling of doom and despair. Every choice you make ends up bad. Every decision causes suffering. There is no hope, there is no future. There is only The Banner Saga.

Hi guys, based on the reviews, I thought I'd give this product a try. I launched this program on two of my laptops to see if there would be performance gains as suggested by some reviewers and the product itself.
(Acer Aspire V Nitro Black Edition 2016)
CPU: i7-6700hq (turbo off)
RAM: DDR4 16GB (2400)
GPU: 960M 4GB (boost on)
OS: Win 10
For my first laptop, I used Tomb Raider's (2013 @1080p Ultra preset) Benchmark and started with a base of: 44.4 min, 66 max, and 55.4 avg. For the second test, I turned on CPUCores and got: 44.0 min, 66 max, and 55.1 avg.
The second benchmark, I used Bioshock Infinite's (Custom/Ultra+High Settings) benchmark and started with a base of: 7.49 min, 121.67 max, and 63.3 avg. For the second run with CPUCores enabled, I had: 7.69 min, 105.35 max, and 64.89 avg.
For the last benchmark (1080p, 8xaa, Ultra Quality, Extreme Tess.), I ran Unigine Heaven Benchmark and got the scores: (489) 6.5min, 41.5 max, and 19.4 fps. With CPUCores enabled again, we scored: (494) 7.2 min, 41.3 max, 19.6 fps.
(Alienware M14x R1 2011 Edition)
CPU: i5-2430m (turbo on)
RAM: DDR3 8GB (1333)
GPU: GT 555m (OC to 700mhz/1000)
OS: Win 7
For my older laptop, I used Tomb Raider again (720p Normal preset) For the baseline, I got: 54.4 min, 84 max, and 69.4 avg. For the second test with CPUCores enabled, we achieved: 54.0 min, 83.7 max, and 69.9 avg.
Used RivaTunerStatisticServer + MSI Afterburner to monitor fps, temperatures etc. In my case there were times the program did help the average but lowered my maximum fps. In others, it lowered the scores all around (1-3 fps no big deal in regards to loss). I would recommend others to try this program for themselves and perhaps may have better luck with performanec gains as gamers all around only want the best.

Ok, I've put a little time into this game. Enough to where I can start to form an opinion on it. First off, let me precede this with a disclaimer. The game is currently in Early Access so parts may change once it hits the final build.
This game does have a dark atmosphere similar to Diablo series of old. I've played around with several different builds to date and they all offer something different. However, the true magic happens once you can combine 2 professions to make your own hybrid class(think Titan Quest and you'll completely understand what I'm talking about). If you enjoy that idea and don't mind some occasional weirdness occuring during gameplay, then this game belongs in your library.
Here is where I explain the weirdness I spoke of earlier. Controls can be a little wonky(there have been times that I've selected the enemy that I wanted to attack and my character simply ran over to stand next to them). You will occasionally come across an area that you should be able to reach but an invisible wall will prevent you(to date, I have only seen this a small handful of times and is nothing too major). Also, there is some popup issues where I had to be actively running to have an object appear in front of me.
If the Early Access thing worries you, then I would state that they appear to give regular updates on the game. I'm unsure if they are planning a final pass once they finish the primary development of the title but since they are apparently trying to create themselves and have shown an openess to the community, I cannot see that they will leave issues remaining in the game.
I currently cannot comment on the co-op as I have not yet experienced it other than saying that the game does offer LAN and Online modes.
If you enjoy ARPG's of old and want to experience something both new and old at the same time, I would recommend this. If you are looking for a graphical masterpiece, then hold off. For myself, I fully intend on grabbing a few copies for friends once it is finished so we can all have a grand old time loot grinding.

Risk of Rain is a 2d sidescrolling Rogue-Like, and well worth your time, provided you're willing to suffer through a few glitches and a matchmaking system that's honestly just a hassle.
Story~  Risk of Rain has a story that a lot of people just kind of breeze by.  It's not told very much outright, but it's a pretty good story about survival and what you're willing to do to survive.  The ideas behind some of the creatures is very interesting as well, though most of this information is found through cards rarely dropped by their enemy counterparts.
Gameplay~  The game is a rogue-like, so expect to die a lot.  The Bosses are pretty cool, as are a lot of the enemy varieties.  Elite versions of enemies will occasionally spawn, and have special properties.  Hell, even the occasional boss can spawn in an elite variety!  This game also has an interesting way of increasing difficulty: by time.  You have to go through 4 stages, each of which has 2 or 3 variations, before finally entering the final stage, but more on that later.  The important part is, you can go through these 4 stages as many times as you'd like, leveling up and accruing more items as you progress.  The only problem is, the enemies around you get more difficult to face as time progresses, so it's a race against time as much as it is a grind for the best gear.
Class Variety~  The class variety in Risk of Rain is great.  Each is unlocked in a differnet way, whether it requires beating a mini-boss, beathing the game on a certain difficulty, finding it in the world, or just collecting a certain number of x thing. Instead of going the Binding of Isaac route, where each character is just Isaac with a few stat changes and equipped with a few items from the starting block, all of RoR's characters are unique and interesting.  There are 12 classes in total, and none of them play in the same way.  From a large robot who punches enemies to death, to a sniper and his drone pal who together are able to one-shot bosses, everyone plays the game differnetly.  Speaking of which...
Relics~  Relics are very interesting ideas.  Each level (save for the last, I think) has a relic, and each relic changes the game in some substaintial way.  For example:  Glass gives you 10% health and 500% damage, Command lets you choose what items you pick up, and Enigma makes your use item a special one that has a different effect each time.  These relics are dificult to find, and often times you won't use a relic you found.  Even so, they make for a large amount of playstyle variety.
Items~  Items are dropped from buyable chests, dopped by bosses, or occasionally found on shrines/earned from shrines.   There are four (sort of 5) item classes:  common (white), uncommon (green), rare (red), boss items (yellow), and use items (orange).  The first 4 are increasingly powerful passive items.  These passive upgrades include extra health, a sort of field around you that does damage to enemies within it, +1 max health for each killed enemy, or even an upgrade to your 4th ability.  Use items, on the other hand, are activated by a button press.  These also have extremely cool effects, from a slew of high-damage projectiles capable of killing a boss by themselves, to the ability to open every chest on screen for free.
Soundtrack~  The soundtrack of this game is absolutely wonderful.  Each track is strange in its own way, and they all help build a level or bosses atmosphere.  I can't not mention the final level's theme as one of my all time favorites in a game.  It's a haunting track that really gives the feeling of "win or lose, this is the end."
Level variety~  The levels in this game all feel very unique.  Each level has 2 variations, usually centered around the presence (or lack thereof) of a relic.  Each level has a unique set of enemies, and a unique roation of bosses (though some bosses appear in mulitple levels).
The U.S.S. Contact Light~  I can't NOT talk about how amazing this final level is.  Not only is the afformentioned musical accompanyment one of the best in video game history, but the level itself is unique and sprawling, with secrets and different ways of going about completing it.  First off, there are four rooms you can unlock with keycards occasionally dropped by enemies.  A few of these rooms can be accessed without the keycards, given you've invested heavily in mobility upgrades.  3 of these 4 rooms contain a peice of equipment that can help out greatly in the final battle, as well as several chests.  There are also many doors between wherever you spawn and the boss.  Each takes 30 seconds to open, and you'll be bombarded with enemies while they do.  Speaking of which, this stage contains several BOSSES from the previous levels as normal enemies, the Wandering Vagrant in particular.  Once you've done all you want to do, you can finally face off against the final boss.  I'm not going to super spoil anything, other than that it's a super difficult, multi stage fight that will take great skill in your character, along with a good set of upgrades (or the glass command relic combo).
Glitches~  This is the biggest problem with this game.  The game can crash sometimes if you're not playing it with the right specs in the right way.  Along with this, you can fall through the map occasionally.  I personally haven't had a great deal of contact with these bugs, but apparently they're still prevailant some 3 years after the game's release.
Matchmaking~  And now to my only real problem with this game.  It's marketed as a multiplayer game, but setting up a match with friends is honestly a chore.  You have to go through an IP adress, and half the time it doesn't work anyhow.  It's unfortunate that this part of the game takes so much preperation, otherwise I'm sure I'd be having even MORE fun than I already am.
Why wouldn't you like this game? ~
~ The lack of matchmaking (1)
~ Glitchyness (2)
~ A good bit of difficulty (3)
What to play instead ~
~ Castle Crashers, (I hesitate to say) Minecraft
~ Binding of Isaac, Castle Crashers
~ Crypt of the Necrodancer, Castle Crashers, Risk of Rain but with the Command/Glass relics on.

Risk of Rain is a 2D platformer, rogue-like game (that means when you die, you start over), with a lot of randomness when it comes to items found and enemies encountered. Some stages are also randomized (I believe every stage has two possible layouts)
Players can unlock more items (to be found randomly in a game), characters, and artifacts (that can be used to modify game rules, making it either more difficult or easier) by doing achievements and tasks.
In the game, each character has 4 abilities, usually composed of a normal attack, an areal attack, an escape/boost ability, and a powerful ultimate. There is an XP system (not permanent, or resets every "run"/every restart), where each "level up" slightly increases health and damage. Lastly, there is a gold system (similar to the XP system: not permanent) which can allow you to purchase items (usually randomized, but there are some where you can see the options and choose one).
The game also becomes harder the longer you survive. After several minutes you'll encounter stronger versions of enemies, with more abilities that will surely bring you faster to your doom.
I find this game very fun to play. I always love difficult games especially ones with randomness and having the ability to choose game rules. The characters have a variety of interesting abilities and play styles, although you start with only one fairly balanced character.
It takes a while to unlock more stuff, especially artifacts, which require some good RNG for the items required to find them. Some of them are puzzle-based as well, which is interesting. One of the game-changing artifacts
. Having that one made runs easy.
The design is good. The colors blend well for a game that needs focus, it doesn't hurt the eye. The music is also awesome. There's some dramatic feeling to it, but not too sad. They fit in well with the setting. Also they're good for doing homework ;)

There’s a multiplayer conversation system (which you can play both sides of if you’re playing a SP game, or assign the second protagonist an AI personality to automatically choose their own lines) which is even better than SWTOR’s because it actually takes into account whether the protagonists agree or disagree with one another; my only criticism is the rock-paper-scissors method of decision resolution if you disagree (it’s also used as the persuasion minigame when trying to convince NPCs).
