SECOND EDIT: They updated the game again, fixing things that weren't broken and adding DLC not included in the season pass, not even a year after the season pass was released. The fall ragdolls are a lot floppier now, which is a minor detail that probably slows the character faster, and the UI looks nicer and more consistent, but it's a little more cluttered. The splash screen at the beginning now has another thing to press through that asks you to buy the DLC not included with the season pass. Performance has dropped, and any visual improvements are unnoticeable.
In sum, the new update is unnecessary and exists only to show people they've updated the game. It's still Steep, and it's still fun, but the season pass was insubstantial and provided practically no content, and new DLC is not included, which feels like a rip-off. I can no longer recommend the game for how the publishers and developers are handling the DLC.
Steep is a gorgeous game.
It's beautiful. Once you get past the admittedly repetitive and bland missions, poorly-voiced characters, and a story so shallow it has negative depth, Steep is a sandbox of exploration, tricks, badassery, beauty, and danger.
As a note before we begin: Steep is not SSX. You won't find that level of ridiculous stunts here, and the game is not as forgiving. It is comparable to SSX, though, and if you liked SSX, Steep can still offer something to you.
Of course, that's when it's at its most poetic. Naturally, the game fills a niche: if you don't like snowboarding, skiing, paragliding, or wingsuiting, you won't like this game, and even if you do, the price is, pardon the pun, rather steep.
If you do like them, and the price isn't a problem, you next have to deal with the missions and, consequently, the voice acting. While some of the voices are alright, the grating radio personality and the bland "boss" voice are the most frequently heard and the least likeable. The best voices are, thankfully, those of the atheletes (snowboarders? they don't just snowboard).
The missions themselves are pleasant at best and teeth-clenchingly frustrating at worst. While the game is difficult on its own, many of the missions are particularly hard, which is poorly-conveyed by the three-star rating system of difficulty. Adding to the problem is that you have to level up to gain access to Mont Blanc, the best mountain for generally having fun, and you have to go through the worst of the mountains to get to it.
The "story" is as follows: you are a professional extreme sports person, you make money of footage and competitions, you are the best at them, go win and you will unlock more of the competitions. Of course, you shouldn't have expected a story, silly. However, the tone is inconsistent: some missions take themselves seriously like the Red Bull invitationals, but others act like you're on a Hellish game show like the missions of the Mountain of the Damned.
The incredible beauty of the game is immediately apparent, though: as soon as you enter, you're dropped in on the mountain range to see the snow-covered hills and glittering snow itself. The graphics are wonderful, and the optimization is pretty solid (my thoughts on optimization are probably not the most reliable, as my rig is pretty high-end). Naturally, though, beauty is subjective, and if you don't like what you see in the screenshots, you won't like what you see in-game.
The gameplay is where the game shines, though please read before downvoting because you had a hard time: the game takes some skill and practice. This isn't to say you're bad, this is to say you need to give it time, get used to and good at handling the controls, and note that the keyboard controls are much worse than controller, but the game is entirely playable with mouse and keyboard. Snowboarding and skiing handle mostly cleanly, though inconsistently: sometimes you get slung off to the side when cresting a hill at an awkward angle. The wingsuiting is fast and requires precision, but use the IJKL keys as a second directional pad to dodge and you can slip through gaps you wouldn't be able to before. The only place where the gameplay falls off is with two things: glitches and paragliding. The glitches are maddening at times: sometimes a jump your character landed cleanly and lightly on a steep slope will reduce their endurance gauge (that's the best I can call it) when they should have been fine, and the paragliding is murkily explained with tooltips that don't give any tips at all. The most helpful thing I discovered with paragliding: the stunts button is not just for stunts. It helps you move down in updrafts.
Overall, Steep is a beautiful, clean-looking sandbox for high-speed skiing, snowboarding, and wingsuiting, and for leisurely hangtime in paragliding. It's a little unpolished, and you will encounter glitches - perhaps it's best compared to Skate 3 in that regard - but it's a fun, satisfying experience if you're looking for a more modern snowboarding game.
TL;DR: Steep is flawed, but it's not bad: the repetitive missions are annoying, the voice acting grates, the keyboard controls are awkward, but once you get past all that and get better at the game, it's a winter wonderland made to be explored and shredded with solid, if slightly inconsistent, handling and beautiful graphics. Use the stunts mode for paragliding if you want to go down fast.
EDIT: Edited for the Steam Awards. They added a jetpack with wings, which is dumb, but it's cool. Lots of fun.

I was very disappointed in this game.
The Good
It's beautiful. The animation and soundtrack are phenomenal. The combat is satisfying.
The Bad
The story is slow to start but by the time it gets interesting the game ends. The story is presented almost entirely through text and that text reads like a "choose your own adventure novel". This would be fine but the quality of writing is lacking and the way the text jumps between third person perspective and second person narrative is annoying. It's especially annoying because there are multiple points of view for a majority of the game.
I'm an avid reader so I don't mind reading in my RPGs but I at least want some consistency.
As for the main game mechanics it's a lot like a 2D Oregon Trail. The campaign consists of two stories following two player controlled caravans as they cross a map. Most of the choices given the player consist of:
Do the smart but heartless thing
Do the dumb but moral thing
Do nothing
There will be other options but they either return you to previous "options" or are just variations on the same.
The main game mechanics  consist of making dialogue choices and trying to keep your caravan of refugees alive by making the correct choices.The entire game is on rails so you don't actually change the story or make meaningful decisions (outside of combat), you just get rewarded or punished for the choices you make.
Summary
All in all the lack of real game content and lackluster story heavily detract from a beautiful game that could have been brilliant but just overall feels lacking. There's also nothing to do after the main story has concluded but play the game again. I would be okay with that if they story had been well written and the other game mechanics had been fun.
If you're looking for a finished tactical RPG keep looking. This is apparently the first of three chapters but it's up in the air if those will be made, and as it is this is not a finished game. It ends abruptly just as the story becomes interesting, and no matter what you do, the ending is the same. The store page should be more reflective of the fact that this is not a single player version of Banner Saga Factions, but is in fact more like Oregon Trail, with some tactical combat tacked on. Or maybe it's the other way around, but either way it doesn't work.

If I had to describe this game with one word, it would be TENSE.
Nosferatu is a charming little horror-themed FPS in which you play a man named James who arrives at a spooky old castle in Transylvania to discover that your family has been taken hostage by the count, an ancient vampire, who plans to use their sacrifices to carry out some profane ritual.
The game is essentially one giant map (the castle) full of locked doors and random items, with occasional loading screens separating the various "wings". It can be completed in a handful of hours, but this is sort of the point; you only have the span a single evening, in real time, to track down and rescue your relatives from certain death. You must then escort them to a "safe zone" at the entrance to the castle, at which point they will reward you with a special item, like a weapon or temporary powerup. Level design is essentially one long key-hunt; without the aid of a map you are forced to rely on your pathfinding skills as a gamer to keep track of where you've been and where you need to go.
Combat is simple, but satisfying. Enemies spawn and respawn seemingly at random to keep you on your toes. Some can only be harmed with certain items, like the crucifix or holy-water. If you fail to stake a sleeping vampire in time, get ready for a fight. The game is littered with unexpected boss fights. Spooky ambient noises and a contextual soundtrack that triggers in the presence of monsters add to the anxiety, considering without a lit torch it is often difficult to see more than a few feet in front of you.
I'm not gonna lie, I almost gave up on Nosferatu early on. I had to jump through several technical hoops just to get it running, and the game is excruciatingly challenging, packed early on with death by misadventure, until you find your first firearm. Technically the game is rough around the edges, which in my opinion, adds to its charm. As I mentioned you'll need a tutorial to get it going in full screen on modern operating systems. I was unable to pick up certain items and my gun was constantly clipping through the wall. The reload sound for the flintlock pistol goes on twice as long as the actual reload animation, which is distracting, and on several occasions I would go to fire a weapon only to discover it needed to be loaded... again... for some reason.
Overall, this is a solid if overlooked shooter from the early 2000's. It's short but fun, and replayable due to a level of randomization in map design and item placement. Most importantly, it's SCARY! The atmosphere is perfectly foreboding and you never feel completely overpowered. There is a delicious sense of urgency as you struggle to save your friends and family in time. I managed to rescue everyone before dawn except poor Melissa, who I was informed via a jarring cutscene had been skinned alive. Oh well, I still got to mow down a demonic horse with a machine gun.

This game is a very specific genre -- lots of shooting, strangeness and upgrading of weapons.
However, it still has a decidedly cheesy side, which disappoints.
For example the "dialog" that occurs with somewhat randomized structure between the first person and an assitant who not only narrarates a bit, but also offers suggestions, is dull and devoid of purpose.  An example of this occurs after the first person has upgraded weapons;  she still says she has to shut down the trading machine soon.  This may be true, but it reeks the broken-style repetition of children's games.  I got the impression they played a bunch of sayings and kept the ones a focus group liked the best.  But there is so much more room for interaction.
Really, it's worse than this.  The randomized sayings from the imaginary first person and second person interrupt each other.  At times, the second person (female) actually says "Ah, I'll be able to bring up the trading post, soon!", after I've already been defeated.
Another example: even if I've already upgraded my weapons, maybe even spent all my money, if I approach the trader post, she still anounces "You've earned the money, now spend it!"  Damn, that's stupid.
Until now, I have only played the solo waves, so I limit my critisism to this portion of the game.  Amazingly, I prefer to fight computerized bots, despite their synthetic, consistent, zombie-like mentality.  I also like eating at Mc Donald's.  There is a connection, I'm thinking.
I have not yet found a way to accelerate my way to using the better weapons.  It disappoints me to play a ten-wave solo session and get killed a few times after just three rounds.  Of course, practice makes perfect, but my time is just too valuable to waste on something I'm not having a truly fun time with.  I would pay real money for the ability to save particular spots, and replay from these points, or to modify how the weapons are order in the next-weapon, prev-weapon list.
Maybe it's from being a veteran, I appreciate that practice makes perfect -- muscle memory is the only thing that counts when the pressure becomes nearly overwhelming.  So the order of weapons is crucial for me.  I start with one weapon, for quick reloading after just a couple of kills; this keeps it reloaded more easily after one or two shots.  Then, I want a full-clip weapon for when I'm likely to be draining the clip each time -- that's what clips are for.
But the "start with basic weapons, advance to better weapons", nature of the solo rounds makes the automatically assigned order of the weapons feel very arbitrary.  In particular, since the weapons I use keeps changing over iterations, I'm constantly forced to remember: "Do I switch up, or down, next?"  And I often get it wrong.  The stupid health sprayer is in there, too -- uselessly.  What am I going to do with that as I'm backed into a corner?  Spray my enemies?
I wonder why isn't there an option to leave this out.
One of my least favorite aspects of the game involve when my characted is defeated.  The system just sits there, locking you in a state of not advancing, but not doing anything else, either while if give you a message telling you, basically, that you can wait a couple of minutes before you can start over.  Sorry?  My time is too precious for that crap.
Maybe, given the intensity of the game, the programmers were concerned they perhaps made it TOO intense, and thus require the user to wait a couple of minutes after each round, just as a breather.  More likely, however, is that this is the standard setup for online games, and it made the programming easier.
This is a very strong programming effort, on the whole.  The programmers use one of the smoothest, prettiest game engines I've ever seen, and they use it to the maximum.
It would benefit from more lively dialog with less repetition and more cleaver lines - hire a creative writer, guys!  Consider creating rules that arrange randomized dialog to make sense.  The game delivers basically, those qualities a child most wants from a game: pretty graphics, combined with convincing physics laws, smooth play w/ very, very few bugs, and ... TEAM PLAY!  YAY!
But, why stop polishing the product, simply because it earns money, and works for the kids?  Doesn't the stupidity of some of the dialog make you WANT to do something about that?
A game should not waste my time, waiting and doing nothing after a defeat (or victory) before it loops around to a point where you can begin again.  Could you please give me a hack to turn that off?  EDIT: after living with the waits, just to play the game, I find it doesn't bother me as much as it did at first.  I would still like a means of reducing the time waiting after a round to zero, though.
A means of customizing the order of weapons in my list would be very, very nice (this is a common feature in FPS).  A means of removing the stupid health sprayer from the weapons list would be nice.
Of course, since I only play the game in solo mode, some will say that I am not using the game the way it's "supposed" to be used. I was a big fan of the original standalone Killing Floor release, and coming into the KF2 beta I was a bit skeptical.
It felt different. The pacing was off, very little content, and various other things that just didn't feel right. The game was of course still being made, but my first impression was fairly dull.
However, following the full release of the game, I'm actually thoroughy impressed. The game looks, sounds, and feels amazing to play and improves on the first in a lot of ways.
++PROS++
Good lighting and shading
Zeds look cool
Amazing sound design
Guns have a lot of oomph and look sexy
Perks feel more specialised and tactical
Zeds are more dynamic now, with more emphasis on their mechanics
Zeds gain additional mechanics on higher difficulties, not just raw number increases
Multi-perk weapon system allows for a bit more choice
Lever-action rifle still feels amazing
Cash is now called Dosh (grab it while ya can, lads)
--CONS--
Can't designate a region for the automatic matchmaker (often places me in servers with 300+ ping)
The boss fights aren't very interesting
Matches do get a bit repetative after a while
Rubberbanding sometimes even at low latency (<50ms, possibly client side)
The Survivalist perk doesn't seem useful
Can't use keyboard commands to call out important Zeds (would be useful for public matches)
No official West London map (I think?)
No lods of emone
Overall: 7.5/10 (8/10 with friends)

I've played quite a few games of Civ V, however I've never been entertained enough to actually finish one, which is rather dissapointing since Civ IV is one of my favorite games of all time. I have quite a few greivances with Civ V so I'll give them in no particular order. The sense of scale of war is removed: entire civilzations fight with only a handful of units, and armies no longer exist due to the one unit per tile rule, which also makes moving a cluster of units for attack into a headache. Growth and expansion are severly inhibited; it takes much longer and imposes many more penalties to found new cities and expand your civ's area of control. Border expansion was previously highly predictable, in Civ V cities take control of single tiles at a time in no apparent order. Commerce allowed for tweaking cultural, espionage, wealth, and science production in previous Civ titles, however there is significantly less control in Civ V, as each is produced by population and buildings, you can't reallocate commerce/gold into research, culture, etc. Interacting with city states is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ and essentially boils down to pouring gold and effort into just pleasing a half dozen or more of these fickle things for the resouces they're sitting on. Feel free to disagree, but this game has almost none of the things I enjoyed about Civ IV, and has left me bored about halfway through each game I've played. Here's hoping Civ VI is better.

Let me preface this by saying that I
recommend the game, but I do
recommend buying it at the full price of $15. I don't think it's worth it unless the game is on sale. That being said, here's my review of the game:
Block'hood is a beautiful city building game that combines the art style of Monument Valley with the upward building idea of Tiny Towers. Its main mechanics are micromangement and resource awareness, as each block requires different inputs and produces different outputs. A balance must be struck so that certain resources aren't eaten up too quickly and others don't pile up and cause negative effects (note, I wouldn't necessarily call them
and
resources, as even resources with negative downsides can be used positively). It is very open in build choices, meaning you can create a full industrial complex, a single cabin in a massive forest, or a harmony of man and nature. The story mode focuses on this balance
The story mode is a few chapters long and tells the story of the main character finding the right equilibrium between machines and animals. The story itself is quite nice, but more importantly it teaches some basic mechanics of the game, ramping up to showing the inner workings of more advanced blocks near the end. I highly suggest playing the story mode after the tutorial. I would definitely like to see more stories available, hopefully this is something the devs are working on
These are, as the name implies, short levels where you try to reach a certain goal, such as producing a certain amount of resource without producing too much of a negative one. Difficulties go from extremely easy to nearly impossible, challenges are a nice follow-up to the story mode but I'm not a huge fan of them. They make it feel like a cheap mobile game and I would much rather see more story options
This is where the game shines the most, in my opinion. Here you're free to create whatever giant world you feel like. You can follow the rules of resource management and try to grow your hood naturally, or you can completely ignore them and build purely for the aesthetics, which make for some gorgeous creations when coupled with the style of the art
Block'hood has a simplistic but charming art style that works quite well with the "artificial vs natural" theme that the story highlights. There are so many different blocks to use and learn the best route for managing various resources. The nature of the game lends itself to sandbox mode. However, I would love to see more emphasis on the devs on new stories. The game is 100% playable and enjoyable, but I do think there are a few unfinished outlets, such as certain resources that cannot be used and just build up forever

The concept for this game is really good. Old school vampire story, Dracula lore based means its a very good premise to begin with. Everybody loves the old scary Dracula stuff. No school like the old school. The different gameplay aspects such as the time limit given to save your 16 family members (doggie bruce not in the list) and the possibility of not being able to save everyone makes it even more interesting. With a huge gothic castle as the location, it makes the plot even more enjoyable.
The maps might not have much variety. But for a game of its size it is acceptable. Tedious and boring at times, but nothing to really intefere with the gameplay. For a gem this old, i think it did a really good job in doing something different for its genre.
On the other hand, old games are bound to be filled with bugs. Enemies don't move properly at times. Can be frustrating for melee but not ranged.  Your family AI can be pretty dumb at following you. I can remember the times when Gregory and Bruce jumped to their deaths off the roof of the castle, because the AI is dumb. Not game breaking, just annoying. But most of the bugs are just minor annoyances, does not make the game unplayable.
Only major issue is the screen resolution problem. When you start the game from steam, the game resolutin won't be right. Might be because of Windows 10. I'm not really sure. Only way to solve it is to download the fixes online. Plenty of it. Just go look for it. Or you can go to your Nosferatu folder and choose the start application in the folder. You get to customise the graphic settings. Not as good as getting a fix. But good for a temporay solution.
Get it while it's on sale. Maybe when its at 1 dollar. Not really worth the full price. The game can be finished in 7 hours i think,or less. Old games should be sold cheap, unless its a rare game.

Now after 1000+ hours of game play, it being completed with a max level of 85 and 3 difficulties.
I believe that I am able to give a decent review of Grim Dawn.
If you are looking for a game which have an awesome desolated atmosphere like Diablo 2 and Titan Quest did. This might be the game of your dreams!
This game has a really well done level, skill and devotion (for really making a character unique) system for players who wanna play a game, where classes never feel the same!
At level two the player can pick 1 out of 6 classes from a tanky Soldier to a High Damage Occultist who specialize in poisens, curses and demons, THEEN! at level 10 you will be able to pick another class that "creates" a whole new class with the skills and stats from the class you ofcourse wanna invest most in. By mixing two classes you can even create alot of different playstyles.
For an example;
I played and leveled a Minionmancer (one who uses nothing but summoned pets)
and a vampiric bloodmage who can pretty much soak tons of damage and replenish the missing hitpoints instantly. They might both be called a Conjurer (Occultist & Shaman) but where the Minionmancer kites and debuffs the enemy so his pets can take down the prey the Vampiric build is nothing less but tanky, with great damage potentiel but have to remain infront of the enemy and take the fight straight on.
Now fighting for your life and the life of the humans you meet on your travels, you have to pick options in a variety of missions. You can forexample pick to choose to help people and befriend them or save them but blackmail them into paying you for it. All these options actually have effect on the game. Some merchants will sell you better gear and unique stuff like Dynamite if you treat them well and dont offend them.
When a hold of people like you enough you get to do special missions and bounties, and they can sell you unique gear. While angering the enemy will cause them to improve their efforts to destroy you and your allies, to the point that they will bring enemy heroes and even a Nemisis which is hard to find and kill but rewards you with a Nemisis loot chest.
With these quests, the lore books you find and the different characters you meet you will find an understanding of this world of Cairn.
The final and properly most important thing about this type of game. THE LOOT!
Finding rare and epics are to some extent easy enough but rewarding as their stats can vary.
But when you hit late game of the first playthrough you will find the LEGENDARY! items which you basicly can build whole characters around. The scaling of stats in items, is easy (No million numbered stats like in Diablo3) While searching for a proper difficult opponent you might look for the portal proof dungeons or even a Avatar of a god.
All in all, I would not have kept playing this past the 30hour mark if it was like Diablo3 or Path of Exile. I find this entertaining and the way they improved it from the many previous builds I have played, they do not disappoint.
I will rate this a  ___9/10___
If you love games like Torchlight ( but look for a working game)
If you love grinding gear like in Diablo 3 (But hate that you actually play an arcade game)
Or love some of the other "lesser" games like Titan Quest (which was done by some of the same guys I believe) or Sacred (which had little in Lore but alot in combat)
THIS IS THE ULTIMATE GAME FOR YOU!

Mirror's Edge is a fantastically presented mediocre game.
While its visual style, music, and atmosphere are top-notch, its core gameplay is, in my opinion, slightly lacking. While the game shines in its free-running segments, pretty much every part of the game where you're being shot at feels like a chore. And these segments are unfortunately numerous.
The main theme of the game is free-running, and the first advice you're given about combat is "avoid the enemy". Naturally, the best option in a game like this, where your character, Faith, is extremely agile and quick, is to run from the enemy, evade them, or sneak by them. However, stealth is impossible; enemies will simply detect you no matter how much care you take to sneak quietly. Additionally, there are many forced combat segments: the game tells you to avoid the enemy, then places you in situations where you are unable to do so. This wouldn't be a problem if the combat were enjoyable, but unfortunately, I did not enjoy it.
The main flaw with the combat is the lack of a learning curve. On Normal mode, enemies can shoot you dead in two or three hits. This means that there is no time for Faith to practice her moves; if she messes up at all, which is inevitable when practicing, she's dead, and you have to start the whole sequence over again. Reaction time does little to remedy this. These segments really throw a wrench in the otherwise smooth action of Mirror's Edge.
As I said, the game is very smooth, and its free-running segments, where your only enemy is a steep drop off a roof, are stellar. It feels very rewarding to get the hang of the controls and totally ace a segment without falling or losing momentum. Unfortunately, these segments are mostly used as links between the combat segments in the later game. I feel as though Dice, a developer probably best known for its shooters, felt they needed to incorporate shooter elements here in abundance. But the game would be much better off if it revolved more around the parkour elements, with combat being optional.
Enough about the combat, let's talk about the better parts of this game: The design is fantastic. The use of strong color and good use of visual filters makes this game look like a work of art. The cartoon cutscenes between chapters are great, if slightly low-budget feeling (many frames are noticably re-used). The music is great, and helps the peaceful sections feel peaceful and the dangerous sections feel tense. The characters, while not explored terribly much, still play their parts well, and putting yourself in Faith's shoes is not hard. The unlockables are a nice touch as well.
Despite its flaws, this game is still solid. But now that I've experienced it first-hand, I wouldn't say it's as great as many people say it is. When I find myself admiring the aesthetics and theme of a game more than its actual gameplay, it's hard for me to recommend it to others. However, if you can get this game on sale, I would recommend you play through it simply for the experience. It's presented very well, and it's a shame it didn't have more dev time (there are some cut things in the unlockables), and it's also a shame that it was so short. Hopefully the sequel can improve on this game's flaws, but as it stands, I'd only recommend it at a reduced price.
Good Points:
- Stunning visual design, amazing aesthetics
- Good free-running segments, Runner Vision is an intuitive system
- Good music that bolsters the atmosphere
- Engaging characters
Flaws:
- Forced combat segments feel out-of-place
- Lack of learning curve, no real way to practice combat
- Too little free-running for a game that's supposed to revolve around it, compared to gunplay and combat
- Pretty short, no expansions or extra story content
- Stealth is impossible, enemy AI is telepathic
Bottom Line: It's a great work of art, but only a passable game. Recommended, but only if it's on sale.

In summary: the perfect entrypoint for someone who wants to get into old-school, DnD style RPGs; especially late-to-the-party generation kids who enjoy the RPG genre.
It's not Game of Thrones, but I'm very happy with the idea of a game that can introduce me to the type of storytelling that doesn't patronize me with the instant gratification of the all too obvious maps, dialogue and waypoints combination we've become accustomed to in contemporary RPGs.
I feel like I missed the generation of DnD, Fallout 1/2, and Baldur's Gate; growing up on what I'd call almost mindless RPGs like Oblivion, Mass Effect, Dragon Age and Skyrim. Games that are incredibly fun, but require very little effort or attention to detail to complete; games that certainly show the hallmarks of an RPG, but lack the complete-formula and romance of the classic pen and paper dungeon crawler.
This game is a step in the right direction, and I look forward to giving Baldur's Gate another try after I've played through this 3 times or more.

I enjoyed the game quite a bit. To start off one playthough takes about 10 hours.
Since the game is fairly different than most games on the whole, I figured it'd be easier to point out the similarities it may have with some established games. The game's a little bit like:
Fire Emblem -  grid based combat, but individual unit turn-based with a strength as hp mechanic and armor -- you can try out The Banner Saga: Factions, the corresponding free multiplayer game to try the combat,
Oregon Trail - you travel along a fairly linear path making decisions as you go with a caravan nonetheless,
Dragon Age - unlike Fire Emblem series where if you lose a character in combat, you lose him/her in the campaign, in TBS you can only lose characters through decisions you make out of combat -- falling in combat will only injure a unit for the next fight, unless you rest at camp or have enough time pass to heal the injuries,
King of Dragon Pass - the decision system is similar and you will be given chances to wage war, however you only control the army by choosing one command, such as Charge, Formation, Defend, etc. which then prompts a regular combat scenario,
---
The campaign affects combat in several main ways. Probably most importantly, it affects who you will be able to play as in combat and which encounters will be combat encounters or bypassed through resolution or avoidance. You can add new characters to your party or even accidentally, or purposefully, kill off members of your team.
Next,  your caravan morale affects how much willpower your team has starting the match. Willpower allows characters to use their special abilities, deal extra armor break or damage, and to move further in a single turn. If your caravan morale is low, your team will start fights with less than normal willpower, but if they start with high morale, they will receive bonus morale.
Lastly, from making some decisions, you can gain reknown (the currency used to level up units and to buy equippment and supplies -- supplies are used to feed your whole caravan and maintain morale).
---
Strengths:
As you'll see stated in most any other review, TBS is a gorgeous game. The combat is equally good and quite strategic.
The vast and detailed world map shows the scope of the game's world in the classic Tolkien fashion.
The characters and decisions are very impactful. You can lose or gain key characters (and their equipment) based on your decisions. Some decisions will have immediate results, while others may show up long after you've made them.
Weakness:
The biggest issue I had with the game is that it felt lopsided on the decision system. If you made a series of a few bad decisions, you wound up always struggling to get supplies, and on the flipside, if you make a series of good decisions, you have a fairly easy time. This is because all of the systems seem to compound on eachother. I preferred to be struggling, because it kept the tension of survival prominent.
I enjoyed the overall structure of the story and the many decisions I had to make along the way, however the dialogue sometimes was poorly phrased, such as by using modern colloquial slurs. Some characters would use lore-based expressions, while others frequently sounded like they were from the current era.
This was an odd issue. Some character and city names I did not know how to pronounce, and so I didn't commit many characters and places to memory.
Lastly, you're always moving forward, from point A to point B. Once you leave camp or town you continue back on your journey. Instead of directly choosing your destination, you're sent in the general direction the story tells you to go, able to take detours or backtrack only when an event decision occurs.
---
On Combat:
If you are not familiar with The Banner Saga's combat, I could see it being a fairly difficult game, as common strategic thought is to kill off units rather than leave them maimed and on the board. With TBS's turn-based system, one character takes a turn then control passes to the opponent to move one character. The order of character movement is established before combat and can be changed only by a few special characters once in combat. Although it might seem odd at first, this system requires much more strategy than just going from one side of the board to the other wiping out all enemy units. Each time you kill off an enemy unit, you are giving the opponent an advantage, slight or large dependent on the difference between both sides' total units.
I find TBS's combat system to be a good addition to turn-based strategy family and prefer it to most other turn-based game systems.
What I'd like to have seen:
Skirmish mode - a mode to fight on all the different maps vs the AI using characters unlocked through the story-mode,
Characters & Maps - story characters/classes added to The Banner Saga: Factions (the multiplayer version of the game);
Multiplayer - The Banner Saga: Factions accessible in-game from TBS's client; I think leaving the two games separate can cause some confusion for players, some may only know about one version and not the other;

FTL is one of the best games I own. It's a small, quick installation of  800-900 MB, yet the game is massive. There is so much you can do and so many ways to play. My 2 gold coins:
It is quite the throwback to classical RPGs because this game *really* doesn't hold your hand. You have to actually read the generally well written, albeit often (deliberately?) cheesy dialogue and pay attention if you want to solve quests. Mistakes will be punished, but it makes success so much more satisfying.
The complexity of the game lies beneath the surface. At first I was disappointed by linear leveling areas and invisible walls, and though I wished they had forgone these aspects of classic RPGs, they have elevated that of meaningful and connected worldbuilding to a higher level. If you kill someone, a relative of that person may refuse you help in the main quest later on, so you should be careful as your actions have consequences beyond "don't shoot civilians or the level ends".
Combat is interesting though it feels too slow, due to limited abilites in the beginning and slow animations dragging it out unnecessarily in later fights. A feature to skip spell/enemy animations would be greatly appreciated. The slow pace continues with general gameplay, mostly because of the sluggish run speed out of fights.
Speaking of combat, it is difficult even on normal, but quicksave and the ability to flee make it forgiving and absolutely manageable even against stronger enemies. Environmental effects are satisfying to use but the AI often misjudges them, leading to enemies killing themselves or damaging their allies. Another thing is the terrible item management. Why can't I have all my character inventories next to each other in one window? Right now, moving stuff around is an absolute pain. Also the bartering window doesn't work with your inventory order.
These problems are annoying and regularly distract from gameplay but the latter is strong enough to still make this a great game if you are willing to invest yourself into a challenging and attention demanding playthrough.

This game is a full-on experience that will give you nearly 100 hours of well-paced, challenging, tactical RPG fun.SCORE: 90/100.
People are not kidding about the roleplaying depth, the massive and interactive environment, the SERIOUS NO HAND HOLDING, the difficulty already (but fair), and the rewarding nature of tactical combat. Co-op adds another layer on an already incredibly complex game.

You will spend hours just moving stuff from character to character, to inspect, sell, store, and more. I don't want to have a journal of recipes outside of the game or constantly referring to websites. Crafting is tedious and not enjoyable. Some will think it is great, but most will hate and or avoid it as much as possible.
This is not for casual gamers, people without patience, or people looking for a hack-and-slash loot fest. This is for people looking for a deep and rewarding game, story, and turn-based tactical combat.

A 2008 3 match game developed by app designers Playrix
There are a lot of OLD negative reviews based on the fact that the game crashes at start up etc. Also that there was no feedback from company which was surprising since they have over 450 employees. However since Mar 7 2017 there was an update and quite a few have remarked since then that game is now fixed and I myself had no problem with game working at all. I guess the moral of the story is check specifications before buying, and that Playrix really needs to work on its customer feedback, playing a more proactive role.
Though the game is a 3 match I really found that it had a rather unique concept in comparison to other 3 matches I have played. Basic goal is to restore 4 elemental magic books, earth, fire, wind and water. To unlock a book you need a key, which you will find amongst an array of objects in a HOS. Once that is completed you are treated to 4 three match games followed by a relatively easy spot the difference this will give you a short read about the magic of a mythical character such as a faerie, a water turtle, a  unicorn or something of the like. Repeat this procedure three times in total and you will unlock all the locks to one of the four books and may then proceed to the next one to repeat the process until you have finished all 65 levels or thereabout levels, learnt all about the magical inhabitants of this mythical world and then rainbows will appear over the Kingdom, the end.
The first two books are so easy thanks to the large generous amount of time allocated to the completion of each level that you could probably watch grass grow between each match up and still successfully complete each level. The last two books on the other hand are so strapped for time you'll probably have to go back to the doctor’s tomo and get yourself a heavier prescription. For instance the last level took me around 16 minutes and I was flying around the map like I was a cat in a room full of rocking chairs.
The main objective of the 3 match puzzles is to get a fluid from the start point to the altar, its exit goal. Unfortunately dirt, blocks and ice often prevent your path. By matching 3 or more gems in a horizontal or vertical fashion will remove the dirt. Making a 5 match adjacent to ice will cause an explosion that will move that obstacle and as for the cement blocks you will have to locate an explosive spear and let the liquid meet that for the spear to shoot off and make contact with another spear or the cement block and obliterate that obstacle. The journey can be quite long as you make the liquid traverse through tight narrow passages and patterned chasms. You have some power ups also at your disposal depending on which colour gems you match up. A spade will unlock one block of dirt (green gem), a bomb can take out the ice and rocks (red gem), a switch will change the position of a pair of gems of your choosing (yellow gem) and random will randomise the gem layout again when you get limited in good options (blue gem).
The game is unique not only for its mechanics, it's board fancy grandiose lay out, but also thanks to its background animations, such as an assortment of fish swimming around in a gigantic aqua world or the waterfalls that emit from the mouth of the altar when your fluid reaches them. Not to mention the barrage of explosions that can occur when you come across a cluster of explosive spears like as if you’re watching a Michael Bay Movie about 3 match extremists.
In final the first two books are really boring they take too long explaining the game, the last two books are worthy of a gamer's attention. Hopefully they will continue with this idea looking into 4 other magical elements like Xanox, Mushroom, Moonshine and Testosterone.

I like this game. It's aesthetically pleasing and very chill. There is a resource management system in place, but the only consequence to it appears to be that if you don't have enough of a resource in the pool for a given block, it'll decay until it stops producing. It's a shame, because minimizing pollution could have been a neat goal!
More of the challenge to the game (as far as I see it) is managing space access for blocks when you're building up a pretty town. It's very much a game of managing aesthetics more than interconnected ecosystems,
PROS:
+ Pretty visuals and music
+ Calm, relaxing fun
+ Just enough of a challenge to make it a game
CONS:
- Challenge is pretty minimal here (doesn't bother me, I have other citybuilders for that)
- Controlling the block placement and fiddling with the camera can be... well, fiddly
So I have to recommend this game, but only on the condition that you don't mind the lack of challenge or you care more about just having a chill citybuilder.

Highly recommended game for fans of any Diablo game, Path of Exile, Titan Quest, Torchlight, Fate etc.
The things that drew me to this game was two things:
1) It has single player (offline with no latency or disconnect issues)
2) Dark atmosphere
Other things that are awesome about this game:
-Grim Dawn developers have paid high attention to details, both visually and also dialogue. Graphics are very nice (although needs optimizing, but that always happens just before actual game release) and dialogue is quite good and sometimes funny as well (serious funny, not childish funny (not that there's anything wrong with that)) and there are no inconsistencies as far as I have noticed such as how Leah in Diablo 3 is powerful enough to open a gate, but the main hero is not, yet can defeat Diablo etc.
-The game is friendly to people with certain disabilities such as sufferers of motion sickness (option to turn off camera shaking) and people with colour blindness (several clolour blindness options to suit the type of colour blindness you have). I cannot tell you how well these options work as I do not actually suffer from these disabilities, but I really like that the developers pay attention to this.
-So the fact that the environments are not randomly generated like other ARPGs worried me a little but they are a large part of what keeps a game interesting for me, but I can assure anyone that the environments do indeed stay fresh because of a number or reasons. There are all kinds of debris that can block your path in one game session, then in a different game session it'll be elsewhere (they vary per game session) meaning you still have to explore the map a little further. There are also many caves/dungeons that are optional but there are many and exploring them does reward you nicely, adding high satisfaction to the gameplay.
-Again, the darker atmosphere of this game is not necessarily scary, but it is indeed gloomy and people who enjoy Diablo will particularly enjoy the atmosphere of Grim Dawn.
-I have not looked too much into the lore, but what I have heard and read about does make me want to look into it further. The idea of the game taking place after a recent kind of apocalypse is always cool and it does make you think of Fallout 3 in that sense. You meet characters in the game who are struggling to survive in the post apocalyptic environment with dangerous monsters (and people) roaming the wilds that were once safe in the past.
-Like a lot of people say, the game is built on the exact same engine that the game Titan Quest (awesome ARPG from 2006 and STILL very good and quite up to date with newer games in every aspect, including graphics). You can easily tell as most of the UI also looks very similar in both structure and art style as Titan Quest. Not only that though, the physics feel exactly like in Titan Quest and the character animation has the same kind of heavy feel to them as well.
-Items. Similar affix system as you get in most ARPGs. Random stats will be applied to each item that you pick up. It's nothing revolutionary, but it's a system that is used in many games because it works and actually manages to keep the game fresh for a while. There are magic items, epic items, legendary items, all that kind of stuff. It's all good though!
-The game has factions similar to ones you see in World of Warcraft. You complete quests for a certain group of people and you increase your reputation with them, making them respect you more and there is a meter in the character menu so you can keep track of it. It's exciting to see what more the developers will do with this as there are a lot of possibilities they could play around with in such a feature.
-Levelling, stats and abilities. Most abilities are cool, but I have not explored it much because I have only played 1 character for about 19 hours as of this review and another small character for less than 1 hour. I can say though that you always anticipate the next level you reach in the game as you get to apply point into stats and also abilities and you do actually feel that your character grows every level. As of this review, the level cap is only 40 which will increase as more of act 3 gets accessible (I think act 3 is the final act..?) but I don't think anybody knows what the max level will be yet but it seems to me that the developers want the game to remain fun and add endgame. They have mentioned on their website that after release they are planning on implementing a game mode where you defeat endless waves of monsters and then you can test how far you get etc, although not much detail has been provided yet.
-Another thing I would like to mention is that the developers do not believe in pay-to-win or small useless DLC updates. However, they do want to create expansions to the game after release (paid expansions such as Lord of Destruction, Immortal Throne, Reaper of Souls etc.) which is awesome really.
-Music is very good.
The developers are very active and update the playable game regularly. Check out their website
for information on the content and features of the game on the Game Guide menu.

EDIT: I would like to add some cons about the game as to not be too biased towards the game.
-So obviously the game needs work on the optimization but that always happens near the end of development.
-Combat COULD improve in a way but is not a large problem. I feel (as a melee character) that not much strategy is involved. My class does not really use energy (mana) and I have never ever run out of it before. A lot of monsters' movement speed is faster than you so you cannot avoid their attacks and it ends up with you using potions. The frequency of using potions is similar to that of Diablo 2, give or take, depending on how much healing your class is capable of. I am okay with this, but I do enjoy the way that in Diablo 3 it is balanced in a different way where potions are an emergency heal with a long cooldown, rather than your main source of healing. Basically the combat could do with slightly more strategy as the only strategy I do is to run away from mobs real quick, heal, then go back but it is far from ruining it. It is a smaller problem than I may be making it out to be. Also it is in beta stage.
-User Interface is not that smooth, but it was not in Titan Quest either but easily forgivable as it is not a huge issue or anything. It isn't unresponsive or anything, just not smooth in anyway, although the placement of the UI during combat or any activity is good and does not get in the way.
Might update this review as time goes on, if I remember ;)

Grim Dawn is an attempt to create an old school RPG in an interesting, industrial world where you wake up to your funeral and thrown into these series of apocalyptic events. - and it does what it claims perfectly with its lovely storytelling, well-designed scenery and lots of details that you'll find yourself paying attention, unintentionally.
It features Dual Class System which is a decent way to theorycraft but not as detailed as Path of Exile. Combat System might seem a bit dull at first, but its a Progressive Game and you'll unlock the capabilities of your characters over time. So if you're giving this a try, you should give it a hell of a try to have fun with it. - Very detailed Character and Item Models; Breathtaking, well-produced Soundtrack; Quite variety of foes; Awesome Storytelling and well-placed Lore elements; Carefully designed world that will provide a lot for those who are observant enough.
This game is going to be strong title and it has a huge potential of being a cult. - Its Development should take the time they need to finish what they've started. So, don't be impatient about it. Action RPG is a hard category to progress on. - and so far, Crate Entertainment is doing a very good job.

Risk of Rain is a rougelike 2D platformer featuring perma-death, unlockable items and characters, and levels with procedurally generated elements. Players both new and experienced can expect a challenge on each and every run due to the item pools associated with opening chests. Although the first few deaths of the game may cause frustration, each run will teach you more and more about the flow and feel of the game. And once you score that winning run, believe me, all of your toil will be worth it. The game features single player and local co-op play; however, if you want to play online, you or one of your buddies will have to port forward or everyone will have to use a software similar to Hamachi. Overall, this game provides challenging, yet extremely fun gameplay and is my personal favorite roguelike.

Mirror's Edge is one of those games that was made a few years ago, but still wipes the floor with most recent games. Don't let EA's involvement in the game throw you off, this one was from before the dark days that give us nightmares every night.
While the storyline of the game is not amazing, it is still pretty decent and is still more interesting than a lot of storylines in current games. The main appeal of this game for me was the apparent freedom of movement you have, even though the levels are quite linear. The wide-open level design makes you feel like the path you take is not necessarily the one and only path through the level, even though most of the time it is. The time trial levels reuse some of the storyline levels, which makes them somewhat repetitive yet familliar in an environment where practising easily makes you more comfortable with the section you are running.
The freerunning mechanics don't feel clunky and with the focus on momentum, they feel really fast and smooth when you are playing well and have a reasonable drop in this when you are not (which still does not make the freerunning feel clunky).
Considering the game was released in 2009 for PC, you don't need one of those new-fangled super-toaster 5000 with four bread slots and fast-defrost action- glueing a few potatoes together should suffice. Since the game is over five years old, it is pretty cheap now, too. Unless you don't like this kind of game, there isn't much argument for not giving it a go.

I've beaten this game twice, once on impossible difficulty, and stuck with it for the 100+ hours that took, so how could I not reccommend it? It's a tactics game in the same vein as tactics ogre, breach & clear, and Shadowrun, mixed with a bit of Roguelike where the random encounters and events can either make or ruin your day exceptionally quckly, which combined with some of the tactics makes this an excellently brutal game on the harder difficulties. I thought the memorial was a nice touch, as it makes it clear the game knows you're going to lose a lot of soldiers along the way, some of them very dear to you. Did I mention it was brutal? This game will have you cursing and reloading saves a lot, unless you have the steel cojones to play it on Ironman mode, in which case, it will mostly be cursing and maybe some fist-shattered monitors. It will throw you under the bus over and over again, and you will love it, because you're just a glutton for punishment like that.
It's not heavy on story, but that which it does have is decent. There's maybe 2-3 true "story missions" but the rest are just random events with story-based objectives thrown in, while you advance the main quest mostly via research and side objectives. You'll want to focus on earning engineers and launching satellites while rushing through the main quests for the early part of the game, or you'll get a game over as panic levels rise. Once you reach the turning point though panic becomes manageable and you can slow down or even stall the game while you build up, train and equip your squad in preperation for the endgame.
I'm a little upset by the inclusion of the Enemy Within DLC achievements in the base game, as you can't unlock any of them without buying the DLC, which is, sadly, criminally overpriced. I'm still waiting for it to come down enough during a sale to make it worth buying, and maybe I'll revisit the game again at that time. Also there isn't a Colonel badge for me, which makes me sad... but these are minor things most wouldn't care about.

A really great game. It's a turn based tactics set in some sort of Scandinavian myths setting. The story seems to be very well written and captivating from the start. But what is really stands out - is graphics. The artwork is astonishingly great. The colors, the details... all is just right and very pleasant to the eye. The overall quality of the game is surprisingly great (in our year and age of rushed releases).
The combat system is also quite unique. Your units can attack armor or strength. If you're attacking strength, you deal damage to health and to enemy's ability to fight at the same time, but this attack will be mitigated by armor. If you're attacking armor, you're not doing any harm to unit's health or his ability to fight, but instead open it for a much stronger attack in the future. There's also an unique characteristic called Willpower. Units can use it to deliver stronger blows or to run further than normal. But it's a limited resource which can be replenished by resting (skipping turns). It's just 2 unique mechanics but they greatly enrich the tactics metagame.
All in all this is a great buy for anyone who loves turn based strategies or wants to try them out.

I have to say, this game is an absolute success, probably my favorite genre of game (Fire Emblem-esque strategy rpg), and has a deep backstory and setting as well. That alone would make it 8/10 minimum, but I think the deciding factor for me was the type of situations they threw at you as far as being the leader of a caravan in a nigh-apocolyptic situation.
It's bleak to say the least.
The world seems to come apart at the seams at a wildly quick pace, it's an absolute nightmare to manage and navigate. I was robbed, beaten, betrayed, almost murdered, and lost a fifth of my caravan to attrition during a bad stretch of road that would have been survivable, if not for the previously mentioned murderous thieves. I lost at least two characters to unforeseen (not plot related) events, and I loved every second of it.
It's a leadership simulation at it's finest, that does not coddle you at all. This game really drives the point that being a leader is not being a cheerleader and making speeches every ten seconds, or planning your every move like you're playing chess, it's making hard decisions. Making decisions that could as easily lose you half your supplies or kill your most valuable fighter, as gaining fighters that are direly needed, or creating a distraction so that your caravan may pass to the next town.
It's incredibly shocking to lose in-game characters to out-of-combat events, but it really helped suck me into the game. I was completely immersed with the dire need to see that caravan through everything, and seeing that my decisions were being affected by conditions completely outside of my control could not have been more depressing. It was the kind of depression that comes with leadership, watching men die because you had chosen incorrectly, and having to pick yourself up and keep moving, because that's what the caravan needs.
This is the kind of game that cements video games as a legitimate form of expression instead of childish escapism, and it does it tastefully without any pretentious subtext, very impressive for a kickstarter.

Steep is a love it or hate it type of game. Its really quite difficult to tell where you'll fall in. This game is about the experience of the mountain and the comraderie of meeting other players to tear up the mountain with.  Unlike older games in the genre like SSX, you don't have a career mode or endless challenges to complete. There are some yes, but you'll finish them quickly. Steep excels in allowing you to make your own challenges and connect with other players.
If you aren't fascinated with winter sports (or similar sports) and aren't really interested in the community aspect, you'll probably finish all the challenges and get bored. The controls are also very tricky. They are intuitive once you get used to them, but having to juggle all these buttons and joysticks to pull of tricks is a bit daunting at first. Similarly the game gives you some basic tutorials, but there is way more to the mechanics than is explained there that you kind of have to learn yourself. If you're riding on just what the tutorial tells you, that's probably only 25% of your capabilities.
In addition to all this the game has some flaws and bugs. The UI is obtrussive and annoying. Riding and tricking is based on physics, which sometimes can flip out and cause your rider to do weird things like fly sideways off a jump or get stuck on a shallow hill. These are minor annoyances in my opinion, but can be frustrating. Especially if you're working on a difficult challenge or other player's dare and get caught out by one.
That being said Steep has many good things that outweight the bad. Switching between sports on the fly is super easy and all the sports are really cool (yes, even paragliding). The environment is vast and gorgeous and the snow deformation is just breathtaking. The ability to teleport anywhere with no loading times is also a technological marvel. There are lots of awesome locations not marked on the map and plenty of cool easter eggs to boot. Character customization is extensive and the character models are highly detailed. And finally the game doesn't take itself to seriously, with plenty of goofy diversions and silly costumes to choose from.
I think Steep is a great game, but I have noticed that people who really aren't into the winter sports or the community aspect are more likely to be put off by the bugs that are present. If you like sports games and played a lot of SSX you'll probably like it. If you're on the fence, wait for some updates and season pass stuff to come out.

First Impressions, review may change after more game time.... First off, I generally really like turn based tactical RPGS/Strategy games like Fire Emblem, XCOM, Expeditions Conquistador, Tactics Ogre, Final Fantasy Tactics etc.  Having recently visited Denmark, and watched the "Vikings" TV show, the Viking style theme really interested me.  I've been looking forward to this, but didn't back the Kickstarter.  I have to say I'm rather disappointed so far.
Liked:
1. Love the artwork. Reminds me of feature length cartoons from the late 70s and early 80s. Very nicely done.
Mixed Feelings:
1. The Viking theme.  A turn based tactical RPG about Vikings sounded awesome to me. But then I realize it has giants, and robotic looking things in it. What, were vikings just not nerdy enough? I guess I was hoping for something a bit more like real-world vikings. Seriously, that would have been cool enough.
2. The turn based combat.  First, I'm eternally grateful for the combat being turn based. However I keep finding the battles to be kind of tedious and dull, especially against the dredge.  So I have to whittle away their armor first, then whittle away their hit points?  ZZZZZ.  Might as well have just doubled the hit points.  Then the enemies getting to move more often, the fewer of them remaining is a bit "different" for lack of a better word. Not quite sure what to think of that mechanic yet.
Dislike:
1. The story and dialog so far.  It's dull. The first hour of the game has not hooked me at all.  I have no interest in the characters or what is happening to them so far.  I can't keep my find focused on the game long enough to play more than 20-30 minutes of it at a time.
2. The village and map interfaces.  It feels like something from a Facebook or browser game, for the villages.  World map is very cluttered and hard to read at a glance.
Hoping it gets better as it goes, but it just isn't inspiring me to keep playing it. Disappointed.

The Banner Saga is a colorful tactical RPG by Stoic Games. The unique art style looks like a hand drawn cartoon but it doesn’t take away from the gravity of the plot.  The game primarily consists of two sections, the caravan and the battlefield.
The caravan is the player’s home base and mode of transportation.  A fair amount of time is spent watching the caravan travel along a 2d map as you travel, you encounter bandits, disease, fire, and numerous other things that can help you or kill of members of your group.  Most of the plot unfolds here as well.  The game does a great job of depicting the hopelessness and fear of your characters, but it’s worth noting that there is virtually no voice acting.  Reading the script isn’t necessarily a bad thing, but keep in mind there is a lot of dialogue to get through and that means a lot of reading. So be prepared.
The combat is reasonably deep and combining health and attack power into a single statistic makes for a unique experience.  Unfortunately there can be quite a lot of repetitiveness in the battles.  After the first chapter or two, all of the non plot related fights feel far too similar.  Add that to the fact that there is no height in the battle field and the fights start blurring together.
The art style has a unique beauty, and the combat is fun, if repetitive. If are okay with, or enjoy reading dialogue and like tactical RPGs then pick up a copy.  If you are on the fence then spend some time with the free multiplayer version, The Banner Saga Factions.  That might be good enough.

But the game simply doesen't work like that,
Blocks only deacy when their inputs run out. This seems logical, but this leads to situations where waste products (like sewage, for example) are either being over or under consumed.
Consume too much, and a sewage-processing block decays (once sewage hits 0).
Now you are over producing sewage,
and the only way to fix this is by hitting the exact ratio of sewage-producers to sewage-consumers.
Or..
Don't care... because THERE ARE NO CONSEQUENCES TO NOT PROCESSING SEWAGE!!!
Aside from that, the gameplay (which boils down to managing an excel spreadsheet) isn't very fufilling.
The game is also plagued by odd bugs & oversights.
For example, you can't change block limits in the "world" mode, in which you can build hoods next to eachother.
(World mode is supposed to have a resoruce exchange system, which might make it interesting, but it hasn't been implemented properly)
If you want an athesticly-pleasing, resource-based citybuilder, go play a game like Anno 2070 (Designed by Game designers, not artists!).

I first stepped onto the Killing Floor in 2015 while the game was still in Early Access, and there were just four perks to choose from (before the incinerate and detonate update).
I'll give you that development saw it's ups & downs with the addition of PvP and microtransactions, but all in all I think it was a well done EA campaign, full of free updates including 6 perks, new weapons, new bosses, new maps, and more.
Now that the game has seen it's full release, here's what the developers Tripwire have provided so far this year, all free of charge:
Tropical Bash update: New map, new weapon, new zed
Descent: New map with new game mode, new weapons
Summer Sideshow: Free event with new map, new challenge mode, new weapons
* 6 player co-op
* challenging horde shooter
* Free updates (so far)
* Scaling difficulty
* 10 perks to choose from, each offering unique styles & weapons
* Guns & gore galore
* Incredible gun animations
* Hundreds of workshop levels
* Kick♥♥♥♥♥metal soundtrack
* Well-optimized (i7/2GB Nvidia on high/ultra)
* Beautifully detailed environments
* Lots of character customization
* Fun community
* Match-making (server browser + filters is your friend)
* Server availability can be low at times
I know that the PvP mode and microtransactions during early access caught a lot of grief, however at least they made the all skins cosmetic, and in the end the developers delivered an absolute gem of a shooter. 440 hours in, nearly all maxed perks, and I'm still going strong without any signs of slowing down.
Highly recommended to anyone who enjoys co-op shooters like Left 4 Dead or PayDay2, or a solid FPS in general.

The text based gameplay is fun and unique in this generation of games. The pixel art style and the music are nostalgic and attention grabbing. The backgrounds are gorgeous and the atmosphere is composed to the player through its style. You feel like you are actually in control, and you empathize with the plight of your crew as you try to survive. It looks like a classic game from the Nintendo era but feels like a modern indie, a combination which is unmatched by anything I've played.  Strategization in FTL is key, you cannot blindly charge through and hope to get far. The game is unforgiving, but still fun. Even though deaths are frequent and permanent, you shouldn't get frustrated. Losing is part of the game, actually, and it's an intregal part of learning. After death, you always come back wanting to improve yourself and do better than before. FTL is a unique game that should be part of every gamer's library. This game is a solid 10/10.

In XCOM: Enemy Unknown, you are waging war against an Alien Force invading Earth. You have to utilize limited resources to manage base construction, as well as scientific research and engineering projects to advance your team of soldiers into what is eventually a sophisticated military unit using hyper advanced technology.
From time to time you are called upon to defend Earth from the invading Aliens, whether it be alien abductions in a major city or a UFO sighting. This is where the meat of the game is. You pick and choose soldiers who level up over time and assume roles like Sniper, Rocketeer or Medic, with permadeath mechanics involved.
The game is really fantastic if you like turn based strategy games. There's a certain tense anxiety that comes from being pinned down by incredibly advanced, extremely dangerous aliens and hoping that one of your soldiers can pull of a shot that will shake up the situation and turn it into your favor.
If you like the game, pick up the Enemy Within expansion as well, which is a comprehensive expansion pack that adds Mechs, Augmentations for soldiers and a new enemy faction.
Shoutout to the Long War mod. If you feel like you've mastered the game, try Long War. It is a VERY expansive mod for XCOM: Enemy Unknown and XCOM: Enemy Within. It adds enormous amounts of content as well as makes an already difficult game relentlessly and extremely difficult. In my opinion, the Long War mod completes this already very fantastic game.

The Banner Saga is a colorful tactical RPG by Stoic Games. The unique art style looks like a hand drawn cartoon but it doesn’t take away from the gravity of the plot.  The game primarily consists of two sections, the caravan and the battlefield.
The caravan is the player’s home base and mode of transportation.  A fair amount of time is spent watching the caravan travel along a 2d map as you travel, you encounter bandits, disease, fire, and numerous other things that can help you or kill of members of your group.  Most of the plot unfolds here as well.  The game does a great job of depicting the hopelessness and fear of your characters, but it’s worth noting that there is virtually no voice acting.  Reading the script isn’t necessarily a bad thing, but keep in mind there is a lot of dialogue to get through and that means a lot of reading. So be prepared.
The combat is reasonably deep and combining health and attack power into a single statistic makes for a unique experience.  Unfortunately there can be quite a lot of repetitiveness in the battles.  After the first chapter or two, all of the non plot related fights feel far too similar.  Add that to the fact that there is no height in the battle field and the fights start blurring together.
The art style has a unique beauty, and the combat is fun, if repetitive. If are okay with, or enjoy reading dialogue and like tactical RPGs then pick up a copy.  If you are on the fence then spend some time with the free multiplayer version, The Banner Saga Factions.  That might be good enough.

There's more focus on action, though, as you're encouraged to jump in and do your part in causing a bit of death and dismemberment of your own. On top of it all is a somewhat basic story, though there is so much character and humor packed in that it still seems fresh and entertaining. To call the game "mindless fun" would be a little misleading as there is some strategy involved in trap placement and personal upgrades, but the real fun lies in watching a group of clueless orcs wandering towards a corridor full of all manner of blades and spikes and being reduced to "orc salsa" while you giggle softly to yourself.

If you've ever played Oregon Trail or its zombie tribute, be very prepared to love this game. If you ever had any reservations about Factions - the multiplayer standalone released last year - put them aside.
Gameplay is split into two portions. The first is the Oregon-Trail-style travelling from city to city, complete with sweeping, sidescrolling landscape as you watch your tiny peoples walk from point to point. As you travel, you have to manage your caravan's supplies, personnel and morale to make sure you can get through the campaign and random encounters. Not enough supplies, and you'll start losing people in your caravan to starvation; Not enough people, and you won't be able to make it past large encounters without incurring heavy losses; Not enough morale, and your heroes start battles with less willpower to spend, while you'll find your caravan having more issues that you have to deal with more often.
The second portion is, of course, the turn-based combat. One of the bigger complaints about Factions was the lack of variety of units in the game (something that I believe they're going to work on now that the main campaign is out), but several new classes make their debut here to spice up the gameplay: The Eagle Eye archer variant can fire an arrow that hits all units in a line in front of her, dealing bonus armour damage; The Spearmaster can attack diagonally or up to two squares laterally, and may impale units, causing them to bleed for every unit moved in their next turn; Wardens and Hunters are nimble, unhindered by teammates when moving around the battlefield.
The writing is generally competent, as expected from a bunch of BioWare ex-employees. The numerous choices that you have to make throughout the epic are usually thought provoking and do a good job of making you feel like you have something at stake. The overarching plot is similarly compelling and most important events rarely feel contrived, making you feel like a part of something much larger in the Banner Saga's huge, rich tapestry (ha) of lore.
It isn't a perfect game, though. I can't help but feel that several of the characters had more written for them while others get far less time in the limelight. Yes, with over 20 playable characters, balancing out screentime is difficult to do; However, I feel like quite a few could have had a little bit more time speaking and less time caving skulls in - especially since in between fights you can stop the caravan at any time, leaving plenty of room for additional conversations. It would have been nice if there were more dialogue options with your party, for sure.
Nonetheless, the Banner Saga is more than a competent game. I may even go as far as saying it's a very good game. A deceptively deep combat system and random encounters break the slow pace of the days passing by as your caravan trundles from place to place; Occasional important decision can abruptly change the party you travel with, leaving quite a bit of wiggle room for replay, and having to carefully manage your resources will keep you on your toes as the game throws encounter after unforgiving, dastardly encounter at you.
Also, it looks great! Highly recommended.

Just beat the game, went co-op all the way through with my best friend, loved every moment of it.  I won't discuss the day/night cycle, as it's been discussed to death.  It works beautifully.
The story is alright, not much to shake a stick at, just the average 'find the cure while gov./big bad tries to exploit your efforts' spiel.  There's also a lot of side quests and random encounters to keep you busy the whole way through.
The gameplay?  Spot on.  Instead of doing what a lot of zombie games do and throw more and more zombies at you in lieu of "difficulty", as the game progresses, eveything gets tougher.  The Goons (8-ft. tall rebar swingers) get upgraded, you are constantly finding new enemies to fight, the walkers get faster and stronger.  Basically, it gives you a reason to keep finding new and better gear.
Speaking of gear, the system works great.  As you use weapons, they deteriorate.  Unlike other games, you can only repair a certain number of times (1 for Gray-rarity, 2 for Green, 3 Blue, 4 Purple, and a full 5 for Orange).  Then, you are left with a broken hunk of metal.  This prevents you from getting too attached to one weapon, again forcing you to constantly seek out more powerful and rare weapons.
Levels are split into three parts: Survivor (basic stuf), Agility (parkour tricks), and Power (attack skills).  Not much more to say, except to definitley get the fall damage reduction skill and the one whichgives your weapons about a 25% chance to not use a repair when repaired.
Multiplayer is where it's at.  Nothing is more fun than running up walls and killing zombies with a friend, or three.
The only real bad thing?
*Spoilers*
THE GODDAMN ENDING SUCKS!
Okay, you've done everything in this game with a friend, leaned on each other's strengths, supported through the weaknesses, and had a hell of a time bashing zombies in and finding just the right way to best your buddy in overall DPS.  What happens at the end?  You're thrown into a goddamn SINGLE-PLAYER segment where you do more running from the zombies than using your shiniest, badassest weapons.  You finally get to the top of the tower, and you face off against the big bad.  Do you use your weapons now?  HELL NO!  ITS A GOD DAMN FICKING QTE SEGMENT!!!!!
At least they didn't end with a non-interactive cutscene.
*End Spoilers*
Even with a bad ending, the game is awesome.  Make sure to get it with a friend.
