I have tried this game on two occasions, once during a free weekend at some point in 2016, and again during the free weekend of June 2017. I can tell that the game has improved a great amount from early access to release, as the gunplay is much more satisfying and the players don't move as sluggishly as they used to (among many other improvements, but those were the two biggest changes to me). The one problem that I have with the game is that there are points where I can not actually play it. The game, for whatever reason, does not have the option to make a friends-only game. After looking online for solutions, the only way to make a friends-only game is to either download a plethora of software and attempt to run a dedicated server, or pay some company to run a private server for you. There also appears to be a "server-takeover" feature, in which an empty server can be temporarily converted into a private server for someone to use, unless the server owner opts-out of this feature. Wouldn't you know it, every server opts-out of this feature, leaving you with the original two options. The final option would be to play in a public server, but after a friend and I getting kicked from servers because of our low level, that is not an option either. I don't believe that I should have to download a bunch of  third party programs or pay someone else money in order to play a game with my friends without getting kicked from a game. The game itself is enjoyable, and hopefully the ability to host a server from the game itself will be available at some point in the future, but right now, I only reccomend this game if you are willing to grind for levels in single player for the community to finally accept you as a valid player.

XCOM: Enemy Unknown, the return of the fabled XCOM franchise. A game of tough choices and the fight to save mankind from the aliens pervading our skies.
Let's start with the obvious, a lot of what was in the XCOM series to begin with has been removed, like having to carry mags around, a proper inventory, stat ups relating to what the soldier has done, an AP bar letting soldiers do an action worth so much and multiple skyrangers to hit multiple alien sites. I myself saw these as disadvantages, going away from the standard formula.
However, with these gone, the game has gotten a lot more focused. The lack of Mags enables you to fight a longer fight against more aliens, forcing you to reload in combat or use a side arm. Inventory has been cut down to one or two items per soldier, and each is given a role in combat, like more health, frag grenades, the like. whilst your squad is limited to 6 members at most, your soldiers are all given a class out of 4, and these are then varied within the level up abilities. The AP bar as been changed to two actions at most, with one for movement and an action beyond that ending your soldiers action. The lack of more then one skyranger is not something that can be remedied, sadly, but this is also counteracted to a certain degree by the variance in the map choice. Want to raid an alien ship? Secure a city after Aliens after attacked it? Fight in a train yard after the X-Rays have launch an incursion? the List is varied enough to keep you going.
The Class System is set up to accommodate 4 classes, your frontline assault specialist, your heavy weapons expert, your sniper and your combat engineer. From these, you also derive your weapons choices, which is sadly limited. Snipers can only use Sniper Rifles, Heavies only get LMGs, Supports get Assault rifles and Assaults get to choose between Assault Rifles and Shotguns. Within the Class is a varied array of skills and abilities, for example, the first class up a sniper gets is a choice between being able to move and fire or to fire at what his squad can see so long as his personal line of sight is clear. This can lead to every soldier being unique, but you will find that there is a way to optimise your soldiers. and considering your main squad is only 6 men, you will want to.
Other then that, Customisation is varied, enabling you to choose everything, like race, armour colours, voice, hair, everything that isn't where they are from and gender. (One of the achievements in game is to field a squad of female soldiers, and admittedly you will find that the soldiers you get are majority male) Whilst the running gag with the base game is that every soldier speaks perfect English no matter where he is from, this is fixed in Enemy Within. Base Building Elements return, but you can only have your main starting base in your home continent.
The game is long, and the Replayability comes from the journey to the end game. Though you will find that it does get....samey after a while.
And then, we get the DLC, Enemy Within. And it fixes a LOT of issues with the game.
First off, the improvements: More enemy variety, more map variety, more base building elements, additional customisation options, altered game balance and the introduction of MELD, a substance that introduces a new way to modify and augment your soldiers, this allows you to bring in the big bruisers known as MEC troops, or to change your soldiers biology, allowing them to do many an amazing thing, like jumping up buildings in a single bound.

South Park: The Stick of Truth is a South Park themed RPG created by Obsidian and published by Ubisoft. Now don't let Ubisoft's name put you off because even though South Park is an Ubisoft game you don't need Uplay to play it. The game is about 10 hours in length even with side quests and most of the time you'll be completing the 10 or twelve story missions the game has to offer. The game is locked to 30 frames per second although due to the aesthetic it actually works in this specific case. The game as a whole is very well put together but since most of South Park is dependent on very subjective themes like humor, reception will vary wildy from person to person.
South Park takes place in, you guessed it, the small town of South Park and you play as a nameless and voiceless new kid on the block. You soon meet with Cartman and Butters and discover the fantasy world that these kids have set up, joining them in the process. This game that the kids play revolves around a "magical" item called the stick of truth and whoever controls said stick can then control the universe. Over the course of the game you run all across South Park gathering support for the humans so that you can assault the elves and take back the stick. Most of the story is just lots of general outlines of what could have been a funny story but instead was stuffed with toilet humor and fan service. A large amount of the lines end up being incredibly cringe-worthy, such as the overarching theme that you should never fart on someone's balls or some of the lines the girls have. The entire story ends up being mostly running around South Park and trying to recruit the various factions to play with you (I.E. The Goths and the girls). None of the characters are anything close to interesting and for a game that calls itself an RPG they really don't explain much about the characters and instead seem to rely on you having watched the show. As most of the characters are dull and repetitive, so too are the environments and in South Park you'll be running back and forth throughout the same environments over and over again for some tedious quest or another and in the end this is just too mind-numbingly boring.
The gameplay, however, is actually pretty well done as far as most RPG's go. You have multiple different methods of attacks: Ranged, melee, magic and abilities along with a plethora of consumables for mid-battle use. You acquire many different kinds of weapons and armor over the course of the story and each piece has its own bonuses that come with it. Most of the armor bonuses are just passive bonuses and thus are pretty boring but there really wasn't much else they could've done with this so I can let it slide. The armor types and models are suprisingly varied and you can get some pretty cool looking sets that really feel like something you would see kids create. You can customize your armor to a degree with various slottable upgrades and different colored dyes but for the most part the main bits of the armor cannot be changed. If you have half a mind and explore even the slightest bit then South Park will prove to be incredibly easy and, as far as RPG's go, incredibly short, as the game should clock in at about 10 hours and that's counting about two hours of exploring that I did early on. South Park has a real problem with difficulty and for pretty much the entire game, with the exception of a fight or two, it's incredibly easy. South Park has a very limited setting to work with and as such seeing the same old parts of the town can really hit you with a feeling of tedium that an RPG cannot have. Most of the side quests are pretty boring too and really end up being either fetch quests or quests you can't finish until later so you forget about them. Since The Stick of Truth is an RPG you can upgrade your character with various perks ability upgrades. Ability upgrades follow a linear upgrade line while perks can be unlocked in any order but also tend to have a more minor impact on gameplay. You unlock perks by getting more friends which you unlock by simply talking to people or doing their quests and it does give the town of South Park a very connected feel as if everybody knows everybody. There's also the buddy system where you can take one buddy along with you to fight in combat and help you out with environmental roadblocks. The buddies are simply a letdown because you end up unlocking the final one not halfway into the game and you are never given any reason to switch off of the first buddy given to you.
An RPG with solid gameplay that's severely hampered by places of cringe-worthy dialogue and overuse of toilet humor. Only for fans of the series.

This is a different take on Match 3 genre. The story isn't anything spectacular (just read the About), but the games themselves are pretty good. Overall, the game isn't really difficult. Some of the later levels may require multiple tries to figure out the best strategy to make your way through.
The gems do not require swapping. Instead, you draw a line through them to make a chain. The longer the chain, the bigger the explosion to wipe out surrounding gems, rocks, and other obstacles. The levels themselves are comprised of a long path that weaves its way to the destination. You must reach the destination before time runs out (the green bar on the right side). Sometimes, you must use power-ups to make your way through. The power-ups are charged when long chains are made. The longer the chain, the faster the power-up charges. The camera will stay still until you clear a path to allow the magic to flow further through the level.
The game is divided into 4 parts (books), of which the following happens: A hidden object game preceeds a book in order to unlock it. Not only must you find the
to objects, but then you must use the object to interact with something on the scene. Eventually the key is found to unlock the book. Once it is unlocked, there are 4 sets of 4 levels, each followed by a spot-the-difference game. In the higher levels, more differences must be found. Once the 4 sets are completed, it moves to the next book.
The biggest problem with the game is the low resolution graphics. Even though it says it was made in 2008, they still could've used better graphics or at least provide a HD remaster. On 1920x1080, the grainy images for the hidden object and spot-the-differences mini-games made it somewhat difficult to complete. Putting it in windowed mode didn't help because then the images are just too small. A minor annoyance I had was the counter in the top-right corner of the screen. I couldn't figure out how to turn it off.
Overall, the game is worth the cost for Match 3 type casual game fans. The level design makes it a bit different from the common single screen ones.

/edit (01/02/16)
Okay. So actually after a few more hours I've found a few answers to the problems I wrote about initially in this "review" (the single sentence at the end). However, I'm still sure there better free shooters than this available. Team Fortress 2 and Tribes: Ascend immediately come to mind though they're quite different games. Warface shares more similarities and is a good example of a greater game if not only due to the solid core mechanics such as movement and aim.
For a start, it wasn't immediately obvious that early new weapons actually didn't take 50000 honour each to obtain as indicated by the "store" tab (of which you can earn around 50-150 per match) and instead they can be purchased for less than 1000 each from the "unlock" tab. I recall starting with 2500 honour, so not bad. This includes the entire range of weaponry from snipers to rocket launchers, so you actually don't miss out too much. And four of us had glossed over this before I eventually found it.
Obviously there is still the issue of having higher cost/level guns doing more damage (and you can also upgrade each gun?) and the consumables such as grenades, airstrikes and medkits need replenishing through purchases (though there is a chance to get some through daily/level rewards). I haven't tried the boosts to stats, but I haven't noticed anybody else with them either apart from one person running at ridiculous speed and therefore will have no appreciation for their existence. At least a rocket launcher is a new solution to the vehicles that still have poor movement.
Another thing I quickly realised was the lack of maps (3) until also discovered in the "unlock" tab was that there were another three to unlock very cheaply at 100 honour each. However, the percentage of people playing on them was about 5%. That is to say, one server for each. This may show how very few others have found this unlock feature.
The maps are honestly probably one of the strongest points of the game. Instead of the map itself, what makes them irritating is the placement of spawn points and that some routes can be linear and predictable. Spawn points are very enclosed which makes spawn lockdown (not quite spawnkilling) fairly common. Also it makes controlling territory very unrewarding as all progress is lost after death. Forgiveable with the smaller maps, due to the spawn lockdown problem, but very labourious on the larger maps. Also glass that can't be shot through. Yeah.
But the main problem is none of this. It is simply the core gameplay mechanics. Sure, the movement is average, the objectives are average, the vehicles are.. average? The problem is the shooting is bad. In my opinion the best strategy in gunplay should not be to jump around corners and unloading. And this combined with having superior guns unlocked with more time spent on the game is what decides matches. Especially on smaller maps. Longer range is awful due to the hundreds of invisible walls scattered over the environment. Random bits of cover where you can still see your enemy will stop your bullets from reaching them. It happens constantly, and is why the above strategy is preferred. Also the draw distance means you can't even see people at a higher range, as well as there being a constant "sway" when aiming with a sniper rifle with no way to steady it whereas each other gun has no such thing.
However, even with all these negatives the game has been a laugh with a few friends discovering all of the hilarity in the animations, vehicles and knife combat and has become a bit of a callback. The negatives at least made the game less serious and opened it up to find the fun hidden inside. I still can't recommend it.

Pro: A very fun and interesting game with lots of twist and turns and surprises that can really get you into the story. The combat isn't ground breaking, but it's a lot of fun and every unit feels different, which is great.
Con: While the story is amazing, it's also the source of the complaints of the game. They tell you your choice matters, but it actually doesn't for a lartge part. The only real affect your actions have are over a few optional characters and fictional numbers that don't really matter. Also, while the game is going to be multiple parts, it doesn't really TELL you that, so unless you research, you're left with a bad impression, asking yourself why there's all the loose ends that there are.
Overall: They've created a very big world with a lot of lore and I look forward to the future of the series, I just hope that the future games (which hopefully will have better funding) can deliver a bit more of a real choose your own adventure story. I don't mind if I always wind up in the same place through the story, but I'd like to actually genuinely have a different adventure then another person, something like letting me go through land or through the sea to a single place. Just beat the game, went co-op all the way through with my best friend, loved every moment of it.  I won't discuss the day/night cycle, as it's been discussed to death.  It works beautifully.
The story is alright, not much to shake a stick at, just the average 'find the cure while gov./big bad tries to exploit your efforts' spiel.  There's also a lot of side quests and random encounters to keep you busy the whole way through.
The gameplay?  Spot on.  Instead of doing what a lot of zombie games do and throw more and more zombies at you in lieu of "difficulty", as the game progresses, eveything gets tougher.  The Goons (8-ft. tall rebar swingers) get upgraded, you are constantly finding new enemies to fight, the walkers get faster and stronger.  Basically, it gives you a reason to keep finding new and better gear.
Speaking of gear, the system works great.  As you use weapons, they deteriorate.  Unlike other games, you can only repair a certain number of times (1 for Gray-rarity, 2 for Green, 3 Blue, 4 Purple, and a full 5 for Orange).  Then, you are left with a broken hunk of metal.  This prevents you from getting too attached to one weapon, again forcing you to constantly seek out more powerful and rare weapons.
Levels are split into three parts: Survivor (basic stuf), Agility (parkour tricks), and Power (attack skills).  Not much more to say, except to definitley get the fall damage reduction skill and the one whichgives your weapons about a 25% chance to not use a repair when repaired.
Multiplayer is where it's at.  Nothing is more fun than running up walls and killing zombies with a friend, or three.
The only real bad thing?
*Spoilers*
THE GODDAMN ENDING SUCKS!
Okay, you've done everything in this game with a friend, leaned on each other's strengths, supported through the weaknesses, and had a hell of a time bashing zombies in and finding just the right way to best your buddy in overall DPS.  What happens at the end?  You're thrown into a goddamn SINGLE-PLAYER segment where you do more running from the zombies than using your shiniest, badassest weapons.  You finally get to the top of the tower, and you face off against the big bad.  Do you use your weapons now?  HELL NO!  ITS A GOD DAMN FICKING QTE SEGMENT!!!!!
At least they didn't end with a non-interactive cutscene.
*End Spoilers*
Even with a bad ending, the game is awesome.  Make sure to get it with a friend.

Seeing how all the negative reviews get 0 out of whatever for the reasons unknown to me, i don't expect my review to be welcomed any differently, yet i'm gonna speak up regardless. Yes, i don't understand how this thing keeps being called great, awesome, cool, with great storyline, great graphics. etc. And no, i don't get it how this horrible abomination of a video game even has what, 4 stars out of 5? It's a great mystery to me.
First of all, i'm no way into bashing old games for being... you know, old. I'm an old fan(g) myself.  I play a lot of old games. For example, i just re-played Clive Barker's Undying for like... 10th time because of nostalgia. I keep returning to Undying because it offers a unique and interesting gameplay, different ways of approaching it, something new every time. One of these games that you can replay over and over again and everytime you would discover something new, something you haven't noticed before. Creative stuff that used to prevail in old games, you know, some really creative interesting ideas. And it's even older than this one. But i know for sure, i won't be returning to Nosferatu, no way.
So i was looking forward to a game to satisfy my strong urge to play a good old school shooter. And i saw this, i saw all the good reviews and i thought: "Hell, how could i even miss it back in years?!". Now that i've seen what it was that i thought i missed... Oh boy, was i thankful i did. So, what do i start with. Boy, oh boy, the choice is wide. First of all, the very first thing i didn't like was the menu. It's simply uncomfortable. Pressing "ESC" doesn't return you back to game or a previous part of the menu. That's uncomfortable. No video settings? You gotta be kidding me. Control settings? Please, there's almost nothing to customize. For some reason, you can run and jump, but you can't crouch. Dafuq, really?
Combat system, absolute joke, from the start we have a sword cane that just looks like a simple medieval sword. I have no idea where they saw a sword cane here. Movements are clumsy, they stutter. There are only 2 "types" of attack with that "sword cane" and they stutter as hell and look very poorly animated. Mechanics... I don't get it. The protagonist can run like a cheetah for a few seconds but unable to perform anything but two pathetic looking sword moves? Dafuq? You see, do you already see that thin line that's been broken, right? A protagonist that can on one side do something... extraordinary where most people would suck a huge dog's♥♥♥♥♥♥but on the other hand can't do something simple? Nah, i'm not buying it. Then, when (IF) you get a first firing weapon... Yes, in this game you don't just simply find new weapons, you gotta work ridiculously hard to earn'em, which is not a compliment in that case. Even on Medium! The firing and reloading animations are horrible. They're just horrible, hands down. They lack. The game is so bugged, half the time bullets don't even hit the target unless you manage to make a straight line of a couple of meters between you and an enemy, they stuck at doorways; stuck at furniture; plus there is no areal damage. Doesn't matter where you aim-to the head or leg, you'll get the same result. There's no aiming (ironsights) btw and mostly no alternative attacks, so yeah, your right mouse button is pretty much useless most of the time, animation is very broken and again, it "stutters", literally. Comparing to Clive Barker's Undying, this game simply seems poorly made in general.
Enemies. Mostly the same all the time, appear randomly. Ugly, bugged, move and attack too "sharply", too "fast" in terms of movements, there's no smoothness. Environment? Now i have no idea whose idea it was to make the castle somewhat random all the time, but it doesn't help at all. If it was supposed to make the gameplay somewhat new with every new game, this idea has failed hard. It pisses off much more than keeps you interested or entertained because with every new game there's just more randomness, annoying backtracking and mess in general cause you simply don't understand where to go and what to do since there's no map or hints of any kind. AI is horrible. I spent good 15 minutes trying to escort some old nag down the stairs cause the damn thing literally kept stopping at every corner saying the same damn thing.
Don't get me wrong, i absolutely LOVE old atmospheric games like Call of Cthulhu, Clive Barker's Undying, Cold Fear, Quake, Scratches, Penumbra, Dementium II, Gorky 17 etc, i freaking love them, the unique atmosphere they provide. I love all these old places, survival aspect etc, but this game is just broken beyond repair, it's terrible. It looks terrible and it plays terrible. One of those rare cases when a video game just plain straight♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off.
I could keep on and on forever mentioning other broken aspects like an absolutely useless ability to pick up health packs even at full health, therefore wasting them - Dafuq?; the fact that they are all different sizes and there's absolutely no way to tell which will it be: small one, medium one or large one until you actually pick up one and see how much health it restores - Dafuq?!; or compass being useless in constantly changing environment; the timer that keeps ticking, oh the timer! If you didn't know, there are several family members that are being kept as hostages in an old mansion and if you don't save good half of them in like an hour and a half of REAL TIME the game ends. I read it on Wiki, since i was too sick of this game to actually test it out myself. Yeah, just like that, apparently it's called a storyline here. Needless to say how much this approach to a gameplay encourages players to explore the place rather than just run like crazy through the levels... Oh wait, that's what you gonna be doing;  or the ability to reload your weapon even if it doesn't need reloading - DAFUQ?!?! No, really, even if your weapon is loaded, you can still reload it, therefore wasting ammo, i'm not joking... And the list keeps on going.
So, if you are feeling nostalgic, like i was, try Clive Barker's Undying or AvP 1999 for that instance, they are so much better than this broken crap. 3\10 at best IMO. I fail to see what all the good reviews are about, people will just buy anything these days.

First, review, ever.
Since Titan Quest, something has been nagging me. Where is a Titan Questesque(word) ripoff? Well, now we have one.
I like the game. Please, don't get me wrong. I have HUNDREDS of hours into Titan's Quest. My Steam account doesn't accurately reflect the hours I have put in. Considering, I bought TQ when it first came out and then proceeded to buy the expansion. Then after a couple of years on the shelf. Steam released the Gold pack, and I couldn't resist.
Simply put, I cannot recommend Grim Dawn.
I like GRIM DAWN, I LIKE GRIM DAWN. I just cannot tell my friends/family to buy this game.
Why?
First off. It looks almost exactly like TQ, but SLIGHTLY updated. Almost, to me, like I just spent 20$ on TQ 1.75, except, 10 years later. Grim Dawn isn't even TQ 2.0. It's unacceptable. Not to mention, the mobs are EERIELY similar to TQs. I'm talking about frames and skeletons.
In this day in age, you cannot pass this look off. Nor get away with reusing skeletons and frames from 10 years ago. This game is a slight a niche market with people pandering to nostaglia. I'm guilty, as charged.
The UI is clunky, unresponsive, and down right ambigious. It's purpose is vague and comes with 1234567. These days, QWERTY is the new setup. It just shows the age on the developers. They are behind the times. Right clicking and selecting makes sense. But it doesn't explain anything. If you are new to the TQ vibe, this is vague. I know, I have been there. At the time(Since TQ), there wasn't a place I felt I could get this across. Hopefully, they take me honestly. I promise, I'm not trolling.
I just started out with a Solider class, typical Tank/Melee build. Charge is broken. Half the time I get stuck, unable to move, it doesn't cast, or it completely locks down the screen. SOMETIMES, I pause, and it stops the problem, sometimes it doesn't. So I HAVE TO die, and lose EXP, or quit the game.
The game is expansive. It's vast, and in that vastness, you get lost. Not finding objectives is common, even with reading quests description. Not enough quest items is common. Which requires farming. Farming content that doesn't have a net gain is pointless. It makes it repetitive and boring.
The game needs fountains like TQ. Call them Flux Voids or something. Having to restart from Devils Crossing, then Rfiting, then backtracking is painful. It doesn't fly by today's standards.
I haven't even done multiplayer. So I won't comment about it. This is JUST a summary of my 11 hours of experience.
So, why do I like Grim Dawn?
Same reasons I liked Titan's Quest. Neat and interesting loot, varied builds, and different. I love Hack n Slash genre. It's my bread and butter, go to, bored game. I supported Titan's Quest TWICE. They have gotten more money out of me, than any other game. (Outside of WoW) When I had seen the game, in 2012? I think. I said, when this goes to Steam, I WILL support the game. Because I had loved TQ so much.
I had hoped that they( Grim's developers ) took a familar but seperate direction. Yet, all I am seeing is Titan's Quest 2, as it should have been 10 years ago. While I will continue to the follow the game and complete the content. This is my own Titan's Quest. I am the solo adventurer in the Grim Dawn. I will not recommend a Samwise to my Frodo on this trip.
If the developers want to get in contact with me. I will give them a better, in depth, analysis. I hope they don't take this personally. This is just an honest review from a rabid fan of previous developments.

I'm a big fan of tactical combat. I still play Master Of Orion II on a regular basis, and I just love the planning that goes into tactical warfare. The tactical combat is great.... you scale up your units, you specialize them to suit the combat strategy you prefer, and you execute your combat strategy and hopefully it goes according to plan.
It has a few misgivings that make it just shy of a REALLY REALLY GOOD game, but I feel that they're kind of glaring and take away from the experience.
One issue I had was with the Fog of War. Normally, in RTS games, fog of war provides a sense of mystery about what your enemy is up to, and lets you use the element of surprise to your advantage. This works really well in RTS games. However, in a turn-based tactical combat game, this means that you ahve to move VERY SLOWLY otherwise you might find yourself  overextended. This is  normally a reasonable strategy to execute, but it drags on with this. Extending the fog of war beyond the engagement zone of your weapons would provide you with a chance to execute your strategy better. This is coupled with a very miniscule AI. There is no squad tactics for the enemy AI. The enemy units are placed pseudo-randomly around the map and they mostly stay put. When they're revealed, they're given a turn to take cover, but it's very stale. The effective strategy becomes to inch forward, go into Overwatch, rinse and repeat, until you encounter enemy units which you can overpower if you progress slowly. It would much prefer to have the aliens converge on my position, punish me for staying put, and force me to diversify my strategy.
The other major issue I had was with the XCOM base. There's really only one effective strategy, and once you've got it nailed down, nothing changes. I would love to see other means for earning income (for example, have the gray market play a bigger role in the game, but if you use the market too much you run the risk of XCOM allies pulling out.) Having an alternative stragy for managing the base give you options and allows for more emergent strategies.
One other small issue I had was with the UI.... with the isometric view (which I love) simulating multiple levels of 3-d environments, clicking on one square can potentially indicate several different squares. A couple times, I would try to send a unit to one place and find it running to a completely wrong place. It became a bit aggravating after a while.
Overall, still a very good game. 4.2/5

A shocking documentary window into the secret lives of cats...or a silly, well-done Japanese homebrew side-scrolling shooter, take your pick.
On a basic level, aside from moving around all you've got to worry about are "shoot" and "bomb" buttons; from there it's all about making sure your salvos land and theirs don't. After selecting one of three available kitties with varying movement speeds and weapons (plus a couple more to unlock), you're off on a brisk seven-stage journey to rack up as many points as you can.
You'll quickly notice that blasting baddies releases blue cat icons, which charge up your single-stock "bomb" weapon when picked up; unleashing said bomb not only damages enemies and grants a few moments of invincibility, but changes unfriendly bullets and defeated targets into gold pickups, which serve as your primary source of points - and extra lives. You'll likely soon figure out that downing an enemy from right up close flashes a
message, and grants extra points and cat items; as such, you'll want to be almost constantly on the move, getting in adversaries' faces during fleeting instances of safety, charging up the bomb, letting it rip where it'll reap the best rewards, and already be working on readying the next one.
It's not the most groundbreaking feature set or gameplay style, especially for anyone with some prior knowledge of the shoot-em-up genre at large, but it is a lot of fun, and solidly put together: three difficulty levels are available to cater to a wide range of challengers, and while things can sometimes come across as a bit too chaotic to keep track of, especially when you're first getting used to the style, your character's hit area is forgiving and openly displayed, and handy visual and sound cues make it easier to focus on the moment-to-moment action instead of whether or not your bomb meter is quite filled yet. On the superficial side, there's a more-than-respectable amount of enemy and background variety (and weirdness) packed into the game's brief running time, while the soundtrack (which, as the description notes, is included gratis) has more than enough quirky energy to keep the journey lively; controller support (both analog and digital, thank heavens) also works well, and the game has no trouble humming (er, purring) right along even on not-so-impressive hardware like mine.
I actually bought and enjoyed the original Japanese version of this several months before it came to Steam, but have no problem double-dipping to support both the developer and publisher for making it available to a wider audience. If you have any inclination towards scrolling shooters, bizarre cat humor, or both, at the very least track down the Japanese demo for this online and see how it strikes you; I'm willing to bet that most who do will find it a most entertaining (ball of) yarn.

Neko Navy is sort of an oddity in the SHMUP genre, and yet is what you'd expect of the genre on any given day. That's the weird thing right off the bat: you've played games like Neko Navy before, but the slight twists that it puts on the game at times are interesting when it decides to showcase them. It's a solid game with good difficulty options and reasonable controls. Its problem is simple: it lacks a KO punch of any sort. Nothing WOWs here, it's all good but nothing is spectular. In a genre that has a lot of old GREAT games coming out via porting, in addition to games trying to specialize in one element of the SHMUP genre, it's going to have problems standing out.
Which is sad, because it's clear that the developer understands the underlying genre and knows some key design elements for it. Granted, that has a hiccup once in the while (the fish section), but overall there's good enemy placement and the challenge does ramp up appropriately as you go through the game. The artwork is solid with an ok soundtrack and ok sound design, basically giving you enough to not be repelled by the game, but nothing to draw you in specifically either.
Basically, Neko Navy to me is a rather simple SHMUP that's a good injection vector for those who want to get into SHMUPs: slowly hand holding you through the difficulties and helping you out with extra credits as you fail over time. The problem for a SHMUP veteran however is simple: the lack of the overall hook that makes Neko Navy something truly unique for you to try. In addition, the lack of content/replayability is what kills it for those hardcore fans in the end: it just doesn't have the bang for buck that games like Roche Fusion and Mushihimesama have. However, it does have a charm thanks to good artwork and just a sense of a developer who “loves” the genre. If you have the extra money, I'd pick it up for a couple of hours of fun, but if you're more frugal with your money, it's a wait for a discount kind of game if you're a SHMUP veteran.

A majority of puzzle games will teach you the rules before then asking you to apply them in some fashion to solve a problem.
Antichamber is different. It doesn't explain its mechanics or even announce that any problem exists. There is no hand holding or even an introduction. Instead, it simply opens a door and invites you to pass through.
The entire game is a grand puzzle where the goal is not only to find the correct answers, but to actually figure out how the world works. It doesn't just force you to think outside the box, it makes you question if the box was ever there to begin with.
Antichamber assumes a lifetime of experience driving what you come to expect from a 3D environment, and works to break all those preconceptions. Its mechanics straddle the line between the third and fourth dimensions, giving the game its inviting appearance while still affording it license to blow your mind at will.
This does not, however, mean that the game is unfair. Although Antichamber continually seeks to warp reality, it does so in a very consistent manner. The world, which may seem obtuse at first, is in fact, incredibly structured and rigidly built, though this may only become apparent once you've drawn back the curtain yourself.
While this does mean that you can really only play Antichamber once, for that one playthrough, it becomes more than just a puzzle game, it truly makes you feel like you're learning to walk all over again.

The levels are generally well-designed with a reasonable amount of variety, though all of the special abilities and level elements are introduced fairly early, so the middle-end still drags a bit just from the lack of anything new. The levels are divided by spot-the-difference puzzles (every 4 levels) and hidden-object puzzles (every 16), which helps to keep things fresh. Worth grabbing for fans of the genre.

South Park: The Stick of Truth is a South Park themed RPG created by Obsidian and published by Ubisoft. Now don't let Ubisoft's name put you off because even though South Park is an Ubisoft game you don't need Uplay to play it. The game is about 10 hours in length even with side quests and most of the time you'll be completing the 10 or twelve story missions the game has to offer. The game is locked to 30 frames per second although due to the aesthetic it actually works in this specific case. The game as a whole is very well put together but since most of South Park is dependent on very subjective themes like humor, reception will vary wildy from person to person.
South Park takes place in, you guessed it, the small town of South Park and you play as a nameless and voiceless new kid on the block. You soon meet with Cartman and Butters and discover the fantasy world that these kids have set up, joining them in the process. This game that the kids play revolves around a "magical" item called the stick of truth and whoever controls said stick can then control the universe. Over the course of the game you run all across South Park gathering support for the humans so that you can assault the elves and take back the stick. Most of the story is just lots of general outlines of what could have been a funny story but instead was stuffed with toilet humor and fan service. A large amount of the lines end up being incredibly cringe-worthy, such as the overarching theme that you should never fart on someone's balls or some of the lines the girls have. The entire story ends up being mostly running around South Park and trying to recruit the various factions to play with you (I.E. The Goths and the girls). None of the characters are anything close to interesting and for a game that calls itself an RPG they really don't explain much about the characters and instead seem to rely on you having watched the show. As most of the characters are dull and repetitive, so too are the environments and in South Park you'll be running back and forth throughout the same environments over and over again for some tedious quest or another and in the end this is just too mind-numbingly boring.
The gameplay, however, is actually pretty well done as far as most RPG's go. You have multiple different methods of attacks: Ranged, melee, magic and abilities along with a plethora of consumables for mid-battle use. You acquire many different kinds of weapons and armor over the course of the story and each piece has its own bonuses that come with it. Most of the armor bonuses are just passive bonuses and thus are pretty boring but there really wasn't much else they could've done with this so I can let it slide. The armor types and models are suprisingly varied and you can get some pretty cool looking sets that really feel like something you would see kids create. You can customize your armor to a degree with various slottable upgrades and different colored dyes but for the most part the main bits of the armor cannot be changed. If you have half a mind and explore even the slightest bit then South Park will prove to be incredibly easy and, as far as RPG's go, incredibly short, as the game should clock in at about 10 hours and that's counting about two hours of exploring that I did early on. South Park has a real problem with difficulty and for pretty much the entire game, with the exception of a fight or two, it's incredibly easy. South Park has a very limited setting to work with and as such seeing the same old parts of the town can really hit you with a feeling of tedium that an RPG cannot have. Most of the side quests are pretty boring too and really end up being either fetch quests or quests you can't finish until later so you forget about them. Since The Stick of Truth is an RPG you can upgrade your character with various perks ability upgrades. Ability upgrades follow a linear upgrade line while perks can be unlocked in any order but also tend to have a more minor impact on gameplay. You unlock perks by getting more friends which you unlock by simply talking to people or doing their quests and it does give the town of South Park a very connected feel as if everybody knows everybody. There's also the buddy system where you can take one buddy along with you to fight in combat and help you out with environmental roadblocks. The buddies are simply a letdown because you end up unlocking the final one not halfway into the game and you are never given any reason to switch off of the first buddy given to you.
An RPG with solid gameplay that's severely hampered by places of cringe-worthy dialogue and overuse of toilet humor. Only for fans of the series.

Pro: A very fun and interesting game with lots of twist and turns and surprises that can really get you into the story. The combat isn't ground breaking, but it's a lot of fun and every unit feels different, which is great.
Con: While the story is amazing, it's also the source of the complaints of the game. They tell you your choice matters, but it actually doesn't for a lartge part. The only real affect your actions have are over a few optional characters and fictional numbers that don't really matter. Also, while the game is going to be multiple parts, it doesn't really TELL you that, so unless you research, you're left with a bad impression, asking yourself why there's all the loose ends that there are.
Overall: They've created a very big world with a lot of lore and I look forward to the future of the series, I just hope that the future games (which hopefully will have better funding) can deliver a bit more of a real choose your own adventure story. I don't mind if I always wind up in the same place through the story, but I'd like to actually genuinely have a different adventure then another person, something like letting me go through land or through the sea to a single place. Both go to the same place, but each bring a different adventure.

The Banner Saga is a beautiful game that is not only an artistic marvel, which in itself is a rarity these days, but also a well crafted turn-based strategy. I find myself attached to many of the characters, especially when a poor turn of fate takes them from my caravan. It says something when a game like ME3 can't get me to care about a character over the course of an entire game when The Banner Saga has me on the edge worrying about every single one of the characters' fates within moments of meeting them. That said, TBS can very unforgiving during combat as well as the caravan and battlefield decisions. I can't help but wonder if there was a better choice so save the lives of my men and varls. If only they put more voice acting in the dialogue scenes then I could love this game more.
Update:
So I finally get BS2 and decide to replay through all of BS1. Can't say it's as good as I remember it being. Now that I've had time to mill over the game I realize it builds up so much, but just leaves you feeling disappointed and relieved it's over. The strong narrative is there, but everything is punishing. Many times you are punished at random for decisions, not completely knowing the context of the universe. There are rarely any context clues to help you on your way. Reknown can easily be wasted investing in a character that dies off. And a lot of them can die off.
Battles can swing very fast, usually against you. Certain units and Dredge summoning can quickly turn a winning battle into a losing one. The final battle is especially guilty of this sudden turn in outcome. Just a really painful two part battle where you have extreme disadvantages. The leap in difficulty, even if you play on easy is crazy. I managed to scrape by on normal thanks to following a guide to maximize my party levels and dedicating certain chars to roles.
Depressing stories and difficult games aren't inherently bad. But they have to make it so the player feels responsible for their actions. Otherwise you just have a frustrating game that you want to stop playing. The double whammy BS throws at you: dark, depressing story with seemingly unfair gameplay can easily turn you off from playing.

With a cool looking linear playthrough, at first glance there's nothing wrong with 4 Elements apart from the fact that full screen on a 1920x1080 monitor is streched with no further display options. I had to play it that small windowed mode with the monitor closer to my face. This, I can take, but already fills up the dislike bar a little bit. Other details made the rest of the work and the bar resulted in this review.
The game itself is fine although a little bit repetitive and not very innovative. If you like lighly washed-on themes of fantasy and match-3 type games, no problem so far. But let's go to the list of annoyances:
- There's one chance to shut the fairy up, when she asks if you want to keep receiving tips and stuff. If you don't shut her at that moment, you'll be stuck with her to the end of the game. The "hints" option only refers to the in-game matches, apparently.
- You cannot choose what book you want to unlock next and there's no thematic justification for that, it is just "later books, harder levels". At least let us pick what card from a book to recover next or something, that would be easy to implement even keeping the levels linear but only changing their name, to present players with a "false choice". Everything is so linear that even this kind of insignificant choice would be cool to have.
- You cannot replay any levels after they're beaten once. W-what?? That is a pain, because there are achievements that require you to start a whole new game if you don't get them at first.
- The Epilogue took so long to appear that I have already clicked the screen thinking nothing would happen if I didn't. It skipped the ending and guess what? Once gone, you cannot access it anymore. In fact, forget your progress. At the time that screen appears, your progress is deleted and the only option is to start a new game. I hope there's a youtube video or something so I can see what the hell the Epilogue was about.
The smaller the game, the heavier these details become. Overall, I don't recommend 4 Elements. Even without all the annoyance, it's still a repetitive and very forgettable game.

A very solid game overall - a must-buy if you're a fan of old-school cRPGs.
The turn-based combat system is extremely deep and (especially in co-op mode) seems to help in making the combat not feel like a chore. It does have issues: often times it'll be hard to see where the edges of ground effects (fire, poison, etc.) are, especially if they're covered by grass. This has resulted in my characters taking unnecessary damage more times than I can count. Often times your character's vision will also be blocked for no reason, which can be frustrating. However, these issues are only minor and I expect they will be patched out in the near future.
The story is engaging and the quests are mostly interesting, but unfortunately (or fortunately if you're like me) there's barely any voice acting. That is forgivable, though, as the game has a gigantic amount of dialogue. If you like reading, just buy the game already!
One additional point I must bring up is the fact that the game starts off in a slow-ish manner. My friend and I were not very impressed by the combat system at the very beginning of the game, but it gets SO MUCH better after a few hours once you start getting more and more abilities to play around with.
To summarize: the game is very good, but not perfect. 100% recommended if you're into cRPGs, otherwise you might want to read around a bit more to make sure that the game is for you.

A very atmospheric, but unpolished game.
While it lacks when it comes to graphic fidelity, it has a solid gameplay. The AI characters and items are partially randomized, which keeps the game a bit more fresh and makes a player be wary of surroundings.
Both enemy and friendly NPCs happen to have issues with pathfinding, which can sometimes be extremely annoying. The platforming elements have problems too, especially given the weird gravity of the game and the tendency of getting stuck on objects.
The game has a nice variety of both enemies and weapons, introducing some original mechanics, which I won't spoil. The user interface adds to the atmosphere of the game. The environments themselves are somewhat repetitive, which, combined with maze-like levels, can make a player get lost easily.
When it comes to the horror elements, they're not on Amnesia/Outlast/Alien: Isolation level, but they work nevertheless, more so at the beggining of the game. While the music is good and helps to build the tension for most of the time, it sometimes gets cut unexpectedly.
The experience lasts for around 5-6 hours (I'm pretty sure I checked every possible room, killed every enemy), depending on your pace, but keep in mind that the game has time-limited objectives, which make you want to be fast on your feet. I played it on normal difficulty, which made the game pretty hard at the beginning, but easy towards the end; for a more horror-like experience I would play on nightmare settings.
In my opinion the game is most similiar (while being somewhat inferior) to Clive Barker's Undying and has a similiar vibe of an oldschool shooter. I would not recommend it to people who hate backtracking and having to navigate maze-like environments without a map. On the other hand, fans of classic shooters should enjoy it if they can overlook some of the flaws.Worth buying when on sale, but for the full price I would only recommend it for fans of games like Undying.

An exciting game. Very enjoyable, given that you know what to expect.
Gameplay: First thing to note - this isn't a traditional CRPG at all. No open world, no exploring, no looting random enemies etc. etc. Basically, the game consists of story given in textual form plus tactical battles. Surprisingly enough, this game is actually very much like a Japanese visual novel: making choices in dialogues with some fighting in between. Nothing wrong with that, but I guess there are people who dislike that kind of stuff.
Combat system: The game has an original turn-based combat system which can be a bit confusing in the beginning, but is, in fact, very consistent and coherent. Fights are interesting and challenging - this game isn't easy at all at Normal difficulty (though it isn't exactly hard, the balance is just right). So that part of the game is very well-executed.
Graphics: The artwork in the game is to die for! For me at least it was love at first sight. I actually find it quite difficult to stop pressing F12 all the time. Every single screenshot is a piece of art!
Music: Good, adequate, though I'm not exactly willing to listen to that soundtrack when not in game. Which isn't a bad thing, there aren't that many game soundtracks that can stand on their own.
Story: I'm not quite finished with it so it's a bit early to say, but so far - not bad at all. And I would definitely play again to see what different choices can lead to. All is well here. If it wasn't for one thing... which is in fact the only thing I didn't exactly like about the game ->
Writing: This is the only thing I find somehow... lacking. Don't get me wrong, I like the plot, I like the characters. I don't like writing itself, because it lacks style, it lacks flavor. It wouldn't be such a big deal if this game wasn't at least 50% textual. I'm not saying that all the characters have to speak like they are in the poetic Edda, but all those "ok", "crap", "yeah" and "everything was a mess"-sort of descriptions are not to my liking. And there are typos too. As a part of the game, it's not crucial, because there's also artwork and music and other things. But had this been a book... I'd probably deem it a poorly-written one.

I have played many many games and very few of them offer the freedom, satisfaction, and fun that Dvinity: Original Sin brings to the table. Most modern RPGs are more action than RPG, and suffer from dumb downed and simplified gameplay to appeal to a broader audience. Well Divinity: Original Sin brings the depth and interaction of older series like Baldur's Gate as well as beautiful graphics and music that really brings the Dungeons and Dragons style genre to the next level.
Quests require you to talk to various npcs, whose dialouges are always extraordinarily written, and read excerpts from journals and books to uncover plots and mysteries as well as unravel your tale as a Source Hunter. There are no quest markers or waypoints, which may leave you lost or searching for what to do next, but as you adjust and learn to put the pieces together you will find yourself immersed in the beautiful world,
Every aspect of the game just feels so finely polished and well made. Dialouges with npcs are engaging and many times hilarous. The word intuitive is thrown around a lot for games, but the crafting system in Divinity definitely deserves it. I don't want to give too much away but one small example is you can take a knife to a pillow to get a feather, which can be combined with the same knife to create a quill which can be crafted into various other things. The world is extremely interactive, rivaling AAA titles like Skyrim with the ability to pick up and move around almost every object, including chests and barrels.
The combat is turn-based, with each party member having a number of action points, determined by various stats, that are used to move, use skills, etc during combat. It is very tatical, and the environment plays a huge role. You can lay down oil, slowing your opponents and limiting their action points for a couple of turns, then even light the pool of oil on fire buring everyone standing in it. There are many combinations like this, such as making it rain then electrocuting and stunning opponents standing in the pool of water that forms. One of the big ways the combat stands out is that buffs and debuffs play a serious role in the combat. Being stunned, knocked, down, etc can take someone out of a fight for multiple turns, creating huge advantages. Fights are very tough, and you are almost always fighting someone a higher level than you are, so utilizing your skills correctly is key to a satisfying victory.
You can also converse with the people in your party, discussing events and things that you've done. You also discuss with your party when making decisions for quests. There are multiple meters for how people percieve you, such as independent/dependent, heartless/compationate, bold/cautious, that change based on the decisions you make and things you say.
The icing on the cake of Divinity: Original Sin is that all of this can be experienced with a friend. There is drop in/drop out co op that is super easy to use. You can split up control of your party amongst the two of you and set off on your adventure.
I can not reccomend this game enough, especially to any who find themselves going waypoint to waypoint completing boring quests or easy mind numbing combat in other games. For casual gamers I would still recommend this game, but heed my warning that you may find yourself lost and not sure where to go next, or having difficulties in a tough fight. You can always turn the difficulty down though if you're having too much trouble.
So get out there. Explore. Discover. Interact.

Seriously, though, Divinity: Original Sin, is one of the finest RPGs I have ever had the pleasure of playing. Clever writing (though, the constant talking of the NPCs in the town can get annoying, they have a tendency to talk over each other), a quite pleasing art style and more stats and skills than you can shake a wizard staff at! Having the two main characters interact is also a great roleplaying mechanic, either with a friend, or even alone.
The combat, especially, is a real treat. Turn-based, eschewing mana or other resources in favour of an Action Point system, a la the old X-COM. Enemies are tough and their favourite past-time is chopping adventurers to bits, so you'll need to use your skills intelligently, especially considering magic and their assorted elemental combos.
Overall, a few minor nuisances here and there aside, Original Sin is a splendid game, well worth your time, especially if you feel casting cold spells in the rain should do more than just increase damage.

As strange as it sounds, this is one of the best Superhero games I've played in a while. Aliens take over Earth and stuff you and your crew into a Matrix-like simulation, where you earn new and upgraded powers to leap, glide, run at lightning speeds, throw fireballs, shrink enemies, toss cars with telekinesis and more.
The story is suitably whacky for a Saints Row game, with the hilarious story DLC content (Dominatrix and Christmas) backing it up. The action mixes up gunplay and superpowers well, ensuring a level of challenge with mixed tactics for different enemy types and a few story-based missions that temporarily strip you of superpowers because the mission would just be boring if you wrecked through it with them.
Lots of variety in the content, though it was somewhat disappointing that all the non-main-story missions boiled down to "Do this random selection of activities on the map because I said to." They even put their own tongue firmly in cheek while ordering you to do them. "Now go over here and slaughter these aliens because it... reminds me of... uh... I got nothing, just go kill em."
Lots of features, lots of content, lots of fun, even if it shares a lot of assets with SR3.

Spider-man meets Mirror's Edge. Apperently you arrive in a poorly written story as a hired gun to do the dirty work for them. You dont even need to play this game for 10 min before you know something fishy is going on with the people he works for. The story is really boring and such a cliché.
What i disliked about the game:
- Noise attracts super zombies, regardless of where you are. Apparently they can hear a gun shot from EVERYWHERE!
- Water, blood, sun and all other annyoing effects blur your vision waaaaaaa(add more a's)aaaaay to much. Half the time you just wait for it to go away so you can see again. (Why make such an annyoing effect and then make so much content in a sewer?)
- The seizures, its so frustrating, not because you feel the agony, but because its just removing any way of playing when he's whimping about. We get it, he's turning, but come on, especially after he says "this can't be happening now", for the 10th time.
- I think theres around 10 different types of zombies, pretty mundane towards the end.
- Way to much time spent in water, why would you do that when the swimming is terrible.
- The melee combat was cool at first, but after you behead a zombie for the 50th time, its not that interesting anymore (Also since its only the same type of zombies that you can behead).
- Weapons; Guns is just frustrating since it attracts super zombies without a question. Why is there no silencers? I see military equipment all over the place, but not 1 has a silencer. Reparing of weapons just leaves you to being carefull instead of careless (I cant use this badass weapon i just made as much as i wanted, because it will break eventually) which is really annyoing.
- Exploding zombies gets boring really quick, since its often just unavoidable.
- QTE bosses is the worst in a fps game, really, if i wanted to press A, S, D or W when you told me, i'd be playing a kids game instead.
- The annyoing Dead Island, FarCry and now Dying Light crafting system, it doesnt offer anything fun, that i have to craft my own baseball bat with nails in it, its a fun gimmick, but also completely irrelevant since most weapons you pick up is better or just not worth the hazzle. If you want to make the player get excited about crafting, make it more interesting or just leave it out.
- The sleeping (I can sleep whenever i want, why make such a fuss about it being night?)
- Weird AI (Ie. 3 dudes is guarding a npc, you kill off 2 of them without the 3rd one even seeing you, but you cant talk to the npc before the 3rd guard is dead)
- The map seems big at first, but its not, its actually kind of limited. Also very repetative surroundings, houses, zombies, safe houses etc.
What i like about the game:
- The fast paced running (Not untill later in the game though), which was really missed in the start of the game. I understand that the character evolves throughout the game, but one would thing that running is something every soldier is trained to do well.
- The slowmotion when you cut of limbs (Could have been way more variations)
- Weapon upgrades (Not the crafting part) is a cool gimmick, they could put a lot more work into it though.
- Side missions (Without it, the game would be very short)
- Co-op is always a huge plus.
- The hook.
- Parkour is always fun, but also a bit crazy at times, to see what he can hang onto as long as you hold space.
Summary:
You can predict anything that will happen in this game, since its so cliché. You know what kind of zombies there will be (Slow ones, exploding ones, runners, huge ones etc.), theres a villan (who almost wins duh), the plot twists, the awkward forced feelings about some random woman who you maybe have 5-8 cutscenes with and then he just falls head over heels for her (i mean come on, make some effort in the character building).
All in all, dont waste your money on this if you already tried games like Far Cry, dead island and assassins creed. It feels like a mix of a lot of games put into one. Also, the game starts out slow, which is understandable, but it also means that when you start to become more agile, strong and fast, the game slowly becomes boring and repetative, which is a shame. This is just my personal oppinion, you dont have to agree at all, but i was just dissapointed with it. Theres absolutely nothing new in this game and i wish the creators were a bit more creative, instead of trying to take good working things out of other games and fitting them into theirs only.

Just beat the game, went co-op all the way through with my best friend, loved every moment of it.  I won't discuss the day/night cycle, as it's been discussed to death.  It works beautifully.
The story is alright, not much to shake a stick at, just the average 'find the cure while gov./big bad tries to exploit your efforts' spiel.  There's also a lot of side quests and random encounters to keep you busy the whole way through.
The gameplay?  Spot on.  Instead of doing what a lot of zombie games do and throw more and more zombies at you in lieu of "difficulty", as the game progresses, eveything gets tougher.  The Goons (8-ft. tall rebar swingers) get upgraded, you are constantly finding new enemies to fight, the walkers get faster and stronger.  Basically, it gives you a reason to keep finding new and better gear.
Speaking of gear, the system works great.  As you use weapons, they deteriorate.  Unlike other games, you can only repair a certain number of times (1 for Gray-rarity, 2 for Green, 3 Blue, 4 Purple, and a full 5 for Orange).  Then, you are left with a broken hunk of metal.  This prevents you from getting too attached to one weapon, again forcing you to constantly seek out more powerful and rare weapons.
Levels are split into three parts: Survivor (basic stuf), Agility (parkour tricks), and Power (attack skills).  Not much more to say, except to definitley get the fall damage reduction skill and the one whichgives your weapons about a 25% chance to not use a repair when repaired.
Multiplayer is where it's at.  Nothing is more fun than running up walls and killing zombies with a friend, or three.
The only real bad thing?
*Spoilers*
THE GODDAMN ENDING SUCKS!
Okay, you've done everything in this game with a friend, leaned on each other's strengths, supported through the weaknesses, and had a hell of a time bashing zombies in and finding just the right way to best your buddy in overall DPS.  What happens at the end?  You're thrown into a goddamn SINGLE-PLAYER segment where you do more running from the zombies than using your shiniest, badassest weapons.  You finally get to the top of the tower, and you face off against the big bad.  Do you use your weapons now?  HELL NO!  ITS A GOD DAMN FICKING QTE SEGMENT!!!!!
At least they didn't end with a non-interactive cutscene.
*End Spoilers*
Even with a bad ending, the game is awesome.  Make sure to get it with a friend.

There are a couple of small problems with the game here and there. I'm a big fan of tactical combat. I still play Master Of Orion II on a regular basis, and I just love the planning that goes into tactical warfare. The tactical combat is great.... you scale up your units, you specialize them to suit the combat strategy you prefer, and you execute your combat strategy and hopefully it goes according to plan.
It has a few misgivings that make it just shy of a REALLY REALLY GOOD game, but I feel that they're kind of glaring and take away from the experience.
One issue I had was with the Fog of War. Normally, in RTS games, fog of war provides a sense of mystery about what your enemy is up to, and lets you use the element of surprise to your advantage. This works really well in RTS games. However, in a turn-based tactical combat game, this means that you ahve to move VERY SLOWLY otherwise you might find yourself  overextended. This is  normally a reasonable strategy to execute, but it drags on with this. Extending the fog of war beyond the engagement zone of your weapons would provide you with a chance to execute your strategy better. This is coupled with a very miniscule AI. There is no squad tactics for the enemy AI. The enemy units are placed pseudo-randomly around the map and they mostly stay put. When they're revealed, they're given a turn to take cover, but it's very stale. The effective strategy becomes to inch forward, go into Overwatch, rinse and repeat, until you encounter enemy units which you can overpower if you progress slowly. It would much prefer to have the aliens converge on my position, punish me for staying put, and force me to diversify my strategy.
The other major issue I had was with the XCOM base. There's really only one effective strategy, and once you've got it nailed down, nothing changes. I would love to see other means for earning income (for example, have the gray market play a bigger role in the game, but if you use the market too much you run the risk of XCOM allies pulling out.) Having an alternative stragy for managing the base give you options and allows for more emergent strategies.
One other small issue I had was with the UI.... with the isometric view (which I love) simulating multiple levels of 3-d environments, clicking on one square can potentially indicate several different squares. A couple times, I would try to send a unit to one place and find it running to a completely wrong place. It became a bit aggravating after a while.
Overall, still a very good game. 4.2/5

If you liked Titan Quest, you'll probably have your portion of fun with this game. If, like myself, you're looking for a more Diablo-style action/RPG you may want to move along.
The negative things:
- Most of the ingame content is not procedurally generated, so there's not much in terms of replayability.
- The maps are huge, but they look almost identical and there's not enough visual variety.
- The AI is lacking. Ranged monsters shooting walls you're hiding behind instead of trying to flank you. Melee monsters rarely trying to avoid your attacks and dying rapidly because of that.
- The pacing is quite slow. The amount of useful loot you get is miserable and you usually don't get enough ingame currency to buy really good items from merchants.
- The skills are somewhat boring. Having something like "Your attacks now deal some extra fire damage" when there's no or very little visual effect is not that exciting. There's not enough "weight" and epicness in the process of grinding monsters into dust.
The positive things:
- There are some dialogs. I can't say I'm a fan of those, especially since there's no voice over for them, but hey, some people like this kind of stuff stuff.
- The dual specialization idea is quite neat. I wish the skills from different specs were synergizing better.
Am I regretting buying the game? A bit, but now I know exactly why I like other actions/RPGs and appreciate the effort their devs put into them.
Update: If you have doubts about buying the game please read the other reviews, both positive and negative. The game seems to have a strong fan community that may be somewhat defensive about the game, thus apologizing certain flaws in the game design or content. That is understandable, but that is not helpful for a consumer.

There's a lot about Block'hood that I want to like. City builders, resource management, production chains, and tile placement puzzles are all some of my favorite things when it comes to games, and good city builders or tycoon-style games are so rare these days. Plus, Block'hood has an interesting aesthetic, relaxing music, and a lot of creative potential.
Unfortunately, it seems to be one of those games that went off the rails while it was in Early Access, resulting in a lot of strange (and often unfinished) ideas.
For example, the game has a short story mode which acts as a tutorial, a challenge mode with beginner levels that act as a tutorial, and an actual multi-level tutorial. The story mode was particularly strange, as it was incredibly slow-paced and stifling with what you could do (like a tutorial), yet I had to stop and redo the whole thing with the help of the other two tutorials. Additionally, the story mode has no save option, and the game crashed three times while I was on the last level, forcing me to restart.
Even more egregious is a UI scattered with blank and greyed out buttons that appear to be future unlocks, but.. aren't. It appears that there are spots where the developer intended to put a sort button on the resource list (which has several dozen unalphabetized entries), but then decided not to without removing the button, and there are four tabs in each building menu labeled I, II, III, IV (falsely implying tiers), despite there only being two tabs of each tile in the game. There's also things like a sound menu that resets itself every time you start a level, and several tiles with incorrect adjacency labels (meaning you have to build certain things like support structures and parks facing the wrong way to get them to function).
Beyond that, there are just so many half-baked ideas. I remember when this game was in development and everybody complained that it felt lifeless without people and animals wandering around. So they put in people and animals wandering around, with likes and dislikes, names, and moods. A neat idea, but there's no reason to actually pay attention to them, and the mood system might as well not be there as they have no actual impact on the game. There's also an event system that doesn't really seem to be well thought-out, and things like weather and a day/night cycle that don't actually sync up with what you're seeing (it'll be dark while the UI says "day" and raining when there isn't a rain event).
And lastly, something subjective, this game falls victim to the same thing that Project Highrise does for me: It's a game about building something that doesn't make sense. I don't mean that it's about building weird abstract art towers (that part's neat!), I mean things like the "Small Appartment" block not looking like an apartment, and instead consisting of a single empty room with a door and a window in the middle (not the middle of the wall; the middle of the room). Given that so much of the game is based on numbers and balancing things, you end up with a hodgepodge of mismatched rooms that require a TON of imagination to view as the nifty vertical societies the game aims for. It isn't about being realistic, it's about looking like something functional.
Most of my issues with Block'hood could very well be addressed in the coming months, and even more if it did something like adding mod support. However, in its current state, it feels like it falls into that "shouldn't have left Early Access" category. Which is a shame. The world needs more building games, and this one has so much potential.

I've played this a while now. There are many good things about this game, and bad, all of which have been given by other reviewers. On the whole, it simply ends up feeling a little empty.
When I'm playing a game like this, what I really feel like I'm playing with is a model of something -- a model of what works and what doesn't; something robust that I can develop strategies for. It doesn't have to be a simulation, but the model needs to have a certain level of complexity to be interesting. Furthermore, the complexity needs to be "deep", not "broad".
Unfortunately, Block'hood seems like an example of "broad" complexity that is actually pretty shallow -- lots of choices of blocks, but many are redundant. The interactions are basic, and boring, once you've grasped what's going on here. Maybe some non-linear limits would have helped, like decreasing returns on similar block business types, or low caps on stockpiled resources, or something.
There are a lot of combinations to explore, and in fairness I've never tried to build some kind of monster block, just a few levels' worth. But I find it hard to care after a while.
I suggest reading the other reviews on here; there are many good ones.

The game looks great. The animations are great. I like the subtle animations on the screen. I like the battle animations. The story so far is okay (I'm only 4 hours into it at this point). I will admit that when I saw the first line "The gods are dead" I rolled my eyes and thought great, it's a cliche in the first line of the game.
The combat is different. Having armor and strength, having to make a decision as to which attack to make -- break armor to reduce the armor and allow subsequent attacks to do more damage or attack strength which in turn lowers the amount of damage they can do on their strength attack. Break armor attacks however are unaffected by strength, so those almost dead enemies can still pose a risk. There's a disadvantage in eliminating low health enemies while there are strong enemies still on the board.
The willpower attribute is interesting in that you have a limited amount of points that can be used in strengthening attacks or moving further. Characters are limited in how much willpower they can expend, which also can be raised. This pool is limited but willpower can be gained when an enemy is killed and there are some characters that can add willpower to other characters through abilities.
Here's what I don't like... the slow moving caravan moves slowly. The world looks great, but I really don't like waiting minutes for the caravan to crawl across the screen to the next destination. I get it, it's probably for effect or immersiveness, but please... can I just fast forward please? The caravan leaves... moving slowly... moving... then an event pops up. Read through it, resolve, hopefully a battle, then back to the slowly... moving... caravan. *sigh*
After 4 hours I got up from playing the game and went to look at the time, thinking surely it was hours later than it was. I was surprised it was only 4 hours. It felt much longer. If this was non-stop action, that would be a good thing.  For this, not so much.
With that said, I like the game so far. I don't regret the pre-order, but I'd be hardpressed to recommend it to someone at $25 unless I was really sure they'd like it. My recommendation is to find the free to play multiplayer "Banner Saga: Factions" and give it a shot. If you're okay with the combat system, then maybe consider the singleplayer version.

South Park with an endearing rpg setting. What more can you get? It was a fun ride all the way through and I might play it again just to try out at least one more class. The main storyline and quests are what really drive this game for me, so fans of the show will have a blast.
I was a bit disappointed in some of the elements of the game however. The weapons are left to be desired since they seem to be less class specific and more whatever floats your boat, which isn't necessarily a bad thing, but sometimes it just felt wrong lugging around huge two-handed weapons and the like when I was a thief class; it could've just been me not exploring the meta more, but I think more class specific weapons would've been nice. Speaking of items, there was a huge saturation of strap-ons, clothes, and weapons right at the very end of the game for some apparent reason. Knowing South Park, all of those things right at the end could've been satirical, but it just felt underwhelming going through the whole game with a lack of items for each class and then suddenly getting a bunch of items at the end. Again, these two points aren't neccessarily bad, but I think they could've been executed better in order for the rpg elements of the game to feel more immersive. Maybe I'm just being a bit nitpicky.
Either way, the game was wonderful and I had a great time. I'd definitely implore those who like the show to check it out; or if you're just looking for a quick rpg that's a little different in story and aesthetics, this could be the game for you too.
