This is my review from Metacritic. My profile and my 5 other reviews can be found here:
Also, if you read reviews saying "They said there was a Day/Night cycle, but it's always sunny!" and "Why can't I turn off the Film Grain Effect?!" Those were misinformed reviews. The Day/Night cycle doesn't start until you finish the tutorial, which happens at the same time multiplayer is unlocked (you have to do like 2 missions before you can play the other zillion with your friends). Also, The Film Grain Effect stuff has been PATCHED, so you can turn it off now, which I was quite pleased about myself.
Anyways, here's my review:
Dying Light is an excellent zombie survival game from the developers behind Shadows of Mordor and Dead Island (the game feels like both of those mixed together, along with 3 grams of awesome salt).
Crafting System: Fun. Find blueprints to modify exsisting weapons with effects like shock, fire, poison, impact, and bleeding, or a number of cominations there of. Requires components you find all over the world. DLC blueprints need some work, they often downgrade your weapons, but I'll overlook that, because 99% of them work. When you mod weapons, there is a visible effect on them by the way, which is always nice.
Customization: There are quite a few options for customization of your character's clothes as you progress through the game (you can't change his face though, so in 4 player multplayer you look like quadruplets, which is creepy, but the guy looks cool enough, and it's first person, so you really only see his hands and feet and hear his voice). Currently, there are 3 outfits you can get from DLC's, including a secret agent and a ninja (with the Ninja being *deep breath* FREAKING AMAZING!). You get a quite a few outfits during the story, and they get cooler as you get them.
Gameplay: Incredible. Really shines in at least 2 player multiplayer, and 4 players is super fun. You can chop off their legs, bash in their skull with your rebar hammer, or grab their neck and slam their ugly face into it. Cool environmental ways of killing zombies, such as grappling them into eachother then throwing a molotov on the pile, or kicking them in the♥♥♥♥♥♥straight off a building. (PS, grapple throwing zombies off of the freeway is soooo satisfying.)
Mob Variety: Mobs extremly varied. Here's a list:
Infected, or Biters (they've been "dead" for awhile, your average zombie),
Bomber (they kinda explode, pick them off first, they can one shot you if they get too close),
Virals (recently turned, very very fast, spawn from noise, and also sometimes speak to you, begging for mercy as they go beserk and try to eat your face),
Gastanks (Guys in hazmat suits that have a gas tank on their back which can be shot at for a noisily efficent form of killing groups of zombies)
(There are also Suiciders, hazmat guys that only spawn at night which charge you and explode when they get to you, like bombers, but harder to kill. Pain. In. The. Rear.)
Goon (really buff slow swinging hammer wielding death zombies... of doom.)
Demolisher (basically a goon, but only seen at higher levels, and has super fists instead of a hammer. Charges you, punches you, throws nearby cars and other big heavy stuff at you, take a lot of damage to kill. have a helmet and armor you have to beat off before you can reliably damage him.)
Volatile (only show up at night, super strong, agile, and really friggen mean.)
Toads (spitters, they don't move away from where they stand unless trying to avoid getting smacked by your crowbar)
Bolters (only spawn at night, do not attack, get scared if they realize they have been seen, spawn in certain marked locations, drop valuable resources for crafting high end gear, usually surrond themselves with less friendly zombies,)
That's about it. The big guys can sometimes be lured into nailing their buddies too.
Leveling System: You have 3 differnet skill trees (Agility, Power, and Survival), each of which level, you get a point for the one that levels when it levels, you spend the point in it's tree, eventually you level enough to have all the skills, just a matter of the order you want to get them in.
Day Night Cycle: Day/Night is very real and very deadly. Don't be fooled by other posts saying "why there no day night cycle?". They clearly didn't finish the tutorial. There is no day night during the first two missions, because you are still learning to play, and night time is very difficult to not die during (death is rather inconsequenstial however, at least by end game. Death makes you lose survival xp, which is gained from quests and surviving nights. But once max survival xp, which happens before you finish the story if you do all quests, you don't lose anything other than current location from death.) Night is when crazy monsters come out, running around outside at night gives 2x xp bonus. Safe Houses let you sleep to make night pass safely. You gotta clear them first.
Parkour: Really Fun, Really Simple. I play Mouse and Keyboard for this game, so to parkour, you just run up next to something climbable, and press spacebar. There are tons of skills to get that let you do parkour faster, and do new moves to help you climb easier (if you can get the skill Tic Tac, GET IT!!! Why? Because... OMG!!!) Or fall more betterer (because you want to fall as besterest as you can!).
Air Drops? Yes.
Dismemberment? Yes.
Scary/Creepy? Lets just say (SPOILER ALERT) that I saw a zombie baby... yeah...
Multiplayer? Yes.
Can I be a Zombie? Yeah. A mean one too.
Fun? Heck Yes!
Should you buy it? Yeah, you should.

Risk of Rain is a highly addictive game of endurance, like most games of the rogue-lite genre it becomes increasingly difficult the more you play, ultimately the goal is to see how long you can survive. each playthrough feels different thanks to the wide variety of passive and active items you can get, these aren't little boosts either they will make or break you. Some plays will have you a bit salty but others overjoyed by the combo of boosts you get.
You start out with one class but there are a handfull of others to unlock and each has a wholly unique playstyle. Some favor run and gun tactics while others focus on keeping distance between the player and the enemy. Each class has 4 skills one is a basic attack with no cooldown while the three others vary more, the commando (starting class) has a dodge roll, a piercing shot and a rapid fire attack that stuns but the bandit class gets a dynamite stick, a powerful shot that lowers cooldown times if you kill an enemy with it and an invisibility period where enemies won't attack. There is a lot of fun to be had in experimenting with each class to find out how it's best used.
Visually the game has a pleasing pixel art style and is accompanied by the amazing music of Chris Christodoulou (also made the music for Deadbolt another game worth looking at)
If you want a game you can constantly come back to and enjoy a good challenge give this game a try!

Short-Description:
A good game about balancing income and outcome of resources.
These resources are consumed or produced by each block, even those that seem to be not that important in other games.
For example Grass is not simply grass to look nice, but also needs water but at the same time produces fresh air and space to relax.
This applies to every block in the game, of which there are quite many.
What i miss are alternative types of the same block, for cosmetic reasons. Like having a grass tile that has some snow on it, or a lightpoleplaza with different types of floor (concrete, grass, plaza, runway).
Thats not a big problem, but would give more freedom in really creating a Block'hood you like.
Positive Aspects:
The music is awesome, as far as i know piano tracks only. You can hear examples in the trailers above.
The gameplay and its complexity is really good and sets the game somewhere between a puzzle game and a build-up management simulation. What i like most about it, is that you can create what you like.
You want to produce a negative ecosystem with powerplants, oildrills and generators, you are free to do that. You want a natural habitat with as few humans possible, or maybe even only wildlife, you can do that.
Or a mix of all of that or even do several themed block'hoods (i for example created a block which dealt with workforce, oilproduction and energyproduction, aswell as fishing, all at a beach. In another i built a big hotel with a park and the nessecary stuff to keep it running.).
I would say, its somewhat like the game Reus.
Very much so, only that you have more freedom and dont need research to get things running.
It also throws a nice mode into the mix that is literally SimCity 4.
You can play Sandbox mode and create a world with different attributes, like how much water, how deep water, have preset biomes (want more tundra-, or desert- or woodtiles?). Then you can select an area and set it as a "hood".
You can make it smaller or bigger.
Then you can choose that created "sector" and start building your blocks there.
Each sector is connected to the worldmap and therefor to all the other sectors you will create and play on.
You can then import and export resources from each sector (hood).
Which is literally the exact same thing SimCity 4 presented and which i liked most about the game.
With that mode, Block'hood receives a relly good and "unique" gamemode that adds to the scale of the game and give even more freedom to not only create a "Hood" in one level and be done with it, but create a whole worldmap with different connected levels.
Neutral Aspects:
Graphically its ok, textures and models are blank colours, but it looks good that way and not somewhat weird or even cheap. More like a good looking,w ell resoluted game of lego.
What i miss a bit though, is a meta game feature connecting all of that and giving the player a purpose to why he/she is doing all of this or even would try and get specific resources.
The polishing of the game is a weird topic though.
(Kind of) Negative Aspects:
On one hand it feels very polished, the menu is nicely done, you can pick from several languages, it has tutorial mode, story mode, sandbox and challenge mode, the options are there and overall it looks and feels "high quality".
The gameplay sometimes feels not up to par with the presentation though.
Not because its bad, but because there are some questions that come up while playing, mostly UI related. Which lets it look inconsistent in quality.
For example, as each block has an input and an output of resources, it is nessecary to find blocks related to each other in the build panel.
The sheer amount of blocks available to the player make this a mess and given that many blocks look somewhat similar its a challenge to find what you need.
To make it clearer, the following situation:
I had the block "Amphitheatre" available to place.
But one resource that serves as input are "artists".
Now i have to find a building/block that is producing artists, so i can generate them to serve the amphitheatre.
To get some help, you can click on the resource, in a resource panel which shows you the actual total income and outcome of each resource, so the game highlights blocks on the buildpanel that either produce or consume the clicked resource.
Problem A: it doesnt filter them so you still have to go through each individual window and look close for the symbols that indicate their relation
and problem B: this is only possible for a resource that is already in use.
Meaning, when i am currently not producing any artists, i cant click this resource (artists) to highlight all blocktypes that are related to this resource.
Which means, i have to first go through the dozens of blocktypes to find one that is related to artists, instead of giving me just the resourcepanel with all resources listed and have me filtering the buildingpanel by resources whenever i want.
Thats one example where the game somehow starts doing something useful (highlighting the buildings related to the resource), but stops at really utilizing this feature properly and with enough thought.
Playing the game for an hour will at one point smash your head against this problem(wall), so it should have been noticed and "fixed".
Resumée:
I hope to see future patches to adress the controls and UI problems.
Apart from that, its really enjoyable and provides enough challenge, freedom and sandboxing to fill hours of play.
Its very well worth the price i think, im even stunned to see it being sold that low.
About the topic of it being out of early access:
I think it should have stayed longer in early access.
In fact i was quite shocked when i heard it will release in 3 days.
I visited the forums a week before the announcement and had a thought of it needing at least another year to be finished properly and maybe also get another feature or two.
This doesnt mean it isnt somewhat ready.
Its a well working game, enough content is there and the whole gameplay loop makes sense and doesnt feel rushed out.
But it also kind of missed opportunities to polish at named places and also to maybe introduce some more features to reach full potential.
As i think it has enough possibilities to be expanded. Maybe with DLC later down the line.
Or with a sequel that might go for multiplayer aswell (sharing the world map feature would be cool, adding possibilities of trade and maybe sabotage to the mix).
Buy it when you are interested in a build-up management and puzzle game about economy, ecology and symbiosis, feeling different but similar to games like Reus and Sim City.
Especially when you are like me and searching for a fresh new mix in these genres, apart from the established games, this title is very welcomed.

By the end of this game I was honestly sad I finished it. When I first began playing I had very mixed feelings about the game. The first half of the game had me feeling very isolated (especially the section of the game where you are mostly just driving along the coast) and made the story feel very slow to progress. Once I got to the second half of the game I was immediately hooked. The game is probably one the most polished games I've ever played. Everything works perfectly.
The story is very interesting. It always had wanting to know more.
The game also had a very nice atmosphere. The world has a similar feeling to that of Orwell's 1984. Very bleak and depressing, dystopian enviorment but also filled with an array of interesting characters.
I don't really have any complaints about the game and would honestly say it has one of the best stories I've ever heard. Now i finally understand why people want a Half Life 3 so badly.

Ps. If anyone is playing this game for the first time, make sure to check out Half Life 2: Episode 1 and 2 as well. They are also very good.

Super Hexagon is a game about recognising and reacting to different visual patterns under stress. It is also one of the greatest games ever made. My grade: 10 out of 10.
That was the short review. It is surprising how much can be written about a game so simple. Simplicity is in fact one of its strengths. It has been compared to Dark Souls for a good reason. Both games require you to learn various visual cues and then force you to react to them under duress. Super Hexagon is special because it implements that concept and leaves only the bare essence, the design of the game is pure, there is nothing superfluous. That is a plus, because it makes the player confront how he plays the game. Super Hexagon in unique, because in order to excel the player must get to know himself.
I didn't always think that. In fact, after I first played Super Hexagon for about 15 minutes, I came to some depressing conclusions:
1. I would never be good at the game. Some skills and things in life are beyond me.
2. I would have to put in an immense effort to be merely average.
3. The game requires you to suffer from insane amount of stress, nobody needs that in their lives.
I was obviously wrong. I'll probably continue with the review at a later date.

Mirror's Edge came out what seems like forever ago. No one seemed to care. I was hyped up like a junkie who just got a sack of coke the size of the average purse. It took me a long long time to get my hands on a copy but when I did I was even more eager to pop it into my Xbox and play. When I did I was more than satisfied. All my waiting was well worth it.
Eventually I lost my copy and re-bought it here on Steam. I'm no master, nor am I very good, but I can get my way around pretty well. The more effective you are at the controls and timing the better the gameplay is. Mirror's Edge is focused around the flow of movements to get you from point A to point Q as fast and as efficient as you possibly can. Jumping, climbing, sliding, ducking, scrambling, etc, over, under, around, on, and sometimes even through, objects in your way to get to your objective.
The game not only looks grand but it showcases a nice little story. If you took the time to watch and listen to the animated trailer that Steam probably auto played, you'll know that Faith is on a quest to find her sister and bring whoever brought this upon them to justice. No matter the means to get to the end. Along the way you'll encounter police and people who you're never sure if you can trust.
The story is told through animated cutscenes that are marvelous to watch as they flow beautifully with out outlines. You jump in and out of buildings and sprint across rooftops for hours. The game makes an excellent use of feeling frail and weak, while still allowing the player to feel powerful. This is presented through the combat in the game.
You will frequently be confronted with heavily armed and armored policemen sent to kill you. You can often times choose to avoid them entirely or take action. You have three ways of stopping them. 1. Physical attacks such as punches, kicks and even nut shots. 2. Disarm and arm your self. 3. Disarm and go crazy with a gun.
Mirror's Edge will frequently stop the player to showcase mind bending puzzles that force you to find "a new perspective on how to get from A to B." The puzzles only grow more complex and even more rewarding. When you can figure them out for your self you feel wonderful because you managed to think like a runner. Which is really the whole point of the game. Be able to flow through it as efficiently as you can.
There are a few chases where you try and out run or keep up with people via parkour and finding alternative routes. After multiple hours of game time you'll find your self running paths you never noticed before. Climbing and jumping and disarming and shooting people so quickly.
Once you feel you've become well acquainted with the controls Mirror's Edge offers you a new mode to test your skills. Speedrun and Time Trial modes are a nice feature. Time Trial has you running to beat a ghost and running to beat your own ghost. Can you out parkour your own parkour? Give it a try. The Speedrun mode has you running against the clock trying to beat the par time and set a new record.
The game has rewarding combat and rewards the player for skill and precision. The story is pretty nice with a great pay off and the difficulty curb isn't too sharp a climb too fast. If you don't love it by 2 hours in there's something wrong.

As a single player game Dying Lights atmospheric tension and challenges are just what you would want from a survival horror game. The squalid and zombie infested environment of Dying Lights Harran somehow manages to retain a certain beauty and the  wonderfully crafted world draws you in making you want to explore every inch. The combat, weapon systems and movement are  beautifully balanced to offer players a challenge without being too tricky to master with a little practice. The night and day cycles require different approaches as night sees a clear advantage swing to the zombies. This game is more about being a  savvy player rather than all out hack and slash or bravely running away as both elements will be required equally, along with a healthy dose of stealth and cunning depending on the situation. There is plenty to keep you busy too with over 50 hours of game play. For the best experience set your gamma up correctly and play in the dark with headphones, it really ramps up the  tension and immerses you deeper into the game.
As with most games these days you get a bevy of unlockable skills which you will soon come to rely as you progress and wish you had from the start. However the best tool by far is the grappling hook as it makes moving across the map and escaping the undead really flow. Unfortunately, you will need to put in at least 10 hours of game play before you unlock it.
This is my review proper, the coop play of Dying Light and where my opinion seems to differ widely from everyone else. I will  say it now, I am not a fan of the co-op in this game. While some elements work others don't and at times it is more multiplayer PVP than it is coop. I increasingly found co-op annoying and more of a hindrance and an intrusion rather than a help. It's far from bad and it has its place, but, for the most part it is not what I would call true co-op play.
Dying Light supports drop-in/ drop-out co-op for up to four players. The entire campaign is playable in co-op, and there are special co-op challenges.
Okay so you got me on this, (with the exception of "Be The Zombie" element which I will come to shortly) co-op combat is actually that as you can't fight each other and can work together killing zombies. However, this brings me to my main problem in co-op combat, it's too easy. Enemies do not scale with the amount of players and it rapidly changes the game of survival horror to hack and slash zombie clearance.
The introduction of "Be the Zombie" is great if what you want a PVP multi-player combat element. It can be hilarious if you are playing with a few friends. However, the intrusion of random players in your game can be frustrating, even when they are not being the zombie and on your side there are some real idiots out there. Go afk for a second or start playing with your menus, etc., and before you know it your dead. I found this element novel at first, but it soon gets old and you find yourself in the menu system opting out of this. "Be the Zombie" is  definitely not a co-op element, but is a multiplayer PVP element.
Dying Light was built with co-op in mind and Mission progress is saved across all players’ games, which can cause problems  when joining a session which has progressed further down the story. This is most notable if you have a group of friends who regularly play and some of you play more often than others. Some of you can lose out on blocks of Story mode and associated  achievements.
Again, these can be fun, especially when playing with a group of close friends, however, they have absolutely nothing to do with co-op play and are purely PVP and yet bizarrely are only available in co-op play. It makes no sense and they break the flow and tension of the game and soon get very annoying. For me co-op play is all about working together and helping each other and these challenges force you into PVP events that I do not want in my co-op experience.
Anytime a dynamic drop hits the map all players get to raid the cache of medicine and supplies. True to its co-op claim,  friends can help a downed ally and all the loot you find is unique to each player so there is no squabbling over drops so this works well.
Character customization options are poor, so don’t expect to be able to play specific roles or even tell each other apart during the early stages of the game.
The lack of a local co-op option is a real surprise as this game would be well suited to a local co-op play between people in the same room playing on split screen. Ideal for keeping the older kids busy or killing some time with your partner etc. But alas, no such option exists.

.

An in-depth role playing game for people who love D&D.
Many RPG's have an open world, but Divinity: Original Sin is one of the few that don't tell you where to go. While it does have a quest log, it acts as an extensive journal of the progress you've already made in quests rather than telling you what to do next. You will never see a quest marker on your map, though you can place markers yourself. When you read a book and unlock a crafting recipe, it doesn't just record the ingredients either; it records the whole book into your journal. You'll actually have to read it yourself.
NPC interaction for the most part feels very alive. Most of them are named, and even the ones that aren't have unique dialogue. You can also open the trading window for any NPC, not just vendors. Though their inventory changes as time passes, the have a limited inventory of both items and gold. If you sell all your items to one person and take all the gold they have, you'll either have to wait until they get more gold or find someone else to sell to. Often, it's easier just to trade goods for other goods. You can also pickpocket or kill any NPC; there are no "essential characters." Stealing only has consequences if you are seen doing it. There is no morale system, but you can get bad reputation if rumors spread that you are killing innocent people.
Combat in Divinity can be very rewarding, but its lack of forgiveness can cause a huge difficulty spike to those who have no idea how elements in the environment can affect the battle. When you enter combat, the game will change from real-time to turn based rules similar to D&D. Enemies you encounter will take every advantage they can, especially enemy archers and casters. Enemies also don't re-spawn, which means that every encounter is unique. It also makes you feel less guilty about using consumables in a non-boss fight. Spells and specialty consumable arrows dominate the battlefield, as well as environmental hazards (almost all of which you can create). You can also perform any action in combat that you would be able to do out of combat (and vice-versa), as long as you have the action points to do it that turn.
Characters are very customizable. You start with two characters, first choosing a class, then editing that class to have any starting stats and abilities you want. The class you choose will decide your starting equipment, but other than that you are free to change the allocations entirely. You can later recruit two more party members within the campaign. At low levels, melee can seem underwhelming when the base spell damage is so high, but after a few levels, one-handed users will start to become tanks that can block every other attack, two-handed users will start to two-shot enemies, and rogue types characters will be able to back-stab numerous times per turn, usually with the ability to escape unharmed or turn invisible.
Each character in your party is completely independent. They have their own inventory, personality, and reputations with the NPCs. In single player, you control all of them and can make them follow you, or you can separate them. There is no limit on how far apart they can be. This translates very well in multiplayer, where the each player controls their own character and may do whatever they wish in the world (even attacking the other player). One player can be in turn-based combat while the other player is walking around town in real time. You can also make your in-game characters disagree with each other. If you have four party members, you can have four human players. It's drop-in-drop-out, making it very easy to jump into a game.
The story starts very basic: You are "Source Hunters," special agents who work to eliminate a powerful and evil magic called Source from the world, summoned to investigate a murder in which Source magic was suspected to have been used. Your backgrounds are left ambiguous. As you investigate and explore the city and the surrounding area, the plot takes many unexpected turns, even connecting with several side quests and branching off into more than one overarching plot. It comes off as very well thought out and planned.
Divinity: Original Sin is an unforgiving, but rewarding game that brings meaning back to the word "Roleplaying." This is not Skyrim or Diablo, and it doesn't try to be. If you love D&D, strategy games, and/or games that use traditional RPG rulesets, this is for you.

Original Sin makes me feel like I've gone back to the glory days of dicking around with a crazy old computer game that was made by fanatical autists. Risk of Rain is a highly addictive game of endurance, like most games of the rogue-lite genre it becomes increasingly difficult the more you play, ultimately the goal is to see how long you can survive. each playthrough feels different thanks to the wide variety of passive and active items you can get, these aren't little boosts either they will make or break you. Some plays will have you a bit salty but others overjoyed by the combo of boosts you get.
You start out with one class but there are a handfull of others to unlock and each has a wholly unique playstyle. Some favor run and gun tactics while others focus on keeping distance between the player and the enemy. Each class has 4 skills one is a basic attack with no cooldown while the three others vary more, the commando (starting class) has a dodge roll, a piercing shot and a rapid fire attack that stuns but the bandit class gets a dynamite stick, a powerful shot that lowers cooldown times if you kill an enemy with it and an invisibility period where enemies won't attack. There is a lot of fun to be had in experimenting with each class to find out how it's best used.
Visually the game has a pleasing pixel art style and is accompanied by the amazing music of Chris Christodoulou (also made the music for Deadbolt another game worth looking at)
If you want a game you can constantly come back to and enjoy a good challenge give this game a try!

Civ 5 is a board game of sorts were you pick a character of a great civilization and grow from there ending the game in several endings rangeing from domination to science. how you play will determine what others think of you for instance if you are a warmongerer people will likey not support you and are much more likely to rally against you the game is quick and the movments between the units are amazing, however that being said i do feel like the best way to play this game is with the brave new world DLC, so if you do want to try this game you sort of have to buy that to get the maximum experiance heres some of my pros and cons for the game

Progression, as you level up your civ you get more advanced units that help you get an edge these units do truly feel powerful if you have the more advanced army which i think they did amazing on.

SUPPORTS MODS, which means you can have limitless fun with the communitys creations unfortunalty most of  them require you to have DLC's

AI's don't declear war nearly as offten as they should

All in all i love Civ 5 it is most certainly worth the asking price and really its worth the DLC to specifically Brave new world, i don't have the DLC on this account but i played it on my friends it is a must and it adds so much fun stuff to it like spies, truly a staple game that i reccomend for those who love stratigy. 9/10

Strangely addicting, FTL is a fun game that makes a lot out of a little.  The graphics are not fancy, but that quickly disappears when you really get into the game.  The premise is simple: get to the Federation with your secret data without being destroyed.  Death is permanent.  When you die (and you will, often) you don't go back to the last save.  You go all the way back to the beginning.  Space can be brutal.  However, play through again...and again.  While you had previously been ripped apart in level 2, you now get to level six every time.  You pick up crew and lose them.  You choose weapons as you come upon them and each battle has the opportunity to be your last.  For the price, it is certainly worth a buy.  I have found it oddly addicting and, of course, it plays on any old Mac or PC.  A solid recommendation to buy if you like the thinking man's space shooter.

One of the most engrossing Tac/Strat Rpg's ever!  Think Orgeon Trail meets XCOM (or FF tactics) The Banner Saga features an interesting new twist on Tac/Strat, with tough decision making and unique army/resource management.  You never know when something around the corner will challenge your ragtag party of warriors and misfits.  The story takes many twists and turns, characters die, and heroes will fall.  Careful planning is required before each challenging battle.  The AI is smart, and will challenge you.  Troop manamgement is fun and balanced, and each upgrade feels important into keeping your band of heroes alive.
A stunning and gorgeous score from Austin Wintory (Journey, Monaco) accompanies your excellent and challenging adventure throughout this Norse inspired story.  The art direction is abosultey fantastic; a heavy fantasy feel is combined with a unqiue storybook vibe along with Disney style animation.
The Banner Saga is truly engrossing.  Hours fly by as you try and last one more day on the road, battles keep you on your toes and the story is very well told and features tough decision after tough decision.  I can't recommend it enough!

You begin the game as a lone, perfect triangle, the last of your kind. You soon discover that you're not the only being in this universe as you are quickly rushed by hoards of irregular shapes, jealous of your perfection. You have been granted with powers of lateral movement, which you can use to inverse-circle strafe. You have no weapons - Fortunately, these irregular shaped beings are not too bright; with a well timed side-step, they'll rush themselves into the void and be obliterated.
This might seem very straightforward, but the universe itself plots against you - warping and spinning the landscape to disorientate the player.
You are not completely alone, however, as a narrator/companion helps you on your way. When you reach certain goals, she grants you various morale boosts. She will let you know when you've achieved your goal, but also gently lets you down when you fail. If you're up for a challenge - you can play for 120s through and unlock the secret dialogue with her.
Upon completion of the game, the universe concedes defeat and no longer pulls its landscape-changing stunts. However, the hoards are ever present, allowing you to play on after finishing the main quest.
Features:
*Six unique universes
*Impeccable naration
*Outstanding soundtrack
*Lots of nice colours

As a father, it's hard to find games where I can literally stop at any point for a given period of time.  I've recently started getting into tactical turn-based-strategy games, and XCOM:EU was a great addition to my collection.  I loved the complexity of the game (do I purchase new troops, research the next greatest technology, or manufacture better weapons for the next mission?)  I also love the fact that deep down, I'm a closet reloader (I make a save point, and when things go wrong, I reload), and the game allows me several options that punish me for that.  The game allows for only one single save, or randomizes enemy attacks each time you reload.  While the game gets easier as your troops progress and get stronger, the missions also get longer, which allow for an increased likelihood that your favorite soldier gets the axe.  Is it worth it to replay a 45 minute level just to keep your soldier?  These are all of the things you must think about when you play XCOM:EU.

The Banner Saga is definitely in the top tier of games that have been Kickstarted. It has a very deep, involved plot from multiple perspectives and is filled with surprising revelations and heart-wrenching endings.
The graphics are a refreshing departure from the norm. The conversation scenes are reminiscent of Fire Emblem's static conversation scenes, while the travel and cut scenes are truly beautiful. The animations during battle are enjoyable to watch, as your character pulls off such a powerful hit and damages nearby enemies as well, or when your archer nails an enemy from across the map after their careful aiming.
The music in this game is just beyond words. Austin Wintory does an exceptional job on the soundtrack. The audio cues seem to hit at just the right moment to strike a chord of fear into you, or even to set the mood for celebration or sorrow. It's not often that the audio of a game ends up being my favorite part, but The Banner Saga really delivered.
The story is very involved and changes based on the decisions you make as you go along. This means that I'll be completing several more playthroughs before I'm done with the game. The choices can really reward you, or even end up in a death if you're not careful. I haven't gotten more involved in the wellbeing of a game's characters in quite some time, though in this game I find myself desperately trying to make the best choices so they can be happy, or even survive!
The combat, though it lacks variation, reminds me a bit of chess. It would benefit greatly from anything that could introduce deviation from the repetitive battles (though some specific battles can be exciting and different). My favorite point of the difficulties though, is that if you choose to play on Easy mode, you can play through the entire story without having to worry about battles, as some can be even skipped! If you choose to play on Hard mode, it is ACTUALLY a challenge. This is a nice change from "hard" modes on games lately not actually challenging their users.
This game is worth the full price, and more. I look forward to any sequels that come out from Stoic.

What a game! I bought this when it first came out, and I would find any moment I can to play it. It's very addicting.
I've played this game first, then the original following and enjoyed them both tremendously.
There is definately a lot of strategy involved in this game, think chess with weapons. It's fun changing your soldiers and naming them after your friends or loved ones. It definately creates great stories to tell your friends what their virtual counterpart has accomplished in the war to save earth, or how they fell bravely in battle.
Gameplay is easy to pick up, once you learn the basics, you'll soon be hitting keystrokes and having everything you want happen onscreen without having to look at the keyboard. Difficulty can be quite unforgiving. For those looking for a more casual encounter, you can definately lower the difficulty level and even "load" old game saves if you screw up a battle.
Basically, this game caters to the casual and hardcore.
Graphics are nice and simple. There aren't any amazing graphical achievments here, but this game isn't about that. It is kinda cool building your underground base and you get to see a cut view of it all. Seeing aliens die in slow motion is always satisfying. And speaking of slow motion...
Sometimes the game tries to get "cinematic" and would zoom in close to any character making a kill... sometimes the camera picks a location where say, a wall, or mailbox, or car is in the way, and all you see is a zoomed up texure, hear gunfire, and an alien die. Kinda breaks the mood sometimes, but it's a minor flaw.
Multiplayer, well, kinda sucks imo. I played with a friend and its fun killing each other, but I wish there was some kind of co-op, he brings his men, I bring mine and we have a common goal.
REPLAY VALUE: SUPER HIGH
Here and there i'll find myself playing this game, this seems to be my fallback game when there is a lull in things to play. Very reliable. I absolutely approve of this game!

Eh, Pongo is an okay game, but I wouldn't recommend it to others.
Pongo is basically a game that consists of 50 levels where simply put, "Get from point A to point B." Some of the levels can be challenging, others can be really easy, but most of all, they also have monsters you have to deal with. If you're planning to 100% this game, then completing the levels would take you a couple of hours at the most, depending on what pace you're taking.
Generally, most, if not all levels take place in the middle of an ocean, containing a lot of islands. You as a player has a pogostick and you use that to manuever through obstacles and get to the other islands in order to get to point B. You also can have another option to switch out your pogostick to a "gun" used to take out the monsters that get in your way.
Since you're in the middle of the ocean, you can fall and drown in the water so you can expect to die like this when you failed a level. You can also die by the monsters, but you get multiple chances based on what difficulty setting you are in. If you die during a level, you go back to the beginning of the level and there are no checkpoints so you only have one shot.
In easy mode, you get three lives which affects how many hits the monsters can hit you and you
which basically means you can still move around while in the air.
In hard mode, you only have one life so you can't let any of the monsters hit you and you
which means that you can only move in one direction continuously while in the air. This is only for players who want a bit more of a challenge.
But it doesn't really matter what mode you take as you don't get any achievements regarding these modes anyway.
They don't seem very interesting and it feels the same every level you complete and they don't feel different whatsoever. The textures are plain and very boring to look at. Some of the levels get very repetitive and you will be bored playing this if you're not planning to get the achievements.
I always hear this kind of music on Youtube, especially ones by Kevin Macleod. There should be more custom, creative music for this game to make it more unique, rather than putting in royalty-free music since to me they don't really make sense when putting it in a game like this.
Oh and I forgot to mention that there are badges and trading cards, so you can "play" this game for the trading cards and you don't have to play it again.
If you're looking for a cheap game, wanting to craft badges from the trading cards, or just wanting to play the game for more easy achievements, then yes. Otherwise, don't get this game.

1. Early Access. Now it's a demo version of the rogue-like game that lasts less than one hour.

Also, if you read reviews saying "They said there was a Day/Night cycle, but it's always sunny!" and "Why can't I turn off the Film Grain Effect?!" Those were misinformed reviews. The Day/Night cycle doesn't start until you finish the tutorial, which happens at the same time multiplayer is unlocked (you have to do like 2 missions before you can play the other zillion with your friends). Also, The Film Grain Effect stuff has been PATCHED, so you can turn it off now, which I was quite pleased about myself.
Anyways, here's my review:
Dying Light is an excellent zombie survival game from the developers behind Shadows of Mordor and Dead Island (the game feels like both of those mixed together, along with 3 grams of awesome salt).
Crafting System: Fun. Find blueprints to modify exsisting weapons with effects like shock, fire, poison, impact, and bleeding, or a number of cominations there of. Requires components you find all over the world. DLC blueprints need some work, they often downgrade your weapons, but I'll overlook that, because 99% of them work. When you mod weapons, there is a visible effect on them by the way, which is always nice.
Customization: There are quite a few options for customization of your character's clothes as you progress through the game (you can't change his face though, so in 4 player multplayer you look like quadruplets, which is creepy, but the guy looks cool enough, and it's first person, so you really only see his hands and feet and hear his voice). Currently, there are 3 outfits you can get from DLC's, including a secret agent and a ninja (with the Ninja being *deep breath* FREAKING AMAZING!). You get a quite a few outfits during the story, and they get cooler as you get them.
Gameplay: Incredible. Really shines in at least 2 player multiplayer, and 4 players is super fun. You can chop off their legs, bash in their skull with your rebar hammer, or grab their neck and slam their ugly face into it. Cool environmental ways of killing zombies, such as grappling them into eachother then throwing a molotov on the pile, or kicking them in the♥♥♥♥♥♥straight off a building. (PS, grapple throwing zombies off of the freeway is soooo satisfying.)
Mob Variety: Mobs extremly varied. Here's a list:
Infected, or Biters (they've been "dead" for awhile, your average zombie),
Bomber (they kinda explode, pick them off first, they can one shot you if they get too close),
Virals (recently turned, very very fast, spawn from noise, and also sometimes speak to you, begging for mercy as they go beserk and try to eat your face),
Gastanks (Guys in hazmat suits that have a gas tank on their back which can be shot at for a noisily efficent form of killing groups of zombies)
(There are also Suiciders, hazmat guys that only spawn at night which charge you and explode when they get to you, like bombers, but harder to kill. Pain. In. The. Rear.)
Goon (really buff slow swinging hammer wielding death zombies... of doom.)
Demolisher (basically a goon, but only seen at higher levels, and has super fists instead of a hammer. Charges you, punches you, throws nearby cars and other big heavy stuff at you, take a lot of damage to kill. have a helmet and armor you have to beat off before you can reliably damage him.)
Volatile (only show up at night, super strong, agile, and really friggen mean.)
Toads (spitters, they don't move away from where they stand unless trying to avoid getting smacked by your crowbar)
Bolters (only spawn at night, do not attack, get scared if they realize they have been seen, spawn in certain marked locations, drop valuable resources for crafting high end gear, usually surrond themselves with less friendly zombies,)
That's about it. The big guys can sometimes be lured into nailing their buddies too.
Leveling System: You have 3 differnet skill trees (Agility, Power, and Survival), each of which level, you get a point for the one that levels when it levels, you spend the point in it's tree, eventually you level enough to have all the skills, just a matter of the order you want to get them in.
Day Night Cycle: Day/Night is very real and very deadly. Don't be fooled by other posts saying "why there no day night cycle?". They clearly didn't finish the tutorial. There is no day night during the first two missions, because you are still learning to play, and night time is very difficult to not die during (death is rather inconsequenstial however, at least by end game. Death makes you lose survival xp, which is gained from quests and surviving nights. But once max survival xp, which happens before you finish the story if you do all quests, you don't lose anything other than current location from death.) Night is when crazy monsters come out, running around outside at night gives 2x xp bonus. Safe Houses let you sleep to make night pass safely. You gotta clear them first.
Parkour: Really Fun, Really Simple. I play Mouse and Keyboard for this game, so to parkour, you just run up next to something climbable, and press spacebar. There are tons of skills to get that let you do parkour faster, and do new moves to help you climb easier (if you can get the skill Tic Tac, GET IT!!! Why? Because... OMG!!!) Or fall more betterer (because you want to fall as besterest as you can!).
Air Drops? Yes.
Dismemberment? Yes.
Scary/Creepy? Lets just say (SPOILER ALERT) that I saw a zombie baby... yeah...
Multiplayer? Yes.
Can I be a Zombie? Yeah. A mean one too.
Fun? Heck Yes!
Should you buy it? Yeah, you should.

I am a big fan of the original Half Life. I've beaten the game several times. It is one of my personal favorites. Now its sequels (Half Life 2, EP.1 and EP.2) are included among my favorite titles.
I really liked the episodes as well. They were too short though. The creators announced that in fact the three episodes (With the third one not released at this point) are just one long game. Of course that brings many negative aspects. For instance if you want to play all three of them, you may want to install them simultaneously, resulting in some big portion of your memory being occupied. But there will be plenty of time to talk about these games. Let's focus on this title for now.
This sequel had a lot of work. It had to surpass the original game. Half Life was a unique game. It has an amazing story, great characters, and was really entertaining. It also had a certain kind of "magic". It became a classic almost instantly. Its second installment kept a lot of the great details that made the original so good and improved them with other features that helped to create an immersing gaming experience. Half Life 2 is as good as the original.
The old characters returned, but with better skins. Some new and interesting characters are introduced. There new and cool enemies (Whose A.I. is good). The graphic detail is incredible. The water effect is by far the best I've ever seen in a game. They took a lot of time polishing this features and it shows. The only negative thing I can say is that this title is shorter than the original.
The plot is great also. It is almost too linear though. We now follow the adventure several years after the events of the first game. The population is being enslaved and is our duty to help them before annihilation. To make the game even more appealing, the creators added the spectacular gravity gun, which is an extraordinary weapon (Well, not a weapon per se). It has the power to lift heavy objects and neutralize their weight. This weapon is almost as important as the characters. We wouldn't be able to solve some of the most interesting physics puzzles without it, and is extremely fun to use. And I almost forgot, the physics are great.
It was extremely difficult to reach the first Half Life game in terms of quality, but I think that this game pulled it off. It has that certain "magic" also. And is highly enjoyable. I recommend this title. It might not disappoint anyone.

Let's put it this way
CPU Cores advertises that it maximises your performance by REDIRECTING processing power from all other porgrams to the one you want, and it does just that, and does it well. Say a game has a reccomended processor of duo-core 3.0 ghz, and you have a duo-core 3.2, in a normal situation you still wouldnt technically meet the reccomended specs because the cpu is busy doing other things as well, but with CPUCores, it'll MINIMIZE the intereference of other programs and dedicate as much power to your game as possible. In the same situation, if you have a duo-core 2.7, you won't meet the reccomended specs even with CPUCore, this is because IT DOESN'T MAKE YOUR PROCESSOR MORE POWERFUL, IT JUST REDIRECTS THE PROCESSING LOADS.
Personally, I have a mid-highish end laptop and I used it on Overwatch. The game normally runs at 60fps for me at medium-high settings, but if there's lots of action on the screen it usually drops to about 45fps. With CPUCores that doesn't happen (or not as much), if it does drop it's usually to 55 or so, so I can personally say it does something.
In conclusion, it will most certainly HELP your fps given the situation, but it WON'T turn your grandmas desktop into a super computer

The game plays like a casual game in most respects however it suffers from being too ramdom. You will encounter randomly generated enemies, space anomalies, rewards, shops with random gear, etc. It is possible early on in the game to encounter, without warning,  a combination of space combat in a hostile sector of space, and be unable to flee or survive it. Moderately rare, however I encountered this situation a few times in a limited number of plays so it is worth mentioning.
Gearing up your space ship with weapons and crew can be problematic due to the very occasional appearance of shops with gear that may end up being equal or inferior to what you already have. Because of this I found it extremely difficult to make any sort of deliberate progress towards being prepared for the final boss fight. A fight which causes the difficulty of the game to spike dramatically. After only a few playthroughs, I could predict my success in the boss fight once I had gotten 60-70% through the game based on the equipment I had accumulated thus far.
The heavy use of random elements and lack of balance as a result speaks to lazy game design. Simultaneous ship and crew combat can make for some frantic moments trying to manage two aspects of combat, causing a spike in difficulty. Though careful use of the pause button helps. The game offers wild swings of difficulty and is ultimately starved for meaningful options.
I think this game will appeal to players who like super simple gameplay, extreme difficulty curves (perhaps so they can call it "hardcore" gameplay), and don't mind having arbitrarily limited opptions. I can't recommend this game. In my opinion, it starts to scratch the "casual game" itch and then splashes in some enjoyable combat craziness, but then it dramatically shifts gears to the ultra tough. Design wise, this game can't decide if it should be casual or punising.

Red Crucible Firestorm is the sequel to the popular game Red Crucible 2. With it comes updated visuals, maps, guns and more!
But is it any good?
The gameplay isn't bad but isn't great at the same time, feeling just like any other FPS available on Steam. Nothing is really unique about it, the controls are the same as per usual with WASD moving your character, space to jump and the mouse to shoot/look down scopes. There are extras you can get sorted into boosts, chests & consumables. Boosts are items that increase a specific stat for a temportary amount of time. You'll most likely forget they even exist for the most part. Chests are basically Red Crucible's version of Counter Strike's cases albeit without the fancy opening animation. These chests come in 3 forms, weapon chests where you spend money to try and win a special gun, rank up chests, that are given each time your rank up and mission chests, chests given after completing certain missions. Both of the last 2 contain nothing useful at all though. Lastly we have consumables, items that are able to be used in game and "help" the player. Some consumables include medkits, airstrikes, mines and parachutes. Some of the consumables can be fun to use but once you run out of them, you most likely won't get them again unless you pay.
When Red Crucible Firestorm was announced, everyone expected it to have better graphics then Red Crucible 2. It passed that expectation but really ruined the feel of the game in the process. Red Crucible 2 played and looked like a arcade game, Red Crucible Firestorm plays like an arcade game and looks like a PS2 game. It really doesn't mix well. The guns are alright though and the look pretty good!
You would really think that with develops that have coded for several years that they would at least have a slightly good physics system. But no, in this game, you can drive straight though other vehicles, launch your vehicle into the sky and drive straight through bushes!
This game is Pay-To-Win, there honeslty is no other way to describe it. There are two currencies in the game, honors and coins. Both are able to be earned by not paying, with 15-100 honors earned by winning a game and 15 coins + 600 honor being earned by ranking up. Here's the problem, most of the "good" guns you can buy from the store cost around 300 coins or 100k honor, if you get to the max level (Level 30), you will have 450 coins, enough for a single store gun... Without including honor earned by winning matches by Level 30 you will have 18k honor, you wouldn't even be able to buy the most basic of the premium guns with that. You can also buy coins with 3k coins being $60 (Wow, what a deal -.-), the top range guns cost around 1k so enjoy your 3 new guns! Honestly, I wouldn't touch this game just because of the currency system.
Red Crucible Firestorm is far from being a great game, the graphics are meh, the gameplay is generic and the pay-to-win model just overall ruins the experience. There are so many other free-to-play FPS games on the market that are so much better that I really can't recommend this game to anyone.

Nosferatu: The Wrath of Malachi is the standout 2003 title from Idol FX, a long-defunct Swedish studio responsible for Drake of the 99 Dragons and so obscure that Wikipedia doesn't have a page on them.
Bring out your garlic and stakes, because we're going on an oldschool vampire hunt.
Nosferatu is a fast-paced action horror where you explore a series of procedurally generated castle wings under a strict time limit, with the goal being to rescue your family and friends from a malevolent Count. Every inch of the setting is drapped in early 1900's gothic horror imagery, thick stone and rickety supports hosting the bloodbath under a early film filter complete with dialogue cards. It's a premise that is far more novel than it should be, and it makes the game vastly more entertaining.
Despite being sold as a horror game, the enemies don't pose much real threat to you and you'll be mowing them down in droves. For all the vampire-slaying weaponry in this game, your best weapons are your fists and a cup of water.
As you explore to the tune of glorious violin scare-chords working in unison to become a soundtrack, you're given 15-25 minutes to rescue all the family members in a particular area and escort them to a "safe zone" located in the main courtyard.
This is where the game's problems start coming into play. The escort AI is incredibly stupid - their greatest nemesis being stairs. From t-posing to changing elevations to cartwheeling in midair while attempting to navigate them, I had to reload a save multiple times from escorts deciding that gravity is a myth and it's time to take a leap of faith.
It runs well, but there's no resolution options. In fact there's no options of any sort. This game has not been updated for modern systems in the least and the options are as barebones as the procedural generation.
Procedural generation that doesn't add an ounce of anything to the game. While it may have been beyond its time, the core game is bereft of replay value and all it changes is whether or not you'll get shafted by family members being hidden in the last possible place to look. It offers nothing over actual designed levels, the actual generated rooms means you'll be seeing the same handful of rooms a bunch of times.
Threadbare design permeates the game. The hyperfast pacing doesn't seem intentional so much as it does a result of poor balancing and easy enemies. There's few weapons, few enemies, few rooms, a small amount of bosses and it reeks of relying on some technical aspects that look good on a box over a game that seeks to entertain in every aspect.
Ultimately, Nosferatu: The Wrath of Malachi is a fun game. Being the Fist of the North Scare is genuinely entertaining and despite the drawbacks it's worth your time. But it's not worth your money if you're after dollar to hour value, you'll blast through this once and never play it again.
I can't complain too much about dollar value, I got it for free. I recommend this game, reader beware.

I'm not going to beat around the bush: This game owns. It's a conditional sort of owning, the kind where the game itself is 13 years old and rough around the edges, but if you can get past that it is a fantastic experience. Your character is meeting your family at a totally-not-creepy-at-all eastern European castle for your sister's wedding, and you arrive in the dead of night to discover the castle is a den of horrors. It's a first-person action game that moves like the Quake II/Half-Life 1 era games, so be prepared for sliding around at 40mph with your cane sword and crucifix. You'll be glad of it soon enough, because the enemies are quick and relentless and you'll need to do some sidestep dancing if you want to survive.
The big draw here is that there's a whole castle to explore to find your family members, and it's randomized with each new game. I've found the layout doesn't change too dramatically, but the locations of enemies and items (including essential items like keys) vary immensely. The first time I played, the East Wing key was sitting right out in the open for me to take, but the second time I had to delve into the cellars and wrest it from a pair of vampires. You find a wide assortment of weapons and tools with multiple uses, like stakes that can be used to pin bloodsuckers or burn as light sources. And you'll need to use them, too, because enemies in this game do not ♥♥♥♥ around.
Again, this game is 13 years old, and looks and feels the part. But as long as you can get past that there's a deep game of terrifying exploration here. The atmosphere is excellent, with dramatic lightning and some chilling musical cues. This one's definitely a stand-out.

Just want to give my early impressions.  Not a full, formal review.
The Banner Saga is a Kickstarter game and it's exactly what Kickstarter should be about: visionaries with bold ideas that probably wouldn't get funded through traditional means.  And that's exactly how TBS feels; it's a game designed by visionaries who love every bit of their craft but that leads to some issues of its own I'll address later.
First off, this is a gorgeous game.  The art style combines the clear-line character art of Ivan Bilibin with the iconic backdrops of Eyvind Earle.  Every piece of art from the intricately detailed world map to the rotoscoped animations is beautifully rendered.  The world of TBS draws heavy inspiration from Norse mythology but there's quite a bit of detail and world building when I was expecting it to be very straightforward.  While it is still a strategy game through and through, fans of RPGs will find plenty to like with the well defined characters and detailed world.
Being a strategy game, combat is at the forefront but has some niggling issues.  It's a very clean move-action system where character order is more important than arbitrary stats like speed.  Being wholly turn based, action economy is the name of the game as you're forced to dominate the battlefield through superior placement of your units.  Combat could be a bit more robust but normal difficulty is a decent challenge so far and there's "hard" for people wanting more of a challenge.  Thankfully, battles are evenly spaced between story scenes so every individual battle feels special.
Unfortunately, my biggest complaint of an otherwise fine system is the speed.  Combat moves at a lethargic pace.  There's no option to skip animations or speed combat and in a game where battles with as few as 4 enemies can take 10-15 minutes average, having a speed-up option is sorely missed.
TBS is immensely pleasurable so far and I can only hope it remains consistent to the end.  I'll update my thoughts as I go along.

Gardenarium is a pastel love song to perhaps the internet’s most beloved art form: the animated gif.
Though it’s true Gardenarium is a game, one played from the first person perspective and consequently fully explorable in real time, it is in many ways something closer resembling an organic museum, shifting and looping pieces hanging in the sky and growing from the ground around you as you journey toward the peak of Cloud 9. Walking is a necessary burden in Gardenarium, but it is the moments of stillness and quiet appreciation that make it so wondrously enthralling. Why you have found yourself in this floating garden and what you are meant to do there becomes secondary to the act of absorbing the environment around you. Geometric flowers sway and shift colors, abstract patterns hang in the sky, and the adorably unsettling populace recite epigrams and rhymes as if life could be so simple. But perhaps here, in this surreal and hypnotic greenhouse atop a cloud, it can.
There is an immediate urge among many I know to label products of the internet age as ephemeral and thematically shallow. But while many of the art forms particular to the modern era are surfacely uncomplicated, their emotional earnestness in many ways seems not a rejection of intelligent thought, but a dismissal of the notion that art must be in some way inaccessible to be deep. In this way Gardenarium’s penchant for blunt, matter of fact wit and uninhibited social commentary feels refreshingly honest. These thoughts may stem from the odd and inscrutable inhabitants of Gardenarium’s organic pastel world, but they carry enough weight in them to pull you out of the clouds and back to earth. Gardenarium is not an exercise in linguistic fortitude, but of accessibility and honesty, spoken in a style too quickly cast aside as the degeneration of literature by the next generation.
Gardenarium arrives at a time when the concept of what constitutes a game/art/literature is being redefined by the day. At this point it seems pedantic to continually qualify what have always been loose labels bestowed largely for the sake of exclusion. Whether or not Gardenarium’s 30-minute walk through a sky garden is a game is irrelevant to the experience itself, one that is both beautiful and poignant, and more emotionally honest than most games could ever hope for. Like its recursive floral installations, Gardenarium is a game I want to get lost in, watching the flowers bloom and dance as I daze into the hazy distance and enjoy the peace of constancy.

A lot can be said about Valve's Half-Life 2. In fact so much has been said that it feels redundant just talking about it. Yeah we all know the games amazing story, and the tight controls, and stunning graphics. I mean JESUS look at those graphics! But what really makes HL2 great, besides just the stuff mentioned? We know its the shining crown jewel of gaming, but do we really know why? The short of it is that the game is extremely solid on all fronts, something that truly can't be said about many games. Everything flows, in a way that AAA games still can't come close to, so much to an extent that I feel people sell Half-Life 2 short, even the people prasing it. Sure games today are made for a wider audience and they get that with shiny graphics and a more streamlined cinematic experience. The games are easier because they don't strive to highlight certain mechanics and instead focus on a wide apeal-story based narrative that can be experienced by everyone. But is that really the case? Truly think about it. HL2 doesn't need to pull you out of the world you have been experiencing in first person to show you a cutscene or have the "tutorial guy" , you never follow a map marker or preform a one button stealth takedown. Were made to think AAAs today are much better because theres more there, bigger maps, better graphics, and new toys all come with having as much cash that the companies making these games are willing to pump into them. We feel a sense of evolution that comes with the silver wraping under the christmas tree and are ready to easily consume more and more of the worlds were presented with because everything is made for that reason only. On the contrary Half-Life 2 did something more. The world is experienced by the player. The story is subtle and it only unwraps itself as you peel back the layers of the Half-Life world and see what Gordon Freeman, or you the player, has missed in the last 20 years. Half-life 2's story has a dark tone, with creative interiors and exteriors that never stray from the world being presented to you, refusing to abandon the lore of the world or dampen the experience all while flowing perfectly with gameplay and mechanics. The basics of Half-Life were run and shoot. And they sure as hell kept true to that in HL which is why the game is still so critically acclaimed. And HL2 does this but even better. Its a game truly worth of a sequel, being able to take what the predecessor had done and improving on every way while making each aspect better. The world you run and shoot in is the same world you live in. What AAA games take the time to truly accomplish the blending of the main concept of their game with every other aspect or even use it as one of their misguided selling points? The game Half-Life 2 truly speaks for itself in many ways. Once you have heard one person say it you have probably heard it all. And while we might not have listened well enough for this message to rub off on other games, the effects of HL2 will be felt by those who truly look for a reason to love it.

Strangely addicting, FTL is a fun game that makes a lot out of a little.  The graphics are not fancy, but that quickly disappears when you really get into the game.  The premise is simple: get to the Federation with your secret data without being destroyed.  Death is permanent.  When you die (and you will, often) you don't go back to the last save.  You go all the way back to the beginning.  Space can be brutal.  However, play through again...and again.  While you had previously been ripped apart in level 2, you now get to level six every time.  You pick up crew and lose them.  You choose weapons as you come upon them and each battle has the opportunity to be your last.  For the price, it is certainly worth a buy.  I have found it oddly addicting and, of course, it plays on any old Mac or PC.  A solid recommendation to buy if you like the thinking man's space shooter.

If you are a fan of strategy games this is a great addition to your library! It is a turn-based strategy with great animations. Though I have never played an XCOM game prior to this one I am a fan of it's multiple layers of strategy, not just those within combat. The player builds a base in an ant-farm style, chooses research projects, upgrades and engineers technological advances for combat units and even makes choices in diplomacy which affect resource income and reinforcements.
Pros -
- Great strategy elements.
- Various layers of choice throughout game make decisions tougher than most games.
- Combat animations.
- Level designs include, not just horizontal but, vertical elements which affect aim and probability.
- Skill trees for individual units let you customize each class. (Ex. you may have 2 assault units in your squad with different abilities).
- Customization for squad composition, base layout, research projects and tech advances.
Cons -
- Combat animations become repetetive.
- Camera catches behind objects and blocks view during animations.
- Story is present but not very in-depth.
Overall: Highly recommended to anyone who enjoys a strategic challenge.

This is a pretty decent match 3 game. Unlock other math 3 games, you match the pieces together to clear a path through to the end. It's fun if you are in to this kind of game. There are about 60 levels, and they ramp up difficulty decently, but it would have been nice for there to be more levels, or perhaps randomly generated levels. Something to keep it going longer. Still, it took me several hours to beat and I enjoyed it.
One thing that annoyed me is that every so often you have to do a "spot the difference" or "find the hidden object" game. These just annoyed me, and I really don't think they needed to be included. Luckily they have a hint button so if you don't care about these you can get through them quickly.
As for the graphics, it's about as you would expect from this kind of game. Colored gems representing the elements. The theme is kind of boring as it is just generic fantasy. You have a little fairy to give you tutorials throughout the game. Still, match 3 doesn't lend itself to having great themes. Gems, candies, what have you, is what people go for. It works. There is just nothing theme wise that stands out.
Anyway, while not an absolute must have, if you like games of this ilk, might as well give it a try if you see it on sale.

I think it's time to update this review to be more modern.
So, first things first, the thing that plagues a good few Early Access Games, the update times.
Grim dawn has always had a bit of a pause between updates, occasionally many months inbetween each update, but the new builds are typically very large followed by a large bug fixing. They do work very hard on the game, and if you want to see what they are working on, they run a Developement forum area which you can check here:
The game itself is very solid, think darker Diablo 3 with lower level caps, slap Early Access on it, and put in classes that are very unique. The loot system is RNG based, like original D3, so you will be getting items that you can't or don't want to use on characters. There is a stash system they lets you transfer them however, so you can use it on other characters.
It has a lot of quests, flavoring, and lore. Suprising amount of lore given that it is early access, but it is certainly there. There are bits and pieces of writing you can pick up to read about the people who lived before things went bad.
The classes themselves fill different roles, such as the Soldier being a dominant Melee/Support class that has unrivaled ability to survive. Arcanist is the polar opposite, being extreme damage potential single target but potato survival. Occultist is the king of AoE killing because of Bloody Pox. Nightblade is unrivaled single target damage since it is melee. Shaman is unrivaled AoE killing with two handed weapons. Demolitionist is the blend of Arcanist and Occultist, bringing high AoE ability at a ranged distance with decent single target damage. The best part is, you can pick two classes at some point in the game, you can be a Nightblade/Soldier, anything you want. But picking a class is a PERMANENT thing. You can NEVER undo this.
The skill system is awesome, basically there are two seperate tracks that tie together. You can put points into a seperate tree, it basically gives you stats and lets you unlock the higher tier skills, or you can put points directly into skills. Basically, if you put points into the stats, you get more stats, and the ability to work your way down the tree to unlock bigger, and better skills.
The skills themselves are interesting, augments typically change how they work, such as giving it more elemental damage at the cost of physical damage. Most skills have progressive passive upgrades that are just... Upgrades, they don't change anything.
Skills can be upgraded through items of course, but these items are reasonably rare. Casters have access to incredibly powerful off hand items that can't be used to block, but power up your skills dramatically.
The bugs are... Well, they are there. But I haven't encountered a single game breaking bug yet. The worst one is when loot will start "Rolling" away off screen very quickly. Nothing you can do unless it hits a solid object.
Graphics aren't bad, aren't great. Optimisation needs a bit of work, game is a bit iffy on the FPS, spikes happen a lot.
Overall, this would be considered a good game without the Early Access title slapped on, I can easily rate this with Kerbal Space Program in terms of promise.

is a fantastic game. I used to play the original game and its sequel back when I was a kid, and again later on as they became available on Steam. However, it should be noted that to get the best experience out of this game, it shouldn't be excessively compared to the original - it's a re-imagination, not a point-for-point remake.
While the strategic gameplay has been greatly reduced from the classic 90's titles that inspired this game, it is made up for by entirely overhauling the tactical missions. Especially on harder difficulties, combat becomes really fulfilling with the fairly effective cover system, varying class-based abilities and, of course, the player's growing knowledge of the aliens, their abilities and warfare.
I've only played the game in the reload-disabling
mode, and as far as I can tell, it's really hard to go back to non-Ironman afterwards. The game becomes infinitely more rewarding (as well as punishing) with it enabled, and forces the player to give much more thought to their actions if they wish to have a chance against the alien threat.
Some of the greatest features in this game include a wide array of customisation options, a variety of maps (even moreso with
), and the general atmosphere of missions. As for the weaknesses, of which there aren't all that many, I would mention the constricting feel of the strategic "geoscape" phase (although its restrictions do serve a purpose and are not in any way an expression of lazy approach or lack of attention from the developers). It involves much less micromanaging than the classic games - whether that's a good or a bad thing is for everyone to judge for themselves.
The leap in challenge from one difficulty setting to another is very noticeable. Even if
difficulty starts to feel a bit too breezy, don't be too hasty to crank it up before you're sure you've got your tactics as well as your general understanding of the game down, or you may be blindsided by the amount of things that are suddenly way more challenging. This is a good thing, obviously - too many games today are simply too easy, going for the "don't upset the player" approach.
All in all, a fantastic game. It has huge replay value, great variety in tactical preferences, and is simply fun to play. I definitely recommend this game.
