This is the best Early Access game I have played on Steam so I felt compelled to write a review. I've been playing almost since it's inception.
If you're looking for a fun Hack'nSlash with replayability this is the game for you. There really isn't much else to do in the game besides wading through hordes of monsters, going back to town and selling loot...but there's a certain appeal that keeps you do it over and over. Finding that one piece of gear to bring your character's dps over the edge, finding that one crafting component that fits nicely with your weapon, specing and respecing your abilities to see what works best...all of these things work in conjuction to keep bringing you back. The graphics are great, the sound track is original and the overal gritty atmosphere give this game an unmistakbable personality that sets it apart from other games of the same genre.
There are a few down sides though. First and foremost the updates are very few and far between. It's been a year since  release and its feels like the current content is wearing itself thin. I felt like I was on the edge of my seat druing the first few months of playing but now I just hop on if I need to kill some time before leaving the house. Everything has been explored and my char has reached a plateau. Playing is rather drab when I know I can't improve no matter what I do.
Multiplayer definitely needs work. The lag is a little ridiculous...expect a 1-2 second delay with every swing and every spell you cast. You also lose connectivity after about 30 minutes of playing. This game is definitlely meant for single player but it would be nice to have some solid multiplayer action.
While the crafting feature adds a nice touch and is fairly easy to learn (basically stack components of the same type, combine them to make a powerful version and drop it on an item) There are some that are ridiculously hard to find. I've been playing for almost a year and have found only 3 of one type, just shy of completing it for an awesome weapon buff. There are others that drop once in a blue moon and I can play for months without ever getting a drop. I've never played an MMO with such rare loot drops.
All in all it's a solid game. I'd definitely reccomend it to a friend. While it is addictive at first, don't expect it to keep your attention for very long like some other games.

Puzzles are rewarding and combine elements together. This helps to keep things interesting while also making the final set a real test of skill. Zenge is a bargon and worth a moment of your time, whether you’d rather take it on the go or add it to your steam collections for that added 100% and trading cards.

is a moderately challenging puzzle game that offers about two hours of decent fun to complete its 70 puzzles. At the price of 99 cents (even less when on sale) it's a no-brainer: if you're at all into puzzle games, you shouldn't hesitate and give
a try.
The goal is to slide the pieces of each puzzle across the lines into their target slots. It starts out very straightforward but every dozen or so levels, the game adds a new mechanic. These mechanics allow and require you to rotate, mirror, teleport, shrink or enlarge pieces, or use certain pieces as a switch to activate color coded lines, allowing other pieces to cross those lines.
Every time a new mechanic is introduced, the difficulty drops for one or two puzzles, serving as a tutorial to familiarize the player with the new mechanic. After that, the difficulty rises steadily until the next mechanic comes along. Overall,
isn't very difficult at all but you do need to think some of the puzzles through or experiment a bit before the solution will come to you. For me, and I assume for most people looking for a challenge but not to the point of frustration or migraine,
's difficulty is nearly perfect for a casual puzzle game.
For a game that has a minimalist look,
's graphics are certainly easy on the eye. When you complete a puzzle, you're shown an artwork in the same minimalist style as the puzzles' design. These are artworks that you probably wouldn't hang on your wall but they're nice to look at for a couple of seconds before you click the button to start the next puzzle.
The music is very basic. You hear a simple but atmospheric melody being played on the guitar or the piano. The sound effects are equally basic, consisting of little else than a very soft 'woosh' sound when you slide a puzzle piece across a line.
If you like, you can disable the music or the sound effects from the game's menu, which is again very basic. There is a third button that allows you to switch between the current puzzle and the level select screen, and that's it. There isn't even a 'Quit' button, you just press Esc on your keyboard to close the program.
has 6 Steam Trading Cards. You'll get 3 while running the game.
There is only one Steam Achievement to be had, an achievement that unlocks after completing the last puzzle.

This is a simple shooter that achieves its goals perfectly. Too many FPS's pretend to be something they are not or try to infuse all known gameplay mechanics to mask the hollow core of its games. You want to kill hordes of enemies, you want a variety of weapons, you just want a quick game to blow off steam or maybe just casually play with your mates, this game delivers. The gameplay is smooth with great little touches and attention to detail that avid players of the genre will appreciate. In this game you can really see the work of a game's creators that want their players to enjoy every last minute, a true testiment to what can be achieved when a developer takes pride in their games.
If I had any criticisms they would include micro payments although these really only unlock cosmetics so it doesn't take from the game's content. Weapon attachments might have been nice but the base weapons are already awesome enough that again this is just nit picking.
A lot of people complain that this game is repetative which is just a pretentious observation that doesn't carry much weight. It is a round by round survival game so of course it is repetative, that is the point. The observation that doing something again here is like playing FIFA and saying "This game could do more than just kick a ball around."
Definitely worth the asking price and provides well over 100+ hours of cathartic fun!

Note for Gaming Laptop Users:
If you are having issues with the game running in a blurry window with no resolution options, or the main menu running at like 1-2 fps and your laptop fans suddenly screaming; you must go into Nvidia Control Panel>Manage 3D Settings>Application Settings>and configure the game for "High performance Nvidia GPU".
In both power saver mode, and performance mode, my Alienware 13, and MSI GT72 both had huge issues with this game, and they were fixed by doing the above.

Music: 10/10 (If you don't like metal, look elsewhere, but since I do, \m/)
Graphics: 9.0/10 (There can be issues with Nvidia FLeX with the gore, and your framerate on even bleeding edge desktop systems. The most recent weekly event where zeds explode when killed illustrated that)
Community/Market (all market items are completely cosmetic): 5.5/10 (The community is often completely dead in this game. Server selection is a pain, and Tripwire Official Servers are often playing odd map/difficulty combos. Look into creating your own server if you want to play with friends. Overall, even if you just want to play offline by yourself, this game is very compelling for your standard first person wave defense junkie. The different zed classes make it fun and varied. There sadly is still only two possible bosses, and I honestly wish there were a couple more.

As others have pointed out, this game is short. If you don't want to play a game you could ostensibly finish in 20 minutes your first try, look elsewhere. Now, a game's length is not an indicator of its quality; games as disparate as Pacman and Dys4ia accomplish a great deal with a brief playtime. The issue with Gardenarium is that it does not do enough meaningful things with the duration that the player spends with it.
Gardenarium has you climb Seussian hillside, collecting trash that causes the landscape to populate with vegetation. Along the way you meet a few nonsequitor characters who tell abridged tales of their life. The game has an abrupt ending where the gameplay perspective changes and asks the player to wander around.
Despite my dry description, there's some actual intrigue here. The aesthetic to Gardenarium is utterly psychedelic, as alien plants pulse and throb with gorgeously animated high-resolution sprites. The flora also grows in amazing patterns that track your movement, similar to the flowers that grow around Ameratsu in Okami. The few charcters you meet also have quite a bit of personality, and some of their lines allude to tragic and humorous anecdotes. The switch of perspective is also an amazing concept for a game mechanic, not unlike what was accomplished by Super Paper Mario, but the promise of toggling between two and three dimensional planes was not used for any kind of clever transdimensional level design. A pity, really.
It's entirely possible that there's some sort of obtuse hidden content that extends the experience past the apparent ending, but I wasn't able to unearth it. On the contrary, there's a lot suggest that this game was intended as more of a playable pitch for a more complete game, or maybe even a portfolio piece. The animation included is obviously very time-intensive to produce, yet the world has little to explore or do in it. The endgame is an interesting concept, but doesn't seem to expand the the game in any meaningful or mechanically satisfying way. Even the vauge theme of corporate disillusionment murmered by the cast doesn't seem very well fleshed out. The game very much feels like it's less than the sum of its parts, as the each individual component seems too compromised.
I ultimately enjoyed the time I spent with this game just because I'm an animation nut, and I'll let the developer keep my money out of appreciation for their craft. That said, I would not recommend the game unless you can't get enough of its visual style. To the developers, I hope you continue animating and eagerly await your future output!

If you're looking for a positive review, then you're in the wrong place, HOWEVER, if you're here for a tremendous chicken Stir Fry recipe, THEN LOOK NO FURTHER!
- Serves 4
- 10 mins to prepare and 10 mins to cook
- 325 calories / serving
- Healthy
INGREDIENTS:
- 1 orange, zested and juiced
- 2tbsp soy sauce
- 2tbsp sesame oil
- 250g (8oz) tender stem broccoli
- 5cm (2in) piece root ginger
- 1tbsp sunflower oil
- 1 garlic clove, finely sliced
- 1 red pepper, deseeded and thinly sliced
- 150g Straight To Wok Noodles
- 400g (13oz) chicken fillet, cut into thin slices
METHOD
Step 1 - Mix together the orange zest and juice, soy sauce and sesame oil and set aside.
Step 2 - Blanch the broccoli in boiling water for 2 minutes, then drain well and set aside.
Step 3 - Finely shred the ginger. Then heat a large frying pan or wok, add the sunflower oil, heat it until sizzling, and fry the ginger till it's crisp.
Step 4 - When it's done, remove with a slotted spoon. Add the chicken and garlic, and stir-fry until just browned. Remove the meat using a slotted spoon and set aside.
Step 5 - Add the red pepper and broccoli and stir-fry for around 2-3 minutes until it's just tender. Add the soy sauce mixture, bring it to the boil then return the chicken to the pan and heat through. Serve with noodles.

This is not the sort of game that you're gonna have fun while playing it. Having that thought in mind, Pongo is the sort of experience that will push you to the edge. I've paid less than a buck for it and this certainly has a major influence on my review. Here're some observations that I've made during my gameplay:
- The graphics aren't bad, they remind me of that game XIII and that's a good thing.
- The soundtrack is kinda nice, although it gets old after a while. I can't say the same about the sound effects, the shooting sound is annoying (by the way, what are those projectiles anyway?).
- The menu options are extremely limited. Even though I'd always choose a mouse over a joypad when it comes to FPS, it would be nice if the game would provide some support for it.
- A simple tutorial wouldn't kill anyone, especially to explain how the power-ups work.
- The concept is rather simple, but it would be interesting if we'd have any kind of story. Like, you're just some white kid who happens live in Waterworld (without Kevin Costner), hopping like a bunny on steroids and all of a sudden there're a bunch of cutthroat creatures trying to kill you for whatever reason.
- It would be more interesting if there was more diversity concerning the environment, like adding some levels with snow, desert etc.

- There's not much a motivation for killing enemies, as they won't give you any point, drop power-ups or nothing. Actually, I'm still asking myself how the hell I've received the achievement for killing 1000 enemies, as I don't remember killing 1/4 of that amount.

- Easy mode should offer checkpoints besides extra lives. Seriously, levels 22 and 35 were especially designed to test the limits of your nerves (it would actually make more sense if these were the latest levels).
- A few glitches here and there. Let's revisit them:
> One of the most annoying and frequent ones is when you're trying to jump to somewhere and happen to land right on the edge. If that happens, you're basically on limbo, pal. In other words, you may choose to kill yourself or... Well, killing yourself.
> Sometimes you kill an enemy and they won't disappear.
> I've seen at least one 'ghost' power-up on this game. By that, I mean that I tried to grab it and I couldn't.
Overall, don't expect much of this game (except for a lot of stress and frustration). Why do I recommend it then? Like, seriously... What game in the world takes pride for counting and achieving 1000 deaths? Well, that's a very good question. I'll let you know when I figure that out.

This is a pleasant match-three puzzle game with some good art and polish, and it's not too long.
In this game, you have to dig through a bunch of dirt so that some liquid can flow to the end of the level. You dig by eliminating tiles on top of the dirt. The camera scrolls on its own as it follows the liquid, and you can't scroll back to earlier parts of the level, so you have to deal with only what you see on the screen. Sometimes the randomness will deal a bad hand, but you can get out of trouble with planning and clever use of powerups.
I admit, I first thought it was a bit easy and simplistic for my tastes -- there are only four colors to match, and the powerups were a bit too powerful. About halfway through the game, I realized the main enemy was the timer, and it could put up a good fight. Later levels got fast and frantic as I had to dig through huge levels in only a few minutes, and the final few levels were quite a satisfying challenge.
Overall, it was pretty good! It seems like something straight out of the golden age of PopCap. If you have fond memories of Zuma, Bejeweled, Chuzzle, Bookworm, and the like, you might find this very enjoyable. For achievement hunters, this is a no-brainer. Get it on sale for an easy 5-7 hour perfect game.

's voice to the character editor, but the rest is mostly reused stuff from its predecessor (and they still haven't bothered fixing stuff in that).
They didn't bother removing certain things that shouldn't have been in Steelport after The Third's story (people who played The Third should know what I mean) and the graphics are still as outdated as The Third's.
Are normal maps that hard to create for a video game studio?
__________________________________________________
And why the heck does it have so much Dubstep? Why do you have to get 250 kills with the Dubstep Cannon in order to beat a challenge that grants you XP and adds to the overall completion of the game?
I'm not a fan of Dubstep, I usually don't complain about it, because I don't bother listening to it and because I avoid any form of contact with it, but this really steps on my foot with a lot of run-up. Yes, there is a "skin" that changes its music to classic while another one changes that to jazz, but you have to BUY a DLC for that!
__________________________________________________
And yeah, the challenges, they became even more annoying:
Get x Kills with y. Kills x enemies with ability z.
In both cases, only alien kills count towards the completion of these challenges (with an exception or two).
Uncreative as hell.
Want 100%? Have fun.
__________________________________________________
Another annoyance is the unlock system.
Here's an example:
Instead of buying shops, you have to hack them, you transfer their income onto your bank account so to say.
Hacking becomes available after 4 or 5 story missions and always has a time limit (60 seconds). Once you run out of time, the shop's security system locks down the whole place and the police is after you.
After beating 2 more story missions, you get additional 60 seconds as a purchasable upgrade.
That's great and all, but if you hacked everything the moment you were able to do that (thus 2 story missions before), THEN THAT'S DAMN USELESS!
I do side missions first, then I proceed in the story with a relatively well-leveled character and a big handful of cash until new side missions show up, then I repeat. Punishing ambition isn't cool.
I don't want to beat the story just to be able to play the game the way I want, damnit!
__________________________________________________
And (still) the biggest let-down: No custom radio station.
Yeah, the "Mixtape" where you put songs from the game's radio stations into a playlist is still there, but I only have 3 songs in that, because the rest is either Dubstep, Reggae or songs you've heard way too often at parties.
__________________________________________________
So overall it's funny, it's ridiculous, it has The Third's weaknesses and it's even worse than The Third.
I'll still play it every now and then, though.

is a fantastic game. I used to play the original game and its sequel back when I was a kid, and again later on as they became available on Steam. However, it should be noted that to get the best experience out of this game, it shouldn't be excessively compared to the original - it's a re-imagination, not a point-for-point remake.
While the strategic gameplay has been greatly reduced from the classic 90's titles that inspired this game, it is made up for by entirely overhauling the tactical missions. Especially on harder difficulties, combat becomes really fulfilling with the fairly effective cover system, varying class-based abilities and, of course, the player's growing knowledge of the aliens, their abilities and warfare.
I've only played the game in the reload-disabling
mode, and as far as I can tell, it's really hard to go back to non-Ironman afterwards. The game becomes infinitely more rewarding (as well as punishing) with it enabled, and forces the player to give much more thought to their actions if they wish to have a chance against the alien threat.
Some of the greatest features in this game include a wide array of customisation options, a variety of maps (even moreso with
), and the general atmosphere of missions. As for the weaknesses, of which there aren't all that many, I would mention the constricting feel of the strategic "geoscape" phase (although its restrictions do serve a purpose and are not in any way an expression of lazy approach or lack of attention from the developers). It involves much less micromanaging than the classic games - whether that's a good or a bad thing is for everyone to judge for themselves.
The leap in challenge from one difficulty setting to another is very noticeable. Even if
difficulty starts to feel a bit too breezy, don't be too hasty to crank it up before you're sure you've got your tactics as well as your general understanding of the game down, or you may be blindsided by the amount of things that are suddenly way more challenging. This is a good thing, obviously - too many games today are simply too easy, going for the "don't upset the player" approach.
All in all, a fantastic game. It has huge replay value, great variety in tactical preferences, and is simply fun to play. I definitely recommend this game.

I played hardcore mode on several aRPGs such as Diablo 1,2,3, Torchlight 1,2, etc. I saw the positive reviews on Grim Dawn and decided to give it a shot with my friends on its hardcore mode.
**I know my review is in pre-release, but unless they majorly overhaul the game MECHANICS it will remain unchanged at release**
THE GOOD
During my first play through the content (currently ends in Smuggler's Pass), Grim Dawn had me hooked. The game is fun, the world is open, and exploration is rewarded. There are many quests that are going on at once and many main and side dungeons to clear along your journey. The enemies are challenging and the bosses are a good rush to fight. The loot is fair in that you get good drops, but it is neither too easy, nor too hard to get decent items. There is a lot of variability in character builds, thanks to the ability to combine 2 classes if you desire. This is a great feature to break from the usual 4 to 5 classes in aRPGs, and allow you to play your character a little different each time they die or you play through.
THE BAD
THE MAP IS NOT RANDOMIZED AND IS REVEALED ON SUBSEQUENT VISITS TO AN AREA. So once you play through once, and come back to a dungeon to farm or for a challenge (the monster levels scale to you), you will notice the map is revealed, making it just a quick walk through the dungeon to the end if you so desire (and why not if you are max level and dont need the xp?). If you've played the diablo series, then you know the random maps are crucial to keeping the game fresh, even if it isnt a big change, it still keeps you on your toes and guessing. With Grim Dawn, there is no guessing, it doesn't feel new, and so grinding the Warden's Lab, Smuggler's Den, or Steps of Torment isn't fun, its just a chore and I have the path memorized. The devs went for a "lazy randomization" technique where the map is the same but different paths may be blocked off by rocks so it isn't always 100% the same. However IMO they need to 1) add more rocks and 2) DON'T REVEAL THE MAP OR THE ROCKS DON'T MATTER ANYWAY.
THE UGLY
So this is the part where I quit the game. This game is so hackable that it isn't fun. The character files are all client-side, when they should be stored elsewhere. This makes literally everything hackable. Don't have an item? You can probably hack it. Did your hardcore character die? Well just make him back alive again! Does your friend want a copy of your epic item? Just dupe it. Tired of grinding for rare crafting components? Just dupe them. Ok you get the point, the game is no fun after the first playthrough and after you realize that its a joke. It doesn't mean anything if you're level 35 on hardcore veteran because that status is easily hackable. That rush you get when your hardcore character almost dies, but you fight your way through, GONE because you can just restore him if you wanted to. People will join your game and offer you dupes and it really ruins the challenge. The other downside is the development timeframe. This game would have been great maybe if it was completed by now or earlier, but now its maybe halfway done, full of hacks, and they are showing no signs of fixing the hacking or map randomization.
CONCLUSION
Buy this game if you are a fan of aRPGs, but won't be playing hardcore mode and don't mind that it doesn't have a lot of replay value. DO NOT buy this game if you are a hardcore fan, looking for a serious challenge.
*some people comment that you can still have the challenge if you don't hack. Well sort of, but it still doesn't make the map not-revealed, and it just makes your accomplishments worthless because some nerd who edits his character file can make a far more powerful character with zero effort, so the feeling of accomplishment is completely gone.

Block'Hood is the game I imagine people in a Utopian future playing, surrounded by crisp, gleaming interiors at a desk that projects the game onto a space in front of the player. Because playing it is, I think, the 21st century version of a zen sand garden, trying to find harmony with nature through human interaction. These may seem like overly poetic descriptions, but the game asks for this kind of reverence and, I think, deserves it.
The game is essentially SimCity with a sustainability focus, teaching the player about the interconnectedness of all things in a community (a "block'hood"), from quantifiable resources like water and electricity to more abstract concepts like knowledge and leisure. For this reason, it doesn't simply reward growth, like the SimCity of my youth, which granted you gifts for hitting population milestones. Instead, Block'Hood rewards you with a tiny ecosystem, like a terrarium you can occasionally water but still get to watch thrive and grow.
Granted, the game doesn't have to be played this way. The tutorials and challenges slowly introduce you to the myriad of approaches you can take to the game, giving you new resources to experiment with and learn about with very little risk for building, say, a bakery before you've planted enough wheat fields and labour to sustain the customers and revenue the bakery brings in. You just "delete" the bakery until you have the necessary supply chain ready, meanwhile probably realizing you don't yet have enough customers in your block for stable income anyway.
I haven't completed the challenges or moved on to the "sandbox" mode yet, partly because the game is still technically in Early Access (meaning the developers are still tweaking things here and there). But the challenges (of which there are several) are short, relaxing, and rewarding, and more than once, I've booted up the game for a short 30-minute session and then headed off to bed, feeling sort of soothed.
And I think this is the game's main draw for me.

This game is so good it deserves an actual review instead of ironic memes.
It's the perfect horror game. The ambient is perfect: a castle in the era of... castles. And it is a HUGE castle. Filled with horrifying creatures (the old graphics help a lot for this!) making very spooky noises. A huge variety of weapons and enemies to try these weapons with. Each enemy has its weakness and it's up to you to figure it out. You must explore the entire castle, rescuing your relatives, finding keys and defeating evil and powerful vampires along the way to ultimately get access to the main castle. It isn't really a linear game as it lets you explore the castle at will, leaving you to figure out where to go and what to try, but as time passes your relatives will start getting killed if you don't find and rescue them!
To conclude, a must have for fans of the horror genre. Without trying hard and failing like modern horror games, this game is so simple yet so terrifying, making you actually jump on your chair without needing actual jumpscares.
10/10 for its time.

This feels more like a puzzle game than a builder game, but in a good way. It's a puzzle game in the same way the old Sierra titles (Caesar, Pharaoh, Zeus, Emperor) are puzzle games: you have a set of objectives (game-set or self-set depending on game mode) and you have to use the available buildings to create a little machine of a city that satisfies those objectives. What you build can be nonsensical or beautiful, as long as your production chains are tightly managed and you leverage the occasional adjacency bonus.
There are a few oversights and quality-of-life problems in this early access phase (some descriptions are too long for  their windows; no way to view the very long resources list or sort them for better viewing) but the game is already very playable and fun. I already find myself thinking about it when I'm not playing, so I am really hopeful that the final game will be even better!

This is fun for one game, because you do pretty much cover all the content in a single one. The main premise is you build a capital city, then can proceed to build stuff in that city or build settlers to establish other cities. You can trade and war with other AI countries, or play online and work with or against other people doing the same thing. All the while you're doing this, you can have your people research new technologies. And what you choose to research impacts the units or buildings you have. So you can be the guy who goes straight for gunpowder, or you can explore all the scientific ones and build a spaceship.
On the topic of spaceships and gunpowder, those are two of the five ways to win a game. Scientific, Domination, Diplomatic, Time, and Cultural. A science victory is obtained when you are the first to build a space shuttle. Domination occurs when you capture all players' capital cities. Diplomatic happens when you are voted the pinnacle of creation by the UN. Time occurs after the year 2050 rolls around, giving the victory to whoever has the greatest score, a mix of troop and city and resource count. The cultural victory has something to do with monuments I think, but since it never happens its not something to worry about.
The game is pretty much exactly what it looks like in the screenshots. My only complaint is that you can't have multiple troops in one hexagon, which was not true for the previous civilization game. This makes coordinating attacks with a lot of troops more difficult than it has to be.
In the end I was bored by it because it's a clone of all the other Civ games. If you haven't played one yet I'd recommend Civ 4 over this one. Literally the only additions here are hexagons instead of squares and an endgame troop called the "Giant Death Robot".

Divinity: Original Sin wants to be Balders Gate, they mentioned classic rpgs and BG nearly every chance they could during it's development, but it really has nothing to do with it what made them great. There's really no overarching villian, no grand quest, there is no memorable characters, or quests, or basically anything you equate with the good ole days of the crpg.
But there is alot of freedom, your can do pretty much as you like with whatever party you choose, but don't expect your choices to actually matter much, e.g.: just because you made the main character a rogue don't think he's going to be useful to you or the plot in any kind of way (I'll eleborate on that in a sec.). You have your typical 4 man party, 2 of which are main characters you create in the beginning, and the other 2 are either generic henchman you get out of a random generator or 2 possible companions with personality that you can recruit in the very first town if you think either is benefitial to your party type. Realistically unless you build your 2 main character's to conform to those 2 whole companions both thru the way you act and what physically completement's your chars your going to be stuck with random henchman who don't say a word the entire game. One thing BG didn't have? Instant death's. Get ready for them because there is a lot of them, you'll dig in the ground, or press a button, or walk in a door and your entire party will instantly die. Why? Because it just does. Almost all of them occur without warning, complete beginnners trap's so you'll need to quicksave constantly or lose progress.
Balancing here is a to be perfectly honest a joke, you'll quickly realize by level 10 how much powerful mages are compared to melee classes and how utterly worthless warrior/rogue type abilties are and you'll find yourself either restarting to build a primarily magic team, sitting your melee's out for caster henchman or offspecing your melee into spells to keep them relevant. I'm not kidding when I say that the difference between survivability of a plate wearing melee and a cloth wearing mage is next to nothing, in fact with all the long range teleports, slows and stuns at the mages disposal I'd say the mages have considerably more overall survivability then the melee do the melee have at best 30% more armor to physical attacks then the mage does and nothing else. The mages also by far do more damage, even against single targets (baffelingly) and they do it at long ranges that would take multiple turns for the melee to even reach the target, and unlike rogues with bows that have to roll hits they never miss.
Outside of class balance, you'll frequently get into fights were you'll be outnumbered 3:1 and success or defeat frequently revolved around who the AI dice roll decided should be debuff/stunned right off the bat for the entire fight or if it ineffectially just attacked the nearest target for miniscule damage. Reloading some fights over and over for outcome I found some I'd nearly instantly lose, win with zero effort, or barely survive, all based entirely on who and what the AI dice rolled to do, there doesn't seem to be any true ai like "Always stun the healer" or "Attack the closest warrior" its all random and so you need to quicksave alot.
Overall I'd avoid it for now, There's alot of bugs and atleast game is patched seemingly once or twice a day, yet finding what's changed is difficult if possible at all since only every other patch gets changelists. It's very easy to render a questline incompleteable either because you hit someone before they were supposed to dialog with you and then start the fight (don't think your going to be rewarded for stealthing and getting the first hit in, thats broke scripts in alot of place, main questline places.) or because you killed someone that your shouldn't have, or because you did a quest out of order.
Lastly, The map editor is also a complete mess that barely functions at best and just crashes at worst, so if you were thinking this is the new age NWN toolkit your mistaken. Maybe in a year down the line I'll check it out again, but for now I'm mostly done.

It's pretty good I guess.  I would give this game an 8 out of ten.  As far as strategy games go, Civ 5 does fairly well.  Early game is very strong and enjoyable, quick progression and visible progress toward what you want your Civ to become.  Mid game you feel like a real king deciding the fate of everyone around you (until you get to king difficulty) while still dealing with challenges.  Late game however is a bit dull, you will spend the majority of your time waging massive wars and micromanaging 30 or so units because you want to make sure everything happens at the right time.  City management will become somewhat of a hassle and each turn will take a few minutes rather than 60 seconds.  Yet, there is something addictive about how Sid Meier set Civ 5 up.  Each time you start you know how you like to play and you try to overcome a few more of your faults, and even though each difficulty hop has a near insurmountable learning curve and may very well be impossible at higher difficulties, keeps you coming back for more.  Many nights have been spent lying to myself about when I will get off.  10 more turns, oh there is a new resource I need.  Well I guess I'll expand my territory out there over the next 20 turns and take that then I'll trade with Byzantium and call it a night.  Oh but Atilla just called my Boy Gandhi four eyes, heck yeah I'll declare war!  100+ turns go by teasing myself with the promise of sleep at the end of a never ending line of side quests.  Only play this if you have time to spare or self discipline of a monk.  Else you wont be sleeping anytime soon.

A few points that could use improvement (perhaps in a v2):
. Once you've solved level 64, and perhaps hunted down the missing achievements, there's no reason to fire up the game anymore.
Suggestions: let the game keep track of your individual level solution times or scores, to add an incentive to replay for better scores. Additionally, the game really should offer a built-in way to replay specific previously completed levels. As it is now, if you like certain levels and wish to revisit them, the game forces you to play all previous levels first to get to the ones you actually wished to replay, or... you have to edit the savegame xml. Ugh.
A slightly more ambitious suggestion: a level design or mod tool would extend the lifetime of this game considerably.
. Well, there is exactly one: fullscreen y/n. Fullscreen appears to be fixed at 800x600 regardless of screen native size, and windowed it cannot be resized either. Trying to find the hidden pixels of a tiny 800x600 window on a full HD (or more!) screen becomes very tiring for the eyes.
It really should not need to be said that graphics and resolution options are a must for PC games.

I have to say thank you to @Flaming Monocle for his review and entertaining video, which is what convinced me to splash out the princely sum of $0.89 on this game!
If you like this sort of matching game I would even recommend it at full price... it's several hours of fun for only the cost of a fancy cup of coffee, and it's much more entertaining than a Caramel Macchiato...  :)
Other reviewers have already covered the gameplay in detail, which consists of three different types of game, but I'll comment on those here too.  'Cause I'm just a rebel like that.
Find the key to unlock one of the books of magic, by playing a Hidden Object Game to construct several items and reactivate an elemental altar.  This is not timed, and there doesn't appear to be a penalty for needing a hint or clicking in the wrong place.  Some of the items you need to find are tiny and/or
well camouflaged - in some cases, even after the fairy helper pointed them out I had to admit I would probably never have found them!
Once the book is unlocked, collect four cards for each one.  Each card is made up of four layers, which are collected by playing the main part of the game - the Match-3 levels.  These start out very easy and progressively get more difficult, although I did find that even towards the end of the game some levels were much easier and quicker than others.  The last two levels are quite tricky, and if you don't do the right thing at the start you might find yourself stuck and unable to progress.  I failed level 63 twice before I realised the trick to getting past it.
These levels, while fun and addictive, are not completely relaxing because there is a timer and you can run out of time to reach the goal.  Again, there doesn't seem to be any real penalty for failure except a few wasted minutes - even the fairy just shrugs and tells you to try again - and if you do fail you generally get an idea of what went wrong and how to do better on the retry.  I wasn't able to figure out how long the timer is, and I think it might vary depending on the difficulty of the level, but my slowest levels were over 9 minutes so in most cases you have a bit of time to think!
Once you have the four parts of the card, you play a 'spot the difference' game to complete the card.  Again, some of the differences require very careful scrutiny to see them as they are quite subtle.  (I didn't feel that the resolution of the game was an issue with either this or the HOG sections; I believe it's just that the details are so small that you really have to look hard to find them.)  Once this part is done, the card is completed and the text becomes unscrambled so that you can read it.
In all, there are 64 Match-3 levels to play through - four books with four cards each, and each card needing four levels to complete it.  In addition there are the four Hidden Object scenes to unlock the book, and 16 spot the difference games to unscramble the cards.  The game saves your progress when you exit, allowing you to continue from where you left off, and there doesn't appear to be any way to skip a section or choose where to go next.  It looks as though more than one person could save a game in progress, as you choose a name at the start and there is an option on the main menu screen to switch this.
The background music was quite pleasant, although it occasionally began to feel a bit repetitive, and I didn't find it distracting.
The graphics, although perhaps a little dated in some ways, were really rather nice.  There are a lot of little details in the background of the level screens that you don't really have much time to appreciate when you're focusing on finding the next group of 'gems' to match (I particularly liked the fish swimming past on the underwater levels), and the gems themselves have different designs on them depending on the element you're working on.
A few pros and cons, from my point of view.
- fiendishly addictive!  Like a good book, I found it really hard to put it down.  I didn't want to stop playing at the end of one section and have to wait until the next day to continue, especially if I was almost done with one of the elements.
- attractive graphics... not top notch, but good enough to not detract from the game.  (In my opinion anyway, other reviewers clearly disagree here. :) )
- pleasant music and sound effects, nothing too irritating.
- new power-up concepts are introduced one at a time to allow you to get used to them.
- the map is a handy feature to help you see where you should be heading, and there is also an arrow at the edge of the screen that points the way for you.  (Actually reaching it is sometimes another matter entirely!)
- the maps sometimes make a picture, which is a nice touch.
- some of the details in the hidden object and spot the difference screens are just TOO small and well-disguised, leading to some frustration with these sections (especially the HOGs).
- at the beginning of each level the camera sweeps back from the end goal to the start, showing you the route you need to take.  This is so fast that I find it nauseating to watch, particularly when the route loops around as it does in many of the levels.
- there is no way to move the camera around the field (at least, not that I could find) to allow you to see what is just around the corner from your current location.  A glance at the map or a look at your guiding arrow will give you an idea of which direction to go, but the map won't show you any of the special flaming arrows you might need to head for or piles of stones/tiles blocking your way.
- the camera follows the progress of the magical energy, which can lead to it swinging around unexpectedly when you're trying to click on something, or to your view being moved further away than you wanted and making it difficult to figure out where to go next.  There are sometimes flaming arrows (necessary to break through some areas) in hard to spot locations because of where the camera has positioned itself.
- the playing tips at the end of each level got very irritating after a while, especially as they were repeating things you already knew towards the end, and I could not seem to turn them off.
- the ending was just a text epilogue which, after the voiced intro, was a bit of a let down.  I was hoping for another word from the wizard after I heroically saved the kingdom!
All in all, though, I found this to be a very enjoyable game.  It does have faults, but they were mostly minor in my opinion and I was able to either ignore or put up with them and still have a lot of fun.  I certainly can't complain for the price I paid for it, and wouldn't hesitate to recommend it - get it on sale if you're still not sure.  :)

What this game does poorly:
In my opinion - nothing, really... I guess the spot the differences puzzles could have had more differences to spot, but then again, it works fine as it is.

A magnificent casual 5+ hours game, with wonderful artwork and fun gameplay, which would cost you under 1€/$ on sale (like right now). This is cheaper than a bag of peanuts or chips, or a beer and will provide you with way more hours of enjoyment. What's not to like?

I played hardcore mode on several aRPGs such as Diablo 1,2,3, Torchlight 1,2, etc. I saw the positive reviews on Grim Dawn and decided to give it a shot with my friends on its hardcore mode.
**I know my review is in pre-release, but unless they majorly overhaul the game MECHANICS it will remain unchanged at release**
THE GOOD
During my first play through the content (currently ends in Smuggler's Pass), Grim Dawn had me hooked. The game is fun, the world is open, and exploration is rewarded. There are many quests that are going on at once and many main and side dungeons to clear along your journey. The enemies are challenging and the bosses are a good rush to fight. The loot is fair in that you get good drops, but it is neither too easy, nor too hard to get decent items. There is a lot of variability in character builds, thanks to the ability to combine 2 classes if you desire. This is a great feature to break from the usual 4 to 5 classes in aRPGs, and allow you to play your character a little different each time they die or you play through.
THE BAD
THE MAP IS NOT RANDOMIZED AND IS REVEALED ON SUBSEQUENT VISITS TO AN AREA. So once you play through once, and come back to a dungeon to farm or for a challenge (the monster levels scale to you), you will notice the map is revealed, making it just a quick walk through the dungeon to the end if you so desire (and why not if you are max level and dont need the xp?). If you've played the diablo series, then you know the random maps are crucial to keeping the game fresh, even if it isnt a big change, it still keeps you on your toes and guessing. With Grim Dawn, there is no guessing, it doesn't feel new, and so grinding the Warden's Lab, Smuggler's Den, or Steps of Torment isn't fun, its just a chore and I have the path memorized. The devs went for a "lazy randomization" technique where the map is the same but different paths may be blocked off by rocks so it isn't always 100% the same. However IMO they need to 1) add more rocks and 2) DON'T REVEAL THE MAP OR THE ROCKS DON'T MATTER ANYWAY.
THE UGLY
So this is the part where I quit the game. This game is so hackable that it isn't fun. The character files are all client-side, when they should be stored elsewhere. This makes literally everything hackable. Don't have an item? You can probably hack it. Did your hardcore character die? Well just make him back alive again! Does your friend want a copy of your epic item? Just dupe it. Tired of grinding for rare crafting components? Just dupe them. Ok you get the point, the game is no fun after the first playthrough and after you realize that its a joke. It doesn't mean anything if you're level 35 on hardcore veteran because that status is easily hackable. That rush you get when your hardcore character almost dies, but you fight your way through, GONE because you can just restore him if you wanted to. People will join your game and offer you dupes and it really ruins the challenge. The other downside is the development timeframe. This game would have been great maybe if it was completed by now or earlier, but now its maybe halfway done, full of hacks, and they are showing no signs of fixing the hacking or map randomization.
CONCLUSION
Buy this game if you are a fan of aRPGs, but won't be playing hardcore mode and don't mind that it doesn't have a lot of replay value. DO NOT buy this game if you are a hardcore fan, looking for a serious challenge.
*some people comment that you can still have the challenge if you don't hack. Well sort of, but it still doesn't make the map not-revealed, and it just makes your accomplishments worthless because some nerd who edits his character file can make a far more powerful character with zero effort, so the feeling of accomplishment is completely gone.

BEST GAME FOR ANY SOUTH PARK FAN
I am a big fan of South Park and could not get enough of this game. I played through it several times and enjoyed every second of everytime. The game itself is very easy, even on the hardest difficulty setting, but the acheivements can get a little more challenging. The mechanics are great and much easier than any other turn based game I've played, especially in the regard that you can block your opponents attacks. There is a large variation in weapons and costumes and the combat is great altogether.
Not only is the combat great, but almost every second of the game relates to the show. Every junk item, except for maybe a couple of them, came directly from an episode in the show. Several lines in the story itself also came from the show, but gave them new meaning. The references go back to the first episode to the episodes around the time the game was released.
The game itself is not long, if you're slow, you can do everything in about 15 hours. I, personally, don't like long games, so this was great. It doesn't have very much replayability, unless you want to go see differences in dialogue and plot when you do certain things. If you want all the acheivements, you will have to replay the game 2 to 3 times.
The DLC for this game was very dissapointing. All that it is, is several costume sets that serve no purpose for most of the game. If the price for the DLC is low when you purchase the game, I say buy them, if it is still the price I paid for them, wait until they go on sale. They are only good until you have to go to the school the first time. By then, you probably have better stuff.
The next game also looks to show lots of promise, and it seems to take place right after this game, so it is recommended to play this game first. Matt and Trey have really poured their heart out in both games (hopefully) and from the sounds of it, in The Fractured But Whole, there will be more South Park locations and beloved characters. This is my favorite game at the moment and would love if The Fractured But Whole puts it to shame.

Preface: Keep in mind that I am going to review this game... without the DLCs. They're not bad. It's just that I haven't bought them... yet. Even though I've had Orcs Must Die for a while.
The story of the game is about a young-adult, sarcastic, nameless Warmage who's defending rifts in dungeons, which is gateways to the Warmages' medieval world, against waves of Orcs.
I do not wish to spoil any quotes or scenes from the game, because that would just ruin everything.
The gameplay is Tower-Defence... but not in a traditional way with a birds-eye-view. You play as the Warmage in 3rd person, like Gears of War(except, you can't take cover).
You run around in the dungeon, place traps and choose which weapon and spell you are going to choose for the wave.
At the end of each wave, you are presented with a high-score. Depending on how well you played, you will earn orc-skulls to level up your traps/magics/weapons.
The Warmage doesn't Level-up. This game is more based on tactics, than brute strength. Unlike Dungeon Defenders, which came out almost in the same time-frame.
The music in the game is medieval but with a crazy tone to it. I like it.
Sometimes when the Warmage kills an Orc, The Warmage makes a sarcastic/hilarious statement. I can't give away what he says. Like I said, it would just ruin the fun.
It is important that you do not mute the Warmages voice. Because the story presents itself on flashbacks and what the Warmage says during gameplay.
It's a Short-and-Sweet game with a special twist to the story and the gameplay.
Orcs Must die! gets an ''above-great'' 9/10. I highly recommend this game.

I've played the game since Alpha and let me tell you this:
This game is everything an adventurer wants, EVERYTHING.
Exploration: 10/10
Multiple ways of ending quests, dungeons with unique layed out traps with randomised loot, different exploration rewards, ... I can't even sum up what kind of treat this game is for exploration. If you want to check every single nook, crack, barrel and crate you may and it sometimes even rewards you. If you want to go dig graves for loot you can if you try. The best part? Most exploration is optional, the only complaint is that some quests do require some thought, but thats what you want, right... right?
Combat: 9/10
It's a classic DnD styled turn system expanded to the smallest detail. You use AP which you generate each turn to do all of your actions, be it slashing, burning, zapping, teleporting, buffing, debuffing, etc... (find out the rest yourself!)
Fighting even takes places in a certain zone, so in multiplayer your partner could be shopping whilst you're fighting off the undead. It should be noted that when not in combat, there are no turns, you walk around and turns are taken on a timer if you're not in them.
This does cause minor exploitation as your partner sneaks around for 5 minutes whilst you stare at the enemy.
The game is also very unforgiving when it comes to making mistakes as you can ruin the entire fight by accidently clicking next to the enemy and run towards your grave.
Story: 7/10
Everything has a story, maybe not as intresting, maybe not as obvious, but its there. View quickly through it or read intensly, your choice.
The game also has a system where you persuade NPC's, enemies or even your own partner. This system is called Rock, Paper, Scissors. The upside of the system allows players to have their characters interact with eachother, be it through Reason, Charm or Intimitating. The downside is when it comes to the NPC's the outcome actually matters much more as it can stop you from obtaining loot or important quest details.

Highly recommended. I can easily say this is one of the greatest games I've ever played. A beautiful, serene masterpiece made with obvious love (something that seems to be rare out of a company like EA). Utterly engaging from start to finish, brilliant gameplay, a gorgeous art style, great level design and game feel, and
The parkour mechanics are polished and engaging; if you play this game, and play another game with a first-person perspective afterwards, you will try to vault over low walls, I can guarantee it. I feel like everything in this game supports a motif of flight (it most senses of the word) and freedom. This is a package where all elements come together to mutually support a brilliant centralized design, without obvious compromise; this feels like the reward EA gave DICE for being their Battlefield factory.
My only big criticism is with the uninspiring story, but this shouldn't bother you too much. I think the world itself tells a story far more engaging than the one directly conveyed. Apart from that, my minor gripes are with the relatively short length (although that's okay too, I really just wanted more), and the way the game can sometimes force you into combat, particularly later on (in some instances this is a lot of fun, but in other situations, particularly those with an arena-like structure, it can become tiresome and slightly frustrating).
But in any case, this game is great. Buy it and play it and EA might not be convinced to ruin the sequel by their stockholders ( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°).

Fight or flight: a physiological reaction that occurs in response to a perceived harmful event, attack, or threat to survival.
There, i just summarized the gameplay in Mirror's Edge. And the "simplicity" of it is perhaps the main strenght in this gloriously original game. You either fight, or flight(run). Or preferably both. It's as simple as that. And it will honestly take you quite a few tries overcoming both enemies and obstacles in your way. I've experienced my fair share of deaths, and especially when you first start out, it can all seem overwhelming. But with every death comes a lesson learned, and hopefully after a few tries you will manage to both run and fight seamlessly without any mistakes or hiccups. And when you accomplish this, it feels like you can take on the whole world(or at least the city's policeforce). There are multiple ways from A to B and the controls are solid(with a controller, never tried keyboard). When you're not being chased or bullets don't fly in your direction, you also get parts in the game where the road you must take isn't always as clear. Normally, you posess something called runner's vision, which visually guides you through the game in the form of the color red(red boxes, planks, doors). But some areas in the game unfolds like a puzzle. You stop up, think, do, die and retry. A welcoming break, in which you also can take into account the amazing visuals or beautifully crafted locations in the game.
Perhaps it is the visually stunning graphics/animations that is the main strenght? It took me quite a long time to finally play this game, i think its close to 3 years. And its too bad and clearly long overdue. The animations are quite smooth, from the fight sequences to the parkour element. The areas are intelligently crafted which in some cases reward your curiosity. And running from cops wielding assault rifles or helicopters with machineguns has never been so adrenaline pumping. Especially when you take leap of faiths and float through the air in what feels like an eternity, all while the sun is shining in your eyes.
Soundtrack is another major plus with this game, with a special mention going to the end sountrack. Overall the soundtrack enchances the gameplay and visuals of the game with a exhilarating sound which fills you  with adrenaline during some of the most intense chase sequences.
This game isn't without some flaws though. Albeit the story isn't necessarily bad, it't only enough there to keep you somewhat invested as you enjoy the other brilliant aspects of this game. The campaign is also quite short, in which i completed it in about 5 hours. Fear not though, as there are other gamemodes to keep you occupied, such as timetrial. The highest difficulty level also unlocks when you complete the game once, so that may inspire you to go for a round 2.
I'm not a fan of giving out a rating in terms of numbers, but i can definitely recommend this game. A truly innovative game in terms of gameplay and visuals(for its time), with an amazing soundtrack to boot. This game can be aquired dirt cheap, and give you an adrenaline kick in your otherwise uneventful life.

I absolutely have no regrets spending under $5 on this game! I will go through and list the positives and and negatives I found after playing this game for about an hour or so, a grain of salt is not provided but feel free to take one if you need to.
Graphics: 8  What do you expect, it's hand drawn on crumpled notebook paper and then animated! The kind of crap we dreamed of doing in Jr. High or High School.
Sound: 8 It is a light blippy and bubbly soundtrack and though I reside on the dark side of the spectrum, I can't help but wiggle and dance just a little bit from the overflowing and overwhelmingly happy music.  The sound effects are equally as happy and add to the overall experience.  I was expecting pew pew pew and got bloop bloop bloop.
Gameplay: 9  This is a top down shooter like Asteroids or Space Invaders.  I can see this becoming engrossing and completely addictive if you have a weakness for casual games.  While the gameplay isn't super face melting fast paced by any means, it is extremely anxiety inducing once you get passed The Leviathon boss.
Replayability: 10  So it is permadeath in the sense you only get one, maybe two chances if you have a shield.  The ability to custom create your own scribble ship allows you to play the same "map" over and over again and each play through is completely different.
So here come the negatives that I found.
-No coop multiplayer.  Couch coop for this game would make it 10x better!
-Not enough variety of weapons: This game needs paint cluster bombs, paint (flame) thrower, proximity mines, paint lasers, something...you get your basic bloop bloop gun and some targeting paint missles but in the hour or so I played the weapons are just more of the same, but faster.
-More backgrounds needed.  I love the fact that when you "destroy" a ship with your paint guns, it is added to the paper background you are playing on.  This only looks so cool for so long...variety is the spice of life.  I would love to see a few more notebooks or desks or tables etc added as backgrounds.  Maybe a bathroom stall wall or something :D
Overall Impression: HELL YES! for under $5 you get a casual game that keeps your interest, supports independent devs, and is an amazingly fun experience.  I look forward to seeing if the devs keep this game fresh and new feeling with updates.  Will this be my main game with 100s of hours, probably not.  Will this be a game I fall back on when other servers are down or when I am feeling casual. Oh yes! This has the potential to be a huge black hole of time, in the most positive sense of the phrase :D

What can I say, I want nothing more than to say this is a juvenile puzzle game with a cutesy story, and zero real plot development and terrible graphics and gameplay.
Most of that however is not true.
Yes, this game does look like it's aimed at the younger casual player, and yes, the story is sugar fried in honey, and the plot is merely a device to keep you playing the game... and yes - the graphics are by no means revolutionary...
But by the gods is this game addictive.
After playing the obligatory amount to formulate a review, I found myself determined to finish the game, which involves firstly 'Unlocking' one of four books of elements - cue an object-finding puzzle, which doesn't penalise you for being slow at, and it's just as well, because the puzzles are very intricate, and have several 'layers' of object mechanics. You may need to find an object to uncover a button which opens a chest which has part of another object inside - and so on. Once you've solved the puzzle and opened the book, you are faced with the task of collecting four 'cards' featuring a different mythical creature or race. You do this by playing two different puzzles - a series of 'spot the difference' games, and the main bulk of the game: a series of four puzzles whereby you must direct the flow of 'magic' to a given point by destroying groups of gems.
The plot is all by-the-by if you just want to play the puzzles, which is great, because the storytelling isn't exactly stellar. But the gameplay more than makes up for it.
I dare you not to become addicted to this game - and determined to keep playing until you finish the last book!

Killing Floor 2 is an improvement on a timeless classic. If you thought KF1 was a fun experience, you'll only have more fun with this one. If you haven't played the first one, you don't need to; KF2 is a completely standalone game and improves in every way. The first Killing Floor was originally a mod for Unreal Tournament 2004, and it definitely shows via clunkiness. That's all nonexistent in this game - Tripwire did a great job with making KF2 feel like it's a standalone game.
Killing Floor 2 has multiple different classes that utilize different weapons and abilities to kill zeds (not zombies, mind you) in a game of 1-6 players. The classes feel well balanced (aside from the insanely strong Berserker) and fun to use. Gameplay is really fluid, shooting and meleeing feels great and it gets really difficult and strategical really fast. It's unlike other zombie horde games, which I don't usually like, but KF2 is different.
You can play as different characters, all with their own tiny little backstories and personalities, like in KF1. Level design is great and there's a lot of maps, even more when you include Steam Workshop integration and modding. To top it all off, the game features an amazing metal soundtrack from various artists to headbang to while playing.
KF1 had a lot of DLC for characters and weapons, so I'm glad to see that Tripwire decided to stray away from those here. You buy the game, you get everything along with free future updates. Killing Floor 2 does have microtransactions with cases, skins and cosmetics, which I don't really care about, but they're never in the way and I don't mind them that much.
The game still gets updates with more content every once in a while, which is cool. It actually takes a lot of effort to get bored of shooting zeds in Killing Floor, which is something you can't say from most other horde mode games. I'd still recommend the first Killing Floor if you're looking for a more difficult and intense experience, although both games are far from casual.

4 Elements, as so many games centered around matching 3 or more same-colored stones, is a rather short and pretty much straightforward game. After every four levels, you'll get to play a short game of "Spot the difference", but that's pretty much all the excitement happening. Oh, and you get to search for objects before you open up another part of the game.
The plot of restoring four books of magic, so that the powers within are in balance again, are a nice little touch, but pretty much all there is to it. After 64 levels, the game is played through completely, and you have the choice of starting all over again. (I played the first 16 levels again to gain the last two achievements, but that's it - I'm done with this game.)
Overall, I wouldn't recommend the game unless you are really a match 3 fan, and find it funny to have a fairy at your side making you think of Navi. Granted, the fairy in this game is not as obnoxious, but not as helpful as Navi either. And that is a feat.
Done with the game, moving on to something more entertaining - at least I hope the next one will be more entertaining.

A good little tool but a bit limited as each application (game) needs to be modified at every change in application. Preferably this should have been kept in memory so you didnt have to manually change the settings from multi core applications from single core applications. Because of this it also does not differnciate from OS related programs like office or a browser etc to use a completly seperate core unless its something like twitch or other like program that the author has specifically enabled the capture of within CPUcores. So while its good it could be alot better with a little more effort by the author by allowing multiple per application configurations to be stored as well as individual executable core allocation.
There are a few complaints about performance drop I've read in the negative section of reviews I can only imagine that this is due to the drop in core resources when you isolate cores to applications, you also have to take into account that memory is no longer being flushed as well as each core will hold onto its own data as it prioritises its need, which is why you should only have one application running at a higher priority otherwise turn it off and let the OS delegate as per normal.

You round a corner and come to a pair of staircases. On the left is a red staircase going down and on the right is a blue staircase going up. You decide to take the red staircase on the left going down. You head through a corridor and round a few corners to find a pair of staircases. On the left is a red staircase going down and on the right is a blue staircase going up. This time you decide to take the blue staircase on the right going up. You head through a corridor and round a few corners to find a pair of staircases. Around and around you go and you can't seem to find anything but these two staircases. With resignation, you surrender to the puzzle, turn around, and try to head back. You round the corner and find yourself in a corridor you have never seen before.
"Antichamber" is a zen puzzle game. It may mess with your head. A lot. However, it is remarkably relaxed about messing with your head.

You are even rewarded for hitting the dead end with some words of encouragement. Then you can just go back and try something different. No worries. There is absolutely no pressure to complete puzzles in time. You are free to take everything at your own pace.

This is fun for one game, because you do pretty much cover all the content in a single one. The main premise is you build a capital city, then can proceed to build stuff in that city or build settlers to establish other cities. You can trade and war with other AI countries, or play online and work with or against other people doing the same thing. All the while you're doing this, you can have your people research new technologies. And what you choose to research impacts the units or buildings you have. So you can be the guy who goes straight for gunpowder, or you can explore all the scientific ones and build a spaceship.
On the topic of spaceships and gunpowder, those are two of the five ways to win a game. Scientific, Domination, Diplomatic, Time, and Cultural. A science victory is obtained when you are the first to build a space shuttle. Domination occurs when you capture all players' capital cities. Diplomatic happens when you are voted the pinnacle of creation by the UN. Time occurs after the year 2050 rolls around, giving the victory to whoever has the greatest score, a mix of troop and city and resource count. The cultural victory has something to do with monuments I think, but since it never happens its not something to worry about.
The game is pretty much exactly what it looks like in the screenshots. My only complaint is that you can't have multiple troops in one hexagon, which was not true for the previous civilization game. This makes coordinating attacks with a lot of troops more difficult than it has to be.

It's pretty good I guess.  I would give this game an 8 out of ten.  As far as strategy games go, Civ 5 does fairly well.  Early game is very strong and enjoyable, quick progression and visible progress toward what you want your Civ to become.  Mid game you feel like a real king deciding the fate of everyone around you (until you get to king difficulty) while still dealing with challenges.  Late game however is a bit dull, you will spend the majority of your time waging massive wars and micromanaging 30 or so units because you want to make sure everything happens at the right time.  City management will become somewhat of a hassle and each turn will take a few minutes rather than 60 seconds.  Yet, there is something addictive about how Sid Meier set Civ 5 up.  Each time you start you know how you like to play and you try to overcome a few more of your faults, and even though each difficulty hop has a near insurmountable learning curve and may very well be impossible at higher difficulties, keeps you coming back for more.  Many nights have been spent lying to myself about when I will get off.  10 more turns, oh there is a new resource I need.  Well I guess I'll expand my territory out there over the next 20 turns and take that then I'll trade with Byzantium and call it a night.  Oh but Atilla just called my Boy Gandhi four eyes, heck yeah I'll declare war!  100+ turns go by teasing myself with the promise of sleep at the end of a never ending line of side quests.  Only play this if you have time to spare or self discipline of a monk.  Else you wont be sleeping anytime soon.

I really liked this game... on my first playthrough.
Puzzles include 4 FROG (fractured object) screens, 16 spot-the-difference screens, and 64 match-3 levels.
The main match-3 levels are different from any other genre game I have played.  I was expecting a classic Bejeweled-style game, but instead of swapping tiles or sliding rows, you form chains by clicking and dragging a path through adjacent matching symbols.  The paths do not have to form a straight line, you can zig-zag any direction except diagonally (for all the explanation the game gives, they never actually tell you this).
As the game progresses, you will encounter obstacles such as ice, immovable blocks, narrow passages, and rocks; however, you will also gain access to rechargeable tools that help you overcome these obstacles.  There is a timer, but chances are you will not need to worry about it until 3/4 of the way through the game, and even if you fail you just restart the level with no penalties.  The levels are increasingly challenging, but never frustrating or boring.  In fact, I found I enjoyed the later levels more because they forced you to use a bit of strategy to complete.
I thought it was a nice touch that each of the four elements have a slightly different level aesthetic, which helps keep the levels feeling fresh.
As great as the gameplay was, though, there are things that destroy the replay value:
- The story is cheesy.  Although, that's to be expected for this genre.
- The chatty fairy.  She was fine for the first playthrough, providing necessary instructions and tips to help you learn and understand the game.  Subsequent playthroughs, though, are a different story - her dialogue cannot be skipped or turned off, so you will have to suffer through "Pop-Ups: The Game" every single time.  This is annoying if you just want to sit down and replay a few levels casually.
- There is no option to select your starting level.  Whether you want to challenge yourself by replaying a tricky stage, or whether you are just trying to go for a specific achievement, your only choices are to continue from your last autosave or to completely start over.  Again, this is fine for the first playthrough, but an unlockable freeplay mode would have been appreciated.
- The achievements are a bear to get.  It took me 1.5 playthroughs to get "Overachiever" because it is partially luck-dependent, and "Quick as a Flash" took 11 angry hours: The first FROG screen does not count toward the achievement because the fairy's dialogue and tutorial eat up so much of your time, so you are left with only three chances per game to earn it (the FROGs for the fire key, the air key, and the water key).  Basically, this means you will need to play through 16 match-3 levels and 4 spot-the-difference puzzles before you even reach the first applicable fractured object screen, and you will be continuously forced to deal with the fairy's "helpfulness."  If you miss the 90-second timeframe on the fire key puzzle, there is no way to just try it again because the game autosaves just AFTER you complete it.  You will either need to restart the game, or hope that you have better luck with the air key.  Regardless, you are looking at another 16 levels and 4 puzzles before getting a second opportunity to win this achievement.
If there had been either a freeplay mode, or a way to turn off the fairy, I might have given this game a 9.5/10 because the gameplay is solid, and it would have been incredibly replayable.  As is, though, I would have to give it a 6.5/10.

Killing Floor 2 is an improvement on a timeless classic. If you thought KF1 was a fun experience, you'll only have more fun with this one. If you haven't played the first one, you don't need to; KF2 is a completely standalone game and improves in every way. The first Killing Floor was originally a mod for Unreal Tournament 2004, and it definitely shows via clunkiness. That's all nonexistent in this game - Tripwire did a great job with making KF2 feel like it's a standalone game.
Killing Floor 2 has multiple different classes that utilize different weapons and abilities to kill zeds (not zombies, mind you) in a game of 1-6 players. The classes feel well balanced (aside from the insanely strong Berserker) and fun to use. Gameplay is really fluid, shooting and meleeing feels great and it gets really difficult and strategical really fast. It's unlike other zombie horde games, which I don't usually like, but KF2 is different.
You can play as different characters, all with their own tiny little backstories and personalities, like in KF1. Level design is great and there's a lot of maps, even more when you include Steam Workshop integration and modding. To top it all off, the game features an amazing metal soundtrack from various artists to headbang to while playing.
KF1 had a lot of DLC for characters and weapons, so I'm glad to see that Tripwire decided to stray away from those here. You buy the game, you get everything along with free future updates. Killing Floor 2 does have microtransactions with cases, skins and cosmetics, which I don't really care about, but they're never in the way and I don't mind them that much.
The game still gets updates with more content every once in a while, which is cool. It actually takes a lot of effort to get bored of shooting zeds in Killing Floor, which is something you can't say from most other horde mode games. I'd still recommend the first Killing Floor if you're looking for a more difficult and intense experience, although both games are far from casual.
