All in all, Block'Hood is an amazing and innovative concept for a game. It's a shame the developers are completely unaware of what makes thier game good.
At first blush, this game might appear to be a city-building game, like SimCity. You have blocks representing houses, shops, trees, etc. that you put together to form a city. However, I would argue that this game has more in common with games like Factorio than SimCity, because of how its resource-management system works.
Instead of these blocks costing anything to place, they require certain resources as inputs, and produce certain outputs, all at a constant rate. There's a variety of resources, and to complete the challenge maps, you have to build production chains of certain blocks to make enough resources. Unbalance your resources and things will "decay", a very nasty condition that you want to avoid. The core decision problem at the heart of the game is what blocks to use to balance out inputs and outputs, and how to structure them to maximize your limited space.
So if you're familiar with other games that have a heavy focus on resource management, this should sound familiar. From my experiences, however, the developers have never heard of this kind of game, because they refuse to follow most of its conventions, and continously weaken the core of thier gameplay with each update.
For one, the game does everything in its power to obscure how the inputs and outputs are currently functioning. They let you see if you are at a net loss or gain of a resource, but it's in different units then what the building will show you when you inspect them. Production of a block may be altered at random through "world events", in amounts generally unspecified beforehand, meaning your production chain may be decayed by things happeneing outside of your control. The UI puts a priority on the amount of the resource you have, rather than the rate of the resource, obscuring the real decision you're trying to make.
I'd say the biggest example of this is the "Zero Footprint" challenge. In it, you have to procude a certain amount of a resource... And none of any other resource. This should be a tricky challenge where Block'Hood really shines- You should be able to analyze the inputs and outputs of everything, and feel proud when you've completed the production chain that balances itself out. In reality, however, it's an impossible task. The UI is bad at telling you how things balance in reality, and it becomes a massive, unpredictable issue with ease, forcing you to intentionally cause decay to drain excess resources. It's easily one of the least pleasent challenges, despite the fact that it should be testing you on all your Block'Hood skills, rather than frustrating you to no end.
(A sidenote: The choice of blocks you have to play with seem... Oddly dualistic. You either have "gentrified neighborhood" or "polluted hellscape" blocks, and that's it. Either "Yoga Studios" or "Garment Sweatshops". Most challeneges end up with you making a 'hood that you're sure has a history of sharply rising rent and middle-class white people pushing the poor out of apartment buildings.)
The game has promise. It really does. The concept of a city building game that relies on resource management rather than unit simulation is endlessly fascinating to me. But there's a long road to go before the good parts of the game outshine the many flaws. What makes the game fun is the resource management and the challenges, but the developers seem focused on making it more like a city simulation. I enjoyed this game, but I cannot reccomend it at this time- There are simple changes it could make to create a truly great game, but I don't see those changes happening in the near future.

I was very undecided when I bought this game. I actually refunded it after buying it and trying it, but then bought it back after realizing how charming it is. You get to build awesome pieces of infrastructure and get to choose how to balance it. Will you go green or double down on green? (Yes I know I am quoting SimCity) The game has its quirks, such as having to turn off decay (if you want to, anyway) everytime you load up a world. Annoying, but not awful. Another thing is that you can't look inside of your huge eco-skyscraper if something goes wrong. There is no "layer view" or anything like that, and that would be very helpful. I would also be very happy if something like roads were added, with cars and such, and that in the "world mode", your "Block'hoods" would be able to interact with each other and you could merge them into one big city. As for the "decay off" bug, I know a little bit about coding and I think it might be from a variable not being passed from function to function or class to class. Possibly a simple fix. Overall, when you look past its quirks and flaws, It's a charming, relaxing , fun little not-really-city-builder but more of an infrastructure and architecture builder. You should support the developers by buying it so they can push out more updates to make the game even better than it already is.

This game is my favourite part of the Anno series, - the microeconomics - extracted and presented in an aestetically appealing style. The puzzle mode is just the right amount of difficult. I'm also very pleased with how it runs on my old laptop. It's snappy and feels smooth and nice.
Overall, extremely good purchase that I will keep enjoying for a while. A must for people who like city builders, microeconomics and cute puzzles. I can't wait to see what future updates bring!

I REALLY wanted to like this game.
However, after 6 hours of play, I just can't take it anymore, sadly.
The beginning of the game was fun, the tutorial dungeon was fun, everything in general was FUN. But then you get to the first town, and it becomes one of the most boring gaming experiences I've ever had. First, you'll have to turn off all the friggin' sound because the NPCs keep repeating their lines OVER AND OVER again and you can't focus on reading the text, which there is ALOT of. I wish it would grey out the options you've already read, since most NPC's just repeat themselves.
The dialogue is good, but it's too humorous. Having humor once or twice here and there is good, but this game has a joke EVERYWHERE, seriously. It gets old, fast, especially since most of the jokes aren't that funny.
The combat and music, are both excellent. Top notch turn based combat. I wish it would tell a bit more clearly if an obstacle is in the way when using ranged attacks, however (maybe make the aiming line red instead of yellow?). The combat is VERY unforgiving. One wizard can stun lock your entire party, which in my opinion is kind of BS.
The thing that made me not recommend this is the PLAIN STUPID walls. The game will LITERALLY BLOW YOU UP if you go somewhere you are not supposed to go. I tried to dig a grave in the main town, and my characters exploded. I hadn't saved in over an hour. FML. No, not FML, but FTG. F this game. You don't do that to players. I tried to dig the grave twice, with my characters separeted by 100 meters. Nope, both still died.
I feel very... sad... for wasting 40euros on this product, and I'll play this again tonight while drunk to see if anything changes. Probably not, but I've been wrong plenty of times.
EDIT: They've fixed a number of things already, which is great. The main thing being the repeating NPC dialogue, AND they muted it completely when you are talking to someone. Amazing!
I'm still not going to recommend the game, but it's going in the right direction. After they explain why my characters just die randomly, then I'll reconsider.
Currently, I've been making progress in the story. The quirky dialogue is still an issue, albeit a personal taste one. I might dislike it, but YOU might love it.
Here's hoping for more updates which improves the game!

I won't repeat all the accolades others have already stated here, but I do want to state one thing about expectations:  this is a "roguelike" game, and therefore "permadeath" is part of the deal.  That means, no saving and then reloading if you die - if you die, you die and your save file dies with you!  You can, of course, circumvent this by simply backing up your save file periodically, but that kind of defeats the whole purpose of a roguelike.  I only mention this because some people don't expect this, and think it "sucks" and that the designer was lazy or something...not true.  This is part of the design of the game, so just make sure you have the appropriate expectations.  (As mentioned, you can cheat your way around it anyway, though I don't recommend doing so - part of the fun of the game is the urgency and tension created by the danger and risk of not being able to re-do anything.)  Anyway, that said, this is a terrifically addicting roguelike that takes a very different tack on the genre.  It has plenty of variety and it's hard to put down once you're deeply involved in a session.  For $10 it's a great deal, and when it's on sale for $5 it's an unbeatable bargain.  If you like roguelikes and sci-fi, this is a must-have.

It's a space roguelike/strategy/simulation. While there is a simple story to follow, it's more about exploring the galaxy and seeing all the cool stuff you can find/unlock. While a typical game will take 2-4 hours, that only covers about 4% of the experience because of all the random encounters and secrets to find. Each ship has a semi-random assortment of weapons and systems which keeps each fight interesting. With each new playthrough, you can learn new tactics and evolve your strategy over time.
The game is deceptively simple as there are a limited number of actions you can take at any given time. However, FTL is one of the few games that really lets you employ unique and creative strategies with the tools you have at your disposal. For example, each room has an oxygen level. Venting your ship's oxygen supply can deter intruders and extinguish fires, but it makes it "uncomfortable" for your crew. At any point, you can stop time with the space bar, letting you examine the scenario and do any commands you need to. This lets you try strategies that require split-second timing and respond to threats with lightning speed.
Just as it says in the trailer, you can be the captain of your ship, and FTL executes this remarkably well. The level of decision-making you have lets you apply your own personal play style and strategies. Every decision you make matters for the fate of your crew. You must assess risk vs. reward with each encounter. Ambitious ventures into uncharted nebulas can reap huge rewards or end in death when an ion storm takes out your oxygen.
You'll find yourself getting attached to your crew members and your ship. This creates an immersive experience and makes all the events happening in the universe seem important. There is a backstory behind each encounter that provides a little insight into the culture and the everyday happenings of the game's citizens. Each alien race has a definite personality that you have to take into account during interactions with them. Interacting with benevolent Engi usually turns out well, however wily Slug creatures are often less than truthful.
FTL is organized very well. Each node/'encounter' is about 1-5 minutes long, there's about 20 nodes per sector, and there are eight sectors. There are many meaningful choices you make along the way, as 'store' or 'distress' nodes are well marked and each sector has an overall theme/alien race associated with it. And, for the entire game, you're being chased by the overwhelming wave of Rebel ships. This gives you an experience that is fluid and fast-paced, but gives you the freedom to think and make your own choices. FTL is totally 100% gameplay, there's no cutscenes or cinematic elements that you have to sit through. (However, you really should read the encounter description or else you might miss something important or make a regrettable mistake).
The art style is really well done. The backgrounds and soundtrack really fit the mood of the game. The graphics are pixelated, yes, but there's a lot of detail and care put into it. It's not 'retro for the sake of retro', but a style that's consistent and perfect for this type of game, emphasizing readability and clarity over flashy or photorealistic visuals.
If you look at screenshots of FTL, every one has a spaceship or two and some HUD icons around the outside. However, the amount of information they pack into every frame is amazing. The combination of audio cues and visual alerts keep you constantly informed without overwhelming you. Because every second counts, you can easily lose if you split your attention, but the interface is really good at showing you exactly what you need to know. Allowing you to stop time at will helps as well.
Seems like a bit of a lame topic, but it really needs to be said. It's such a small dev studio but it produced an experience that really feels 'complete'. You don't feel like anything's missing or done poorly. That's more than you can say for even big-budget games these days. Whether or not you enjoy the game, you must at least notice that the game is pretty much flawlessly made. It's detailed and nothing seems out of place.
It's harder than most games even on Easy mode, a real challenge that doesn't always give you a clear path to success. The randomness doesn't help this at all. Going in, you have to be prepared to build up a ship you think is 'good' only to have it crash and burn in the next encounter. The defining moment for most people is if they give up before they start realizing the more nuanced strategies and tactics you have at your disposal. However, it is possible to win (even with some of the weaker ships you unlock).
This turns some people away from the game (if not the entire genre). There are 'unwinnable' scenarios, especially if you pick a bad ship and it's early on in the game. However, if you get good, you can survive in any ship at least to the last sector. This is not a game that tells you a predefined story or sets you off on a path to a destination. It's a simulation with a bunch of random events, and really random stuff will happen to you in space.
You can only have one game saved at a time, and if you lose, the save is deleted. It's a system that fits with the rest of the game, but can be annoying. Allowing for multiple save states would ruin the randomness of the game, so if anything it's a necessary evil.
Though much of the game is based on exploration, there are time constraints that force you to move forward rather than explore around the entire sector. Some nodes are just impractical to reach because you're being chased by rebel forces. You have to balance your curiousity for the game's universe with your need to stay alive. This is a bit of a struggle because the game shows you so much awesome stuff but doesn't let you visit all of it in one playthrough.
While there is a lot of content in the game, there are some nodes that are rather empty, or just have a token Auto-Assault Scout to fight. Almost every ship is unique due to the variety of weapons and configurations available, but many of the random encounters are pretty similar. Recognizing some of the same events occuring over multiple playthroughs can break immersion a little. These filler nodes can be helpful though after a tough encounter if they give you a break from the action. (e.g. ship is still on fire and you jumped away from an asteroid field and you have intruders)
Overall I highly recommend this game.

This is not an exceptionally long game. You can beat it and earn all the achievements in rather short order (my play time includes needing to start over again roughly halfway through due to computer issues). Yet, it's well worth getting on sale. Basically, it's a match-three game in which you attempt to create a path for yourself through each level, using power-ups to assist you as needed. Longer chain matches lead to ever bigger explosions, making your work easier and faster. There are some fun twists to some of the levels, each world has its own feel to it, and it really is rather relaxing. To be honest, there were very few levels in the game that I was not able to beat the first time without running out of time, and none that took me more than two tries, so the degree of challenge might not be quite enough for some, but I view it as a positive. While beating the game is faster that way, it is also rendered largely free of the frustration that comes with countless deaths on the same level. Overall, if you like casual/match 3 games at all, then this is one to check out.
It does seem fair to warn you of some negatives before you do so though. First, and most annoying, while there are hidden object and spot the difference style mini-games that you play at regular intervals to advance further in the game, the images are in rather low resolution, making what you're meant to spot rather difficult to see much of the time. Fortunately, there's a hint feature and no time limit, nor is there any penalty for random clicking, so when you can't see something these levels are still easily beatable. Also, as a fairly unimportant negative to the game, all the story elements that go along with the gameplay are not exactly going to fill you with excitement, if you care about such things in this kind of game. At least you'll now be a bit aware of what to expect though.

Mini games and colour maching, the game.
introduction:
To start out with, you are introduced to the story, wich involve the elements running amok in a magical world. We are told to restore peace to each element; earth, wind, fire, and water. On the menu screen we can see all the levls representet by books and gems, and we get an idea of how long this game is going to take.
Therefore I felt the introduction to be really boring. It shows the whole game from the get go, and there are no surprises along the way. Then again for a game like this, you would not expect much more than that. I still fell like they should wither have focused more on the story or less, since it keeps domping lore on us, and you quicly forget there is a story all together.
Gamplay:
The gamepaly is split up into 3 diffrent games, where one acts as the main game, while the others are mini-games. The main game is very simple, match coloured blocks in a chain, in order to make sand dissaper. When the sand is gone, the water you need to get to the end of the stage can continue to flow. After you let the water flow to the end, you win the level. The gameplay is really relaxing and well made, since you cab conect more coulors in order to make bigger combos that can be so satesfuing
The levels have diffrent obsticles along the way that can block the way to completion, these items is for eksample rocks.
The levels are getting harder along the way, but you also unlock power-ups, that will help you to remove opsticles and reach the goal. The power-ups fells really overpowered at times, and can easily make the game a win for you, nearly every single time. This was a huge letdown for me, since I never really felt challenged. The powerups can be things like changing around blocks and blowing up paths.
The two mini games are done, in order to unlock new levels. The first one is a "spot the diffrence" game, where you click a place on a picture, to spot the flaw on the other picture.
The other part is a "find the objects" game, where you must spot things hidding in the background. All the games are controlled by simple mouse-clicking., and it fells rather slow and now and again. The overall games are not boring as such, but it quikly get`s repetative.
Charecters:
Well there are only two charecters in this game, and they are both not important. This game is clearly not story driven, but in my opinion, they did not need to include these charecters to complete a already unnesesary story. The charecters are a wizard, which we never see after the starting scren, and a fariy which guides you throughout the game. There is not much to say to this part, so let`s move on.
Visuels:
The game looks ok, but I really did not exspect anything brillaint to be honest. The overall visuesl in-game are accually pretty fluid, and looks fine. But when you do anything outside the main game, the grafics fells weaker and more bluery. It`s hard to explain, but I felt there was something off.
Sound:
The music is acually ok in this game. I fellt it was a nice thing to include, and the diffrent themes are acually not that bad. Other then that, there are not much to say to the sounds other than the start theme will blast your speakers out, it is so loud!
Story:
So the story is pretty basic as said, clear all levels to controle all elements. The boring part is that the story really has no twists and turns, instead it fells like it only is there to give you a reason to why there is 4 main levels.
The other mini-games really has some cool story. Not so much the hidden object part. But when you complete the spot the diffrence game. You see the real picture, and get`s the lore of the charecter on it. This was some intresting reading, and felt like a nice inclusion to the game, and the lore of the establist world. I would just wish they acually used these charecters, and made the game a bit more alive.
But this is also where I don't really understand why they would create so mutch lore to a matching game. it feels really unessesary.
Conclusion:
The game is far from a masterpice, and it really is just another time killer game. This dose not mean I dislike the game at all, I am just saying you can find better games of this type out there. I completed the story and it really is just a congratiolation screen and nothing more. But if you are looking for a simple game to sit down and play, this one could be a nice choice.

UPDATED REVIEW:
So, Grim Dawn has been finally Released and I beated the game, I am very happy with this game, TQ Devs did a great job in TQ and GD.
Grim Dawn in the Release had, and maybe still has, some issues with AMD gpus but also my NVIDIA card burned to death in a area that I don't wan't to spoil but be ware of Mid Act 2 Side Area.
It has a controller support, i haven't really tested but my Wireless Xbox 360 Controller was automatically dected.
Now let's talk about my impressions about loot and Gameplay,The Loot might be better than Diablo 3 for you but for me, who played Diablo 3 Trial to level 15, It was way better.
The Game has 4 difficulities which 2 are given by default and 2 are given when you complete the game on that Difficulity for Example:Normal,Veteran->Elite->Ultimate(yes those are the 4 difficulities).
If you play on Normal you will play like a normal ARPG but in Veteran you will get much better loot than Normal, also the monsters are a bit difficult for Casters, for me a tank self healer, it was easy to defeat every boss.
The World is very big and it might get bigger(I saw some fields on the map very far from the towns and in Beta there was a Area that got cutted).
Gameplay wise, it's a ARPG which you control your character with your mouse and has 1-0(10) Skill hotkeys and LMB,RMB, also it has an additional quickbar by pressing Y,also like i said you will love loot in the final difficulities, though it might get borring finding the legendaries you want.
Conclusion:The game has a lot of quest to offer; 1 endless dungeon for loot; 4 difficulities,which in 2 of those you have to start over its like NG+ don't worry you won't be naked but you might be if you didn't prepare for Ultimate or Elite, hehe, Anyway I think this game is worth the money and if you want to play their old games, buy TQ(you might notice it's not made by Crate Entertaiment. Crate Ent. is the newest TQ company that has old members of TQ company)

Xcom came to my library in the strangest way... I was in the Warhammer 40k: Chaos Gate remake forum in the community when someone said XCOM had similarities with CG, at first i didnt put a lot of attention to it, but later in the infamous summer sale (Thank you Steam...sarcasm btw i saw a great discount and took the opportunity to research the ame a little bit...
Now i have been playing it like theres no tomorrow, its a real delight for turn based strategy lovers like myself, heres my humble view on the good stuff and the annoying stuff:
Good Stuff
- Good Graphics and scenery
- Gameplay is simple and fluid
- AI is a ♥♥♥♥♥ sometimes...yes a good stuff
- The HQ management and item progression has a lot of variety
- Customization for Squads is awesome as well as the promotion scale
- Lots of sidemissions and you choose when to continue the main campaign
- The money management needs some thinking, otherwise you can bankrupt the xcom project
- Camera rotation, angles and voice acting is great
Not so good stuff...more like annoying
Frankly there are no such things i considered bad, more like annoying details:
- Soldiers can panic and sometimes while they are scared they shoot friends
- Personally i would prefer more story background of the beginning of the alien invasion...maybe xcom the bureau: declassified has it, i dont know
- Sometimes a % of a success shot its not accurate with the reality of covered enemies or own squad
- Saving and loading needs a simpler method...come on its a turn based game...basic.
Overall its a terrific game, if i had known about it earlier i would be replaying it at this moment, highly addictive and frustrating too, which is a good thing...sometimes when in a single turn the enemy crushes you and the last saving point is 3 missions back..its just lovely

So before I even get started, at the time of this review, this game is in early access. THAT MEANS IT AIN'T DONE YET! So just bear that in mind. Now, that being said, this game actually has a bit of a pedigree behind it. This game is a dungeon-crawling, action based rpg much in the vein of Diablo, Path of Exile, etc. Now if you've seen any game footage of Grim Dawn already, you may be thinking "Hmm, this gameplay and talent interface sure seems familiar". Well there is in fact a reason for that. A few years back, there was an action rpg based very much in ancient mythology called "Titan Quest". Several of the original developers from TQ are now working on this game. Much like Titan Quest, this game has what I would describe as a "Hybrid" class system. Meaning your character starts as a blank slate, then after your first few levels you get to choose your class specialization. A few more levels down the line, however, you get to pick ANOTHER talent specialization, merging the two into a hybrid class (ex: If you start as an Occultist, and then merge it with Demolitionist, you will become a Pyromancer).
The game also has a unique blend of dark age/black powder technology with a sort of Grim, Victorian aesthetic, which I personally really dig. Although the game still isn't technichally finished, I feel I can safely recommend it seeing as the developers behind it have some credible history in the genre, and the game still feels functional in its current state.

First up. I have never played a strategy game that I really liked. I got this for free when I pre-ordered Bioshock Infinite, along with Civ 5 on GmG. I tried Civ 5 first, but really couldn't get into it at all. So I am only now giving this game a fair chance. I literally said to my best friend that this was the last strategy game that I was going to play if I didn't like this one.
This game though...This game is great! I can't fault it so far. It sort of feels like a game of chess in a lot of ways. Nice graphics and art style too. Actually, the visuals and music remind me of Deus Ex, which is great. It sounds like the same composer to me.
There are also a lot of familiar voices, which is actually kind of distracting, because I am trying to figure out where I know the voice from and not concentrating on what they are saying...The council guy sounds like the narrator from Screenjunkies 'Honest Trailers' lol (It IS him!) :D
Haha, and I guessed the other one right too! It's the Dharma Initiative guy from LOST! :D
Ha! again! It is the Deus Ex Human Revolution composer too! :D
Anyway, the gameplay and strategy elements are very engaging. You need to plan your moves and take good advantage of cover while getting your squad into position.
Then there are squad member promotions, weapons upgrades etc. which offer some interesting choices. The engineering and research aspects are very interesting too. You need to prioritise what to develop, research, build etc.
At certain points you have to choose where to go and who to help, which causes panic levels to go up in the regions you don't help. So you have to manage panic levels too.
There is a lot going on here, a lot of re-playability, and very satisfying gameplay. I am finding it quite addictive so far and I am glad that I have finally found a strategy game that I like. This is definitely helped by the way the game is designed and the intuitive, easy to learn UI, which is a big reason why I haven't liked other strategy games that I have played.
So yeah, very cool game so far.

I do mostly recommend that you play this game. The story line is decent, drop kicking the zombies is fun, all of the free running mechanics are fun, and the coop is pretty fun too. I DO NOT recommend playing the Be the Zombie mode. It is horribly imbalanced towards the human side, despite numerous requests to the devs for balancing. The human players can counter just about everything the zombie player can do. The human players can get more life than the zombie, as well as two/three shot them with any melee weapon (or one shot with the drop attack thing). Zombie have to hit human players with the EXTREMELY slow claw attack far too many times in order to kill them. The tackle and ground pound abilities can deal moderate damage IF YOU CAN EVEN LAND THEM. The newest update and the new DLC add-ons allow the zombie to become EVEN WEAKER by choosing to "mutate" (level down willingly) at a chance to earn new abilities. Mutating, however, removes ALL of your hard earned skills and makes the scales tipped entirely in the human's favor yet again. So over all, the game is great, just don't be the zombie. You won't win and you won't have fun.

I am not often writing recommendations, but for this gem I got to. Larian Studios have done a fantastic job in bringing out a game true to the golden age of CRPG. What you get with Divinity Original Sin is a mix of Baldur's Gate and the original Fallout. Attention to detail is fantastic, although the text elements might sometimes get a bit too heavy for some of you. The combat system is dead on right for me, with a good mix of tactical elements, decision making and choices on how to best approach an enemy. The story is deep and you have plenty of well designed side quests to keep you happy four countless hours. I have the habbit of taking it slow and explore every corner of the enviroment and I can tell you, it is a blast exploring in this beautifully crafted world. Divinity gives you various options on how to approach quests or areas and you are not necessarily bound to have specific character classes with you in order to solve or explore specific areas. In most group RPGs I try to have at least one rouge class character with me (although I do not necessarily prefer it), just to be able to open every chest or get into every location. Larian Studios has managed to prvide access to many areas or access to various situations without depending too much on specific character classes. Just to give you one example, I was surprised to find out that after using my rouge to unlock a door to an abandoned house I desperately wanted to get into, I could have broken down the door with a character that had enough strength or, after managing to get in, I saw that there was another secret entrance through a well in the countryside. Allaround a well designed game!

Divinity Original Sin is a game for those of us who fondly remember old CRPGs such as Planescape: Torment, The Ultima series ( NOT 9!!!) and the old Gold Box D&D games, and heck even Bard's Tales 1-3 ( Not the hysterical remake ).
I must admit that as an older gamer I was salavating at the chance to play a no training wheels hold your hands and powder your bottom style old school RPG.  Sadly that's just what I got.  Now let me expand upon this before people think I don't like the game.
First off let me just say that D:OS is likely the best isometric PC RPG made since Planescape Torment.  In fact I prefer it to Baldur's Gate 1 & 2, which is saying a lot since My name is in the credits of those two great games.  However having said all that, the new era of gaming has poisened my mind.  For anyone who has played the Witcher series or Dragon Age origins your in for a big surprise.  Namely you going to be surprised at just how much those other games hold you hands and pat you on the back.  D:OS is a HARDCORE CRPG.  Most likely you will end up with several profiles once you learn how everything workls.  Technically any class combo will work, however your going to learn through trial and error what works for your playstyle and what doesn't.
This game is fantastic if and only if you have the patience and mindset to play a game that harkons back to the 1980's - 1990's style of CRPGs.  If your looking for a diablo, sacred, divine divinty style game TURN BACK NOW.  Those games are for hyper people where as this game is more akin to playing Chess while reading a Fantasy Novel at the same time.
Here is where things get weird.  I've been playing The Witcher 2♥♥♥♥♥of kings lately and after playing D:OS I can say this :
I have more fun playing TW2AoK.
I think D:OS is a better game.
???
See what I mean.  D:OS despite what I just said IS fun to play, very much so.  It's just a different type of fun.  Kind of like this :  D:OS is like Final Fantasy Tactics + Disgaea + Planescape Torment.  It's a Strategy RPG as much as it is a CRPG.  Baldur's gate was just a CRPG since any strategy you had was destroyed thanks to bad pathing as a result of that game being psuedo turn based with invisible dice rolls wrapped up in what appeared to be real time.  D:OS however is TURN BASED as in you take turns and time stops while your turn is decided.  Much like FFT and Disgaea.
Should you buy this game?  I . . . .Don't . . . . . Know. . . . .?
Sadly I think a lot of people who think they enjoy this type of game will confuse this game with Baldur's Gate where as this game plays more like Fallout 1 & 2 only slower and better.
If I had to describe this game in three words, they would be Fun, Addicting, Frustrating.

Like it's predecessor, Killing Floor 2 is a wave based gorefest even gladiators would be envious of. With superb graphics, and many customization options, this a game you'll always come back to. The dev team is very active in the community, however, the player base could improve. Unlike many other shooters, each perk class has a role to fill in a match, and all too often two or more teamates will not fill their role, nor do they understand key gameplay mechanics that are essential to a successful map clear. I.E. The medic won't be healing, or a teamate will enrage a scrake and then leave it for somebody else to deal with. Or teamates will not take down the larger zeds when they appear and leave them up to be a death sentence later. Too often you will be vote kicked if you try to explain this to call of duty fanboys. I love the game and have been a fan since Killing Floor 1's release, but I'd love to see a ranking system in effect down the road to weed out all the terrible players that one must deal with every other match.

I did some benchmarking with CPUCores & GameMode on reddit, i'll just post the full text below:
I wanted to test the effects Windows 10 Game Mode and the utility CPUCores have on a CPU limited game on a weak CPU, and i chose Hitman 2016 because I have it installed, it has a benchmark showing off a real level and it pushes the CPU hard.
I had a couple programs running in the background on a second monitor:
Telegram, Whatsapp, Discord,
Musicbee playing music,
Chrome with 3 active tabs, one of which being
, which i had set to automatically scroll down through during each test
Excel with the worksheet below
Steam, GOG Galaxy, F.lux, Rivatuner, OneDrive
I tested DX12, DX12 with Game Mode, DX12 with CPUCores, DX12 with Game Mode & CPUcores, DX12 with CPUCores & disabled Game Bar (to test for overhead caused by it), DX11, DX11 with Game Mode & CPUCores
Hardware:
AMD A8-7600 @ Stock, 16GB 1600mhz DDR3, RX 470 @ Stock
I used the integrated benchmark, always completely relaunching the whole game between runs to make sure everything was properly applied. I also used the settings i use to play the game regularly, just with disabled vsync.
Here are the results:
FPS:
Frames:
I don't think the minimum FPS are helpfull, as in each run the 2nd frame was a big hitch as you can see in the full reports here:
We can see that regular DX12 offers an increase in Avg FPS of ~17% over regular DX11,
DX12 boosted with Game Mode & CPUCores even ~19% over DX11 boosted.
Game Mode increases DX12 Avg FPS by ~27%, CPUCores by ~35%, and both together by ~36%.
Disabling the Game Bar did not make a difference
I might update this at some point with a more detailed analysis of each run's frametimes, they are in each run's report in the OneDrive folder above, to see if there are differences in regards to FPS spikes
/UPDATE
I am currently using an AMD A8-7600 CPU, and initially tested this program with just the integrated GPU, and noticed much more stable performance in CSGO & Bad Company 2, with much fewer FPS dips.
Now i added an AMD RX 470 and tested BF1, where this program also gives a noticeable boost, going from 45 fps to 54 fps in a cpu limited scene in the singleplayer. (this was while origin was busy installing the rest of BF1)
I must add that i generally have a lot of other apps such as messengers, music players & a browser running in the background, which is why i see such a noticeable improvement.
If you already have a strong CPU or don't multitask much then you probably won't notice as much of an improvement, but I can say it works as advertised!

First up. I have never played a strategy game that I really liked. I got this for free when I pre-ordered Bioshock Infinite, along with Civ 5 on GmG. I tried Civ 5 first, but really couldn't get into it at all. So I am only now giving this game a fair chance. I literally said to my best friend that this was the last strategy game that I was going to play if I didn't like this one.
This game though...This game is great! I can't fault it so far. It sort of feels like a game of chess in a lot of ways. Nice graphics and art style too. Actually, the visuals and music remind me of Deus Ex, which is great. It sounds like the same composer to me.
There are also a lot of familiar voices, which is actually kind of distracting, because I am trying to figure out where I know the voice from and not concentrating on what they are saying...The council guy sounds like the narrator from Screenjunkies 'Honest Trailers' lol (It IS him!) :D
Haha, and I guessed the other one right too! It's the Dharma Initiative guy from LOST! :D
Ha! again! It is the Deus Ex Human Revolution composer too! :D
Anyway, the gameplay and strategy elements are very engaging. You need to plan your moves and take good advantage of cover while getting your squad into position.
Then there are squad member promotions, weapons upgrades etc. which offer some interesting choices. The engineering and research aspects are very interesting too. You need to prioritise what to develop, research, build etc.
At certain points you have to choose where to go and who to help, which causes panic levels to go up in the regions you don't help. So you have to manage panic levels too.
There is a lot going on here, a lot of re-playability, and very satisfying gameplay. I am finding it quite addictive so far and I am glad that I have finally found a strategy game that I like. This is definitely helped by the way the game is designed and the intuitive, easy to learn UI, which is a big reason why I haven't liked other strategy games that I have played.
So yeah, very cool game so far.

Stilton, Pear and Walnut bread
(Makes one small loaf)
Ingredients:
500g Strong White Bread Flour
10g Salt
7g satchet instant yeast
20g Unsalted Butter, diced and softened
320ml water
200g Stilton Cheese
100g Walnut Peices
1 pear, peeled, cored and diced
1. Tip the flour into a large bowl. Add the salt to one side, yeast into the other. Add the butter and 3/4ths of the water, then turn the mixture with the fingers of one hand. Add the remaining water a little at a time, continuing to mix untill all the flour is taken in and the dough is soft and sticky; you may not need all the water.
2. Coat the work surface with a little oil to prevent the dough sticking. Turn out the dough and knead for at least 5 mins, until smooth and no longer sticky. Lightly oil a bowl, return the dough to it, and cover with cling film. Put in fride for an hour, so it has doubled in size.
3. Line a baking tray with grease-proof paper. Scrape the dough out of the bowl and fold it inwards again and again until all the air is knocked out and it is smooth. Add the stilton, walnut and pear peices to the dough and work them in well.
4. Shape the dough into a rectangle 30 cm long, roll it up into a sausage, then flatten it out again and roll it up a bit tighter this time. Tuck the edges under and neaten the loaf by rolling the edges to taper them slightly. Put the dogh on the baking tray with greaseproof paperwith the join underneath. Place the tray in a plastic bag and leave to prove for about 40 mins, until the loaf has doubled in size. Heat the oven too 200C, or Gas 6.
5. Just before baking, gently rub flour over the loaf, then make deep diagonal cuts alo9ng the top, first in one direction, then the other, to make a criss-cross pattern. Bake for about 30 mins, until well-risen and golden brown. Cool on a wire rack.

I can never forget that day.
The day when my grandpa died.
I was only 8.
He called me to his bedside and whispered to me, in a voice feeble yet somewhat unsatisfied.
He said to me, "My lovely grandson, I have nothing to give you in this life, as I have been poor and unfortunate,"
"Money and fortune, women and sex, lush and class, I can give you none."
I wasn't feeling any bit of dissapoint, as I knew very well of him, of his life, of his potential, of the legacy he could leave to his descendants.
And then there was, as I remembered correctly, a short silence.
"Except for this."
My hand was tightly grabbed and, the next thing I remembered, was a 4-GB-black-Kingston-flash-drive-like object being secretly put in my hand, so secretly that not even the people around me had noticed.
"Finish my life's work." Those were his last words.
After years and years of attempting to figure out just what that only file in the flash drive was, here I was, sitting in front of my laptop, Civ 5 was released.
The next thing happened can only explained by me as providence: I copied the file to civ 5 save folder, opened civ 5, attempted to load the file.
It loaded.
It was a Marathon game, on its 284th turn.
There was only one city left, and it was surrounded by enemies' scouts.
The city health bar was already depleted, and I had 23 workers that were, even the closest ones, at least ten tiles away from my city.
........................................
Years have passed.
There is, like the beginning, only one city left.
Except that one city, is the only one not owned by me.
My right hand trembled as I reached the "Annex the city" button, never knowing the cause of the tremble being either years of non-stop playing, or the fact that I am now only one button away from fulfilling my grandfather's wish.
I looked out the window, tears in both my eyes formed two vertical lines across my face.
Noticed the image in the window, the reflection of yet another old man with eyeful of tears, crying, yet satisfied.
I stared at the blue sky, whispered:
"I finished your work, grandpa."

This game came out recently and I've dropped about 20 hours in, so here are my thoughts!
In Divinty: Original Sin you play two source hunters who have come to Cyseal to solve a murder. From there, the plot escalates and the setting becomes increasingly varied and interesting. Exploration is a highlight in this game with tons of secrets, quests and character to be found often tucked away in little hidden areas. You are given the chance to create both source hunters at the start of the game. Original Sin follows a classless system that encourages minor multiclassing without becoming a jack of all trades, as certain enemies are immune or even absorb certain elements.
The gameplay of D:OS is a highlight and one of the most talked-about features. There are dozens of interesting reactions between spells, skills, status effects and different types of terrain. A charging warrior can slip on ice, a cloud of steam can be zapped to turn into a cloud of static, or a wet, chilled enemy can be frozen on the spot. All of this makes for fun, tactical combat. It initially seems slow but you'll want the time to plan, as the game is incredibly difficult, especially during boss fights are fights against large amounts of enemies. They too use status effects often.
Now, for the graphics and sound. The visuals are highly customisable via the settings, allowing the game to run on old machines, whilst also allowing for some impressive visuals and effects on newer rigs. Animations are average, but spell and skill effects look very nice. One negative is the enemy animations. Some get unique effects, but I often saw generic enemy mages using generic animations for spells of different elements, which was boring and a little confusing. The sound is fantastic, the game has high-quality voice acting for both the player characters and NPCs. There's ambient dialogue which repeats a little too often, but has a very charming Fable-like to it. 'Noone has as many friends as the man with many cheeses!' The music is absolutely top-notch in every respect. Eargasms all round.
Thank you for reading my review!

Grim Dawn, even at this early stage, is an excellent effort with very nice graphics, nice procedural loot drops, and some decent animations however two things really stand out as issues to me.
The skill reward system sucks. You can spend numerous character levels doing absolutely nothing but adding ticks to a "class" progress bar with no new skills or tangible rewards at all.  To work around this deficiency they've baked in a skill respec NPC so you can spend your points on improving currently attainable skills until you save up enough to then downgrade those skills to waste points on that damn class progress bar to get a higher tiered skill. In a word, it's depressing.  It was a bad system in Titan Quest many years ago and it hasn't improved over time.
I've mostly played a pure Occultist and pure Nightblade however my time spent with both were just... boring. The only thing that kept me going was to see the next area or monster type.  I had zero attachment to the gameplay itself which I think is my biggest complaint.  The combat mechanics aren't fluid or inspiring enough to evoke that feeling required to want to do the same thing over and over.  I can't quite put my finger on it but the reality of wasting my time clicking a mouse while staring at a screen is never washed away by what I'm doing.  When I play D2 or D3 I can get sucked away within the first few moments of combat and spend hours doing the exact same thing, always striving to improve my character.  With Grim Dawn it felt very mechanical and I had no desire to keep clicking anything.  I sincerely hope they recognize this and manage to make the combat mechanics more enjoyable.
There's quite a few positives to be found in the game and it's worth the cost of admission by today's standards but I just can't see myself playing it beyond the first playthru and I suspect that I'm not alone.

Orcs Must Die is easily my favorite downloadable title for 2011. Why? Because it takes classic tower defense and makes something new, innovative, and fun out of it. The game blends third person action with tower defense strategy creating a very unique experience. The game is very well designed on that regard, meaning that it is impossible to beat a level using only traps or only spells (you must use both). You play as a War Mage able to use spells and weapons to stop the Orcs from entering the Rift. You also have the ability to lay traps throughout the environment. Each trap is uniquely designed and offers different gameplay elements. Some examples of traps are tar traps to slow enemies, swinging maces, spike traps, arrow wall traps, etc. You play a good amount of levels progressing through a very simple but entertaining storyline. Overall, Orcs Must Die offers a very new and unique experience for Tower Defense fans. To put it simply, if you like tower defense, GET THIS GAME!

Dying Light, what can I say, an exceptional game that is definitely the best game I've played in a long time, parkour is smooth, seamless, fun and rewarding. Better than Mirrors Edge though I would have liked a wall run, but I easily forgot about it and didn't even miss it as much as I thought I did, this is even better than Brink which tried hard but failed. The First Person combat and Parkour in this game is what most other games should be aspiring to be, it's THAT good. The learning curve is easy, it just takes a little bit to get used to if you're using a controller, "A" for jump on a Xbox controller or "X" for jump on a Playstation controller is now your "RB" on Xbox or "R1" on Playstation. so it takes a little bit to get used to but it doesn't take long.
Now the story, it wasn't the greatest, but it wasn't the worst, I've seen better, but it didn't break the game for me. What makes it for me is the multiplayer along side with side missions, challenges, invasion, etc. It all adds up to a superior multiplayer experience and the world is nice, big, and diverse. There's plenty to do, and plenty to do with others, even if it's as simple as just killing zombies for fun, or exploring the world.
There's a variety of weapons, and weapon mods, as you progress there's plenty of options to upgrade. There are guns but there's minimal use for them and not to mention the noise from them attracts the more volatile of the zombies, so beware, DO NOT use guns unless you have to, but afterwards, bail as quickly as possible, don't stick around that area for too long.
Now if Walking Dead was a game, I'd imagine it to be something like this, but no parkour. The scare factor of this game is pretty intense at night when the stakes are higher, you can easily die at night, whether it's a walker, runner, or volatile. Daytime is just a walk in the park, though I have this habit of testing the waters and even during the day being very cautious, and I was right to do so very early on in the game.
Overall this game gets a 10/10 from me, even with a lacking story, this game made up for it in all other aspects. LOVE IT!

Lots of fun. While many people say it's not replayable, I've gone through the game a good ten times and enjoyed each run. Memorizing spots to speed up your runs that you may not have known existed during your first playthrough and seeing a great running combo pay off is very rewarding, which adds a sense of replayability to the game and also makes second and third runs faster and more fun.
On the flip side, by giving players such an intensely graceful experience, after a few runs the player starts to play overly recklessly and hectically as they try to keep the flow going, which often results in death and frustration. Going fast for the whole level is incredibly addicting, and I hope Mirror's Edge 2 either adaps to or changes this. Give the player an incentive to ever stop going very quickly, like a decent combat system or a small chance to explore and see what the safest/fastest routes through a level are and make your choice. Otherwise, make sure the game flows as neatly as possible and feels graceful and fast the whole way.
For what it is, Mirror's edge is definitely worth the buy, especially at $4.99, which I've seen it go for many times.

I did die playing, so you do feel a sense of loss and achievement when completing a difficult mob or boss fight. Warning! In act 2, there is a dungeon. Have plenty of pots for if you don't, you are going to die and not be able to enter again without spending $20,000 bits and rare materials for a skeleton key. Once the game is completed or, perhaps, next act is released, I intend to start with a new toon and try a hybrid. An excellent product that met all my expectation with only a few annoyances.  Bug count was 2 or 3 and fairly minor--transported for no apparent reason to a body of water and had to exit or quests that I could not complete. If you run into oddities with quests like I did, exiting and re-entering the game may permit completion.

This review is for GD's ALPHA. Nevertheless, the game is in a perfectly playable state and is very fun too.
Grim Dawn is an unusual spiritual successor to Titan Quest, to whom a few of the people working on it had a hand in making. Stylistically, the games are quite different- between the vibrant fantasy Greece of TQ and GD's own grim take on Victorian fashions and weaponry. Mechanically though, it's the perfect successor to TQ, taking the good aspects of TQ's 2-mastery system and deepening it with a greater variety of skills available per mastery. Item drops are far improved over where TQ was, with a far better rate of blue items
The amount of actual content the game has to offer can't rival that of many other ARPG's, past or present, but Grim Dawn's lengthy amount of time spent refining what is there isn't an accident- it's a lean game with a focus on replayability through quality and a small amount of variation in your journey through some minor randomization. It's a small thing, but entrances to underground areas changing to be located somewhere else drastically changes the pace of going through zones you already accomplished with another character before.
And, as a final selling point for Grim Dawn, as with other popular ARPG's these days, support for the game won't end upon final release. It's a bit far from now, but future expansion including new areas and masteries, just as meticulously crafted as those in the original, are something to look forward to- and with GD's current record, unlikely to suddenly go awol as the developer decides to work on other projects.

Oh so addicting.
This game does everything right to pull you in from the start and make sure that the only time you want to stop playing is to create a new a character to try a different build using the +poison damage gear you've found. At the same time the game doesn't restrict you from changing your current build. For example, 8 hours in I respecced from building around two active abilities and fire and burn damage damage into two different active abilities and cold and lighting damage. I was having some trouble with certain situations and was finding my damage output lacking against bosses so I looked at what gear I had and what I could change around with my skill points and after a few iterations came with a mostly different build which performed better. The change felt organic. The game strikes a very good balance between giving players the freedom to change their current build and making them feel like the choices they made are meaningful.
Everything about the game feels like it takes the better elements from its predecessors and organically combines them into something that has its own identity. The atmopsphere is gritty and dark like the Diablo series but with a futuristic twist as early forms of firearms and explosives are available. The dual mastery system from Titan Quest is back but the skill trees have more synergy within themselves and each other as the damage and damage bonuses in most abilities are split between two different types. But more importantly the game isn't afraid to add something new. The crafting system and the faction system along with quests that offer some meaningful choices are the big things that come to mind at this stage.
The game world feels much more alive and interesting than most other games. The dialogue is organic and appropriate to the situations. For example, at one point you may encounter a pair trying to scam some money off you and you can decide whether to respond with violence or allow them to join the community you're building up. If you choose the latter and talk to them later on they will express their gratitude for not killing them and how they probably had no chance in combat against you. They also share how they struggled to survive prior to the current encounter. Encounters like these make the player feel invested in the gameworld and builds up the atmosphere, soemthing a lot of modern games fail to do and instead rely on a few cinematics and a diary entry around every corner. While this game has the diary entries, they are well spaced out and actually anwser some of the burning questions the player might have about the gameworld so unlike many other games, I actually read most of them.
Another thing that adds to the atmosphere and to the experience as a whole is the dynamic weather system. It also acts as an important offset to the lack of randomly generated levels. I have no complaints about the level design itself but running through the same exact level tends to get old after a while and the dynamic weather spices things up a bit.
All in all this game is shaping up to be one of the best ARPG out there and thats bound to improve as development progresses.

FTL:Faster Than Light - Review
This indie game combines strategy and micromanagement. Similar to the IOS title "Star Command" the player is in charge of a spaceship with a big amount of equipment. Ranging from missiles to Drones. But he also controls the crew which can contain six different races with different abilities.
You navigate your space vessel from one sector to the next where each sector contains a bunch of randomly generated waypoints. The path through the sector is the player's desicion. It is most likely that you will encounter a hostile ship though.
As many other indie titles FTL has a retro pixel-graphics design, which in my opinion perfectly fits into the overall game design.
Very worth mentioning is the impressive soundtrack of the game!
The gameplay mechnics are very focused on management. You have to decide whether you want to use your ship's energy
for a stronger shield or maybe invest it in your medical bay where you can heal your crew members. Will you power your drones which can be very helpful in combat or will you just avoid confrontation?
At the end of the day FTL is a very consistent title where gameplay sound design and grafics all fit perfectly. What I liked about this game personally was the amount of luck which is involved here. You very much depend on the encounters that occur and the amount of scrap (game currency) you earn. You could lose the game by simply running out of fuel. This said I found FTL a very difficult game especially in the beginning but this isn't a problem at all as the random world generation and the new ship types one can unlock Faster than light has a very high replay value.
I will give FTL 8.0/10 points.

Pongo is a really nice idea, but very bladly executed. It's simply bad in too many ways. Level design is almost non-existant, the art-style actively goes against the gameplay, the combat is not only unnecessary, but also badly designed, and even the physics' system is artificial in a way that, again, hinders gameplay.
I'll explain what I like about it first, and then go quickly over all of the negatives mentioned.
I really like this idea! I've original, and it could have led to some really interesting platforming sections! And I don't dislike the way it was implemented: as in, you have 3 Modes: a shooting mode, where you can't use the pogo to jump; a normal mode, where you charge the jump and then jump, and a true pogo mode, where you automatically jump when you hit the ground. It's a bit clunky, especially with the transitions between them, but over all, it's pretty cool.
A really annoying thing was how there's absolutely no difference between the pogo and the true pogo mode, visually... They look and sound exactly the same. This means that you may expect to be in a certain mode, but realize that you're not, dying as a result... There should definitely be
feedback...
That's about it, really.
Why do I say the level design is non-existent? Well, there are 50 or so levels. BUT, only 2 are memorable. And they're memorable for their gimmicky way. It could have been a very nicely used gimmick, but no. The developers were simply like: "Hey, look at this cool level design!", but the levels provide absolutely no challenge, and remain an idea in a vacuum...
The game is only mildly fun when you try to """speedrun""" it. And I'm intentionally using those many quotation marks. Speedrunning, which seemed the perfect direction for the game, only works as in: run without stopping to kill anything, and pray that the level is timed accordingly. Some levels are. Others aren't. There are moving platforms that take up to 20 seconds to complete their cycle. It's really fun to wait for them.
Then, there's the fact that there is almost no variation. Sometimes a new obstacle appears, but they're not used intelligently or anything. They're just there.
There's also the mind-boggling fact that they levels sometimes have these "sidepaths" or new islands to the side. These serve absolutely no purpose. None. At all. They're just there. Is it to trick the player? Some even have power-ups, that vanish within 10 seconds, making them worthless. I don't understand. There are no collectibles in the game, no story, nothing... Why are these even there?
Then, there are some challenging jumps. These are really annoying. Why? Well, the levels are arranged in hexagons, for some reason. Meaning that you'll having to aim for the outer points of the hexagonal platforms. And jump out of them as well. You'll also have to time it perfectly, otherwise you'll miss and fall to your death.

The other problems are dependent on other systems. The graphic style, for example. It's cute. It looks like a pretty nice, low cost way of creating a game. But not of this type! There's zero perspective on depth. The colors have no shades or anything for one to gauge where the platforms are. So, half of the time, you'll time jumps inappropriately, because you couldn't see how far the platform was.
To make matters worse, the moving platforms are timed never to top. And they change direction at the absolutely farthest point that you can still jump on them. (An awkward way of phrasing it, sorry!) It's possible to jump on those platforms, but it's precision for the sake of it.
There are a few levels like this, those being very frustrating. It's not interesting design is any way.
It also pairs very badly with the levels' length. They usually take 50 seconds (short-ish ones), with some taking up to 2 minutes. 90% of the hard levels aren't hard. They're mostly running forward, or doing a couple of short, easy jumps. Until you reach the hard jump. They're a time waster. And they'll extend the gametime by a lot...
What's wrong about the combat? Lack of feedback. The lives are on the corner, not standing out. But that's not the big problem. What is? The fact that there's no visual indication of when you hit. And even the sound doesn't play properly. It's barely noticeable!
Then, the enemies' attack animations are in no way connected with you taking damage... you take damage at an arbitrary time, even without playing the animation... it's pointless.
But hey, you can simply evade all of the combat without a worry. They're too slow to pursue you, and so are bullets. It's really a completely pointless "feature". It makes the game slower without any benefit.
Finally, the physics. On a basic level, they're solid. The game is a bit too slow, but other than that, it's satisfying to jump and run, when you nail it. The problem comes with the moving platforms. The developers had no concept of momentum. So, if you jump out of a moving platform, it will be as if the platform wasn't moving. That's really weird. It feels very, very wrong, and will totally destroy your timing.
Even worse, is how artificial they've made the player stay still in a moving platform, since momentum is non-existant. I'm pretty sure it's a simply check of "if the player is exactly on the platform, his base speed in the same as the platform". Why am I sure? Because the game has some environmental pieces: small rocks, and destroyable nubs. These would serve very little purpose, being there just to provide some variety. However, if you step on a rock in a moving platform, you will NOT move with the platform. The platform will move without you, and then you'll most likely fall. See where the momentum would have played a very important role? These things happen a lot. And they just make the game feel incomplete and amateur. And still being sold for 10$... It's irritates me, honestly.
In a physics based game, at least study physics a bit more... especially when it negatively affects your game.
The interface is generally bad as well, not giving you good information when you need it, and so on. I won't dwell on that, since it's not too important.
Overall, the game had some potential. But the fact that the level design is so uninspired, and even "broken" in some sections make the game really bad. It's unfortunate. 50 levels that are mostly filler do not, in any way, justify the price. And it's a real shame, since I really like the idea.
I almost forgot one thing! The power-ups. There are 3: rapid fire, high jump, faster running. The first two are useless... The high jump is useful, but only in very, very specific obstacles and don't play a role in the general game.
The speed one, however, is really, really fun! The game is slow paced, making timing more controlled and important (not in a good way), but the speed power up changes a lot. The game suddenly becomes fast paced, making you time jumps while in the air, trying to traverse the levels quickly and in a risky way. It's great! Unfortunately, it's only used is a few levels, and never an explored machanic. Makes it feel like the developers didn't really try and see where the fun in their game was... Oh well.
If there is a revamping of the game, please, please, make it faster, and more interesting!
Ah, one last thing. The game has 5 music tracks. Some are nice. But they have no solid connection to each other, and they just play... one after another. It's like you having your own 5 tracks in Winamp, on the background. They just repeat, one after another... What's the point? Just goes to show how little thought went into the game. It's kind of sad, sometimes. I'd like to think that when someone makes a game, he would think of the experience as a whole, and try to make every aspect interesting... and then I look at Steam and I get disappointed.

TL;DR: This game is the definition of shovelware-made-for-mobile-hidden-object-game trash. And if youre looking for a Match-3 RPG DO NOT look here!
Ok, so the tags are misleading. This is mostly a fantasy themed HOG (Hidden Object game), not a match 3 RPG like Puzzle Quest.
It has a tiny "match 3" component, if you can call it that. Basically, youre trying to draw a path from a start point to a finish point by breaking the "rock" by linking gems, which breaks the background "rock" and creates an open path. You select gems by dragging over them with a mouse. In any direction, including turning while dragging. Its so easy it isnt even funny. It goes HOG scene, where you have to find the pieces of various items in a picture, then use the items in the picture to open more scenes (IE a pickaxe to break a cave in). That gets you a key to open a book.
Then a few rounds of the aforementioned match 3. THEN a "find the differences between two images" HOG. You do that a few times in each book before going back to the "find pieces of items HOG" to get the new key to open a new book.
Theres no choice, no choosing of puzzles, and a very weak fantasy plot with an annoying fairy that constantly flits around the screen. Its like its badly built for 5 year olds. If you like HOGs (oh god, why??) theres WAY better ones out there. And if you like Match 3 RPGs theres way way better ones.
This MAY entertain a 6 year old. But I doubt it. Do yourself a favor and dont waste your cash.

As for currently I can't recommend due to a long lists of bugs and inconsistensies ranging from gamebreaking to slightly obnoxious.
Few examples:
-Menu might at random bug out. Disallowing you to play. Restarting the game is a gamble, good chance it just crashes again(and the game has an unskippable prologue)

-Very inconsistent building mechanics, very clumsily put together

-Inhabitants are dumb as hell, and do nothing but walk up and down. They're purely cosmetic, but they're not very pleasing to look at due to their simplistic AI
-Some blocks glitch through each other. For example the staircase clips through the block put upon it
-Sometimes you can't build upon another block at random. When reinstalling the block below it'll work again for no reason
-Alot of blocks don't make any sense in terms of in- and output
-No multiplayer aspects. The building sharing is purely local
And way more.

I can never forget that day.
The day when my grandpa died.
I was only 8.
He called me to his bedside and whispered to me, in a voice feeble yet somewhat unsatisfied.
He said to me, "My lovely grandson, I have nothing to give you in this life, as I have been poor and unfortunate,"
"Money and fortune, women and sex, lush and class, I can give you none."
I wasn't feeling any bit of dissapoint, as I knew very well of him, of his life, of his potential, of the legacy he could leave to his descendants.
And then there was, as I remembered correctly, a short silence.
"Except for this."
My hand was tightly grabbed and, the next thing I remembered, was a 4-GB-black-Kingston-flash-drive-like object being secretly put in my hand, so secretly that not even the people around me had noticed.
"Finish my life's work." Those were his last words.
After years and years of attempting to figure out just what that only file in the flash drive was, here I was, sitting in front of my laptop, Civ 5 was released.
The next thing happened can only explained by me as providence: I copied the file to civ 5 save folder, opened civ 5, attempted to load the file.
It loaded.
It was a Marathon game, on its 284th turn.
There was only one city left, and it was surrounded by enemies' scouts.
The city health bar was already depleted, and I had 23 workers that were, even the closest ones, at least ten tiles away from my city.
........................................
Years have passed.
There is, like the beginning, only one city left.
Except that one city, is the only one not owned by me.
My right hand trembled as I reached the "Annex the city" button, never knowing the cause of the tremble being either years of non-stop playing, or the fact that I am now only one button away from fulfilling my grandfather's wish.
I looked out the window, tears in both my eyes formed two vertical lines across my face.
Noticed the image in the window, the reflection of yet another old man with eyeful of tears, crying, yet satisfied.
I stared at the blue sky, whispered:
"I finished your work, grandpa."
There is just something so beautiful and perfect about this game.  Get it now.

and grew extremely addicted to the gameplay. I became even more excited when the release of Super Hexagon first released on iOS. However, even playing it before it's PC release, it would still take me FOREVER before I could finally finish all 6 levels.
Super Hexagon is such a simple game that it's difficulty is what really makes you hate yourself. It's never the game's fault for your mistakes. The one thing that kept me from just quitting the game was how easy it was to jump right back in when you lose. A simple press of the space bar (or the up arrow key) and you're off again.
The graphics are simple, but colorful (possibly even distracting to a fault, at times).
The music is also quite nicely done, being that it was composed by chiptune composer Chipzel. If you're not a fan of chiptune, you may be better off playing with the music off.
You will hate yourself as you play this game. But it's super addicting.

Fighting feels wonderful, tactile and with the "oomph" you look for in a game like this.  It is also quick and fluid, unlike Path of Exiles (which was really my biggest gripe about that game).  The skills are all fun, and the leveling system and how you pick your skills is a great nod to customization, replayability and feeling like you have control over who your character is and how they play.

Wish there was more to it, can't wait for updates.

This review is for GD's ALPHA. Nevertheless, the game is in a perfectly playable state and is very fun too.
Grim Dawn is an unusual spiritual successor to Titan Quest, to whom a few of the people working on it had a hand in making. Stylistically, the games are quite different- between the vibrant fantasy Greece of TQ and GD's own grim take on Victorian fashions and weaponry. Mechanically though, it's the perfect successor to TQ, taking the good aspects of TQ's 2-mastery system and deepening it with a greater variety of skills available per mastery. Item drops are far improved over where TQ was, with a far better rate of blue items
The amount of actual content the game has to offer can't rival that of many other ARPG's, past or present, but Grim Dawn's lengthy amount of time spent refining what is there isn't an accident- it's a lean game with a focus on replayability through quality and a small amount of variation in your journey through some minor randomization. It's a small thing, but entrances to underground areas changing to be located somewhere else drastically changes the pace of going through zones you already accomplished with another character before.
And, as a final selling point for Grim Dawn, as with other popular ARPG's these days, support for the game won't end upon final release. It's a bit far from now, but future expansion including new areas and masteries, just as meticulously crafted as those in the original, are something to look forward to- and with GD's current record, unlikely to suddenly go awol as the developer decides to work on other projects.

After a substantial amount of testing on various games, some of which are simply unoptimised and some of which are well optimised but CPU reliant I can safely say that I have seen across the board increases in framerate using CPUCores. This most definitely varies between games and I have seen a lot of negative reviews on here stating that people saw zero performance increase OR that there was a mild performance increase but the same thing could be achieved with one of those "videogame booster" programs.
So I thought I would clear a few things up about what this program is actually here to achieve.
I should clarify at this point that this product will NOT improve the overall performance of your games unless you already have a clearly identifiable CPU bottleneck on your system (as I do).
Looking at the specs of those who did not notice an increase in performance I believe the culprit is that their CPU isnt enough of a drag factor on their machines performance to notice any substantial changes.
I have been awaiting with bated breath the release of the Ryzen processor and up to this point have been running my R9 390x alongside a FX 6300 processor, I was well aware of the bottleneck this would cause but financial constraints being what they were at the time of building... I decided I would just limit CPU intensive effects such as shadow draw distance/Godrays/Shadow quality and so forth.
Unfortunately this simplistic adjusting of in-game settings will only go so far and would work far better in tandem with freeing up some processing power. Which this program does very well.
It is true that, were I not incredibly lazy, I could have gone into my task manager and individually have stopped processes I wasnt using to boost the performance of my games but that is an extremely ball-achingly time consuming process that I just couldnt bare the thought of, additionally I don't know enough about non-essential windows processes to confidently begin turning them off and on.
Which brings me onto why this program is worth more than the "Engage gaming mode" button that can be downloaded free through various sites.  Those pieces of software do exactly what they say on the tin, they stop non-essential programs running in the background.
However CPUCores goes one step further in integrating with both steam and also optimising the OS itself around the game being run, one user suggested this was as simple as running the game program under a higher priority; however even doing that AND shutting down all non-essential programs is not as effective as isolating your entire OS to your first core. Which is exactly what CPUCores does while still stripping down all processing power that isnt necessary for key windows processes. It's essentially the OS equivalent of running a skeleton crew.
But I am not a man without an investigative bone in my body. I ran skyrim and fallout (both games I play often but could do with a few extra frames on) with Iobit and razer game boosters and noticed a stark 10 FPS jump only in CPUCores. If there was any increase with Iobit/razer I certainly couldnt see it. But feel free to try it for yourself!
I understand peoples reservations, I was skeptical at first I must say but I cannot suggest more giving this program a go if you know your computer to have a CPU bottleneck, I can say for certain I do not regret my choice to buy this. But forewarning; make sure you are going to benefit from it before you buy.
One small gripe with the steam integration, I understand that encoding and streaming is a CPU intensive process; but often I am willing to ditch some frames to let some friends watch what im up to. I have noticed that when CPUCores is running it refuses outright to broadcast. The only improvement I can think of on it is if it were possible to have a tickbox to allow broadcasting. But other than that love the program! Give it a go!
