Kingsway is an amazing game in nearly every regard, but with one fatal flaw that hinders the experience quite a bit. You begin Kingsway just like any other RPG game, create your character, pick a class, and get thrown into the game with limited tutorials so that you can figure it out on your own. It was actually very easy to pick up and play, and the operating system aesthetic of the game allows players to have the game layout be however they want. It basically offered a whole new level of player choice that I found really enjoyable. Onto the actual gameplay itself. You select areas on the map you want to travel to and as your character moves, you run into various monsters that you will have to fight. Monsters can drop loot upon defeating them that the player can use to their advantage, or just become a horder. But the amount of random loot frops, weapons, and skills that the player can obtain guarantees that you will have a different experience with every playthrough. The world is also randomized so the player will also be met with new dungeons, maps, and possibilities with every new character they make. It makes it hard to develop a strategy, which just gives it that much more replay value.
So lets just quick run through the pros:
-Amazing user interface
-Infinite replay value
-Easy to pick up
-Genuinely fun
-Player gets to choose how they want to play
But now lets talk about the fatal flaw I mentioned, and that is that the game is not infinite, and you can not keep using the same character forever. The game is set on a small island and the player must move from the left side of the island to the right in order to avoid an evil shadow monster that is set to cover the world in darkness. At the end of the island lies the final boss, where *SPOILER ALERT* the player sacrifices themself to defeat the shadow monster. Your character dies, and this game does have permadeath, so thats where the game ends, and you can decide there to either make a new character or just quit. I would have loved the option to have an infinite world and carry my character up trhough level 100 and fight insanely difficult monsters, and be able to grind for EXP and go on quests. But sadly the game will foce you to face the final boss anywhere from 2 - 4 hours into the game, and then you either die, or win and also die. I just completed the game for the first time after 11 attempts and I dont know if I can play it again knowing I already experienced everything this game has to offer. Let me make this clear, the game really only has one story that you just repeat over and over again. It was a fun ride but now the ride is just over, and I dont even have my character to show for it.

Kingsway is a rogue-light, You're a fantasy adventurer who has to travel the lands, light the beacons, and get to the king's castle. Its main gimmick is that the entire game is reminiscent of the win98/95 era in terms of interface.
Your bags are windows and icons on the desktop, enemies sometimes shoot projectiles in the forms of popups you have to close before they hit you, the enemies themselves sort of drift around the screen at times.  The playable classes are pretty similiar, and even share a bunch of skills between them.  The gameplay isn't bad, it's just lacking in any sort of depth.
They hit upon a wonderful premise of a classic windows style operating system to play the game in, and then barely do anything with it. Oh, one enemy minimizes your windows, great. A few enemies place a couple of annoying popups on your screen. It's so restrained with its gimmicks that after the first hour or so none of them have any impact on you. Compared to undertale, which took its "dodge'em up lite bullet hell" concept and explored plenty of different attack patterns and silly gimmicks, Kingsway doesn't. And without its gimmicks it's a terribly boring and snore inducing roguelite.
TL;DR Kingsway is a wonderful concept that isn't utilized at all, leading you to play a boring click attack simulator.

Kingsway is a roguelike RPG controlled through a user interface that heavily evokes Windows 95. If you're not familiar with those genres, this means that there is permadeath, and the crux of the game is managing resources against a timer (in Kingsway's case, the arrival of a Galactus-style world eating alien known as The Sky Eater) rather than plot.
The main genius of the game is the user interface. If you've used a PC for any period of time, it'll be pretty immediately intuitive how to do things. It's a game that barely needs to tutorialize because you're already on a PC.
The classes also do a fantastic job of feeling different from each other, and having multiple viable builds. My glass cannon mage ripped through everything before getting hit, while my adventurer focused on shields and slow, strong attacks, nullifying all damage before killing things in a few, big hits. There's no doubt in my mind I could have pushed them (or the other classes I've played) in multiple viable directions, and it's tons of fun experimenting, figuring out what works, then taking a honed build to absolutely murder things.
The one thing I'd caution people on is if you're a roguelike diehard it might be slightly easy for you. I've only got a dozen hours of experience, and I feel like at this point if I can get established in the first fifteen minutes I'm making it to endgame. I haven't done a ton of experimentation yet with the Ring of Pain starting item (which tooltips denote as a hard mode), so that might ratchet up the difficulty. Even so, I think that the user interface and really great class design is a good enough hook to get a few dozen hours of enjoyment out of this. For 10 bucks? That's rock solid.

Okay, so I finally decided to give my thoughts on Trench Run. Here is why this game is not worth it's price tag, and should never be bought for the multiplayer.
I really wanted Trench Run to succeed. Honestly. However, it sucks to say that due to awful marketing and general apathy from the developers upon launch, the game died in such a short amount of time, I was not even aware of it.
This game probably does not even deserve to be on Steam anymore, as all possibility of it ever being remotely successful (and for the matter, nearly as successful as King Arthurs Gold) has been killed by the developers. On top of that, the game's servers are so barren that the chance of finding a player in any of the 4 avaliable servers in the span of a month is nigh impossible. This game was only and I say
advertised to players of King Arthurs Gold (and ofcourse players of any other game made by Transhuman Design, but who has any of those?). This means that the already miniscule population of King Arthurs Gold is the only crowd that this game is being propogated to. This is EXTREMELY bad for a game, especially one that relies on a healthy and active community.
The answer is simple: the developers thought the concept of Trench Run was interesting. They decided to work on the game for some years, until they decided to release the game bare, to test the waters. The unfortunate part is, they can't just release a game and expect it to take off. As previously stated, a game will not go anywhere without proper care to marketing. Even games that seemingly had no advertising techniques, such as Undertale, took off due to a cult following and hype. This is not the only reason the game failed though.
The game itself is not very unique. Sure, the lobby system is fun to♥♥♥♥♥♥around in, and multiplayer, Co-Op or PvP can be fun if you have some friends over or something. The issue is, was this game even that much of a challenge? Anyone who has played King Arthurs Gold will immediatly be able to see that almost everything about Trench Run was ripped straight from King Arthurs Gold in some way. The engine itself is identical to KAG (King Arthurs Gold), the artstyle and movement also have no differences what so ever (aside from the artsy pallette). The gameplay itself is all just a rip of TDM from KAG and run mode is the only new tech they probably even added to the game. I could easily see this entire game being a well crafted mod for King Arthurs Gold, which has a healthy modding community.
Well, there is a lot to say about how great this game is. Ofcourse, all of those questions are hypothetical as this game will never reach it's full potential due in part to the previously mentioned.
But there is one salvation that may make you want to sink in a few hours (or less) into the game. Single player/local multiplayer. This is one of the modes THD (Transhuman Design) really wanted to sell when describing the game in forum posts. This mode allows you to play with your friends via couch system, or just play by yourself. The game itself can be quite fun (if not redundant, short living, and frusturating) for a few hours when hanging out with friends. The gameplay it self offers a nice silly and action filled game with 4 different classes that have two different functions unique to them. Not sure if those maybe 3-4 hours of enjoyment are worth the price though.
The gameplay in Trench Run can be pretty fun for a little while, until ofcourse you start noticing the horrible flaws. I have played around 3 hours of the game in it's beta state, and around 2 in its released state. In that time, I have soaked out an adequate amount of time out of each class and gamemode. The result? Redundancy. The game is exactly the same everytime. Same 4 maps. Same 5 classes (one of which is exclusive to the elusive
mode). That is it. There is no other gameplay element at play other than "Shoot/Stab/Blow up the other 3 people and don't get blown up" yet the developers say that this game can be played seriously? I can sum up each class in 10 words or less:
: Left click to shoot, no aiming. Grenades.
: Wait a minute, wasn't this the engineer?
: Hold left click + release, die.
: Right click to hide, click on people.
: Oh sorry, this is only avaliable in
mode.
The classes bring nothing else to the table other than that. The maps get boring and stale fast, as does the redundancy of the gameplay. The only good portion of the gameplay (which hilariously also gets boring fast) is the lobby. Yes, you heard me right, the ♥♥♥♥ing lobby.
So, when a game decides to focus more so on the literal loading screen of the game more than it does the
, you know there is a problem. So, what is so great about the lobby? The fact that 90 percent of the entire attention of THD was focused on making that place pimp as ♥♥♥♥. There is a bar, where you can pick your choice of beer or wine, listen to some of the legitamately good music that the band there plays, or hang out in the VIP club which has various bonuses. There is a pet shop where you can buy some neat pets to follow you around the lobby, there is a hat shop to make your character look sweet. Most importantly, though, there is a basketball court where you can play legit games of basketball that are sometimes more engaging than the actual game. The lobby even has a creative way of announcing updates (on the billboard) which are non-existant and queing you for a match (via truck). The problem with all of this? You actually need to play the game to use the lobby. Playing the game provides you with coins, which you need to do ANYTHING in the lobby. Honestly, even if the lobby was technically incomplete (they had many more plans to improve the lobby further), I feel like the coins system is my biggest complaint about it.
So? Final thoughts? Should you buy this game, or even follow it at all?
I think its plain to say that the answer is NO.
The amount of time (and frankly, fun) that you get out of this game is so limited in its current state (which will most likely be its permanent state) that it is not even worth the small price tag.
Every function of the game (not even mentioning the amount of bugs in the game) is detrimentally flawed in some way.
Trench run should not be purchased and is not worth the money. This is because the community is more than dead (it has transcended dead, somehow) and the gameplay itself is not even all that spectacular.
If you liked the concept of Trench Run, but want a game that is alive, here are some:
: If you are here, you probably know about this game. If not, you have at least seen me refer to it a lot during the review. It is essentially Trench Run with mod support and a semi-active community.
: Another game you probably know about. Multiplayer servers on Terraria provide plenty of free for all or team PvP fun.
: A combination of epic pixel graphics, badass gameplay, and sweet campaign that can also be multiplayer make Broforce an awesome counterpart to Trench Run.
With that I shall conclude the review.

My experience with the game was limited to its main "Run" mode. Unfortunately, even accepting that the game's extremely limited player precision, weapons, effects, enemies, and level variety are somewhat inherent to the retro genre it portrays, I would not recommend this game even to diehard fans of retro / 8-bit, as its gameplay is so utterly simplistic and inaccurate.
I had no idea I was buying some "arena" game where the primary purpose is moving from left to right on very small maps before the opposing team (or  in my experience, bots...) gets to their "side of the level" first. It's a really odd mechanic and doesn't seem to fit this design very well. The game itself lacks much of the implied "fast pace" action as seen in the trailers, and instead you meander your way from left to right (or right to left) over a short distance within a limited 1:00 minute time span for each map, clumsily lining up shots and grenades and hoping you can make it to your side of the level first instead of the other team. The strange multiplayer insistence really hinders what could have been a cool aesthetic for a military game with a campaign / progressive levels with more of a through line. Instead, you face off on 5 levels which all mostly look the same (this one has snow though!) to see who can get to their side first the most, best out of 5.
Your character despite having full controller support seems to steer incredibly vaguely, with there not even being a traditional jump button. Instead you hold right and / or up / down and watch as your character automatically bounds over whatever is front of them, which makes for really imprecise shooting. You can't seem to aim up or down with your regular machine gun. You can stop to press A to awkwardly align a reticle over the area you want to shoot a missile or grenade toward, but then it's mostly crossing your fingers that the enemies happen to be within range of it, and it seems like most of the time you just end up clipping some outcropping barely in front of you and killing yourself instead. While this is funny the first few times, it makes for a frustrating, inaccurate experience before too long. Your medic seems to crap out health / revival orbs at random and the game advises you to "stick close to your medic" but with most all the characters on either side of the game looking like the same pixelated, small design it's hard to distinguish which one that is.
The old school military graphics, explosions, and ragdolling / amputated crawling the characters do all looks good, and overall the design / aesthetics replicate the feel of an old NES game well. The sound effects seem fitting to the events on screen with funny but brief character moans and screams amidst explosions and the like. The soundtrack is easily the worst part of the game for me with its incredibly repetitive, out-of-place plunky / lighthearted guitar and feels more like they're squeezing out a song made for the main menu across every single level. It reflects the light-heartedness of the game, but I wonder if the game had embodied more of a Medal of Honor / epic orchestral type soundtrack if it would have been a little more immersive and less elephant in the room, in your face all the time.

It may be more fun local coop in its versus mode, however I never had the chance to play this option. I could see it still wearing thin pretty quickly.

DEEP IN THE QUANTUM RABBIT HOLE:
It has PHASE and follows the actual math of QM. Moves (both classical moves (Cm's) and quantum moves (Qm's)) apply quantum gates involving 2 or more squares, and collapse happens whenever two different type and/or color appear on the same square. Collapse is random in accordance to the laws of QM and so introduces luck into the game, with the addition that capturing Cm's remove the wave amplitude in the destination square off the board (Qm's can't be used to capture).
We are allowed to make moves for e.g. a Knight where is some amount of Knight at the origin square and the destination is within 1 (Cm) or 2 (Qm) Knight moves away. Cm's apply the NOT gate while Qm's apply the sqrt(NOT) gate. Every piece except unprompted pawns can make Qm moves, and even pawns can get involved in the fray when they i.e. capture half of a rook's wavefunction.
How does phase matter? Consider white knight moves from B1 to C3. White doing the Qm version of this move twice is applying sqrt(NOT) twice, which is the same as applying NOT (a classical move). However, if white moves Qm, Cm, Qm, the Cm move (which will not appear to have done anything when it is done this way) means our total gate equivalent to applying the NOT gate 1/2+1+1/2 = 2 times, i.e. doing nothing at all. Thus a move that seems to do nothing (the intermediate Cm) actually had an effect. In a real game, more complex phase phenomena show up.
When there part of a piece in the way (and only one path from A to B) we apply a CNOT gate for a classical move, which means that the ordinary NOT gate is "controlled" by the absence/presence of the blocking piece. If there are multiple paths through blocking pieces, multiple other pieces can get involved. Handling all of this complex and intuition is built gradually, mastery is hard but possible. In general the game favors parsimonious rules over what a human would expect.
And by the way, two of the same piece/color combination are identical particles (spin 1/2 fermions).
BRING A FRIEND:
Overall the game plays well. It has a balance of obvious and deeper strategy and tactics with luck thrown in (whenever a collapse happens). There is no easy trick to force a draw, etc (no, splitting the king over and over again won't work. The opponent can capture most of your king, split his pieces to fill all vacant squares, and mop up your remaining sliver of king).
The graphics are pretty (don't use the 3D view). Two main downsides: I don't think there are enough people for reliable online play yet; there is no AI to speak of (it is horrible and it will be much harder then chess to develop a good AI). However, this game makes a good cofeeshop topic with a friend. And the fact that developing an AI will (I think) be so hard means we can hone a skill that is both fun and beyond what machines can do, a claim few board games have.

This is my new favorite power-fantasy game.  It's not an objectively good game, but just from personal taste, I love it.  It really goes all-out with the first person view, most immersive I've seen without a VR headset.  I've always wanted a game where I can walljump or roll in first person, and now I have it!  Faith's acrobatics *feel* more powerful than pretty much any shoot-em-up or stab-em-up, it's simultaneously lower-power and way more superpowered than anything you can pull off in Skyrim.  The fight sequences aren't too exciting, but it's a really nice change to disarm enemies with good timing (and then throw away the gun because seriously who needs guns) instead of blowing them away.  Of course you don't have to throw away those guns, I'm sure my playthrough would have been a lot easier if I wasn't playing pacifist, but it felt more natural that way.  Weird.
It's your standard Prince of Persia jumping-puzzle fare, which means there's spots that can be really frustrating to get through, but that only caught me a couple times.  Checkpoints are pretty liberal, so getting stuck is always "Getting past this part is hard", not "great, I need to backtrack through half the level again".
Other comments...well, it's always nice having games with female protagonists and no romantic subplots.  The game feels a little short, but it was worthwhile, it didn't feel tedious.  There's hidden collectables (like pretty much every Prince of Persia style game) but there's not a whole lot; completionists won't lose whole weeks of their life over it, thank God.  It doesn't have achievements, which is really annoying considering that the console versions did get them.  Despite the fact that it's a console port though, the controls still feel simple and natural.  Fascinating bold use of colors in the game, I liked it a lot aesthetically.
So, yeah.  In summary, it has cool aesthetics, and it makes you feel like a superhero more than any superhero game.  Very worthwhile diversion that won't eat up a lot of time.

REALLY wanted to like this game, and for £30, I expected more. Lets start.
Personally, I LOVE the design, this game is entirely right up my street. RPG's being my favourite genre of game.
Firstly, NO quest markers, with the Dev's saying they're never going to add them, try and ask people for help in game and you'll be lucky to get any other reply than "Figure it out yourself" or "We're not going to hold your hands through it" The dev's share this sentiment.
So this then means that you have to use your journal, another normal thing for deep RPG games to have. So you consult your journal, to be greeted with a VERY brief description of one of the 8 or so "quests" you'll pick up right at the start.
Thankfully, important places do eventually get added to your map in the form of markers, BUT ONLY WHEN YOU HAVE BEEN THERE!
So this leaves you wandering around, listening to the HIGHLY repetitive voice ambience that goes on in the first main area. Cluelessly trying to find the places you need to go and the people you need to speak to.
So around a hour in you'll be in a inn, then suddenly magically teleported to "the end of the world" wherein a imp begins to prattle on about something you honestly don't know or care about. Typical time's ending blah blah blah, no real emphasis on character developement or any real "reason" as to why this is happening. there just happens to be "Stones" (Real imaginative I know) Laying around that you need to collect.
The best thing about this game is the turn based combat, with actually harkens back to the old tactics games some of us grew up with (shining force, star ocean, final fantasy's)
The Graphics are fantastic and I very rarely seemed to lose frames for the time spent playing as well, the voice acting on the part of the main characters is incredibly well done and believeable, it's just a shame the more important dialog isn't fully voice acted as well.
Hopefully (I really really want to keep playing this game) some kind fellow will create a mod which adds the quest markers that the dev's believe are not needed, because either they come from a community of elitist's or have never actually watched someone play their game for the first time like I did.
Hopefully the community aspect also turns into something a little bit nicer and welcoming than what it currently is. As asking politely for help can get you a whole lot of agro.
At the moment, the game is a 6/10 based simply on the choices of the dev's and the obvious hard work gone into it.

Many people like to compare this game to the portal series or other first person adventure puzzle games, but it's not like those in the fact that it never holds your hand. Instead, it finds a way to teach the player indirectly through experimentation rules in the game that were never in the tutorials preceding. It's like doing math in that respect.
The game also has some metroidvania premises to it, you can't solve this puzzle until you upgrade your gun, an open world that you can freely roam, and a end goal that's so open to interpretation, an alcholic could probably have just as good a guess to the meaning.
So yea, a game about thought, deceit, math, and metroidvania design.
This could either be a chore or the best thing since butter on sliced bread.

Great hack and slash. Like Torchlight, the game plays like Diablo. However, unlike torchlight, the story is actually somewhat interesting and the western/Baroque setting is very unique and unlike any other canon I've seen. Another plus is the fact that even though this is technically an "Early Access" game like many others on steam, it has all the aspects of a full release. Especially now that multiplayer has been added, the game really only has to add the Arcanist class before its essencially all there. Mechanically, the game is well made. Not too HD but just enough clarity to help the game keep its gritty look. While it's technically designed and designated an Isometric, the camera can still be turned with "," and "." allowing for a much less restricted feel like many other over the head games. The class system is also very intuitive allowing for any of the 5 classes to be combined with another class, allowing for a variety of different combinations. The classes are also very accomadating to different desires and styles. The Soldier is essencially basic tank n' slash. The occultist is for people who like edge and magic, the demolitionist for gun people, the nightblade for burst/stealth people, and the arcanist for people who like not edgey magic. Overall, I believe this game is worth about $40, not $25.

As far as roleplaying goes, I don't find much there in terms of speech options. Generally when you talk to other characters, you just click the questions in a list until you've asked them all.
I would give this game a 6.5/10

Once in a while a game comes along that you have a hard time putting down, sometimes it's losing track of time, sometimes it's a case of one-more-turnitis, sometimes you even fight to keep going that little bit longer...
Grim Dawn is one of those games, (in the 'Little bit longer' category), the story is interesting and well paced, the estimated timeperiod I would say feels almost early Renaissance in the vibe it tries to capture and the gameplay elements are solid.
The only major complaint I have against it is the MAJOR disparity between selling prices and buying prices, I'm not talking 50% off here, I'm talking in the ballpark of 80-90% off the buying price of the item to sell it off, after the first five levels or so it's not even worthwhile to pick up items that aren't magic to clog up your inventory.
A few minor complaints include the overly large and unnecessary visual UI, it gets in the way at times, and the camera pan is a problem when heading downward, I always get blindsided by some critter as I'm going towards the UI on the screen as it takes up so much real-estate I can never see 'em coming.
The lack of visual cues for breakable or openable objects is also a bit of a pain, I've taken to blasting the stuffing out of every item I see that might be breakable, chairs, tables, cabinets, headstones, etc. because some breakables have items in them as I found out to my surprise during one firefight.
Finally, more on a feature / preference front, there really is no visual customization for the player character, you're male or female, that's it, beyond that it's all in your rusty, fleabitten, bent, and corroded hardware you find and strap to whatever you feel needs the most protection. Now for single player mode this isn't a big problem, but with the new multiplayer it can be a bit of a bother if three fellows are standing shoulder to shoulder and looking practically identical.
All in all it's got a lot of promise, if you enjoyed the Diablo series the mechanics will be familiar to you, one thing to remember, with firearms / ranged weapons, the shift key is your friend, you won't chase the baddies from here to hell's half-acre or start trying to squaredance with them.

4 Elements is an old tile matching game where you instead of moving tiles around to form links just point out to the game links that are already there. It takes you through a fairly lengthy single-player campaign and even manages to mix in a few Hidden Object and Spot the Difference mini-games. It is however not a game that can stand up to the more modern tile matching games and it's attempts at branching out, through the use of a small storyline and the previously mentioned hidden object games, does not add much to the experience.
The gameplay is simple enough, you have to lead a liquid from the start of a maze to the end by matching tiles to open up paths. Most of it is pretty straight forward but the game does add in a few special puzzles and traps as you progress however the really interesting ones only show up in the very last levels and you don't really feel challenged until then. You get a few special abilities that are charged by matching tiles of a specific color however their use is mostly limited to the areas where they are required to progress.
One bug that kept annoying me throughout the game was that the on-screen arrow that shows you which direction you need to go always blocks your view of a tile.
All in all there is not much to see here. The game is not impressive or interesting and the fact that the individual levels are fairly lengthy means it does not even qualify as a decent timesink. Not a good game to buy.

The problem that I find a lot of games tend to run into that leads to poor reviews isn't any lack of quality in the game, but rather, misleading marketing. Trailers that leave out the important parts that actually define the game. Or trailers that focus on certain elements that lead you to believe the game is about something that it's not. Or even predecessor games in a series that set up an audience with certain expectations, an audience that isn't suited for the change of pace the developer wants to try out with their newest creation.
Any of these things can lead to a game that, while exceptionally good at delivering to a specific audience's tastes and desires, gets tons of negative reviews anyway simply because the game accidentally attracted a bunch of people who didn't understand the game wasn't meant for them. This is a game that absolutely does
make that mistake.
When you watch the trailer, you know
what this game is about. You can tell if this is the kind of gameplay that you find rewarding. It's fast, it's tough, it entails intense focus, and that's all there is to know about it. That's all you need to know. I love how elegant that is.

TL;DR: Interesting game, good to try out, but is easy and gets a bit stale relatively fast. Good as an indie game, but don't expect too much.
My review is a bit harsh, I'll admit it, but the game isn't bad. It's just that I hyped too much and expected much more of it. My first run was a blast, if you only want to try out you'll have lots of fun. But if you want more, don't expect much for now.
I'll be honest, Kingsway looks more like a self-made project you'd do for your early portfolios than a real, finished game. I've still liked it so I'll recommend it anyway.
First of all, don't be fooled by my big play time. 40% of it is time spent AFK/alt-tabbed but with the game opened, and a good chunk was me testing the limits of the game. I maybe got 15 hours of real gameplay, though I would've been done much faster if I didn't go for 100%.
So, the game is buggy. Are those gamebreaking bugs that make it impossible to play? No, but they're annoying when you notice them.
Passive effects don't stack. I had the Keen skill (+1 stats on lvlup) and got another one from a boss gear. Didn't get my promised 5 points each level, still 4. Haven't made the maths on Bandage, but I didn't seem to heal much with two of it either.
You can enchant and disenchant items infinitely, but if you leave the game with an enchanted item it'll get stuck when you come back: you'll be able to disenchant it, but not enchant it back (its name won't change either when you disenchant).
Skill books will tell you if you can't learn a skill of if you already know the level 5, but for skills that have only one level the books will get consumed for no benefit.
Ending #5 didn't give me the Beastkin End achievement, though I did it as Beastkin.
I'm probably forgetting some more.
There are design choices I disagree with.
Many items give you a very vague description. I still have no idea what Lucky Coin is supposed to do, I barely used Potion of Attack until I found out the only drawback for overconsumption was poison (drink them all, antidote, poof)
Some items have no purpose... at all. I still have no idea what I'm supposed to do with these Strange Rubble and Horns, all I'm told is that "someone may want this"
Nowhere in the game are you told how to get a Full Rune. It's not that complicated, but it's near impossible to do anyway. I cleared all caves each run, and I regularly stocked up on one or two runes, getting sometimes a third as well. But all 4? Good luck.
You find healing wells in which you can drop and pick up coins. One at a time. What it does is cool, but without a touchpad to go faster it's horrible.
You can find level 11-13 gear on mobs level 5. With bags so limited in size, not very useful.
Enchanting an item increases its level requirement by 1. If you keep disenchanting and re-enchanting an item, it will eventually require a level you can't even reach (you usually reach level 20 but an item can ask hundreds, see my screenshots). And the bonuses aren't scaling with level, a level 1 ring can be enchanted to require level 20 and still be a crappy +1 str.
Skill speed don't make sense. Two skills with the same shown speed have clearly different cast speeds, like Black Fireball and Astral Storm : both are "Very Slow", but AS is like 3 or 4 times faster than BF.
Agility is worthless, I spent like 90% of my points into it and I wasn't much faster than monsters. My Mage with 3 Agility was just as fast.
The only scrolls that have a noticeable effect are the healing scrolls, in combat the time to use them you're likely to miss an attack. They're just not worth it.
Finally, the game is fairly easy. If you can survive through the first two or three levels you're almost sure to go to the end. Gold is an issue very early, but you quickly get flooded with it and you can't even spend it all unless you keep hopping between shops to buy stuff. The hardest part is managing weight, because I'm a hoarder, but the extra gold isn't very impactful.
You can go all the way with only the basic attack and a heal spell (if you can learn it or find a book), I've even leveled up my MAGE by bashing people manually (even though all my stat points were put in intel), and only switched to spells when I got a high level Black Fireball (that got quicly replaced when I found a book of Astral Storm). All you have to do is put your first few stat points in strength to double your damage. The special pop-up attacks are not a big deal, even if you don't put any point in agility. Really, I died only twice during my runs: when I wasn't paying attention at all, and when I tried hard mode with the weakest class (two bandits when you deal 0 damage as first battle isn't easy).

This game goes hard after Windows 95 nostalgia (if that's a thing?) and absolutely nails it. It's a pretty basic RPG style game where you have to travel around a world lighting 3 beacons to unlock an end boss. There are 4 different classes with different abilities and spells available to learn but I'm not really that sure about the variety because, despite there being permadeath, I actually finished the game with my second character and I'm not feeling the desire to replay the game for a few reasons.
The aesthetic is just really cool and fits with the game's mechanics really well. Your character sheet, the world map and bags are all just icons on the desktop that you open up and can move around and resize at your will, which is actually important because space management on the screen and clutter became a bit of an issue. Things like travel time and attack timers are all loading bars, and the combat is real time and uses the windows in pretty interesting ways. Each enemy opens a new pop-up window and moves around the screen slowly outside of your control while you're clicking on buttons in the window to execute the combat. Some monsters have special abilities that ♥♥♥♥ around with this too, there's a shadow bandit who occasionally uses his turn to minimise his window so he's just attacking in the background while you're frantically trying to get the combat back open. Some monsters shoot arrows that are a small window with a "dodge" button on that fly across your screen from right to left and there are a small number of other spells that use a variety of moving windows with dodge buttons. The issue with combat is that everything is great fun and makes you panic the first time you see it but then extremely quickly becomes 2nd nature which reduces the combat to spamming the attack button over and over with minor breaks. You also see all of the different in combat effects early on and after that just meet stronger versions of the same monsters so it really doesn't develop in a way I thought it could after seeing the cool things it was doing in the first 30 minutes, almost as if they ran out of ideas.
The game took 3 hours to finish, across both characters, so it's very short. That actually turns out to be a bit of a blessing because it was getting very repetitive for me already. The most frustrating part is that the final area of the game is absolutely full of random encounters with absolutely no variety. None of the enemies cast spells forcing you to react or do anything interesting with your windows, so you just spam attack until they die and move on to the next irritatingly frequent random encounter. There are a load of unlocks that carry across characters such as health boosts or starting items so I guess they want you to replay the game multiple times but I have no interest in playing it again, it's looks alone are what got me to finish the first run. It's a really neat game and I'd definitely check out a future Kingsway 2 but the first iteration falls short in a few places for me -

One of the greatest games I have ever played.
Pros
+ Beautiful, colorful, and unique atmosphere which really portrays the "Utopia" that the runners live it
+ Replayability. After I had completed this game I found that I kept coming back to it and replaying different parts of it.
+ A wide variety of parkour moves and martial arts that are at your disposal.
+ Wide and large maps that actually have driving cars and walking NPCs below you (that's always a plus)
Cons
- Not very many routes you can take to get to the set destination. For a game focused on "Making your own path" there weren't many options.
- Buggy. I encountered several bugs throughout the game, but they weren't really a problem unless I went looking for them really.
- Not very many different enemy NPC models. I swear I've killed hundreds of the exact same cop in several different locations (unless they are all twins or something).
- Crashing. During the chapter Pirandello Kruger it will always crash for me unless I walk REALLY slowly in this one part of the map.
-Storyline. The storyline is okay, but it's kinda generic and hard to follow sometimes.
-Length. For the style that this game protrays it would have been nice if the game didn't take only a few hours to complete.
So, overall I most certainly would recomend this game. It may have some flaws, but it is most certainly worth playing.

I might get some flack for this review.  I honestly don't know if it deserves to be bought or not.  To put it simply, it is a good game.  Actually, it's a damn good game.  Yet there is one flaw, and it is embedded in the game to the point where if you took it away, this game wouldn't be itself anymore.
Let's focus on the good first.  It's definitely Star Trek-like.  You have your crew and they fulfill different roles, you are part of a Federation defending yourself froma  rogue empire that wants to destroy you.  So you have to explore planets to find resources and parts to fight other pirates or ships, or even solve problems in order to get more fuel or scrap (money).  You can answer distress calls, buy stuff at space stores or upgrade your ship including your crew, combat weapons, using droids or other things to support your ship in battle.  This definitely makes it not only fun, but damn interesting strategy wise.
Now for the flaw: it's random.  Let me explain: when you are being chased by the rebels, you can't explore every planet and fight every battle, so you have to be choosy about what you do, and how you do it.  Then when you go to the next sector you have to do the same thing.  But every planet, every sector, every thing that happens is a random occurence.  From an outside perspective this sounds awesome.  But when you can't explore everything, so you can literally go through an entire sector, blow all your resources, missiles, and scrap, and when you get to the next sector have nothing to do except hope that people give you free resources, and enough to outrun the rebels.
This randomness literally kills a lot of the fun in the game.  When it happens 2-3 times it becomes game-killing.  I even looked up strategies on the internet, but you can't strategize really well in randomness.  Even the online strategies admit to this flaw in the game (although some don't view it as a flaw).  To me, the randomness would be fine if I weren't so hastefully forced through the system.  Maybe if it was a controlled randomness where some things are meant to be there and some things change all the time, then sure.  But total randomness just doesn't make it for me.  I like the unknown, but I don't like being forced and rushed through it.  It makes the unknown pointless and forever unexplored.
So do I reccommend this game?  In the end, yes.  Get it on sale though.  Don't buy it at full price.  If you like it, then okay, but if you are disappointed then you spent 5 dollars on it and shouldn't worry that much about the waste you might have had on it.

I currently run a i5-6400 @ 2.7Ghz (3.2Ghz boost) with a MSI GTX 1070 X 8GB
Immediately found a 5-20 FPS boost, but thats not the best part.
CPUCores is helping resolve a preexising issue I have with unstable frame-rates.
3 easy examples are as follow:
FarCry Primal boosted from 42-50 FPS in 1527p* Ultra to more stable 58-61 FPS in 1527p Ultra (Using 60FPS lock, V-Sync OFF)
Fallout 4 boosted from 38-56 FPS in 1527p Ultra to a solid 60 FPS in 1527p Ultra (Using V-Sync ON)
Witcher 3 boosted from a 55-81 FPS in 1080p Ultra to a more stable 79-85 FPS in 1080p Ultra (Using 'Fast' V-Sync**)
My preexisting issue is that my GPU is bottlenecking my CPU. This causes unstable framerates in any CPU intensive games (most of the recent AAA titles). One moment I can have a steady 60FPS and then it'll studder and drop to the high 40's - low 50's and moments later jump back up to 60FPS. CPUCores is a GREAT solution to that problem (and I'll continue to use it even after I upgrade my CPU). The program is optimizing core priority to the game and its processes allowing a more CPU "power" availability dedicated to work with my GPU and running my games at a more stable frame-rate!!! And no matter how big or small it WAS increasing the framerate too!!
----------------------------------------------------------------
*1527p is 2715x1527 DSR (Dynamic Super Resolution) - The game is rendered at a higher resolution, then downscaled to my monitors native resolution of 1920x1080 (1080p) to enhanced image quality. In almost all games the GTX 1070 can produce identical framerates whether in 1080p or 1527p when running any settings so I just default on 1527p for a better image!
**Fast V-Sync is NEW to all Nvidia GeForce graphics cards starting from the GTX 960's and UP. It allows the graphics card to render the game @ higher FPS than the monitors refresh-rate without sreen tearing by collecting the best frames produced and tossing aside the left overs. This allows for a crisper and smoother experience for 60Hz monitors without the performance impact of running Vertical Sync. OPEN NVIDIA CONTROL PANEL -> MANAGE 3D SETTINGS -> GLOBAL SETTINGS TAB -> VERTICAL SYNC MENU DROP DOWN-> SELECT 'FAST'

A pretty OK "match 3" game with 70+ large levels and a few mini games added.

Gripes:
I. The UI neglects in helping you figure out what is causing decay. "Decay" is an ambient destruction of usable blocks into unusable blocks that you must replace (as far as I've deduced). Optionally, you can play with decay off, which presents a much nicer free building experience, but when playing with it off from the start (as the default settings are configured), you have to build fast otherwise the decay sets in, which is the opposite effect that you would want when taking time to beautifully place down all your buildings.
II. Building large projects is clunky, I was filling in an ocean and beach in a max size map which took some 5 minutes, why is there no fill tool or mass placement option? Holding your build button down for every tile when you're placing almost 100 of them or more is just a waste.
III. Resources barely do anything; the only thing that matters is making sure everything is green in the production screen. The game gives you arbitrary goals to work forwards to, but the only real goal I've been able to come up with is build something without decay turned on then figure out what you need to make all the numbers green and build around that.
IV. Deliberate lies. In some of the levels you're allowed to build tiles which you cannot support in that level. In the second challenge mode for example (or around the early ones, can't recall precisely which), you have the option of building a cafe, which consumes bread. What produces bread? The UI isn't going to help you (why no option to search for "produces x resource" or "takes in x and produces y"?) so once you finish scrolling through all the build options you come to the realization that you have literally nothing to produce bread. What actually produces bread is a bakery but you won't learn that until you have access to it.
V. Moving the view port is annoying, up and down but not left and right? I'm an avid city sim player and I'm willing to learn a few shortcut keys to move the screen and rotate, just copy an existing scheme like the Sims.
VI. Once my GUI disappeared and there was no option to restore it. I tried pressing all the F keys and most keyboard keys but I had to destroy what I was working on.
VII. There's icons on the inspect mode such as a cog wheel that the game neglects to tell you what they're used for.
VIII. So many tiles with no clear indication of how they interact visually upon first inspection. OK, so from doing the tutorial you will have an idea of what feeds into what, but the game isn't going to bother telling you this or help you out. Are you missing a resource you need? What needs it? Where can I get it? All questions you will be asking and not getting answers to until you spend about half an hour watching chains of buildings decay and you replace them over and over until you finally figure out how many X you need to support 1 Y building.
IX. I had nearly 900 greywater from apartments in the third challenge level that had no relevancy, despite tooltips claiming that it would have implications. What crazy amount can my simulation tolerate before something bad happens? Can't I at least get a warning? In said level I didn't even have access to buildings to process the greywater (Which is like waste water produced from certain buildings notably apartments).
A short description of what the rest of the game entails:
Keep the numbers green and produce enough to stop decay while processing away waste. You can build some advanced buildings that require a more complex support system but you don't really have to. Once you get the numbers green in challenge modes you can just go watch Youtube or something while you wait as there is no speed up simulation button. There's also buildings which synergize together and others which have anti synergy, but again this barely matters.
All in all I'm bored after my time spent playing, there's also some inhabitants that you can work towards unlocking and watch meander around your simulation, but they don't have any specific differences or benefits that I've noticed.

The problem that I find a lot of games tend to run into that leads to poor reviews isn't any lack of quality in the game, but rather, misleading marketing. Trailers that leave out the important parts that actually define the game. Or trailers that focus on certain elements that lead you to believe the game is about something that it's not. Or even predecessor games in a series that set up an audience with certain expectations, an audience that isn't suited for the change of pace the developer wants to try out with their newest creation.
Any of these things can lead to a game that, while exceptionally good at delivering to a specific audience's tastes and desires, gets tons of negative reviews anyway simply because the game accidentally attracted a bunch of people who didn't understand the game wasn't meant for them. This is a game that absolutely does
make that mistake.
When you watch the trailer, you know
what this game is about. You can tell if this is the kind of gameplay that you find rewarding. It's fast, it's tough, it entails intense focus, and that's all there is to know about it. That's all you need to know. I love how elegant that is.

4 Elements is a match 3+ game that captures the fun and unique essence that is generally missing in all the bejeweled clones. It isn’t as genius as any of Popcap’s creations but it does have a place on the list of casual games worth playing; especially if you are in to the Match 3+ type games. The game plays pretty much like any other match 3 games, except with quite few more additional twist. You can directly chain multiple gems together to create larger explosions to clear paths to reach the end goal while at the same time build up magical energies that match the colored gems destroyed. These magical energies unlock powers that include re-randomization of the game board, defrost/destroy gems, etc. In addition to the already huge amount of game changing twist, at the end of each book chapter you have to undergo a spot the difference and hidden object challenge. The story, while very limited in scope, is a nice touch and it adds on to the overall theme of the game.

A very clever puzzle, neighborhood building game that gets you thinking about sustainability and flow of materials.  It's all about balance and planning - just like any effective community planning.

Unlike many strategy games of this genre (e.g. Sim City) where money is a primary focus, in Block'hood the "money" is a variety of materials: water, electricity, fresh air, labor, consumer, fish, organic waste, inorganic waste, sickness, etc. (there is a huge list of these materials - including money itself).  Every building you create has an inflow requirement (e.g. a small apartment needs water, electricity, and fresh air) and an outflow (it produces organic waste, grey water, labor, and consumers).  Each building has a unique list like this.  As you develop your neighborhood you find yourself juggling these resources to various objectives.  If you don't meet your building's needs with the correct balance of material flows, your building will deteriorate and require replacing.
The game has a Sandbox mode wherein you can attempt to create a neighborhood of whatever size you desire (be careful as the more you add the more you must juggle).  Or you can play in the challenge mode where you must meet certain game objectives (e.g. collect 500 beer without accumulating more than 100 wheat).
As I said before, it's a clever game.  If you enjoy puzzle and Sim games you'll probably like this one.  If you're interested in learning more about sustainability this is also a neat way to learn more.  I have had a lot of fun with both the challenge and the sandbox mode.  I have not experienced any technical problems with the game so far.
It's still Early Access and therefore the challenges are a little limited.  The ones available are almost more like an extended tutorial.  I'd like to see these expanded in the near future (I'm sure that's on the way).
Sometimes the game is a little slow. I would like the option to accelerate the game clock (like many strategy games have).  I understand not having a pause option, as it's part of the material flow strategy but once a neighborhood is setup I'd like to be able to let it run at 10x speed to meet an objective.
A fun title absolutely worth $10 if you are interested in the Sim/Strategy/Puzzle genre.

South Park: The Stick of Truth is an RPG developed by Obsidian Entertainment and released in 2014. It's really like playing a series of South Park episodes in a video game format. Having Trey Parker as a writer and voice actor makes the game all the more authentic.
this game (and the show) has earthy and shock humor, South Park is basically TRYING to offend you, and I wouldn't recommend it to most younger gamer's or anyone who is sensitive
. Honestly I haven't even watched very many of the episodes but I have watched some.
On that note though,
. I kept having this sensations that there were a lot of in-jokes that I was missing out on, because I hadn't watched all the South Park Episodes. But that being said I still enjoyed the game as a whole, read on to see why.
You play the game from the perspective of a silent protagonist who has moved to southpark to avoid.... something! You just overhear your parents talking about it, but you character is about as uninterested as possible. The dialogue is quite comical since your character doesn't speak and all the other characters acknowledge it.
An example would be from the early dialogue in the game "do you know why we moved here?" *blank soulless stare* "Honey, I don't think he remembers...." "Good! Now go out there and make friends, son."
Really the only type of interaction I had with the NPC's was by hitting them in the shins with my weapon, or farting in their general direction.
The story is surprisingly longer then I excepted, right when you're bringing one chapter to a close, you go home, go to bed, and wake up to find there's a whole new crisis to deal with. On that note the over all theme is that you're playing an "imaginary" (ish?) game with the south park kids. There are two factions, the humans and elfs, whom are at waring over the stick of truth.
The whole inventory, equipment, quest log, etc, is all done like it's on social media, there are several hilarious jokes that revolving around this theme. Although I did feel a pang of guilt since I only check my own social media once a day and never touch it again. This game has a lot of polish, but what really stands out to me is how organic it is. Here's an example:
Early in my first playthrough, I wandered into a house looking for medical items to loot. I heard a noise behind me, and saw a zombie coming in; instinctively I swung with my baseball bat and knocked its head off, but I could see another one coming behind it, and then a hazmat-suited zombie with an explosive tank on its back. I could take them both in a fight, but I didn't know how many more would be coming behind, and if I blew up that tank indoors I'd be dead.
So, I ran deeper into the house, hoping this building had a second door; it didn't, but it did have a window. At the time I didn't know if windows were passable or even breakable, but I gave this one a kick, and sure enough it broke open, letting me flee out into a ditch as the zombies shuffled in behind me.
As a set piece, that would be pretty lackluster; but, it was 100% organic. Every component of that emerged from gameplay and simple rules; the situation made a thread that would have been trivial out in the open into something life-threatening, I responded as if I really were a scavenging survivor, and the game's mechanics supported my strategy.
Also, day one Linux release! Techland earned a lot of loyalty from me with this game.

These reasons are only a fraction of the game and why you should buy it. To review this game is like a puzzle in itself.
Antichamber is a inspiring indie puzzle game that does not hold your hand and pits you little to none explanation in a strange maze with Escher-like architecture, in search for ways to truly escape it, an endeavor that requires the use of several "color guns" scattered across the map. These guns allow you to do some fantastic things with the games little cubes, and so the adventure lays itself upon you.
The paths will elude you, your perspective on things will be challenged, and you bet the puzzles of this game are as hard as they come. The problem is that the game "cheats" you to boost that said difficulty, by purposedly keeping you ignorant of the game's mechanics and its own "laws of physics".
Truth to be told I could only go so far without help after grabbing the Green Gun, because there is a trick that you must learn to procede (to the Yellow Gun) that is almost impossible to figre out on your own. Seriously. In that point I felt compelled to search for outside help, which broke the experience for me; to add insult to injury, I faced a few others "obligatory" puzzles (the game has a very open world structure, in that you can finish it but not see all it's content) with a solution that broke down to the use of a "hat trick" that was never, ever teached by the game - I can only assume some people discovered it by accident and the word spreaded.
The lack of a more elaborate story is also a negative point, because the developers made such an intriguing maze that the absence of a proper story is felt like a missed opportunity.
Overrall, Antichamber is a beautiful, ingenious game, that deserves to be played simply because it is really mentally challenging. It is nowhere near a good experience as Portal, for example, but it was worth the ride.
Super recommended

XCOM: Enemy Unknown offers a lot of fun for fans of turn based, tactical game play. It has good level design, interesting game mechanics, with smart(ish) AI that can offer you a challenge. You will get emotionally attached to your squad of heroes as you level them up and unlock new technologies. You will weep and want to through yourself from the highest building when they get slaughtered by Mutons or mind-controlled only to be turn on your own guys.
My only real critique of this game is that the maps aren't procedurally generated, thus you're sure to see the same maps over and over, with various permutations in terms of enemies encountered - but this isn't enough to develop the one-size-fits-all strategy you can develop for each map.
Graphics: 6/10. Offers some visually pleasing graphics, but won't blow you away like games running on the latest Unreal engines.
Story: 5/10. It's a generic story of "Aliens invade Earth and we need to stop them. ZOMG HOW DO WE DO THAT? I know, let's form an elite team of heroes to take on the entire invasion."
AI: 8/10. If you make a mistake, the game WILL punish you - severely. Though once you get your squad to higher levels with better equipment the game does get dumbed down a bit.
Game Mechanics: 7/10. Interesting game mechanics, from the turn based strategy to the macro management of your base to the micro management of your squad.
Overall: 7.5/10. Fun game, with a multitude of different modes, but the same maps over and over gets old, fast.

Generally speaking, the game plays like an RTS without shortcut keys when not in combat, in which the minimap doesn't function for anything.

I could write ten thousand words of praise for Antichamber and still not sufficiently express how deeply I love this game.  It's a first-person puzzler in the vein of Portal and Quantum Conundrum, with a catch: surrealism.  Much of the game takes place in impossible space.  Rooms are bigger on the outside than on the inside, walking through a doorway and back lands you in a different room than the one you started in, and sometimes walking backwards is the key to moving forward.  The minimalist visual style is clean, the music is ambient and soothing, and the puzzles are works of mad brilliance.  Antichamber won't scratch an actiony itch, but fans of puzzlers and/or weird games ought to check this one out.  And wear good headphones, because seriously, that soundtrack is phenomonal.

This is very much like playing your way through a South Park episode, and you'll get to see all kinds of places that will be very familiar to you.  If you like South Park, you'll probably like this game.
I found the combat system to  be pretty interesting ... I am usually not a fan of "quick time" events (which are those things where you have to press keys in a certain order to get through a section -- kind of like playing Simon), but South Park does them really well.
You pick your ability or your attack, and then you usually have to do a sequences of buttons or clicks to get the maximum effect of your attack.  It is not as annoying as it sounds (or at least I found it to not be annoying -- and I have a very low tolerance of this stuff) and actually adds a good flavor to an otherwise pretty typical classic "Final Fantasy" style combat system.
The game has a really good length to it; towards the end, I was starting to get a bit tired of it, but when I actually finished it was pretty satisfying.
All in all, I'd say it was surprisingly good and very well made (in South Park style anyway).

4 Elements is a gem-matching puzzle game that won't challenge your brain too much.  Four elemental books need to be unlocked and pieced back together, and each starts off with a hidden object puzzle to find the key.
Once you unlock a book, you start working on the meat of the game: matching gems to clear a path for the energy contained at the starting point.  The energy spreads as you match gems to remove environmental obstructions beneath them, and your goal is to clear a path for it to flow to the objective.  Maps can be quite large with multiple rooms and corridors and all types of obstacles, and time is limited.  There are four powerups that help you get past difficult situations.
After each four puzzle levels, a page of the book and an art card illustration is completed. You play a short minigame where you spot the differences in the cards.
64 puzzle levels, 16 spot the differences puzzles, 4 hidden object puzzles.  Graphics are nice but locked at 800x600. Very casual.
It's like playing three episodes of South Park. Crude humour, many Easter Eggs - recommended for fans of the series.

This game is awesome.  The definitive proof that graphics do not make a game!  The concept is so simple, yet so amzingly, frustratingly addictive and rewarding.
You pilot your ship from one end of the system to another, undertaking tasks, fighting pirates and basically keeping your crew alive and your ship in one piece.  But that belies the hidden depths this game has; the quandries you face...Do you spend your last credits on upgrading your weapons system, or your shields?  Do you attack that pirate or slink away in shame, justifying the decision with a embarrased cough and a barely audible muttering of 'Well, my hulls been damaged and he probably had missiles'.
The gamut of emotions it provokes...horror when you're weapons tech, who you've spent the last hour training to the highest degree gets wiped out by a mear chance of fate!  The sense of smugness when you realise the pirate who attacked you doesn't have the firepower to breach your shields and you have multiple ways of repaying his badly thought out decision with interest (go with the fire beam!).
This game will swallow hours of your life and you will give it willingly, and all the while thinking why didn't I think of making this?

This game has a lot of polish, but what really stands out to me is how organic it is. Here's an example:
Early in my first playthrough, I wandered into a house looking for medical items to loot. I heard a noise behind me, and saw a zombie coming in; instinctively I swung with my baseball bat and knocked its head off, but I could see another one coming behind it, and then a hazmat-suited zombie with an explosive tank on its back. I could take them both in a fight, but I didn't know how many more would be coming behind, and if I blew up that tank indoors I'd be dead.
So, I ran deeper into the house, hoping this building had a second door; it didn't, but it did have a window. At the time I didn't know if windows were passable or even breakable, but I gave this one a kick, and sure enough it broke open, letting me flee out into a ditch as the zombies shuffled in behind me.
As a set piece, that would be pretty lackluster; but, it was 100% organic. Every component of that emerged from gameplay and simple rules; the situation made a thread that would have been trivial out in the open into something life-threatening, I responded as if I really were a scavenging survivor, and the game's mechanics supported my strategy.
Also, day one Linux release! Techland earned a lot of loyalty from me with this game.

Mirror's edge is a first-person parkour game developed by EA.
The story is somewhat unique. You play as Faith Conners a 'runner' (courier) who works for a revolutionary group trying to resist the dictorial govenrment's control. The plot is mainly told through animation cutscenes.
Gameplay is Mirror's edge's main selling point. As a 'parkour' game, it is all about using your environment to get to one point to the next. This includes running up walls, jumping across buildings, sliding, running on walls etc. Another aspect of the game (if somewhat weaker) is combat. Combat revolves around using melee attacks such as punching and kicking to knock out foes. You can also pick up guns from fallen foes, but you have to drop them when proceeding with parkour activities. The problem with the combat is that thers nothing really appealing about it. Furthermore, it can get quite annoying trying to take out when gaurd while others are easily shooting you. Another issue I found is that there are no manual saving in the game, meaning that when you die you have to rely on the auto save feature which takes you too far back and forces you to redo alot of your moves. This might not sound like such a bad thing, however in a game where a single mistake could bring death, choosing where and when to save is important at reducing frustration at repeating the same actions again. Finally, there is minimum objective indicators on the hud which can make it difficult to figure out where your supposed to be heading.
The level design is great. The colourful graphics are quite appealing to look at, especially when you look at all the details in the textures. Furthermore, there are plenty of objects to jump over, climb and run on. There might be some situations where  there is only one way to reach a desired location, but most of the level design is quite open.
Music does a  good job at instilling the techno atmosphere. You get a somewhat sci-fi feel when playing the game which is quite refreshing. Voice acting of characters are decent.
The controls a somewhat a 'hit and miss' scenario. When the conrols work everything is fast and amazing to experience. However, sometimes you may face some unresponsive keyboard inputs, which result in you failing to jump at a crucial moment and the result is death. Add in the fact that you can't manually save the game, this can get annoying quickly as you have to repeat your moves to get back to where you were before death.
Besides the main campaign, there is also a time trial mode. In this mode you have to get a series of maps. In each map you have get from one point of the map to the next as quickly as possible.
If your looking for a visually appealing first person running game and have some patience, this is the game for you.

Dying Light is first-person zombie parkour game, mixing Mirror's Edge's parkour, Dead Island's large amount of weapons, and Dead Rising's way to create modified weapons.  You then will get Dying Light.
The Story fits you as a GRE officer trying to take intel back, as it was stolen from someone dwelling within the city, you soon get used to the many survivors in the city trying to survive, as you help along side them, doing quests for them and such, but overall I give the story an 8.
The Gameplay is fantastic, allowing you to climb up almost anything you want to climb, and do what you want;  Do you want to run into a horde of zombies swing your Electrified Rebar around?  You Can!  Do you want to stick to the rooftops and gun down any enemies down below?  You Can!  With the wide variety of melee weapons and blueprints, you can use whatever weapon fits you, how about a Blunt Baseball Bat?  No?  A Sharp Machete?  No?  Or how about a pistol?  You choose what you want to do, you can also obtain a wide variety of skills, from Drop-kicks, to making grappling hooks, to jumping on zombies heads!  Overall the gameplay deserves a 10.
You can also play in Co-Op.  Co-Op has you and your friends (or random people) completing the story together.  Or how about being a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and becoming a mutated zombie, known as a 'Volatile' invading other people's games and killing them, fitting your needs?  9 for the Co-Op.
I don't really need much else for this review, so please support the creators and buy Dying Light.  (And plus it's 25% off this week, there's nothing better than a sale on a good game, right?)

If you were a fan of King Arthur’s Gold then I have some delightful news to share with you – if you weren’t already aware. Transhuman Design are back with their second Steam game. This time the indie geniuses have put their mind to a multiplayer intended action game that features a sweet singleplayer mode for those who can’t get into a multiplayer game. To date Steamified have featured several multiplayer (including local multiplayer only) games that have been pretty much presumed dead on arrival for a lack of a competent singleplayer mode. I’d like those developers to cast a watchful eye over this game and study it. You can create a game that is fully intended to be played as a multiplayer game – which I believe Trench Run is – and have a successful and well implemented singleplayer mode. It may not save your game entirely but it will give those who gave you their hard earned cash the ability to play your game and not immediately utilize Steam’s refund system.
The fact of the matter is that I have yet to get into a local or online multiplayer game of Trench Run. This could have annoyed the hell out of me. I could have screamed blue murder at the developer but they implemented one hell of a singleplayer mode that makes me think that the game is a worthy purchase even if you never end up playing the fully realized multiplayer game. Yes, I’d love to get a game but  I haven’t had any luck yet. That’s okay because I play on the Australian servers and usually at weird times. I’m certain that I will get into a game at some point. I can try to play on other servers but as is generally the case with region specific servers I fear that the lag would make the game unplayable for me and that I would be at such a disadvantage as to not make the game a particularly enjoyable experience. This is not on the hands of the developers but a simple reality given the quality of Australia’s Internet and the distance data must travel.
The lobby is one of the best for any online game I have ever seen. I love the fact that there is quite a bit to do in this mode while you wait for other players to come on board unless you want to get straight to the action and play the single player mode which is, I believe, the same as games with real players but where you play against bots so that you can get into games quicker. The bots aren’t just a pathetic challenge either as their AI has been programmed very well. Other players, who I hope to play with at some point, have argued that their AI is much better than a lot of the players that they’ve had actual matches with so I have to give kudos to the devs on a job well done.
The pixel graphics are fantastic but that was one of the trademarks of King Arthur’s Gold so it is a continuation of what we have come to expect from the devs. I love the choice of music as it really meshes with the gameplay that I have experienced thus far and it makes for a fantastic touch to the lobby.
Just as I was about to quit my session another player came on and we were able to have a game with bots. Thanks to ‘Iron Raccoon’. The game was fun and very similar to the normal bot games but Iron Racoon ended up winning the game and doing very well.
Unfortunately the game currently lacks achievements and trading cards so I hope that they are added in the future.

Now that the game is released I can share my thoughts and experience with it and hopefully help someone make the choice if this game is for them or not.
I bought the game during its early access stage and completed the first portion it had (25% of the total game) for two times, then fiddled with it after each major update and I have to say that the game has evolved quite nicely, much better than I thought it would be.
The final version is great and works. I have heard of people experiencing some problems (or finding bugs), I've yet to find anything however so I won't say that its bug free or otherwise.
But how is the game itself? First of all, this is not your standard RPG like Diablo or Skyrim, its much more tactical. Think back to games like Dungeon Siege 1 where you had a party and each battle depended on the action you told each member to take, it depends on how you approach the battle and how well prepared you are.
At the same time the game does not hold your hands at all. You have a quest book which gives you information about what you need to do but most of the time it won't tell you where to go directly. It will however give you hints and its up to you to find out how you can complete the quest. This is much more refreshing since it opens up the world a lot, it makes you think and revisit people and places to get more clues and ultimately complete the quest. Overall, once the quest is completed it feels so much more rewarding.
The game is also pretty much open world. Its not as open world as Skyrim for example but its so much more than Diablo, meaning that its not a linear experience of going to point B from point A but at the same time those points exist. Its up to you how you get from one point to another and especially when you go. No one said you can't go from point A to point G from the get go, just be ready to face some strong opponents on your way.
The NPC's in the game (friendly) are also very alive, they won't just sit idle while you steal from them, or rob their house. You can steal everything you want, just don't expect them to sit quietly and watch you take it all away. First they will stop you, then they will call the quards which in turn will land you in jail (if you do not stop stealing). But that doesn't mean the game forbids you from being an♥♥♥♥♥to the world. As long as no one sees you, steal as much as you like (since its so damn rewarding).
Finally, the combat. Like I said in a previous paragraph, its a call back to the older games. The combat is turn based. You and your enemies take turns on hitting each other. You have a set about of Action points (AP) that you can use to do various things like moving, attacking, healing and so on. Once you run out of AP its time to end your turn and let the enemy do his thing.
Because of this turn based system the game feels much more fresh and at the same time much more harder (which is very good for this title). One mistake might cost you the lives of a team member or your own (thankfully you can revive them as long as you have a ressurection scroll). Play your cards right and you will win battles with ease...you just need to pay close attention and think before acting.
I personally recommend the game to RPG fans, especially those that loved the games of old and even more to the new people that haven't had the chance to try one of the old games due to various reasons.

For example, waiting for a bar to be filled before attacking. Or a unique dodging mechanic and counter attacks. Just to add a little twist in a game that just is about fighting goblins, slimes, and skelebones. Kingsway has some of these functions and it makes it what this games is.

Addictively fun and compelling. You start up the game thinking that you're going to play for a bit to pass the time, you better make sure you had nothing to do that day; or rather that week. In a market full of shooters its definitely a sigh of relief to see that this game did not set up shop in the same crowded district. Xcom is made by a niche audience for a niche audience. It combines a good mix of base management and turn based strategy and is not afraid to punish you for not strategizing accordingly. While not  flawless, the game is notorious for its unfair Rng on rare occasions, especially at higher difficulties. Lady luck is a promiscuous little harlot at times and she will either kiss you and whisper sweet nothings in your ear or take a big steaming pile on your chest, rob your money and deem you as a threat to national security by your own  government. The dice rolls you get at times will have you pulling out your hair. In batches or by individual follicles depending on your nature, but in a good way. Oddly enough the game's difficulty frustrations add to the fun. Some odd bugs may pop up here and there and camera glitches can break the immersion at times. Still, If you're a fan of the genre, this will tide you over. Add the exceptional expansion pack and dlcs and just be sure to stock up on supplies for that season's hibernation.
