I don't get what all the reviews are about. Obviously terrible graphics which is to be expected, but then no resolution options besides a hack you need to install online. No saves whatsoever as you have to remember to quicksave or all progress is lost. There is no story, you just wander around a castle and try to find your family. There is no map and no indication for where people are, you just pick one of the 5 ways to go and then backtrack and go the other way till you find them. There are many gameplay problems. You pick up health even when you cant use it and it makes it wasted. You also can pick up ammo, even if you cant use it, again wasting it. You can only carry 15 bullets for your pistol which makes no sense. The combat is just terrible. You use your fists or a sword and just mash attack and sometimes it hits them and sometimes it doesn't due to the poor hitboxes. Sometimes while you're hitting you they can suddenly also attack you and sometimes that can't, showing the lack of any consistency in the system. And since each hit does like 20 damage and you will be fighting 2-3 guys in a row its just stupid. There are spawners that just keep popping out guys and the only way to destroy them is attack the portal, but you have to kill the guys or you die, but they keep coming. Its annoying and poorly done. Also the guys take 20 hits which makes combat tedious and long without reward. I get it that the game is trying to be survival horror, but I have played games that actually accomplish it and they don't need to make terrible combat and way too strong enemies and a lack of being able to hold ammo and wasting resources. You die so quickly and easily, but since you can't sneak or avoid people..... you just die, hope you saved, reload, and repeat. Apparently weapons can randomly be in spots so just based on luck you can have guns sooner or not, which is dumb. Also I was playing on medium, not even hard. I don't know if it's just for nostalgia's sake people rate this because they have fond memories from childhood, but like many old games there are dumb and poorly implemented and outdated mechanics. You also find a bunch of gunpowder and bullets but you can't do anything with them at that point of the game. Not to mention your family can die and you lose the game and there is nothing you can do but restart the game completely since you can't beat it. Having the built-in timer is annoying and further ruins the game because instead of being able to play the survival horror at your own pace, you have to run quickly or you lose. Always having to hurry and pay attention to the timer ruins the atmosphere.  3/10

After some hours and finishing act 1, I have to admit that this game has the chance to be the real Daiblo II sequel (in terms of gameplay). Though, the developers have to take their chance and there is still a lot of work to do.
Pros:
- Skilltree, finally a game that allows tinkering with skills and spells.
- Two "classes" in one, or second spec.
- Typical Diablo like Hack'n'Slay
- You are responsible for stats assignment
- Has this "I want to see more and gather items" feeling or at least unleashes it
- Futurue support or partly supported already: Crafting
Cons:
- The Titan Quest engine, yes, someone may say it is doing a great job but there are many things this engine is not capable of (e.g., missing shadows, performance issues, etc.)
- The gameplay is not that smooth yet.
- Only 2 acts until now (CONSIDER: Early Access!)
- Crafting is currently not really balanced
- Level cap
The game has a lot of potential but the devs need to unleash its potential. There are still some things that are not yet finished and will need a lot of polishing.
Finally, I recommend this game to everyone who is searching for a old fashioned Hack'n'Slay.

Mirror's edge is a first-person parkour game developed by EA.
The story is somewhat unique. You play as Faith Conners a 'runner' (courier) who works for a revolutionary group trying to resist the dictorial govenrment's control. The plot is mainly told through animation cutscenes.
Gameplay is Mirror's edge's main selling point. As a 'parkour' game, it is all about using your environment to get to one point to the next. This includes running up walls, jumping across buildings, sliding, running on walls etc. Another aspect of the game (if somewhat weaker) is combat. Combat revolves around using melee attacks such as punching and kicking to knock out foes. You can also pick up guns from fallen foes, but you have to drop them when proceeding with parkour activities. The problem with the combat is that thers nothing really appealing about it. Furthermore, it can get quite annoying trying to take out when gaurd while others are easily shooting you. Another issue I found is that there are no manual saving in the game, meaning that when you die you have to rely on the auto save feature which takes you too far back and forces you to redo alot of your moves. This might not sound like such a bad thing, however in a game where a single mistake could bring death, choosing where and when to save is important at reducing frustration at repeating the same actions again. Finally, there is minimum objective indicators on the hud which can make it difficult to figure out where your supposed to be heading.
The level design is great. The colourful graphics are quite appealing to look at, especially when you look at all the details in the textures. Furthermore, there are plenty of objects to jump over, climb and run on. There might be some situations where  there is only one way to reach a desired location, but most of the level design is quite open.
Music does a  good job at instilling the techno atmosphere. You get a somewhat sci-fi feel when playing the game which is quite refreshing. Voice acting of characters are decent.
The controls a somewhat a 'hit and miss' scenario. When the conrols work everything is fast and amazing to experience. However, sometimes you may face some unresponsive keyboard inputs, which result in you failing to jump at a crucial moment and the result is death. Add in the fact that you can't manually save the game, this can get annoying quickly as you have to repeat your moves to get back to where you were before death.
Besides the main campaign, there is also a time trial mode. In this mode you have to get a series of maps. In each map you have get from one point of the map to the next as quickly as possible.
If your looking for a visually appealing first person running game and have some patience, this is the game for you.

In a gritty, post-appocalyptic world where you're being chased by---oh wait wrong game.
In a beautiful clean world where you can interact with just about any surface using parkour and cool tricks it is your job as a runner to deliver valuble information. You play as the character Faith a totally kick-butt-awesome girl who knows how to kick her enemies where it hurts and is determined to set things straight.
The Mirror's Edge world is famous for its clean art style and sparring use of color (usually resulting in a single primary color per area). It's a nice change of pace compared to the gritty stuff coming out left and right and is incredibly eye catching. The game which came out in 2009 (If memory serves right) still stands up ok graphically, while perhaps not the best with the passed time, it's by no means sore on the eyes.
The game is also famous for being the only game of it's type- a super awesome parkour game in which almost everything you can reach can be grabbed on to, wall ran across, jumped off of, etc. which with practice can be incredibly fluid and you can breeze through the level... until it comes to the fighting that is. The combat is also made in a similar fashion. You can run on a wall jump off and use the enemy as a landing pad, you can run up to them and slide between their legs to hit them where it hurts, you can kick them off edges of things, you can counter attack and grab their face with your leg to slam the into the ground, etc. my point is, it's awesome, fluid and incredibly satisfying as weel as working well with the enviroments.
There's also a speed run mode for those who like to put the pedal to the medal and challenge your friends.
The fact that this is in place also give great replay value to the game.
I also highly recommend playing it multiple times because even after beating it somewhere around 10-15 times, I still find new short cuts that I didn't see before to help beat my previous best.
I have notivced that as I've been playing a fair number of attempts to grab edges or this or that have failed resulting in death, I wouldn't quite call it a bug, but very much percision is required due to all the ways you can traverse the map and what might be right for the situation, every now and then the game will see it slightly differently than you and you may mess up, but you know, it happens.
Also, I've noticed that this game is not Alt-Tab out friendly, it will crash the game nine out of ten times mostlikely and nobody likes that so it is seggusted you are not doing something actively in another window.
It has beautiful scenery and a wonderful, clean art style. It has very satisfying movement. It has lots of replay value. It has misjudged jumps/ weird no grab moments. It is not Alt-Tab friendly.
Rating: 8.5/10

This is likely the best puzzle game I've ever played, perfectly toeing the line between being esoteric and intuitive. Each new puzzle feels utterly impossible, until something clicks, and then it's suddenly laughably easy. No other game I've played managed to capture such a contrast without feeling contrived or frusterating, but this one has. With its "story" conveyed by little tiles on the wall, and its interface never once showing you a menu in a conventional sense, this game managed to be immersive in the face of a massively surreal environment, leading me to feel as though I was actually in this odd place. Given the nature of the setting, this was utterly shocking. This game is not so much a game as a work of art in the interactive medium.

Excellent party game or buddy-buddy co-op experience.
Multiple difficulties for any level of player, from EZ PZ mode for the casual player just wanting to chill with friends, all the way up to "You made a single mis-step and now you've wasted 40 minutes of fighting for every breath" - The difficulty scales with the number of players in the server, so soloing isn't impossible and is still a fun challenge if you don't have any friends around (or at all...), but partying with 6 players isn't always beneficial because the bigger enemies become VERY hard to kill by yourself. If everyone dies but you, better hope you brought a few spare mags in your undies. You'll need them. ._.
Gunplay is visceral and feels pretty nice, and the reloads are usually pretty realistic except for the revolvers and sci-fi weapons. But you better get used to hip-firing. Guns maintain 99% accuracy while moving and hipfiring as long as you only fire once, so it's best to keep your speed rather than slow to a crawl and get swarmed when you aim down sights. Kinda goes against what most players are used to, so it definitely takes some getting used to. But it's not a chore, and actually feels really rewarding when you learn exactly where the center of your screen is and never need to play games with a crosshair again. :v

I got a pre order key of this game and have been hyped all the way. And lets just say it met my expectations.
It is a fun and a very fast paced game. Every round can last a minute, and some of mine have lasted a just two seconds. The unpredicatable mechanics turn every sniper shot into a cross map scenic flight, grenades into trick shotting basketballs and rockets into ridable objects of mass destruction.
Some people may be put off by the 'aim with wsad or arrow keys' for sniper shots, rockets, grenades, basketballs and flashbangs. It takes a while to get used to it, but once learnt makes the games so much more enjoyable. Heated battles are ensured when a commando is running up behind you, and your sniper aim is pointing the other way. Who will win?
The fact that you can be blown across the map, into a medic kit and instantly start shooting again adds another dimension. You are no longer the 'spectating, bored, dead kid' when shot. Now you can watch people slash at your crawling, feeble corpse or jump in front of a sniper shot and get flung into a building.
And the lobby, don't get me started on the lobby. You can 'booze out' with your friends, buying wine, beer, cigars and even coffee with coins earnt winning games. You can grab a insulting parrot, a fluffy bunny, a crocodile or even a boring old potted cactus or fern at the pet shop, Or why not dress up as your favourite class, a horses butt, a stylish shoot or the rare IM RICH suit. You could also play fetch with a dog, bounce on your croc or try to play fetch with your pet fern. You can also chill with your friends playing basketball, or throw your pet chicken at each other.
The fact that the matches last for no time at all, allow collecting coins quickly. I spent half an hour to get a pet fern, then a chicken, a horse butt costume then finally an assault class costume.
The only downside at the moment is the lack of players, but that is due to the fact that it has just been released.
Buy it, you are missing out. Also explosions, many, many explosions.

The game tries to redeem itself with a lobby area. Here you can buy things with coins (earned from winning games) such as beer, wine, clothes, pets. This part of the game feels pretty tacked on, and is unrelated to the main part of the game. There are not very many people online right now, and filling up games is very difficult. The game seems to be using the exact same engine as KAG, which makes the experience feel more like a cheap reskin than a full new game.
I felt the core game to be pretty uninteresting, and you can see the majority of gameplay in about 20 minutes. This game definitely feels like an Early Access game, and I was suprised it wasn't one. I hope the developers can turn it around, because at the moment I feel that purchasing this game is not worth the price.

Trench Run is a 2D multiplayer shooter that is exclusively about shooting people, blowing them up, and having fun in the process
The gameplay is very simple: you control your characters using only only 2 buttons and direction keys (you could play with a NES controller), the maps are small, there's no story, no base-building, no leveling system… You can immediately buy the game, join a server and blow stuff up. The game is very fast paced, with explosions all over the place, corpses flying across the map, buildings getting blown up, it's very hectic and hilarious to see.
There are 5 classes available that play quite differently:
- the assault has an automatic rifle and grenades
- the demolition has a rocket launcher and C4
- the commando has a knife, flash grenades, can climb walls and defuse C4
- the sniper has a sniper and can camouflage
- the medic, only available in “Run” mode, has a shield, ammo boxes, and can revive his teammates
There are 2 game modes: Run and Skirmish. Skirmish is self-explanatory, it's 4 players trying to kill each other, the player with the most kills win.
Run is a team vs team mode where the goal is to run to the other end of the map while dodging enemies and killing them. There's a bit of tactic involved : you can try to be sneaky, hiding in a bush or using a flash grenade, or defend a strategical corridor from a window, or be a medic and help your teammates with ammo and health.
Outside of the 2 main modes there's a lobby where players can meet in between matches, chat, play basketball, buy pets and costumes and drink beers.
There could easily be new modes, maps and even classes created for the game as it's entirely moddable, and you can run your own private servers.
So this game is awesome, but it has a population problem. There's generally always someone to play with, but the most I've seen online was 6 players and sometimes I have to wait 10 minutes in the lobby for someone to connect. You can still play with bots, they're not too bad, but playing with real people is obviously way more fun. If you're lucky and have irl friends who are into fun games, you could play with them in local multiplayer too (up to 4 players).

BEST ABOUT IT:  Hack n slash with tons of loot and ways to build your character, cool dual-class options.  It’s essentially a modded version of Titan Quest which was a fantastic game, and you don’t even have to squint to see that this is Titan Quest underneath, yet this is also one of its weak points.
WORST ABOUT IT:  It’s about the most unimaginative game possible.  It’s essentially a modded version of Titan Quest skinned with generic post-apocalyptic elements.  I’ve seen little that has improved anything, although having a layered health meter was a good idea, eating rations to keep a secondary health meter up will allow your health to quickly refill, but even that “survival” feature isn’t immersive as you can’t hunt, cook, or even carry food in your pack, you eat upon touching a ration (seems like a tacked on zombie survival gimmick but it actually does add a useful mechanic that replaces constant regen) and you'll still be waiting on your energy bar or chugging down blue potions.  Auto pickup of iron (currency) is appreciated, as is the ability to start an item combination from your vault.  But I think there were many more ways to improve on the engine other than a cosmetic extreme zombie makeover.
GAMEPLAY:  You squeeze screenfulls of monsters to death with your mouse clicker in an effort to obtain xp and loot to build up your character to be a BAMF.  You’ll also likely be drinking lots of potions and comparing stats in your stuffed packs of gear.  If you've played Titan Quest you've played this.  Diablo 3 is very similar too and I remember playing Titan Quest in anticipation of Diablo 3.  Now that we have Grim Dawn and Diablo 3 I would still prefer to play Titan Quest.  [8/10]
CONTROLS:  Great responsiveness but nothing that strays at all from the already well established action RPG genre and nothing that wasn’t already built in its Titan Quest foundation.  There's a heavy load on your mouse finger as you use it to move, aim, and attack, while your keyboard hand doesn't do much especially if your character doesn't rely on many active skills.  [7/10]
STORY:  I guess you’re a soon-to-be-zombie in some other universe that’s mostly  like a post zombie apocalypse Earth and you were in the process of being executed by a town of survivors but then weren't and now go on to start your quest of robbing monsters of their loot.  [3/10]
GRAPHICS:  At this point they're awful and remain awful on all settings.  I'm not even referring to the bland and muddy palettes we get here and in most post-apocalyptic games.  They look ok when the screen is still but as soon as it starts scrolling everything except the main character shakes hyper fast so I wasn't able to focus my eyes on anything but my own character.  I also experienced bands of horizontal tearing.  If you just sit there with a 10 yard stare in a daze (like a zombie I suppose) you can progress but this was actually painful and my eyes were crossed after playing.  I reloaded Titan Quest (released in 2006) for comparison and experienced nothing at all like that and was actually amazed at how much better Titan Quest’s graphics looked than Grim Dawn’s.  Also Grim Dawn wouldn’t even launch at all (because I have 2 monitors hooked up) until I manually edited a game file.  What’s more, if any change at all is made to the options menu while in game it will crash to the desktop and attempt to send a crash report which errors out presumably without sending.  Some of the special effects look wrong, like weather effects just seem off.  [3/10]
PERFORMANCE:  Many areas of the maps cause extreme drops in FPS, even after cleared of enemies.  Loading screens are frequent (something that TQ had almost none of) and often lead to your demise as you enter a new area and monsters pounce you before you have control.  Game was stable once running, so long as you don’t alter any options.  [4/10]
SOUND:  The guns don’t sound like guns, more like bongos tapped gently, and the music sounds like someone just randomly plucking at an electric guitar and plinking keys on a piano.  The music does fit the mood of the game but it would be better if it was less repetitive.  The human enemies sound…special, as the yell “heeeey” when they see you and I wasn’t sure if they wanted to tell me a joke or kill me like every other moving object ever on the screen.  Of course I assumed the latter and shot them dead.  [4/10]
DIFFICULTY:  Currently there's just normal difficulty and it's not too challenging, I was able to run away, kite, or warp out if I ever got in over my head (I played both a melee soldier and a ranged demolitionist), but the monsters do scale to your level and respawn every time you enter the game.  [5/10]
REPLAYABILITY:  There’s a lot of potential replayability due to the versatility of the multi-class character builds, random loot drops, and respawned enemies.  You’d probably want to try the various classes and after doing so would likely experiment with different combinations.  You can freely swap most items between characters so your main could be the vanguard who assembles epic gear for subsequent play-throughs on alternate characters.  [8/10]
MULTIPLAYER/SINGLEPLAYER:  It's currently a planned feature but is not implemented yet.  The single player mode is incomplete and it doesn't take all that long to hit a bridge that is uncrossable because the content on the other side isn't done.  [0/10]
CONCEPT:  Although it's not novel in any way, there is a place for this game if it's done well.  As long as they're already jumping on the zombie survival craze I personally would have liked them to take the survival aspect further, along the lines of Project Zomboid.  [7/10]
SUMMARY:  Just as we'll likely be salvaging derelict ships and airplane fuselages in the inevitable zombie apocalypse to survive, this indie team has recycled the remains of a dead company's game to make a profit.  However in its current early access state it somehow does not quite reach the height of the game whose shoulders it stands on.
I FOUND SIMILAR TO:  Titan Quest, Diablo 3, Torchlight 2, Drox Operative
RECOMMENDED PURCHASE PRICE:  I do not recommend that you buy yet.

MY RATING AS OF 7/30/2014:  49/100

If it works this is a great game. However it is plagued by some awful performance.
I have a pretty powerful computer and know my way around but I get massive framedrops, sometimes into the single digits pretty regularly. I've looked around on the Steam forums, dev / game forums (Chucklefish), and the general internet. I found some tips but nothing helped permanently. Sometimes it happens after an hour or two of playing, other times it happens within 10 minutes of launching the game. Sometimes enabling frame skip works, other times it doesn't. Enabling it halves the framerate cap to 30 though. The same with switching quality settings, it's only temporary (or doesn't help at all).
I really wanted to play more of it, but it got so bad, it just wasn't fun anymore.
If the game works well for you, it's really good. The soundtrack is great (buy it from the composers bandcamp page!). The characters are varied, though I haven't played all of them. The relics can also change your playstyle pretty drastically.
I feel the difficulty is a weakpoint. When I started out, easy was too easy for the most part but normal was far too hard for me. Once I unlocked the Glass and Command artifacts this really changed. Glass sped up the early game so you get to a critical point where you have enough items, and are pretty much unkillable, faster. Command is also completely overpowered and as long as you survive for a bit and get a few items you shouldn't have many troubles, even on the hardest difficulty.
If you can you should definitely try out the game first to see if it runs well for you!

What do I like having played it through (on easy!). Random levels and enemy placement, tension of wanting to move slowly as the game seeks to scare, with needing to move quickly to save relatives. Tension caused by enemies slowly respawning randomly with limited ammunition.
Do I want to play it through again? Not really, but I did enjoy it and I would recommend picking it up on the cheap.

I loved this game back in the day and I still love it now. Nosferatu: The Wrath of Malachi is a very interesting little horror FPS. It takes heavy influence from the classic horror films backing in the early 1900s (Nosferatu, Dracula, The Cabinet of Dr Caligari, Frankenstein and so much more) and brings it all together into an old school first person shooter much more akin to Wolfenstein 3D. The story is, your sister is getting married to the son of a wealthy count in Transylvania where you and your family have gone to visit to take part in the wedding ceremony but you arrive late to the party and it soon dawns upon you that things have gone horribly wrong, only to find out that the castle is haunted by vampires, wraiths, zombies, ghouls, demons and what other kind of classic monster you can throw in there. The count aims to resurrect the almighty Malachi and to bring the world to an end and it's your job is to save your family and to put a stop to the count from resurrecting Malachi.
Since this is a Steam review, I want to break it down into simpler, more straight forward lists of pros and cons:
Pros:
- Open, explorative level design
- Interesting weaponry
- Fun gunplay
- Great aesthetic, has that German Expressionism vibe to it
- Really creepy and atmospheric
- Old school, using medikits to heal as well as allowing you to carry all weapons and as well as powerups throughout
- Very challenging even on easy for your first run
- Randomly generated castle with each new playthrough (Some landmarks will stay the same but it's so you're not lost)
- A wide variety of nasties of the night to fight
- Enemy and item placement is randomized, leaving you wondering what's around the next corner
- Fantastic amounts of replayability
- Captures the feel of the classic horror films pretty much perfectly with it's soundtrack, story, theme, melodramatic voice acting, etc
Cons:
- Some of the geometry can be very dodgy, making you get stuck or fall through places
- The geometry can glitch out really badly sometimes, leaving holes to the neverending void of nothingness
- The graphics look a lot like Quake 1 despite being released in 2003
- Animation quality is quite laughable
- The Wolf 3D maze-like levels will confuse a lot of people, just make sure you remember the layout when exploring
- You are timed against a pretty strict clock, while times moves realistically you will often find yourself too late and some of the people you're meant to save will die off (The level design makes that even more of an annoyance)
- Hit detection can be a pain sometimes
- Not enough powerups in my honest opinion
- Health and ammo is a little too plentiful, it can kill the survival horror element of it sometimes
- The last boss is far too easy and underwhelming despite his cool design
- The game runs for roughly 2-3 hours, that's too short for most
I think Nosferatu: The Wrath of Malachi is a really great game with awesome ideas, good level design, solid gunplay and great survival horror experience. Taking ques from Wolfenstin 3D and being inspired by the films in the early 1900s makes it a pretty fantastic game for horror fans or old school FPS fans to pick and play for a little while. The level of replayability comes in by obviously completing the game in several difficulties but also saving your family members and completing the game as fast as possible, that leaves plenty of room to replay the game if you're really into it.
Overall I would recommend this with all my heart and soul, it's so much fun to play and with it's short length, it's great to kick back and relax and watch the afternoon or evening go by playing this, by then you might have beaten the game already. But it's always fun to come back to every now and then. Your first playthrough will take you a lot longer, respectively, and you will lose some of the people you're meant to save and by the end of the game you will just want to hop back on the horse and do it all again, this time doing it faster so you can save everyone and that makes it a very fun and addictive game to play.
If you like strategy games and if you are a fan of them. This is one of the games you have to try at least one game

Nosferatu: The Wrath of Malachi is a very different game than all the other horror games I've played. It is very unique in the game design, the level design is very good, and the randomization of the castle means that the locations vary and never are in the same place twice when you die.
The story is pretty bland, you inherit a castle, you arrive a bit later than you're family, then when you arrive to the castle you suddenly find out that you're family is missing and you need to search round the castle to find them and not let them die, pretty boring stuff and it feels the same as any old horror movie
The game design is pretty good, the atmosphere is really creepy and well thought out, with the design of the monsters and creatures and the sound effects that play all around you. Although the combat is weak and the hit detection seems a bit off, it is still fun to play
The level design is pretty good as well however when you die, you might see a lot of the same rooms over and over again due to the randomization of the castle, that also counts for the monsters too, you will see the monsters over and over again, although the game does randomize, it is pretty repetitive
The level of difficulty is alright, challenging but fun to play and scary, however when you die, there are no checkpoints (you have to save regularly to continue from where you left off) and you lose everything and have to start all over from the beginning
However this game is fun especially with the lights off, headphones and a couple of buddies around you, this is a great horror game. It is pretty much a hide and seek game with a few enemies here and there, but it is worth it especially during Halloween!

This is likely the best puzzle game I've ever played, perfectly toeing the line between being esoteric and intuitive. Each new puzzle feels utterly impossible, until something clicks, and then it's suddenly laughably easy. No other game I've played managed to capture such a contrast without feeling contrived or frusterating, but this one has. With its "story" conveyed by little tiles on the wall, and its interface never once showing you a menu in a conventional sense, this game managed to be immersive in the face of a massively surreal environment, leading me to feel as though I was actually in this odd place. Given the nature of the setting, this was utterly shocking. This game is not so much a game as a work of art in the interactive medium.
tl;dr
I cannot recommend this game enough.

Antichamber is a really enjoyable puzzle game. The difficulty and game length felt right, and the puzzles' basis in illusion felt unique and interesting without being overwhelming. You don't need an understanding of some higher order math to finish this game, but it is still satisfyingly challenging. I appreciated that if I ever was stumped by a puzzle, it didn't usually mean I was *stuck*, because at any time there were usually several puzzles available in other areas that I could switch over to solve.
The game also has a cool atmosphere supported by its minimalist visuals and ambient music/sound. I especially loved the harmonic, electrical hum that your gun has while using it. Any story is left to implication, so doesn't interfere with the game play at all.
Definitely worth playing.

Battles are extremely short, even most boss battles take 3-4 turns while other fights will take 1-2. This is because damage over time is sooooo strong that you can stack it up and watch the boss lose 50% of their hp in a turn. Attacks that do not stack damage over time are extremely weak comparatively, so combat is not balanced and there is essentially no challenge.
The story itself is also far too short; there are several side quests, but that doesn't make up for it. The level cap is only 15 and you will hit the cap before the end even if you skip all side missions.
Keep in mind these points take into consideration that this is supposed to be a casual and silly game. I wasn't expecting Final Fantasy, it just still could have been better in some areas.
Negatives aside, combat as well as the journey are extremely hilarious and fun your first and second time through the game. Skills in combat are really fun to use and have cool animations.
If you don't mind paying $1/hour or even $2/hour it's worth it at full price, but I hope it's on sale when you choose to buy it.

PROS:
Intuitive UI
Interesting resource balancing concept
Very zen, meditative, pleasing.
CONS:
At the moment, lacks penalties and consequences for negative effects, somewhat limited in scope of building tools, though devs are supposedly adding more. Minor bugs and glitches. Sometimes elements can be frustrating or impossible to place.
Requests for devs, if they read these.
Please add...
Railings/borders
Curved roads/more curved elements in general.
Monetary/resource cost for element construction (with option to toggle on/off)
Allow supports to be built on other elements, such as grass.

So something not particularly well addressed in other reviews is, exactly what IS Trench Run? In short, it's sort of a Smash Bros. take on 2D arena combat games like... well, like Soldat. Except it's kind of pared down. You have two real game modes: free-for-all and team play, supporting up to 4 and 8 players respectively. The twist is that nobody ever dies; although you score "kills" for walloping the hell out of another player, it's more like a game of tag. If you're "killed" you're reduced to crawling and hopping around at a gimped rate, and can't attack. If you can snag a random medkit, you're back in the game but the healthier players can and will swipe these to keep them from you.
There are all of two modes available: Free-for-all deathmatch, and team play (4 and 8 players respectively). Free-for-all is simply a series of single-screen arenas that will shuffle when one player is left standing, and the first one to 10 kills wins. Team play features objectives like "reach the other team's end zone" and maybe other stuff I dunno.
When starting a game you can pick a class that determines what two things you can do; sniper can disguise as a bush and snipe, demolitions can chuck missiles and set mines disguised as crates, etc. This is all well and good, but... it's where I start to realize that the game is minimalist to a fault.
There are two bare-bones game modes. The maximum players in any game is either 4 or 8, even online. The arenas are tiny. You have two action buttons per character. Only the winner gets coins to spend in the lobby, on things like booze, coffee, costumes, and pets which only persist in the lobby where you can't really do anything. On top of all this the game's color palette, which while undoubtedly an accurate recreation of an EGA palette or something, hurts my eyes. It's predominantly sickly tones of yellow, brown, and green.
And finally, we're about two days out from the Steam launch and the servers are DEAD. As I type this there are no player-hosted servers, and nobody at all on the US server. There was apparently a record of 31 people playing throughout the entire day.
I admire the concept and it's briefly amusing to watch the sprites ragdoll all over the place, but I just don't think it has an ounce of staying power as it is now. It looks like it's maybe still in active development(?), but if that's the case it really should've been listed as Early Access.

In short:
A lot less technical than the original XCOM games, but still worth every penny.
Longer version:
Compared to the two original games (UFO / Terror from the deep), there is a lot of differences in design and gameplay:
- You can only perform (max) two actions per soldier and turn... either run a short bit and shoot, run longer, run and reload etc... no more tweaking exact movement distances. I don't mind that they changed it, even if it sometimes feels a bit dumbed down.
- Don't expect to be able to field more than one team at the time, meaning you'll be forced to forfeit some missions - a feature that actually gives the game a greater sense of urgency and at least a fleeting feeling that your choices has an impact.
- Don't expect to be able to customise your soldier's gear beyond main weapon, armour and utility slot(s)... No more ammo, extra grenades and backup weaponry. Another change that does work in the games favour, even though the threat of running out of ammo is gone...
Those were the three major things that I noted when comparing the new and old XCOM... granted it was a decade or two since I last played UFO.
I for one loved this game, and if you loved playing the old games like I did (and can adapt to a modern, less complex paradigm) I feel confident you'll love this one too.

Zenge is a lovely little puzzler, all about fitting pieces together and slotting them into the right-shaped spaces on the screen.   similar in playstyle to Hook, the order in which you place the pieces means that you may not be able to place others, so you might have to backtrack to find a different order.
The game is very soft and warming.  It's kind of like a warm cup of cocoa, while wrapped in a snuggly blanket on a summer's evening.    The levels take anywhere from 5 seconds to 4 minutes to finish, and there's around 60 of them, I think, so it takes three or so hours to play, perhaps a little more if you're not so great at imaging how things look when rotated or flipped.
The pieces can all move around on a track, and when you click them together, you can pick up more pieces and move them about.  As you play through the game, a wordless story unfolds of a little guy searching for the pieces to help with the puzzle.  Each frame of the story is told between each level, and follows the little guy as he reaches for the moon, then uses stepping stones to head towards the sun, find its key, unlock it, and by taking the essence of the sun, to work wonderful magics, search parallel universes, and collect the various operators which help you move bits around the board.  they're rotators. flippers, shrinkers, teleporters and various coloured pads which unlock some moves which might not be previously possible.
The background music is lovely, and just tinkles away in the backgound, giving the game it's lovely ambient air.  The art style is lovely too, with gradual fade-ins for the story frames , and how the pieces you're fitting together make those frames.
The feedback when you make bad moves is very good, and in a subtle way makes you more careful.. in the same way that you know if you spill your cocoa, you're going to have to get up and find a wipey to clean up, which is far too much hassle, so better to just take it slow and relax...
End to end I really enjoyed this game. It's got heart and soul baked into it.  It's not hard, and very seldom does it throw you a level which needs more than a few minutes of playing about..  there were two which required you to fit some pieces together in a specific place, although other places should have worked just as well, but they're not too frequent.
Very well worth my time, and I feel very relaxed and like I've experienced a lovely fantasy tale too.

I've played this game for a bit in my free time at work and I think I've summed up a good idea of how this game is now and where it is headed.
This game "is a passion project by a small team of experienced developers" and it shows in many ways. There are a lot of fine details that you wouldn't expect and a lot of overall design that shows that they have their vision and are following it quite well.
Some examples: The Art direction is fantastic. The character models are well designed, albeit very limited, in that all players look the same currently with only the armor and weapons distinguishing them. This shows they wanted to spend their important resources on great looking armor and weapons, but that they may not have the time to implament individual models which is a great trade off.
The combat is mostly balanced with a lot of small changes expected before release. Some skills feel underpowered or clunky while others shine brilliantly. The skill I'm thinking most of is the skill where your soldier charges to an enemy. I love the concept, but the execution of it bugs out and sometimes I'll permenantly run into a wall twitching out. Although trying the demolitionist gave me a complete 180 and the skills feel great and mesh well together. Although some builds are more viable due to the lack of support gear designed to allow a greater range of builds. Most resistances on Armor are pretty useless as there aren't enough enemies with strong types of damage to worry about covering your resistances especially Chaos damage. Only damage type I've had annoyances with were Cold, Poison and Bleeding.
Pets feel underpowered to me, although I haven't taken Pets up to max level range at this time and tried a full pet build. I can't imagine them clearing swaths of enemies like my Bullets can or my Passive arc attacks on Soldier. Will change/update if I get the opportunity to test them more thoroughly.
The game runs fairly smooth, but at this time it feels like it drags. In time I expect optimization of the game to bring a smooth experience to a wider range of computers. I'm running a i7 4700 and GTX 765M and I have a hard time keeping a smooth frame rate in larger crowds. Although I get similar performance on my on die GPU so it shows that not only will the game potentially run fantastic on more modest computers, I expect with some time they will have a premium experience on nicer hardware.
The town upgrading feels very underdeveloped currently. I'd love to see it flesh out considerably and would love to see the rift sitting in town work double to allow access to the Aetherial Realm and possibly a Chaos Realm giving it more purpose than a quick hub to dump stuff and grab a few quests.
Monsters feel varied enough, although it feels kind of off. I wish some monsters would have more mechanics than "RUN AND HIT" or "RUN AND SHOOT". I like some of the goblin type monsters who can heal and the summoner type who raise mobs to swarm you. I'd love to see the beasts who shoot you from range unleash a thorns effect if you get close causing you damage for being close or to see the zombies get up a second time occasionally. Although I'm happy, that would be a fine touch that would definitely go a long way to making the world feel more fleshed out.
The Lore is great, but I want more. The universe is fantastic.
Overall I feel this game is a solid 7/10 right now for being early access. It's very fun, worth every penny they ask for and definitely a promising game with a bright (Grim) future. Looking forward to seeing some truly devious things come from these developers.

FTL: Faster Than Light has you commanding your very own spaceship as you blast through the galaxy, being persued by rebel raiders.
FTL is fantastic, allowing for almost sim-like control in a sci-fi environment. You can control the ship, it's systems, it's weapons, it's engines, mostly everything. The game gives you a great sense of control, but sadly, there is a thin veil of RNG which surrounds it.
I may be wrong, heck, I am a lot of the time, but after 33 hours of play it felt as though randomness played too big a part of this game than it should. Now, don't get me wrong, I loved the game! 33 hours of playtime is a heck of a long time to keep my attention! But, on the harder difficulty (Normal, strangely, being incredibly hard, and Easy being of normal difficulty) it felt as though there were situations were you just could not win. After spending about an hour on a no-win situation became kind of disheartening.
And that, sadly, was where I gave up on it. Again, I hugely recommend this game. It's incredibly fun, with tonnes of really great and interesting sci-fi scenarios to play out, just like you're your very own space captain!
But, with so much praise for the game already out there, I figure I'd highlight what I feel is it's biggest fault.
Anyway, enough out of me. 33 hours of playtime should tell you all that this title is well worth purchasing, and is usually priced incredibly cheaply!
Thoroughly recommended!

Dives so far into the parody of The Matrix that it unintentionally becomes the best Matrix game possible.
All difficulties are extremely easy on the PC, because having the ability to aim accurately invalidates the need for super powers or "high powered" weapons: just tear everything apart with the starter handgun.
Lacks the diversity of hilarious minigames that made SR3 such a delight (no sewage truck, flaming atv, etc.).  Retains some of the silly minigames from previous (Streaking, etc.), but they're pared down and simplified (Insurance Fraud has no set boundaries once started, etc.).  Because of the introduction of superpowers and over-the-top weaponry, several of the retained minigames are lackluster (especially Property Damage: TANK-KUN, I CHOOSE YOU!).  While some of those that were the most iconic were left behind (Gameshow).
Also sorely missing is the turf control aspect of the game.  Granted aliens and rivals spawn in clusters to control areas, there's no feeling of progression to wiping them out.  You don't feel like that particular group of enemies mattered, and there's no real reason to stop and clear them when the only discernable reward is a comparable amount of pointless XP as any other activity would provide.  The non-core game feels sparse and directionless, in a license that thrived on the quality and variety of the non-core minigames it brought to the table.
While I still highly recommend picking it up due to it being the best and most faithful recreation of the Matrix concept, I can't recommend it over SR3 from a mindless fun perspective.

.  The game that changed everything. Before this the
series was just a man with a ponytail and some Gearbox expansion characters hiding in vents and assaulting things with a crowbar, and a rather disappointing short film with that guy from
. But this game didn't just change the way people viewed the series; it changed the way we look at video games.
Let me tell you a story. Back in 1993, the video game
was released. The people at Valve, being innovators in video games, wanted to make a video game that "scared you as much as
did", and this originally manifested itself as Valve's
famous unreleased game (and apparently Gabe's pet project, if some sources are to be believed),
. Whilst the game itself never made it to Alpha stage, you can see fragments of it in most Valve releases - particularly in
.
The original pitch for
included a feature about the new game engine, that apparently featured improved physics and graphics. But wait, they're talking about GoldSrc? The game engine that's definitely not based on the
engine, which itself is definitely NOT the id tech engine series? Surely GoldSrc is the last engine you would think of when talking about game physics?
But whereas
was more action and exposition-based, it's successor was more aimed at creating realistic and fully-fleshed out characters, scenarios and locations for the player to explore at their leisure - whilst obviously keeping within the parameters of that world and it's restrictions. And this is where half of
's success lies. The characters are brought to life very convincingly with a combination of excellent animation and superb voice actors on top par. If Barney was the gamer's fan favourite of the 90's, Alyx Vance is undoubtedly the favourite of the the last decade - and beyond. I'm not a
fan so I don't rate Elisabeth, but I get why people like her. It's for the same reason they like any video game companion: because they're sharing in the adventure and loving it. I'll bet there were plenty of teenage boys out there who considered Alyx a legit girlfriend. Well, we can all dream. Ooh baby baby, yeah some more... Uh, what? No, I'm not doing anything... *cough* Uh, anyway... Moving on.
I'm not going to gush about the Beta content, because everybody knows about that. As much as I do think there are some excellent unexplored ideas in there, that's not the focus of this.
So how does the game fare today? You would think that after over 10 years at the top, surely it feels a little bit dated? Well, actually, no. It doesn't feel the least bit dated, it feels just as fresh as if it still had the pre-wrapped packaging on. Admittedly, it doesn't share the polish of some newer games, but is that inevitable for a game that's just celebrated it's twelfth anniversary? Maybe, maybe not. I think that the only thing that dates the game is the light effects. I'm not knocking it, but these days you expect some JJ Abrams-esque lensflare everywhere.
But that aside, the game is undoubtedly fully deserving of its title.

- Antichamber.
is one of those games that goes beyond the expectations and ideas of a game is or should be. With a minimalist design and mysterious atmosphere, its world comprises of non-euclidean geometric spaces that appear illogical, but more accurately, are hyperlogical - abiding by their own predefined rules and logic; most evident in the trailers and screenshots above.
This is a mind-bending little game so full of depth and complexity and meaning that it's hard for me to really present to you what it is and can be. It's a puzzle game with no fail state — you can't die. It's a puzzle game where the levels are all connected together. It's a puzzle game about life. It's puzzle game about a lot of things.
The game has 120 signs, each with unique advice that fits not only in relation to the game's puzzles, but also as a reflection on the ups and downs, lefts and rights, weird-bending corridors of life. They're probably my favourite part of the game, and I have them all as a slideshow for my desktop wallpaper.
In conclusion, I think Antichamber is a beautiful game that more people should play, because even if you are the world's top Global Elite player, or a sad Silver 1 like me, we all have our own ups and downs in life that deserve to be addressed.

First off, I am a huge South Park fan, so I'm bias.
I thoroughly enjoyed this game and the RPG elements were pretty great. My 30 hours on record are from three different playthroughs, so take that into account. The game is short and, oh, how I wish it was longer! I hated extinguishing everything there was to do and going to the endgame.
I would highly recommend this for any South Park fans and old-school rpg lovers. If you aren't a South Park fan, you most likely won't enjoy it either as much or at all. If you're easily offended by South Park, completely avoid it. It crosses the line on quite a few subjects, which I personally love dark and messed up humor. Lots of fart jokes, too, which are meh, but didn't ruin anything for me even though your Magic ability is basically fart types.
Gameplay is solid. Lots of different weapons and customizations, though you'll be switching out equipment on a regular basis. Battle is turn-based, you'll almost always have one partner with their unique moves and abilities. You can switch between different characters in and out of battle, which is nice (though it takes up their turn when in battle). Difficulty, even on hard, is pretty easy when you have the option to use an item then attack/use magic.
It's similar to Mario RPG (on SNES) with timed attacks for extra damage, so it's somewhat interactive though can be annoying.
Story is great, though what few decisions you have, don't have much of an impact on the game and both decisions lead to the same outcome. It pretty much is just an interactive episode of South Park.
If you like the looks of this game, but still on the fence, I'd say wait for a sale before getting it. You always have Steam refund options if you don't like it, which you should be able to figure out within the first hour or so of playing.
My only complaint is that I wish it was longer and not so many timed button pressing events (I forgot the proper acronym and term for that).

As a puzzle game, I highly recommend AntiChamber. Puzzles that change the way you think in subtle ways, juggling your perceptions with indirect, and sometimes very direct means. I found more than a little enjoyment experimenting with new ways to solve the puzzles; because as with all truly great puzzle games, there are more ways than you think to solve a given challenge. The best moments, in my estimation, come from realizing just how much the game has shaped your understanding, as puzzles you would knuckle your head in frustration at suddenly break open before your newfound circuitous thinking.
That's not to say it's all gravy, though. There were a handful of situations I found myself beyond frustrated at, as even knowledge of what I was supposed to do didn't translate into the ability to do it. In one instance in particular, a minor slip up destroyed all progress I had made, forcing me to begin anew. These moments of rather stone-faced "un-puzzling" if you will, are some of the (personally, anyways) minor tarnishes on an otherwise highly polished game.
Storyline-wise, or in this game's case, a lack of storyline, is understandably bland, as the game prefers to let the puzzles speak for it. A stellar story/storytelling should not be the reason anyone picks up this game, in my opinion, but anyone looking for an incredible and thought-provoking puzzle game would do well to give this one a shot.

In short:
A lot less technical than the original XCOM games, but still worth every penny.
Longer version:
Compared to the two original games (UFO / Terror from the deep), there is a lot of differences in design and gameplay:
- You can only perform (max) two actions per soldier and turn... either run a short bit and shoot, run longer, run and reload etc... no more tweaking exact movement distances. I don't mind that they changed it, even if it sometimes feels a bit dumbed down.
- Don't expect to be able to field more than one team at the time, meaning you'll be forced to forfeit some missions - a feature that actually gives the game a greater sense of urgency and at least a fleeting feeling that your choices has an impact.
- Don't expect to be able to customise your soldier's gear beyond main weapon, armour and utility slot(s)... No more ammo, extra grenades and backup weaponry. Another change that does work in the games favour, even though the threat of running out of ammo is gone...
Those were the three major things that I noted when comparing the new and old XCOM... granted it was a decade or two since I last played UFO.
I for one loved this game, and if you loved playing the old games like I did (and can adapt to a modern, less complex paradigm) I feel confident you'll love this one too.

Xcom, a good addition to strategy games.  You get a basic squad of up to 6 units, that you can outfit with armor, weapon, and gear.  Each soldier is more or less unique, and all class up to a few classes such as; medic, sniper, assault and so on.  Even researching new tech, a long with mapping out your base.
There is definintely difficulty in this one, especially since your squad size has been reduced to 6, down from the classic's 20.  A lot of the controls from the classic have been simplified, and turns don't take forever with a smaller more focused squad.  It is disappointing though that the enemy count as well, has been lowered.
I personally feel it falls short on a few things the old classics had, such as base construction, and management from hiring scientists for research to engineers for production, as well as the smaller enemy count.  However, if makes up for it in a good challenge, and strengthening what it does provide well...that being a tacticul squad-based turn-based strategy.

First off: Thanks ArchDaily for introducing this game on their site. The nearly simultaneous release of this game and Dungeon Defenders has led to inevitable comparisons between the two games, and rightly so. Both games are Tower Defense games played on a personal level rather than a top down perspective. Both have the player control a character that can run the course of maps, place a number of defenses and traps, use different abilities and go toe to toe with the advancing mobs with melee and ranged weapons. The difference comes in the approach. Dungeon Defenders distributes the different abilities among different classes making the game virtually unplayable in single player especially if you’re playing a support class. Orcs Must Die has no multiplayer but gives all the abilities to one character with new abilities with each successful mission. Orcs Must Die also feels much more action oriented. If you’re looking for a good tower defense game that you can play by yourself, look no further than this game!

Unless you haven't bought this game yet, or if you haven't seen the trailer, you MIGHT be asking, MohawkGoatyGoat, what in the name of dank memes do you do in this mighty-fine Hexagon-based action game of actioney action? Well, I can answer that question WITH a question. Who likes to move around dodging things with the middle (Hexagon) going ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ spinning around like a charged up spin-dash, while looking at pretty colors? I made the game seem bad, didn't I?
Well, this game is NOT bad! Lemme tell you why plz.
In Super Hexagon, you move around dodging the obstacles that come in front of you. They ONLY appear in patterns with other obstacles. There is the C-pattern, the Bat pattern, and so many others (yes, I'm getting the names from a Steam guide). It's REALLY hard, well, that's because Terry Cavanagh has been notorious for creating some of the most nightmare fuel challenges in a video game.
Once you survive a level for 60 seconds, the hyper version of the level engages, which is basically a much harder reincarnation. Once you survive 60 seconds in a hyper level, you go to (what I call) a hyper INSIDE a hyper. OOooooo. Basically, it just adds pretty colors. Only exclusive to the 1st level (and it's hyper counter-part), the shape can change into a pentagon and a square. NEATO!
The middle Hexagon is spinning while you play, so you need to have a high attention span. This spins you, and the obstacles that come down. This feels like it makes the game a lot harder. When really, it's the same, but it can throw you off guard at times.
I know I haven't said much here, but this is a great action game that has it's own law around it. Don't check it out, and you go to jail, without being able to redeem you get-out-of-jail-free card.

This is a definite diamond in the rough. WoM was released in 2003, so it obviously shows it's age in it's graphics but contains excellent ideas implemented very well for that era of gaming. The AI is aggressive, doesn't hold your hand at all when it comes to enemies, and is smart enough for your family memebers to stay out of your way when you're being attacked, or help you if they can.
You will die, probably several times, but it will always be your fault, which is actually really refreshing. In these days of cover shooters and regenerating health, your ability to screw yourself into a corner by needlessly engaging with multiple enemies instead of carefully taking one or two at a time is a nice nostalgic touch which meshes very well with the overall story and aesthetic, as you are supposed to be just a man, confronting horrible unholy abominations in an effort to rescue your family.
The random element is a great touch, meaning you can find family memebers in different places every time you play. The clock counting down to sunrise adds to the pressure and stress you feel as you come across room after room with no one in it. You might almost catch yourself yelling for Melissa or Gregory, or finding yourself a little sad when you fail to save one of them in time.
The weapons are nicely varied. Your fists are your default, allowing you to smash face on little goblins and even stunlock early vampire enemies. Stakes are both weapon and utility, allowing you to stake sleeping vampires if you're quick enough, or being lit on fire to provide a portable light source in super dark areas. The guns are by no means overpowered, given the Flintlock's long reload time and the Revolver's 5 shot cyclinder. The cross is a highly unique weapon, as it can cower low level enemies but not harm them, be charged up and released to provide a bright, brief flash of light to help guide you through a room, and is the ONLY weapon which can destroy Shadow vampires.
Some AMAZING sound design rounds out this old beauty. I would seriously recommend turning off the lights and playing with a decent set of headphones, but even on older tv speakers 6 feet away from me, the sounds and ambeint music are very very well done. Creepy noises, creaking doors, moaning ghouls, growling devildogs, all coupled with an ambient music score which was crafted by someone with an obvious love for old horror cinema.
I definately recommend giving this game multiple playthroughs, but even once is enough to put this one in my favorites list.
Cheers.

X- Beyond the Frontier.  I bought this game origianlly the year it was released.  It required the CD-ROM to be inserted due to digital rights management.  I lost the original game years and years ago during a move.  Today, I found out it was on Steam.  How could I resist?
I'm not a fanboi.  You need to know this.
If you're looking for instant gratification and eye candy thrown at you because you rolled your face across the keyboard, this will not be the game for you.  If you like to prove to the micro-universe inside your hard drive that you can conquer any hardship thrown at you, then this is certainly the game for you.  It's about beating the odds.  No, not quite.  It's about ripping the arm off of the odds and beating it to death with its own appendage.  Yeah, that is the kind of game this is.
I will not sugar coat this review.  I've cussed at the screen as many times as I've cheered.  This is a multi-layered game.  First layer, trade your way to better stuff.  Second layer, become a business owner and make NPC traders work for you.  Third layer, catch pirates if you want, but you must deal with a growing xenon threat, which will target your NPC traders and blow them out of the sky from time to time.  Yeah, you lose the cargo haul when that happens... which is all the motivation you need for going after the xenon to end them.  Fourth layer to this game, follow a storyline that ends up with you ending the xenon threat once and for all.
So basically you start with 100 credits, a broken ship and owing the local militia forces 3500 credits.  Don't leave the starter system without paying that off, or the offended race will Kill On Sight (KOS) you.
Nothing easy, but like real life, anything you work hard for and gain, you will better appreciate those gains.
In this game, you can go from that broken ship, a hundred in the pocket and a big bill to having a whole host of stations that you own, rocking shields, death weapons and a fleet of NPC fighters at your back.  It's not handed to you.  It's not gift wrapped or slid under the table in your direction.  Something may seem completely ridiculous but later on, you nod and go, "Ah, so that's why I couldn't find any Stott Spice factories in Teladi space."
Most important aspect of this game, many people think the game is over once the main story line is defeated.  It's NOT.  You can still build an empire worthy of your greatness.  After the main story is done, there are Nine Xenon Sectors to clear out.  It won't be easy.  Once they're all dead and completely gone, you now have nine sectors to build an empire beyond imagining... or can you survive it?
My original game owned more than 1000+ hours, my own empire was making tens of millions by the hour as I built factories in five of those cleared out xenon sectors, and those factories are defended by their own fleet of ships...
All from a broken slow ship and 100 creds.  Dare you take that challenge?  Can you survive the whacked alien mentailies from a handful of different races?  I loved this game back in the day, and I'm loving it all over again.
I arrive, I suffer their madness, and I conquer them.  What more could you want in a space simulation?

I've played this game for a bit in my free time at work and I think I've summed up a good idea of how this game is now and where it is headed.
This game "is a passion project by a small team of experienced developers" and it shows in many ways. There are a lot of fine details that you wouldn't expect and a lot of overall design that shows that they have their vision and are following it quite well.
Some examples: The Art direction is fantastic. The character models are well designed, albeit very limited, in that all players look the same currently with only the armor and weapons distinguishing them. This shows they wanted to spend their important resources on great looking armor and weapons, but that they may not have the time to implament individual models which is a great trade off.
The combat is mostly balanced with a lot of small changes expected before release. Some skills feel underpowered or clunky while others shine brilliantly. The skill I'm thinking most of is the skill where your soldier charges to an enemy. I love the concept, but the execution of it bugs out and sometimes I'll permenantly run into a wall twitching out. Although trying the demolitionist gave me a complete 180 and the skills feel great and mesh well together. Although some builds are more viable due to the lack of support gear designed to allow a greater range of builds. Most resistances on Armor are pretty useless as there aren't enough enemies with strong types of damage to worry about covering your resistances especially Chaos damage. Only damage type I've had annoyances with were Cold, Poison and Bleeding.
Pets feel underpowered to me, although I haven't taken Pets up to max level range at this time and tried a full pet build. I can't imagine them clearing swaths of enemies like my Bullets can or my Passive arc attacks on Soldier. Will change/update if I get the opportunity to test them more thoroughly.
The game runs fairly smooth, but at this time it feels like it drags. In time I expect optimization of the game to bring a smooth experience to a wider range of computers. I'm running a i7 4700 and GTX 765M and I have a hard time keeping a smooth frame rate in larger crowds. Although I get similar performance on my on die GPU so it shows that not only will the game potentially run fantastic on more modest computers, I expect with some time they will have a premium experience on nicer hardware.
The town upgrading feels very underdeveloped currently. I'd love to see it flesh out considerably and would love to see the rift sitting in town work double to allow access to the Aetherial Realm and possibly a Chaos Realm giving it more purpose than a quick hub to dump stuff and grab a few quests.
Monsters feel varied enough, although it feels kind of off. I wish some monsters would have more mechanics than "RUN AND HIT" or "RUN AND SHOOT". I like some of the goblin type monsters who can heal and the summoner type who raise mobs to swarm you. I'd love to see the beasts who shoot you from range unleash a thorns effect if you get close causing you damage for being close or to see the zombies get up a second time occasionally. Although I'm happy, that would be a fine touch that would definitely go a long way to making the world feel more fleshed out.
The Lore is great, but I want more. The universe is fantastic.
Overall I feel this game is a solid 7/10 right now for being early access. It's very fun, worth every penny they ask for and definitely a promising game with a bright (Grim) future. Looking forward to seeing some truly devious things come from these developers.

- Antichamber.
is one of those games that goes beyond the expectations and ideas of a game is or should be. With a minimalist design and mysterious atmosphere, its world comprises of non-euclidean geometric spaces that appear illogical, but more accurately, are hyperlogical - abiding by their own predefined rules and logic; most evident in the trailers and screenshots above.
This is a mind-bending little game so full of depth and complexity and meaning that it's hard for me to really present to you what it is and can be. It's a puzzle game with no fail state — you can't die. It's a puzzle game where the levels are all connected together. It's a puzzle game about life. It's puzzle game about a lot of things.
The game has 120 signs, each with unique advice that fits not only in relation to the game's puzzles, but also as a reflection on the ups and downs, lefts and rights, weird-bending corridors of life. They're probably my favourite part of the game, and I have them all as a slideshow for my desktop wallpaper.
In conclusion, I think Antichamber is a beautiful game that more people should play, because even if you are the world's top Global Elite player, or a sad Silver 1 like me, we all have our own ups and downs in life that deserve to be addressed.

As a puzzle game, I highly recommend AntiChamber. Puzzles that change the way you think in subtle ways, juggling your perceptions with indirect, and sometimes very direct means. I found more than a little enjoyment experimenting with new ways to solve the puzzles; because as with all truly great puzzle games, there are more ways than you think to solve a given challenge. The best moments, in my estimation, come from realizing just how much the game has shaped your understanding, as puzzles you would knuckle your head in frustration at suddenly break open before your newfound circuitous thinking.
That's not to say it's all gravy, though. There were a handful of situations I found myself beyond frustrated at, as even knowledge of what I was supposed to do didn't translate into the ability to do it. In one instance in particular, a minor slip up destroyed all progress I had made, forcing me to begin anew. These moments of rather stone-faced "un-puzzling" if you will, are some of the (personally, anyways) minor tarnishes on an otherwise highly polished game.
Storyline-wise, or in this game's case, a lack of storyline, is understandably bland, as the game prefers to let the puzzles speak for it. A stellar story/storytelling should not be the reason anyone picks up this game, in my opinion, but anyone looking for an incredible and thought-provoking puzzle game would do well to give this one a shot.

What is it? 3-d Non-Euclidean story-lite puzzle game.
Graphics: Minimalist black and white graphics puctuated by garish saturated bursts of color. The graphics work pretty well for the game by eliminating superflous details and highlighting only what's needed to solve the puzzles. The minimalism also helps add to the disorienting atmosphere of everything.
Gameplay: Antichamber's most unique feature is its confusing, non-Euclidean geometry and the various ways it plays with spacial perception. There are a dozen or so puzzles, right at the very beginning, that involve navigating the rooms of Antichamber. These are truly clever, I've never seen anything like them before. Then you find your first "upgrade", which is effectively a less inspired version of the Portal Gun from Portal, and the puzzles turn into standard puzzle game fare using this tool.
Story: There is no plot, but there are some loose ideas conveyed through patronizing aphorisms found on the walls, which are pseudo-deep and meant to be applied to Life but are written poorly enough to be unconvincing. There is an ending, but I don't have the foggiest idea what, if anything, it was trying to convey and I suspect you won't either.
Difficulty: I got stuck on quite a few of these puzzles, and had to look up the solution to one or two. There are some mechanics that are very subtly telegraphed, and most of the rooms don't work as you'd expect them to work in the real world, so it takes a certain bending of mental rules to figure these puzzles out. A few puzzles also require precise execution. Expect to have a pretty hard time compared to most modern puzzle/adventure games.
Value/Replayability
It took me almost 10 hours to solve all of the chambers and see the ending, about $2/hr at full price. I wouldn't play it again after solving everything.

block'hood is a relaxing city-builder (or neighborhood builder I guess) with a charming blocky aesthetic and a potential for some really impressive looking structures.  This city builder differentiates itself from the pack by making it more about resource management than anything else.
By my count, block'hood has (at the time of reviewing this) about 96 different things you can build to produce resources.  Unlike most games where you build stuff, you don't require the resources at the time of building, rather they're required to output their resources.  Because of this you can rearrange your city as much or as often as you please, as long as you constantly have input for any given building, or it will DECAY!
In my time with the game I didn't find anything antagonistic, so it really seems to be just about planning and executing.  If that's something you enjoy, and if you're happy with a secondary goal of making something as beautiful as it is self-sustainable, then you'll probably really love this game.

Tripwire Interactive has become a beloved developer/publisher to me over the years. From my perspective, they have a proven record of accomplishment of releasing games that fill an underrepresented niche and do so with passion and expertise. Then they provide best-in-class support to those games over years, actively support modding, and release tons of free content and updates. Killing Floor 2 development trudged along unflinchingly through the early years when salty Steam keyboard warriors flooded the store page with thumbs down reviews and tears. I am glad they persevered because, man, what a game they have delivered. I have something like 42 hours in KF2 at the time of writing this review and there is so much to the game that I have barely scratched...I can see putting hundreds of hours into this game before even a hint of being bored.
Tripwire Interactive games deliver some of the best gunplay (animations, feedback, audio design, models, creativity) and multiplayer (especially co-op) available on the PC. There is something special about their games. Rising Storm 1 was one of the few multiplayer shooters where I intentionally cranked the soundtrack up to the point of almost drowning out all other game sounds because it was that good and that evocative of the setting and theme (it gives me chills to this day). The gunplay in Killing Floor 2 is almost addictive to me it is so well executed and always compels me to play one more match when I should be going to bed.
Sorry for the rambling review but I unequivocally recommend Killing Floor 2. When I see the Tripwire Interactive name on a product, I know I can pre-order without hesitation or fear. They have earned their pedigree and Killing Floor 2 is no exception. I enjoyed it from the very first Early Access days straight through final release and post-support.
If you love strong compelling gunplay, a wide variety of playstyles, and are looking for an elegant co-op game Killing Floor 2 fits the bill.

This is the best CRPG to come out in years, make no mistake. Divinity Original Sin boasts a highly enjoyable combat system predicated by quality encounters which are challenging enough that if you die, it's entirely your fault.
The skill tree is classless but has presets for convenience rather than necessity; melee characters will want healing spells and mages can benefit from using ranger or rogue escape skills.
If there's one thing that's been done right, it's being careful not to overdo old school CRPG mechanics. Quests don't have GPS coordinates and blatant markers like Bethesda games and require some old fashioned thinking and reading.
The multiple ways to resolve problems, quest structure should you decide to kill people and light-hearted humor makes the world and NPCs engaging for a playthrough that might span between 60-100 hours.
That's only talking about the base campaign. Larian intends on having a thriving mod community like Neverwinter Nights with their modular construction of maps but that remains to be seen as people come to grips with the SDK.

Super Hexagon is a mixed bag. With seizure-inducing graphics, sudden difficulty spikes, and infuriating vocals, I considered not even recommending this game. But as all Terry Cavanagh games do, there was one gameplay element that spoke through to me:
The menu system. Yes, you heard me right. As an avid gamer, I have seen too many AAA titles have a long, drawn out menu systems. They usually involve many button presses, logos popping on the screen, lag from background elements, etc. Sometimes it takes two minutes to even get into proper gameplay. One time, I ordered a pizza while a game was loading, and it had arrived and I had finished eating it before I realized that the computer was off.
But this...this game is something special. You can open up the game, start playing it, stop playing it, and close the game in a total of 6 seconds. That is incredible. There is no game that is its equal. The length of time playing the game juxtaposes the amount of time wasted in the menus. For most games this is inversely proportional.
Terry Cavanagh, you are a masterful game designer. You took a bad game and made something irresistable about it. Something that tricks you into playing it for 30 hours, even if it's bad. And that makes it good. For that, it deserves a spot in the 2016 Game of the Year nominations.

A bit of missed opportunity.
The moment you start playing Mirror's Edge you immediately feel that it is something special. The view of the city below you, the pure and sterile look, the smooth and seamless acrobats.
The problem is, the more you play the game, the more it feels unfinished.
Don't get me wrong, Mirror's Edge is a good game but it gives you the feeling that had the developers had a few more months to smooth out the edges, it could have been a masterpiece.
The frame rate occasionally stutters horribly. The story barely glues the levels together. The pacing of the game is all over the place for no apparent reason.
As it stands, what you get is an awesome game concept sitting on a very pretty game engine and it still worth exploring for any gamer. No other game will give you the Mirror's Edge experience.
Here's hoping that the eventual sequel can remedy the mistakes of the first game and reach the heights that it was striving for but never got to.
