The short version:
Divinity: Original Sin aims to be a modern day Ultima 7 and is reminiscent of many of the older games in the genre, it will make many of you who did like games such as Baldurs Gate II and Planescape Torment very happy indeed, especially if you also like turn based tactical combat. Players will be able to create a team, make choices and see how the consequences of their actions bear out.
The long version:
This is a game with little to no hand holding and it does not insult your intelligence by making this game accessible to your five year old sister, no this game is a deep tactical turn-based RPG experience.  Not only will you have freedom over your choices in the story (consequences and choices, even disagreements, will affect how things go), but also in how you get there.
You will be forced to interact with the world and speak to the people in it to gain information and quests, this is especially true as there are no exclamation marks over their heads telling you that this person is important or that they have information you need. It's also a game that rewards exploration, should you be careless enough you could find yourself completely missing out on certain quests. You can even kill most npc's in the game should you wish to do so (with the exception of a very few plot specific ones), but be careful of what you decide to do, there will be consequences for your actions.
There will be puzzles, lots of traps and mysteries to solve and interesting ways to approach many of the quests, you have the freedom to go wherever you want and the areas/monsters -wont- scale to your level, meaning you could die a very horrible death by exploring too far when you are low level. You could also be very skillful with the items/weapons at hand and somehow actually kill that level four troll while you are just a meager level two knight.
Being a rogue is especially fun as you can steal nearly everything, including snatching paintings off the walls, pick pocketing their weapons or even keys to their homes for a later "visit". Stealth is also very viable when stealing, but be careful, if you are caught people will dislike you and that will affect prices and information you can get, eventually you will be thrown into jail. Once there your partner can either come and bust you out or... well.. i wont spoil the surprise for you, suffice to say that there are more ways than one to get out of jail.
Party-based turn-based combat will encourage players to shape and control the game's environments, and to discover and utilize various skill and spell combos that you can choose for your party members
But the best part is the superb co-op experience, gone are the days when only player 1 gets to decide upon important decisions. You can both talk to any and all npcs and you both take part in dialogues during important events or with certain npcs, and should you two disagree on how to resolve a quest or dialogue you can have your characters argue over it. They will also react to certain things, for example, if you steal something your partner can start up a dialogue with you to either condone your actions or condemn them.
As to not spoil anything in the game this example is merely fiction and not present in the game. (Not to my knowledge at least)
example: You find a valuable gem on the beach and player 1 wants to sell it while player 2 wants to try and find the owner of it, stating that its immoral to take such a valuable object from someone who obviously dropped it.
Player one then gets a few different dialogue options to try and talk some sense into the other player's character, he can choose between a string of diffrent types of retorts and some might be intimidate, persuade, charm etc. After he has chosen his retort player two can choose a counter argument and will utilize the skill you chose and a game of rock, paper, scissors will commence, you will utilize the skillpoints in that particular skill you choose to gain an advantage over your friend in this game.
Depending on the outcome it will either be in favor of your decision or not, this will also give you points in various personality traits such as romantic or pragmatic depending on what you choose to say and these points will net you bonuses to your personality and other skills. Also it can be quite possible to make the two characters hate/love each other in the end.
This went on far longer than i intended so i will end this here by saying that the game is great and hopefully it will stay as amazing as it is now throughout the whole game (currently playing through it). Also, im Swedish so my english and grammar is not perfect, apologies for that.

After 100% Kingsway, I decided to write a review for a game I really liked. For those who do not know, Kingsway is an rogue-lite RPG with the UI of an old windows OS. It's neat. I would like to get this out of the way, I don't get the negative reviews with them expecting more out of the game because of the trailer. All the trailer states is customizable UI and nothing else. I can say the Trailer is a bit vague, but because of the vagueness of it, people projected what the game will be like and overhyped it for themselves. This, of course, disappointed those people. I guess I will start with the pros:
Pros:
Cool Aesthetic
Combat is fun for the most part (Little windows pop up and the enemies move around the screen and you have to defend and attack at the right moments, use spells/abilities, or choose to escape)
Unlockables that make starting the game again easier
Great Soundtrack
Unlike some other people, I actually enjoy the different classes.
Varied enemies as the game progress. Some are pretty interesting, like the Phantom (Who can close your UI windows) or Shadow Bandit (Minimizes his battle window so you have to manually click it open)
Very few bugs
Neutral:
It's fun to get a broken combo of legendary items that give skills that your class usually doesn't get and you are able to cheese your way through some bosses. This is could be seen in two areas.
Cons:
Can get repetitive, however, it depends on the type of person, since I had fun for all the hours I played. The game lacks a lot of events, so events start to repeat. It takes about 2 or 3 playthroughs to see all the events in the game. Events range from quests, dungeon events, and overworld events that give items or buffs.
Some enemies are purely attack and defend, which works for some and not for others. E.G. The sea serpents and goatmen.
In some ways the game is a bit too easy, I usually am able to complete an ending on my first or second try with any class. Once you get past level 10, and you aren't stupid, it pretty much guaranteed that the run is going to be successful. The only class I had to repeat 3 times was the beastkin was because a bug stopped me from getting the "Complete the game as a beastkin" so that was annoying, ending 5 "Sacrifice" is the bugged ending.
Overall: I think it is a solid game and worth a buy. For achievement hunters, it's quite good and for someone who looks for a casual rogue-lite experience, it's also great. If I would give this game a number rating, I would give it either a 8/10 or 9/10.

A really interesting visual novel with a unique spin on making choices.  Rather than selecting choices from a menu, you decide when and how often to make use of an interesting mechanic in which the main character can read the minds of those around him.  What he/she learns or doesn't learn dictates how he reacts to different situations.  It's a nice change from the usual modus operandi of visual novels.
The story's themes are rather existential and interesting, framed in a somewhat typical science fiction setting.  The art is rather hit or miss, with some of it being really beautiful and other aspects being rather poor.  Personally, I was a little creeped out by the way smiles were drawn on the characters.
Overall, it's an excellent entry into the visual novel genre.  Somewhat short, but with excellent replay value.  I'd definitely recommend it for anyone who enjoys a good story and is intrigued by the concept of personal mental privacy.

for all those who are unfamiliar with the Xcom franchise, xcom is unlike your traditional strategy game experience
for starters it is turn based, instead of real time, and second of all the live of your men (of which you have few) are extremely valuable
the game starts out extremely challenging (especially on higher difficulties) and you will find yourself losing men and money everywhere, but as you progress in technology and experience (both your own and your troops) the game rapidly becomes more managable
this is unfortunately one of the games largest downsides however,
the game struggles to maintain its punishing level of difficulty, and by the end of the game you will literally roll over the now pitiful alien menace
the graphics and gameplay are solid, though there are the occasional bug (and missed shot) which can be frustrating, but will rarely ruin the game for you
the game is very replayable, but suffers from a short variety of maps, so after just 1 playthrough you will easily have memorised every map
the xcom enemy within dlc helps fix this, but ultimately furthers the difficutly curve, as mech suits and gene mods only make it easier to destroy enemy resistance, and go as far as to make the early game a bit less challenging too
all in all however this is a great game easily worth your time

I've seen a lot of people calling this snake oil, so I was curious if it actually did anything. I benchmarked a couple of games using my mid-high end gaming laptop and a garbage-low end work laptop. Here's what I found out.
After benchmarking demanding games like Battlefield 1, the Division and Star Wars Battlefront on my better computer with a quad-core i7, instead of increasing FPS, I noticed CPUCores increased my stability and reduced frame drops and CPU load significantly.
On the other hand, I tested the same games on my low-end laptop with a dual-core i3 CPU. Using CPUCores actually made an impact on the FPS, but less so on frame drops and stability.
The most significant improvements were in games running borderless windowed mode. For example, on my better computer Battlefield 1 runs at 54-60 FPS when walking or driving, and around 30-45 FPS when in a firefight. On a best-case scenario with CPUCores, I benchmarked 57-60 FPS when walking and 51-58 FPS in a firefight.
In conclusion, don't expect it to magically make 5 FPS playable. On the other hand it can really help with frame drops, freezing and general stability.

XCOM: Enemy Unknown is turn-based strategy (maybe not EXACTLY strategy - but it's the best genre that describes it), is remake of XCOM: UFO Defence from 1994. Like every remake - it's simplified. Very. Luckily, lack of some machanisms, that made '94th version so hardcore, makes this one a good beggining for ones not familiar with XCOM series.
Game starts as player becomes Commander of XCOM project - international organisation, created to face extraterrestrial threat. Main characters we cooperate with are central officer Bradford, responsible for providing us informations and contacts with council, dr. Vahlen - chef of science team, providing us with new technologies, that eggheads invent from our captures. But there must be someone who construct their ideas - this person is Dr. Shen. Using their help, we hae to repelate alien threat. In base game, we meet aliens on various missions, eg.: Abdustions, terrors, crash/landing sites, alien bases and so on.  Almost every mission reduces panic level in countries. That is necessary, because when panic level is too high - country leaves XCOM - we lose country that is funding us, which means we get lesser amount of money, scientists and engineers. And when 8 countries leave XCOM - project is terminated, and we lose game (imagine losing in the middle of storyline - sad, isn't it?). Game progresses with story progress - every milestore we reach - capturing live alien, base assault ect.  makes game harder, which means more enemies during missions, new species trying to kill us, but also new items to fight, new upgrades and more, so game will be fair no matter of what, if you keep up with reserach and upgrades.
What to add? Our "little army" can reach higher experience levels, unlocking new abilities, skills and so on. When they level up for the first time, they get randomly one of 4 classes: Assault, Heavy, Support and Sniper. All of them have diffrent skill tree - so eg.: Heavy can fire from rocket launcher, and Assault can fire twice to same target in one turn. Be careful, because once soldier is killed, his skills are gone. Just a little remider :)
To sum up, I'd recommend XCOM - it's good succesor of old ufo defence. Sometimes easy, sometimes challenging - but isn't that the way game should be?

I’d sum up Antichamber as an illogical, logical puzzle game. I had to think more abstract and “outside the box” than any other puzzle game I’ve played before. It’s frustrating, rewarding and beautiful in a minimalist way. All of which comes together as a fantastic game.
You’re immediately thrown into the game. No menu, just instant gameplay. Great for quick 10-20 minutes sessions but also has the ability to eat up hours while you try to get past a seemingly impossible puzzle.
The first thing you’ll notice are the visuals. It’s minimalistic and heavily based on lines and outlines with vibrant colors. It’s beautiful and unique but also doubles a way to easily draw your eye to important things.
Music and sounds are also good. The background music is always there but never got in the way and I never got tired of it. In fact, I typically wouldn’t even hear it since I was concentrating on a puzzle.
Gameplay is going to be a tough one to write about, so I’ll be as brief as I can. There is no traditional story and I think the hints you gather along the way form a story about life and questioning yourself.  You must make your way through various puzzle rooms. The main room, which you can exit to at any time, serves as a map and to show your progress with the “hints” you have gotten along the way. The hints are posters you’ll see on the walls and serve as cryptic messages or meanings to solve the puzzle. Most of them have you contemplating your own life decisions, haha. You will eventually collect 3 guns that allow you to manipulate, store and shoot cubes to solve puzzles. Each gun will allow you to do a little bit more with the cubes, letting you get past puzzles you may have been stuck on before.
Antichamber is difficult, but only because it’s difficult to think and twist your mind in order to come up with a solution. I’ll admit I looked at a guide more than a handful of times. It’s frustrating in the beginning because you are not accustomed to the style of puzzles but eventually you start to always think outside the box. Looking back, it’s pretty funny how much you change your thinking from beginning to end.
+Unique and beautiful visuals
+Unique gameplay
+Rewarding
+Changes how you problem solve
+Hint system has you questioning life
+60fps
+Frustrating at times
+Better anti-aliasing solution could be used

Finished SR IV the other day. It was a good but uneven ride. The story, as it unfolded through the missions and side missions, was pretty good, very funny at times and an interesting bow on the series (although it makes you wonder where they take the franchise from here). Game play wasn't quite as solid. Some parts were fun like the super powers but then they'd shoehorn in some trash platforming mechanics that were just tedious. I don't know why YOU play the Saints Row games but it's probably not for 3D platforming, lame hacking minigames or playing some poor man's version of Audiosurf. Later in the game, you're forced through the same mechanics a second time even if you avoided all the voluntary instances of them up to that point. There's also some design choices that get old such as the eternal night of Steelport and (intentional) graphic flickering. If you've played -- and liked -- the previous games in the series, you'll probably want to play this one just to see what they do with it and the call-backs. If you never have, most of that would go right past you and you're just stuck with a pretty uneven experience.

Worth the 10 bucks and I'm going to try explaining why through a bad review
1) First of all, the aesthetic for anyone that likes the look of old PC-98(?) or ancient MAC-OS, as the game is a tiny mix of both. I'm stuck on windows 10 because of my specs so that's definitely refreshing.
2) Probably not for everyone, but I got attached to the music after a while. The soundtrack is definitely gonna loop a few times during a full playthrough as that's probably gonna be around 3 hours and the playlist is about 30 minutes long or so. not a musical expert (read: a ♥♥♥♥in idiot) so I don't have much to say about it besides "it's neat.".
3) The pacing of the game. After a few minutes you'll already get what you're going to do in battles for the rest of the game without it becoming too grating, as the different characters and the pop-up attacks from various enemies keep you on your toes.
Lest you wear the ring of pain, the shadow moves slowly enough for you to grind peacefully on the left-mid side of the map until you're actually ready to move towards the end of the game. Even then, the shadow isn't like in One Way Heroics. It just changes the enemy type from being biome-specific enemies to an ambiguous "shadow" that can be fought and still gives XP, but no items.
Complaints:
If anything, I feel like the quests are lacking. I've seen the game streamed firsthand and I thought the game was going to be absolutely massive and a playthrough would take ages, but despite the map being randomized every playthrough, the quests you get are generally pretty static. There isn't exactly a ton of enemies either, you'll just encounter the Cultists in the mountains, the Clot in the catacombs, stronger variants of previously fought enemies as you go to the right side of the map (with a few original enemies here and there like the goatmen).
Also, a more detailed stats menu showing some of the more auxilary stats (like the magic power boost you get from Warded enchanted items) would be nice.
Overall, trying to get the 5 different endings with a different character each time is how I recommend playing, as you'll probably get the most of your money's worth that way.

Cons:
-The game has some bugs. The first time I got very powerful and 80% through the game, when I saved and came back later, the game couldn't load my save without crashing. After that, on my next successful playthrough, I always kept the game running so I didn't have to load a save, just in case.

The game has a somewhat interesting presentation, but the interface felt clunky and the gameplay was not that fun (as warrior class). Beat it on the second try, not going to play again, even though there are other endings to get.
I think what bothered me the most was the combat system. You pick your attack by clicking a button, then a little bar fills, and when it's full you attack. The enemy does the same (minus the button), and of course keeps attacking no matter if you act or not. You have to pick your attack quickly so you don't waste time, and while you are doing that the button actually moves around. I got used to that quickly, so after a while the moving wasn't challenging anymore, just annoying. Also occasionally enemies do special attacks that you can dodge by clicking some other suddenly appearing moving buttons. What it boils down to is that I had to put actual effort into controlling my character. The very opposite of tight controls. Getting your character to do what you want is part of the challenge, and constantly drains your awareness. I like turn based games, and I like action games, but in this weird mix the two components only took away from each other.
Other than that I was mostly annoyed by having to use purely mouse controls for everything (you can actually unlock hotkeys later on, great...). And a bunch of things just felt clunky. For example the inventory. I spent a lot of time dragging little item icons from one window to another, either to loot them or to organize the items. It really does feel like organizing files on an old OS, and you have to do it purely with your mouse. And after every fight you have to click loot, take the loot, then click that you want to continue. It drags on a bit after a while.
The difficulty curve is as you would expect from a casual game with permadeath. If you survive the early game, there is very little risk of dying if you play a beefy character. I was pretty bored by the end.
There are much better roguelikes available that are just as easy to get into and are more fun. Some of them are even free. This is not a bad game, but I wouldn't recommend it.

Dialog and exploration is the game strong point.
Unfortunately at present the mix between text dialog and voice dialog is terribly confusing because they overlap too many times and too quickly so you kinda miss stuff especialy if you like to take your time as in an RPG and enjoy the character interactions.
As per the turn-based combat, is realy good tbh. Very intuitive to visualy and quickly understand how many action points you still have until you "pass" and it's realy not overly complicated nor terribly slow/tactical. Animations in combat are realy flashy so that helps a little for it not being boring or slow.
Coop is a diferent world that what we are used to see. If you play with a friend the dialog options (and decisions) are shared by both and both can disagree and that leads to truly fun discussions. I just love making my wife mad by just disagreeing with everything she wants in-game, it's priceless.
About the game uniqueness, i believe it's the "old school" vibe of RPGs, and especialy the feeling that you are not being "led" and "hand-hold" by the game. When you discover something or acomplish something cool, you feel proud because you were smart enough to do that on your own and don't feel you were pushed into it. Also the freedom to do whatever you want in choices and still be able to progress in the game. You can kill a quest giver you don't like because you have the "urge" to do it, and it's fine most of the time you can get a similar quest in a diferent way later on.
It's a game that chalenges you to do what you feel it's interesting. It doesnt scream at you to do stuff the way the developers wanted because they think its the proper way to do it, it doesnt punish you too much if you want to experiment alone. It has that old school vibe in a time that games were suposed to be about player interaction, and not so much as watching a movie on trails.
Can't explain much better. If you like 10 hour action packed games that look like a movie, don't play this. If you like a chalenging and rewarding game that doesn't tell you everytime what you "should be doing" this is worth it.

**What's new since last review?**
Last time I reviewed this game, I had 20 hours of gametime. Now I'm sitting at almost 70 hours, this being one of the 5 most played games in my entire library. This is, without a doubt, my most favourite ARPG, and I have a LOT of ARPGs. There is so much depth, detail, and pleasure in every bit of this game. The loot has improved much since my last review, and now there are ways to imbue items further, combine weapon imbuements, use dynamite to blow up equipment for base materials, and a special smith who can craft even better loot, using the things you've acquired in the game.
Act 3 has been added to the game in less than the time it has taken me to get through all that Act 1 and 2 had to offer. I've just walked into the first location on the map where Act 3 takes place. Seeing how big the world is, I know I have a lot more to look forward to.
Additionally, the inclusion of bounty and reputation into the game has been the icing on the cake. I absolutely love taking bounties and using rifts to quickly travel to the locations mentioned in the bounty description, kill the target, and impove my reputation with said faction. The more they like me, the more discounts I get, and with each new tier of respect, I open new items and equipment I can buy.
Grim Dawn is such a good game.
**UPDATED IMPRESSIONS**
After just having finished Act I (20 hours into game, give or take), I can say that I am much more impressed by the game than I was originally.
The loot system appears to get deeper and deeper, with the expected rare, epic, etc loot system. Add to that the ability to re-run dungeons after going back into the game, each time, and how varied the stats are on items, the looting in this game is an absolute pleasure.
All of the environments are a joy to explore, and the mobs are very nicely detailed.
The questing system is fun, and there seems to be ample content in each area, giving you lots of reason to go further and deeper into the world that has been lovingly crafted by the devs.
I have been playing as an Occultist, and the skills are just phenomenal. I was a big fan of Torchlight 2, and I tried my darndest to enjoy Diablo 3, but this game really takes the cake for my ARPG needs, and it isn't even finished yet.
If you have any joy for deep item loot, crafting, hunting, and questing, you'll do well by grabbing this game.
It's a complete pleasure.

The only place to go from Saints Row 3 was crazierways, and they sure kept up the good work on making everything as nuts as possible without taking itself too seriously at any point. The powers are fun as hell to play around with, but the bad guys' firepower is a bit scaled up as well, and dealing with them can be a little annoying if you're not using all your best weapons sometimes.
Co-op is still great and all, but is way buggier this time around -- my partner in crime has actually gotten his save more or less corrupted a couple of times. Keeping your current and completed quests in sync is kind of a headache, especially in the odd case where it doesn't even want you to do the quest in co-op. But hey, it's still superpowered mayhem with a friend, so you can't hate it too hard.
Car customization is still in, even though most players will probably rarely even use vehicles once they're 15 minutes into the game. They quite improved the color finishes, too. There's also a degree of weapon customization, which is pretty swank if you ask me. Character customization is at least as robust as 3, and you can even just import your SR3 characters if you've set up your online whatnots right, though some of your wardrobe items might no longer exist (I went through the intro mission shirtless, which was actually strangely appropriate).
There's as much Saints Row humor as ever, and also kind of a lot of referential humor this time around, which is all good and well for me. Basically the game is an escalation of the same old, which is... well, pretty much what you want it to be. It still knows exactly what it is, and it's still fun as heck.

Ok so lets say you find a resturaunt that makes a dish so unbelieveably devine that it escapes description. So you go there for the first time with a friend and find out the hype is all true, you wish you could live there it's so good.
A week later you go back with a date to find out that they not only upgraded the tables and chairs of the resturaunt they also upgraded the menu as well. After dinner you and your date talk about your amazing experience for weeks and suggest all your friends and family eat there.
A week later when you go back again they say that things have changed. Instead of being a sit down and order your meal resturaunt they just do deserts to go now. Which isn't the end of the world you grab a slice of chocolate cake and when you take it home and eat it you are reminded why you keep on going there even if the feeling is short lived.
3 weeks later when you go back they say they are renovating and you will be able to get a slice of cake soon but wont tell you when and all the cooks went to work at different resturaunts.
You go to visit these resturaunts every so often and you can taste their contribution to the meal and it tastes good but it isn't the otherworldly decidence provided by the original meals you enjoyed.
Then it happens, after years of renovation signs and promises from the owners and chefs, they finally announce they will never open their doors again...
You know that if they ever did open up again it might fall short of your expectations, but that haunting memory of that excuisite cake keeps you up at night. You continue living going from bakery to sweet shop trying to find it's equal or even something to put your mind at ease to know that that level of quality can be matched. Instead the truth is that every single sweet treat you put on your tongue brings your closer and closer to the realization that nothing will ever measure up and you are doomed to an eternity of trying to find anything to measure up but you know you never will.

This was the discovery of 2013 for me (it was released in late 2012 but I got it a few months later).
Very cool design, beautiful soundtrack, and gripping gameplay. Certainly not for those that can't handle losing, as you WILL be punished for your mistakes and there is no loading, which is why every decision you make is all the more important.
There's a variety of ships and you'll keep trying out new ones before getting even remotely bored by the ones you already used. The game is very replayable (I've spent 50+ hours on it now, even though each successful playthrough is some 3+ hours, and well, many fail halfway through :))
All in all, very fun to play, and it's beautiful to just be in the game.
You will be losing a lot at first, but keep going, as the more you discover the game, the better you'll do and the more you'll love it.
Highly recommended for anyone who's not dependant on save/load mechanics ;)
